title: DexLink: Synthesizing Dexterous Behaviors from Chained Hand-object Poses
authors: Meenal Parakh,Deep Patel,Beining Han,Jia Deng
abstract:
Synthesizing diverse dexterous manipulation policies is challenging: existing simulation-based approaches rely on human demonstrations (Jiang et al., 2025; Mu et al., 2026) which are difficult to scale, or use generic reward functions (Kedia et al., 2026), which provide limited control over the hand-object interactions. We propose DexLink, which addresses these limitations by synthesizing diverse dexterous behaviors from sparse, reusable hand-object interaction templates. Given key task waypoints, DexLink retargets static interaction templates to target objects using an optimization that preserves
spatial hand-object relationships. It then links the retargeted poses into an approximate reference trajectory and uses residual reinforcement learning to refine this reference
into a closed-loop policy in simulation. Experiments spanning single-hand, bimanual, articulated, and dynamic tasks demonstrate that DexLink provides fine-grained control over
task timing, grasp types, and high-level execution. The modular interaction templates transfer reliably across object scales, instances, and categories; without object-specific
human demonstrations, the framework also matches the performance of dense reference-tracking methods. Finally, zero-shot deployment of policies trained purely in simulation shows promise for the simulation-based framework.
https://dex-link.github.io/
introduction:
Learning from data is a key paradigm in robotic manipulation and relies on the ability to collect large, diverse behaviors (Khazatsky et al., 2025). For dexterous manipulation, this requires coverage over diverse tasks, objects, and interaction behaviors. Obtaining such coverage is challenging: dexterous hands involve complex, contact-rich dynamics that make teleoperation cumbersome and expensive (Handa et al., 2019; Tao et al., 2025).

Simulation provides a scalable platform for synthesizing dexterous behaviors, with potential for real-world transfer (Jiang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2023). Yet, specifying which tasks and behaviors to generate, and how, remains an open challenge. Existing work often relies on human demonstrations (Jiang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025) to generate robot data, creating a scaling bottleneck, or limits generation to only specific skills such as grasping (Ye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). We aim to address these challenges, enabling simulation-based synthesis of general dexterous behaviors.

Towards this goal, we present DexLink, a simulation-based framework that enables generation of dexterous behaviors across a diverse set of tasks and objects, spanning single-hand, bimanual, long-horizon, articulated, and dynamic tasks. Further, DexLink allows control over behavior synthesis: object goal poses, hand-object interactions, task timing, and high-level execution strategies (Figure 1).

Importantly, DexLink provides these capabilities without requiring costly human demonstrations or cumbersome per-task reward engineering, which existing works often depend on. Existing generation methods vary in how they input task-related information, from indirect optimization objectives to full task demonstrations. Indirect objectives such as task-specific reward design (Chen et al., 2021; Kedia et al., 2026) or hand priors (Mandikal and Grauman, 2022; de Bakker et al., 2026) in RL indirectly guide policies toward specific behaviors: while such guidance is easy to obtain, it provides only weak control over learned behaviors and can produce unnatural robot motions or interactions that fail to satisfy downstream task requirements. In contrast, methods such as Jiang et al. (2025); Li et al. (2025); Mu et al. (2026) provide task supervision using dense demonstrations obtained from teleoperation, motion-capture data, or vision-based annotations, respectively: the dense supervision provides more control over learning but is costly to collect and, when extracted from video, depends on the accuracy of vision modules. Further, the generation is typically tied to the specific task-object pair represented in the demonstration, limiting scalability.

DexLink instead achieves the diversity and control over behavior generation by assuming a sparse, compositional task representation which
combines a sequence of object-state waypoints with hand-object interaction templates assigned to selected waypoints (shown in Figure 2, left). The object waypoints describe the desired task progression, while the interaction templates specify the desired spatial relationship between the hand and object. Importantly, these templates only specify local interactions and can be reused across tasks and objects and chained with other templates along the waypoint sequence. Selecting different waypoints and interaction templates allows the target behavior to be varied, or controlled, as desired. These templates can be obtained from motion-capture frames or static hand-object reconstruction methods (Yang et al., 2022; Fan et al., 2023a).

Obtaining a physically grounded trajectory from this compositional task representation presents a challenge: we need to preserve the desired interactions, goals, and phase timings, while remaining dynamically feasible.
DexLink addresses this grounding problem by decomposing it into two steps: constructing a reference trajectory that preserves the task intent, and refining the reference for dynamic feasibility.
Specifically, an object-aware retargeting optimization adapts each interaction template to the target-object geometry, producing approximate robot anchors. These anchors are linked along the waypoints to form an intermediate reference, which is refined with residual RL in simulation. The intermediate reference narrows RL exploration around the intended behavior, while RL corrects its dynamics, contact, and timing errors to provide a physically grounded trajectory (Figure 2 right).

Our experiments, covering a diverse set of tasks, evaluate the framework’s flexibility: interaction templates can be reused across scale, within-category and across-category variations, and generation can be carefully controlled by varying the task specification. Ablations establish the importance of each component, and we show that the framework supports sparse interaction anchors, while performing on par with other approaches for dense object tracking. Finally, zero-shot deployment of policies trained purely in simulation demonstrates the potential for zero-shot real-world transfer.

In summary, our contributions are: (i) a simulation-based framework for synthesizing diverse dexterous behaviors across tasks and objects;
(ii) an approach that converts composable sequences of object-state waypoints and hand-object interaction templates into physically grounded policies;
and (iii) systematic evaluations in simulation demonstrating coverage over variations in object geometries and tasks, and zero-shot real-world deployment of simulation policies.

title: MERLoc: Robust Robot Localization in Dynamic Environments with Pose-Based Retrieval over 3D Gaussian Splatting References
authors: Michael Baumgartner,Dario Mylonopoulos,Sammy Christen,Markus Gross,Moritz Bacher
abstract:
Robots operating in previously mapped spaces must localize accurately despite moving people and rearranged objects. Most localization pipelines match the query against a sparse set of captured reference images retrieved by appearance, which is brittle under scene change and repeating structures. We present MERLoc, which turns a single metric 3D Gaussian Splatting scan into a dense Functional Reference Memory.
Reference views are sampled over the navigable space for the robot’s morphology and sensors at a target density and rendered offline. Pre-encoding them for the chosen off-the-shelf localizer removes the reference encoder from inference.
A pose-based retrieval strategy then selects references by spatial proximity and viewing direction rather than appearance, sidestepping visual ambiguities whenever a prior exists. Across one classical and four learned localizers in simulated and real dynamic scenes, pose-based retrieval matches or outperforms appearance retrieval in most cases, even when the latter is gated by the same prior. On real data, it lowers position RMSE by 15–60 % in nine of ten backend/split combinations, and the rendered memory outperforms real-image caches posed by Structure-from-Motion.
The system runs onboard a Jetson Orin NX at 5 Hz5\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}, enabling a navigation policy to successfully traverse a hallway with people roaming and rearranging objects.
introduction:
Robots deployed in homes, hospitals, and warehouses operate in spaces that are easy to scan but rarely remain identical to those scans over time. People walk through them, objects appear, and furniture moves. While structural elements provide reliable localization cues, these dynamic changes introduce distractors and ambiguities that degrade localization pipelines built for static scenes.

The dominant localization pipeline for previously mapped environments queries a sparse set of posed reference images [1]. References are posed offline by Structure-from-Motion (SfM) [2], retrieved online via appearance descriptors [3], and passed to a relative localizer.
Frozen at mapping time, the reference set is limited to the captured viewpoints and can neither be densified nor adapted to a robot’s sensor suite.
Furthermore, appearance-based retrieval is prone to visual aliasing, where distinct places look alike, such as repeated corridors or identical doors. Aliasing and scene changes since mapping both lead retrieval to return confidently wrong references that no relative localizer can recover from [4, 5, 6].
Recent feed-forward localizers replace the geometric solver but inherit both limitations; even when trained on dynamic scenes [7, 8, 9], most are, as we show, more sensitive than classical pipelines to aliased or changed references.

We propose a 3D Gaussian Splatting-based Memory Encoding and Retrieval Localization (MERLoc) framework, which replaces the rigid, captured reference set with a controllable, backend-adaptive, rendering-based memory. Given a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [10, 11] scan of the environment, we sample reference poses over the navigable space at a specified density, height range, and orientation profile tailored to the robot’s sensor suite. We then render these views and encode them offline in a representation customized for the relative localizer. This forms a Functional Reference Memory (FRM): its content is determined by the target backend and robot morphology rather than by the scanner that captures it, e.g., depth-lifted keypoints for classical pipelines [1] or encoded visual tokens for latent-conditioned architectures [7, 8, 9, 12]. Because of this customized encoding, the relative localizer runs entirely off-the-shelf, without per-scene training or adaptation, and without encoding any reference at runtime, which removes one encoder pass per retrieved reference from the online path. Furthermore, the FRM density becomes a tunable design parameter that trades accuracy against storage without increasing online inference cost.

To select references, we index the dense FRM by pose. Given a pose prior, typically the previous estimate or odometry, we gate candidates within a radius and rank them by viewing-direction alignment and proximity, falling back to appearance-based matching only for initialization or recovery. Unlike SLAM, which routinely gates retrieval with a propagated pose [13, 14], localization pipelines still retrieve by appearance alone.
Neither the dense FRM nor pose-based retrieval suffices alone: pose-based retrieval starves on a sparse reference set, and appearance retrieval still aliases on a dense one. Together, they make classical and learned relative localizers metric, more accurate, and more robust to scene change without touching backend weights.

We claim that (i) MERLoc turns one metric 3DGS scan into a Functional Reference Memory whose density, height band, and encoding are chosen per robot and per localizer, so that classical and feed-forward backends run off-the-shelf without encoding references at runtime (Sec. III); (ii) on real data, this rendered memory outperforms real-image caches of the same scene posed by SfM, even at a lower pose density for the classical backend (Sec. IV-D); (iii) pose-based context retrieval over this memory lowers position RMSE by 15–60 % relative to appearance retrieval for nine of ten real-world backend/split combinations and, under simulated scene change and human activity, matches or exceeds prior-gated appearance retrieval while clearly exceeding plain appearance retrieval for four of five backends (Secs. IV-B–IV-D);
(iv) the system runs at 5 Hz5\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} on a Jetson Orin NX, enabling a navigation policy to reliably traverse a hallway while people move around the robot and displace objects (Sec. IV-E).

title: One Ocean, Many Tasks: A Data-Grounded Simulation Suite and Benchmark for Marine Robotics
authors: Shuaijun Liu,Qifu Wen,Xingwei Chen,Xinwen Hu,Feiyang You,Sijia Chen,Ningxin Su
abstract: Simulation is essential for marine robotics, yet existing platforms often trade off between visually realistic worlds, high-throughput experimentation, and ocean-condition realism grounded in real data. We present OneOcean, a data-grounded simulation suite and benchmark built around a unified spatiotemporal ocean-environment product that harmonizes bathymetry with data-driven currents and tides, with optional pollution fields for cleanup-related evaluation. On top of this environment representation, OneOcean defines a task ladder spanning navigation and station-keeping under currents, waypoint and route following, depth-profile tracking, area scanning, pipeline inspection, and multi-agent coordination, including formation transit, fish protection and patrol (herding), and surface pollution localization, containment, and cleanup. The suite supports multi-agent settings with 2–10 vehicles. Our simulator supports three to six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) and produces standardized metrics and reproducible run manifests, enabling consistent aggregation across tasks, difficulties, and scaling settings. Experiments across dataset variants and scenes systematically stress planning and control under data-grounded disturbances and reveal trade-offs among heuristic baselines, Behavior Cloning (BC), and a Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner.

title: Memory Is Not Ground Truth: Revising Navigation Authority under Unreliable VLM Evidence for Persistent Semantic Navigation
authors: Sumukh Shrote,Shenbagaraj Kannapiran,Eric Eaton,Camillo Jose Taylor
abstract:
Vision-language models (VLMs) enable robots to reason about semantic and spatio-temporal context, verify task-relevant objects, and guide sensing and navigation in complex environments. Persistent memory can further reduce redundant search for field robots, but raises an important question: when should those memories continue to influence behavior? Repeated negative observations can be used as evidence that a memory is stale. However, our experiments show that such observations may remain ambiguous under VLM-based
perception. Using a Boston Dynamics Spot equipped with four fixed cameras and a persistent spatio-temporal visual memory, we measure negative-verification behavior across targets, viewpoints, language queries, and repeated revisits. False-negative rates vary substantially across objects, nearby revisits often reproduce the same detector outcome, and some matched target-present and target-removed experiments yield identical miss histories. This ambiguity persists under changed observation geometry, identity-preserving query reformulation, and conditioning on a previously verified target image. These findings led us to separate two questions: is the object still there, and is this memory still useful for navigation? We introduce a dependence-aware, reversible memory-update mechanism that avoids double-counting correlated misses and stops repeatedly using unsupported memories as direct navigation goals without claiming that the object is absent. Memories are preserved for later positive recovery. One resident onboard VLM is shared across memory verification, semantic frontier reasoning, and in-motion perception. In three matched real-robot decision contexts, an episode-local baseline selected a stale memory as its navigation objective in 3/3 cases, whereas our method selected semantic frontiers in all three cases. A complementary trial re-verified the target during motion and promoted fresh memory. These results support revising memory actionability rather than interpreting failed detection as object absence.
introduction:
On-board foundation models allow mobile robots to use natural language task inputs along with visual observations to reason about task-relevant objects and where to direct navigation effort. For field deployment, however, this reasoning must happen while the robot is moving, sensing, and sharing limited onboard compute across multiple tasks. Cloud access may be unavailable or undesirable, and loading separate large models for perception, memory, and navigation is often impractical. Recent systems combine VLMs with semantic maps and persistent memory to support long-horizon embodied tasks [1, 2, 3, 4], reducing repeated search but raising a new question: when is a remembered observation still worth acting on? Memory creates a new problem. Suppose a robot previously verified a red stool, later returns to the remembered location, and fails to detect it. The stool may have moved or been removed, but the VLM may also simply have failed. Negative evidence depends on the target, viewpoint, visual conditions, and language query, and repeated observations from similar geometry may reproduce the same failure. The robot can therefore either discard a useful memory or repeatedly spend navigation effort on one that is no longer useful. This distinction matters because memory is not passive storage. A retrieved memory determines where the robot moves, what it observes, and where expensive VLM inference is spent. For an onboard system, deciding whether a memory remains useful is therefore also a resource-allocation decision over motion, sensing, and computation.

Existing memory and observation-model approaches can reduce
confidence when expected detections fail, accounting for factors
such as visibility, geometry, or detector uncertainty [5, 6].
However, when detector failures are systematic or correlated,
accumulating negative observations may remain insufficient to
distinguish environmental change from perceptual failure.

We study this question on a Boston Dynamics Spot with four fixed cameras and persistent semantic memory. The robot follows a memory-first search strategy and falls back to semantic frontier exploration when no memory is trusted. One resident onboard VLM is shared across scene verification, memory verification, frontier ranking, and in-motion perception.
The experiments reveal more than ordinary detector noise. False-negative behavior varies across objects, nearby revisits often reproduce the same verifier outcome, and several target-present memories produce exactly the same miss histories after the target is physically removed. Changing observation geometry, reformulating the query, or conditioning on a previously verified target image does not always resolve this ambiguity.

As illustrated in Fig. 1, this leads us to separate two questions: is the object still there? and is this memory still worth acting on? We address the second question through memory actionability. Geometrically distinct negative-evidence groups can move a verified memory from VERIFIED_ACTIVE to SUSPECT and eventually DORMANT_UNTRUSTED, while repeated local misses
are not double-counted. The memory is preserved, no absence claim is made, and later positive evidence can restore its navigation authority.
Once direct-navigation authority is withdrawn, the robot resumes semantic frontier exploration while perception continues during motion. CPU-based CLIP screening limits expensive VLM calls, and all semantic reasoning shares one resident onboard VLM.

Our contributions are:

We experimentally characterize negative VLM evidence in
persistent semantic navigation, demonstrating target-dependent
false negatives, redundant repeated-revisit evidence, and
identical detector histories under target-present and
target-removed conditions.

We introduce a dependence-aware, reversible
memory-revision policy that separates memory actionability
from physical-staleness claims. Redundant local misses are
not double-counted, unsupported memories lose direct-navigation
authority, and later positive evidence can restore it.

We develop a resource-aware architecture in which one
resident onboard VLM is shared across memory verification,
semantic frontier reasoning, and asynchronous in-motion
perception, with lightweight CPU screening used to gate
expensive VLM calls.

In matched real-robot decision contexts, an episode-local
baseline selected a previously failed memory as a direct
navigation objective in 3/3 cases, whereas our method selected
semantic frontiers in all three cases. A complementary trial
demonstrates asynchronous target verification and fresh
memory promotion during motion.

Persistent VLM-based navigation should therefore decide whether a memory remains worth acting on rather than equating failed detection with evidence that the remembered object is gone.

title: Cairn: Object-Centric 3D Trajectory Priors for Steering Frozen VLAs
authors: Agelos Kratimenos,Kostas Daniilidis,Evangelos Chatzipantazis
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are capable low-level controllers, but they tie where objects go to the layouts
they were trained on: when objects are moved or obstacles block the way, they carry them to the wrong place or into
collisions. Fine-tuning on new layouts needs robot data for each one and erodes skills the model already has. We
introduce Cairn, which keeps the VLA frozen and steers it at test time along learned 3D trajectories of the object
in its gripper. A small prior reads point clouds of the scene and the held object, along with its pose when grasped and
the instruction, and samples SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) trajectories up to its release that lead it around obstacles and turn it to fit
through gaps. The prior and the VLA form the two levels of a hierarchical planner in which feedback runs both ways: the VLA’s intended motion chooses and reshapes the
trajectories, and the chosen one guides the VLA’s denoising. Its predicted actions, mapped to the held object’s
poses through the grasp, are pulled toward the next waypoint, while the VLA’s weights stay untouched. Across 1,941 held-out
LIBERO scenes with displaced objects and obstacles, Cairn raises the success rate of a frozen π0.5\pi_{0.5} from 24.5% to
95.1%, above that of a π0.5\pi_{0.5} fine-tuned on our training layouts, without hurting standard LIBERO. On the
third-party LIBERO-PRO benchmark, it raises success from 27.3% to 38.0%, and from 54.4% to 81.1% on the episodes it
steers. On a
real Franka, with a prior trained purely in simulation, it guides the frozen DROID π0.5\pi_{0.5} around an obstacle and to a
placement at the limit of the arm’s reach, where it otherwise fails. All code, models and data will be made public.
introduction:
Moving into a new home calls on two abilities: lifting and setting down a bookshelf are skills one brings along,
while where it should stand and how to get it there, around the sofa and tilted through the doorway, depend on the new
home. Vision-language-action models
(VLAs) [6, 39, 4, 3, 59] have the first:
trained by imitation on large robot datasets, they grasp and place many objects from images and an instruction. They
largely lack the second. Deciding one short action chunk at a time, mostly from 2D images, a VLA absorbs where objects
belong and how to reach them from its training layouts; moving objects collapses its
success [93, 20, 73, 19], and obstacles cause
collisions [67, 51]. An obstacle calls for a detour chosen before it is
reached, and a long object may need to turn to fit through a gap. Both depend on the scene’s 3D geometry and the
object’s shape. The
motor skill is in place; the route is missing.

Fine-tuning a VLA can teach it those layouts, but it needs robot demonstrations of every new scene and can make it
forget skills it already has [95]. Guidance instead changes what a generative model produces without
changing the model: each denoising step is nudged along the gradient of an objective. It has spread from image generation [15] to inverse
problems [13, 66], trajectory planning [35] and robot
policies [75, 17, 51]. Since current VLAs generate actions with flow-matching
experts [4, 3, 59], the same recipe applies to them with no robot
data or training: OmniGuide [67] steers frozen π0.5\pi_{0.5} and GR00T by back-propagating 3D energies
through the robot’s kinematics. Its targets are local: a collision field does not know the goal, an attractor
pulls straight through obstacles and can get stuck in local minima, and both act on the gripper, not the object it
holds. The open question is not how to steer a frozen VLA, but where to.

A route that helps a frozen VLA must meet several requirements, and existing planners each meet only some of them. It
must be metric and three-dimensional, unlike image paths, which lack
depth [25, 45]. It must describe the held object and how it turns, not only the gripper
positions of 3D path predictors [34, 33]. Models of 6-DoF object
motion [84, 87, 64] plan the object, but learn from human data, without
its shape or the robot’s reach. It must cover the whole carry and find the goal from the instruction, whereas motion
planners [40, 70] must be given the goal. It must reach the VLA without
retraining it, whereas hierarchical VLAs [45, 34, 7] train their low-level
policy to follow plans. Above all, the route and the VLA must agree. Together they form a hierarchy, a planner of the route above a planner
of actions, and in hierarchies the high level usually commands while the low level is trained to obey. A frozen VLA has its
own preferred motion, and a route chosen without it has to be forced on it. A high level that offers a distribution of
routes can instead couple with the VLA at test time, with feedback in both directions: the VLA’s intended motion chooses and reshapes the route, and the
route steers the VLA.

We present Cairn, a framework that steers frozen VLAs with 3D trajectories of the held object that account for the
scene, its obstacles and the object’s own shape. The name comes from the stacked stones that mark a hiking trail: a
cairn shows the way but carries no one along it. In the same way, Cairn marks the route of the held object and
leaves the moving to the VLA. To meet the requirements above, it builds a two-level planner from a small 3D
specialist, which plans the route, and the frozen 2D generalist, which plans the actions (Fig. 2). The specialist is a motion prior built like 3D point-cloud
policies [23, 24], but it predicts where the held object travels rather than
how the robot moves. From point clouds of the scene and the
held object, along with its pose at the grasp and the instruction, it samples with rectified
flow [52] a route to the release as SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) waypoints. It is trained without robot actions, on
simulated demonstrations generated with moved objects, obstacles and several routes per scene. At test time the prior and the VLA
steer each other. The VLA’s intended motion weights and refines the sampled routes that clear the scene. In turn, at
every denoising step, the object motion that the VLA’s action chunk would produce is pulled toward the next waypoint of
the chosen route. The VLA’s weights are never changed.

We evaluate Cairn in simulation and on a real robot. On LIBERO-Shift, 1,941 held-out LIBERO scenes with moved objects
and obstacles, it raises the success of the frozen π0.5\pi_{0.5} from 24.5% to 95.1%, more than fine-tuning
π0.5\pi_{0.5} on the same layouts, which also degrades π0.5\pi_{0.5} on standard LIBERO, where Cairn leaves performance
unchanged. On LIBERO-PRO [93], a third-party benchmark of moved objects, it raises π0.5\pi_{0.5}’s
success on the episodes it steers from 54.4% to 81.1%.
The coupling between the two levels helps where success has room: under LIBERO-PRO’s layout shift it adds
2.3 points over a route fixed at the grasp, and where the VLA’s intent changes the route it makes motion
smoother and safer. On a real Franka, with a
prior trained only in simulation, Cairn steers the frozen DROID π0.5\pi_{0.5} around an obstacle and to a
placement at the limit of the arm’s reach, where π0.5\pi_{0.5} alone fails. Our contributions are:

Cairn, to our knowledge the first framework that steers a frozen VLA with learned SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) routes of the object it
holds, from grasp to release, conditioned on the scene, the object’s shape and the instruction.

A hierarchical planner whose two levels, a learned route prior and a frozen VLA, inform each other at test time
in both directions, without retraining either.

A generator of varied LIBERO demonstrations, with moved objects, obstacles that force detours and turns, and
several routes per scene, and LIBERO-Shift, a held-out benchmark built with it.

Extensive experiments in simulation and on a real robot showing that Cairn makes frozen VLAs robust to moved
objects and obstacles, outperforms fine-tuning without its forgetting, and carries over to a third-party
benchmark.

1. Cairn, to our knowledge the first framework that steers a frozen VLA with learned SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) routes of the object it
holds, from grasp to release, conditioned on the scene, the object’s shape and the instruction.

2. A hierarchical planner whose two levels, a learned route prior and a frozen VLA, inform each other at test time
in both directions, without retraining either.

3. A generator of varied LIBERO demonstrations, with moved objects, obstacles that force detours and turns, and
several routes per scene, and LIBERO-Shift, a held-out benchmark built with it.

4. Extensive experiments in simulation and on a real robot showing that Cairn makes frozen VLAs robust to moved
objects and obstacles, outperforms fine-tuning without its forgetting, and carries over to a third-party
benchmark.

title: FineDex: Bridging Fine-Grained Human-Object Interaction Generation to Dexterous Humanoid Manipulation
authors: Yujia Zeng,Yuxin Chen,Yuzhen Song,Runhan Huang,Chensheng Peng,Yiyang Shao,Koushil Sreenath,Masayoshi Tomizuka,Yilun Du
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Dexterity is, at its core, finger-level control, yet existing dexterous manipulation and
human–object interaction (HOI) generation methods rarely let one specify how an
interaction is performed: five-fingered hands are often reduced to grippers, or finger usage is
copied from individual human demonstrations. We present FineDex, a framework that makes finger-level intent both
expressible and executable. FineDex learns coordinated human body, hand, and object motions that
follow fine-grained instructions on hand selection, individual fingers, and contacts with
articulated objects.
To bridge generation and execution, FineDex leverages generated interactions
as actionable priors for an agent that discovers physically feasible
contact strategies through practice in a physics-based digital twin.
By adapting at test time without per-instance retraining,
FineDex generalizes
across fine-grained instructions and object configurations.
Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art HOI generation quality
and fine-grained controllability, substantial improvements in dexterous
manipulation success, and successful
deployment on a real dexterous humanoid robot.
introduction:
Dexterity is, at its core, finger-level control: humans press with a fingertip,
hook with a specific finger, brace with the palm, and switch hands when one is busy.
Yet existing dexterous manipulation and human–object interaction (HOI)
generation methods are evaluated mainly by task completion
alone: many effectively use a five-fingered hand as a gripper for
pick-and-place [25, 28],
while others copy whatever finger usage appears in a specific human
demonstration [7, 24]. Meanwhile, human interaction data offers a scalable source of rich
finger-level behaviors. The missing link is a model that can express such intent
on demand—which hand, which finger, which contact—and a way to realize
it on a physical robot.

However, existing methods fall short on both fronts. On the expression side, text-conditioned HOI generators
synthesize coordinated human–object motion [3, 23, 1, 21],
but they respond almost only to task-level descriptions: asked to use the left hand or a
particular finger, they produce the same interaction regardless. On the realization side,
generated motions are not physically exact, and differences
in robot kinematics and contact dynamics make direct
motion replay unreliable. Existing pipelines bridge this gap by training
reference-tracking policies [7, 4],
but their reliance on reference-specific training
limits scalability to diverse fine-grained instructions,
object configurations, and robot-specific constraints.

Our key insight is to decouple fine-grained intent generation
from its physical realization, treating generated HOI
as a sketch of the intended interaction.
What a human would do is best captured by a generative prior
learned from fine-grained human interaction data.
How the robot can do it is best discovered through
test-time practice in a physics-based digital twin.
Generation supplies the finger-level intent;
practice supplies its physical grounding.

Building on this observation, we introduce FineDex, a framework that makes
finger-level intent both expressible and executable. As shown in Fig. 1, FineDex learns
to generate coordinated body, hand, and object motions
conditioned on fine-grained instructions specifying hand selection,
individual finger motions, and designated contacts. For execution, FineDex treats generated interactions as
actionable priors for an agent that proposes contact programs, practices them under
randomized dynamics, and commits to the most reliable behavior, which
is then executed on the robot. Because adaptation happens through practice, the same system
generalizes to new instructions, robot-specific constraints,
and object configurations without retraining.

To measure what task success alone cannot, we introduce FingerBench, which evaluates
whether generated motions follow hand- and finger-level instructions and whether robots
realize them in physics-based execution. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art HOI generation quality
and finger-level controllability. In physics-based execution, practice turns generated priors into reliable
contact behaviors where direct replay rarely succeeds while preserving designated finger contacts. On a real Unitree G1 humanoid, FineDex completes
articulated-object tasks under constraints it was never trained for, such as operating
with the left hand only or with a single designated finger.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

Finger-level HOI generation. A generator of coordinated body, hand,
and articulated-object motion that follows fine-grained instructions on hand selection,
specific fingers, and designated contacts, with state-of-the-art controllability
and quality.

Finger-level HOI generation. A generator of coordinated body, hand,
and articulated-object motion that follows fine-grained instructions on hand selection,
specific fingers, and designated contacts, with state-of-the-art controllability
and quality.

Practice-grounded dexterous execution. An agent that grounds generated
interactions through practice, adapting to fine-grained instructions and object configurations
without retraining, with deployment on a real humanoid.

FingerBench and fine-grained ARCTIC annotations:
a benchmark for evaluating fine-grained instruction following in HOI generation
and robotic execution, and fine-grained annotations for
training instruction-conditioned HOI models, with the latter to be publicly released.

1. Finger-level HOI generation. A generator of coordinated body, hand,
and articulated-object motion that follows fine-grained instructions on hand selection,
specific fingers, and designated contacts, with state-of-the-art controllability
and quality.

2. Practice-grounded dexterous execution. An agent that grounds generated
interactions through practice, adapting to fine-grained instructions and object configurations
without retraining, with deployment on a real humanoid.

3. FingerBench and fine-grained ARCTIC annotations:
a benchmark for evaluating fine-grained instruction following in HOI generation
and robotic execution, and fine-grained annotations for
training instruction-conditioned HOI models, with the latter to be publicly released.

title: RePace: Reasoning about Demonstration Speedup for Faster Vision-Language-Action Policies
authors: Insup Lee,Hojin Jeon,Sunguk Shin,Seoungbin Bae,Taekwan Kim,Jinwoo Shin,Dongsu Han
abstract:
Since vision-language-action (VLA) policies can inherit the slow pace of human demonstrations, accelerating these demonstrations before fine-tuning can lead to faster VLA policies without an additional speed-selection module at deployment.
Several offline speedup methods have focused on identifying segments that require less precision and assigning predefined speedup factors to the segments.
However, even within a single segment, a speedup factor suitable for steady motion may be too high when precise alignment is required.
To this end, this paper presents RePace, an offline reasoning framework that determines how much to accelerate each part of a demonstration.
For the same recorded movement, RePace measures how much each candidate speedup factor shortens the sequence and compares the resulting observation-action pairs used for training.
Given the task instruction, a pretrained language model uses the visual context and original motion of successive windows to interpret these candidate retiming effects and select a speedup profile for the complete episode.
Experimental results demonstrate that RePace outperforms the baselines in overall task execution efficiency on both LIBERO and RoboCasa-Kitchen.
On all three tasks with a gripper-equipped Franka Research 3 arm, RePace matches or exceeds the acceleration baselines in success rate and completes successful trials faster.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models extend pretrained vision-language representations to robot action prediction [5], and researchers have evaluated these models on various real-world manipulation tasks [22].
A pretrained VLA policy can be fine-tuned on demonstrations of a new task to predict robot actions from observations and a language instruction [17].
Practical deployment of these policies requires both successful manipulation and timely task completion.
However, since even experienced demonstrators may move the robot cautiously to avoid mistakes during teleoperation [38], a policy trained on these demonstrations can inherit their slow pace, even in open space where the robot could move faster.

For faster VLA policy, there have been two primary approaches to accelerate policies at different stages: (i) test-time policy acceleration and (ii) offline demonstration acceleration.
Although several studies have focused on acceleration during execution (i.e., test-time policy acceleration) [1, 18, 13, 10, 32, 33], the task success rate can decline when predicted action chunks are directly downsampled at higher speedup factors [8].
Meanwhile, other studies have addressed the acceleration of demonstrations before policy training (i.e., offline demonstration acceleration) [8, 15, 30, 6, 27, 24].
Although the overhead of VLA fine-tuning makes it difficult to use downstream policy performance to guide demonstration acceleration, we focus on the latter approach, offline demonstration acceleration, because it enables faster VLA policies without a speed-selection module at deployment.
Several studies have addressed the question of where to accelerate demonstrations offline.
DemoSpeedup [8] uses action entropy to identify segments with different precision requirements, while VOLT [30] uses a vision-language model (VLM) to interpret visual context for segment selection and assigns a human-defined speedup rate.

Even within a segment selected for acceleration, we still need to decide how much to accelerate each movement.
For example, suppose that we treat the entire approach to a cup before grasping as a single segment.
The gripper may move straight toward the cup and then shift slightly to one side to position its fingers for the grasp.
A lower speedup factor may preserve the observation at this change in direction, while a higher factor may combine successive commands and omit that observation.
Our key insight is that, before policy fine-tuning, we can compare candidate factors directly by examining how many steps each saves and how each changes the observations and commands used for learning.
In consideration of these changes, how should the recorded scene and motion guide the choice of speedup factor throughout a demonstration?
In addressing this question, we have derived the following three challenges in offline speed selection.

Challenge 1) How can we compare the effects of candidate speedup factors before policy fine-tuning?
A shorter demonstration may omit details of the movement that the policy needs to learn.
The choice between two speedup factors therefore depends on how many additional steps the higher factor saves and which details the lower factor preserves.

Challenge 2) How can we determine which data changes matter for the task?
The significance of a change in the training data depends on the scene and the recorded motion.
For example, a few observations may capture a straight path through open space, while an intermediate observation can show how the gripper adjusts an object to fit through a narrow opening.

Challenge 3) How should the surrounding movements guide the choice of speedup for each window?
A short window of consecutive demonstration steps may show how an object moves without revealing the purpose of that movement.
For example, seeing the object placed in a holder in the next window can help explain why a small rotation just before placement may warrant a lower speedup factor.

To this end, we propose RePace, an offline framework that selects a speedup profile for the complete episode, as shown in Fig. 1.
We measure the effects of each candidate factor under the same retiming rules used to construct the accelerated demonstrations.
A pretrained language model [29] interprets these measurements considering the task instruction, scene descriptions, and recorded motion from successive windows to select the profile without requiring window-level speed labels.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows.

We propose RePace, an offline demonstration acceleration framework that uses large language model (LLM)-based reasoning to select speedup factors and construct accelerated demonstrations.

We propose RePace, an offline demonstration acceleration framework that uses large language model (LLM)-based reasoning to select speedup factors and construct accelerated demonstrations.

We define three inputs for effective speedup reasoning: visual context and original motion describe the recorded demonstration, while candidate retiming effects quantify the changes produced by each candidate speedup factor.

We evaluate RePace using both simulation benchmarks and a real-world Franka Research 3 robot, showing that demonstrations accelerated via RePace contribute to faster VLA policies while mitigating decreases in task success rates.

1. We propose RePace, an offline demonstration acceleration framework that uses large language model (LLM)-based reasoning to select speedup factors and construct accelerated demonstrations.

2. We define three inputs for effective speedup reasoning: visual context and original motion describe the recorded demonstration, while candidate retiming effects quantify the changes produced by each candidate speedup factor.

3. We evaluate RePace using both simulation benchmarks and a real-world Franka Research 3 robot, showing that demonstrations accelerated via RePace contribute to faster VLA policies while mitigating decreases in task success rates.

title: Real2SimLab: A Unified Platform for Real-to-Simulation Transfer
authors: Yongchang Zhang,Jie Huang,Yunhe Ni,Ningyu Zhou,Guangyu Zhao,Ruixun Liu,Rui Huang,Yidi Wu,TianZe Zhang,Zixiang Jiang,Xiang Li,Kevin Shen,Yiwu Zhong
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Real-to-simulation transfer, which builds simulations from real-world observations, has long been studied in research and industry.
Recently, coding agents have become capable of generating simulation programs from video recordings, and several benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate them.
However, each individual benchmark defines its own inputs, deliverables, and scoring pipeline. This leads to N×MN\times M integrations when evaluating NN methods on MM benchmarks.
To this end, we present Real2SimLab, a unified platform for real-to-simulation transfer.
It evaluates a method by running its written program and scoring the output simulation with the original scorer of each benchmark.
Moreover, Real2SimLab provides a pipeline to create training data and reward annotations for real-to-simulation methods.
Our pipeline carefully avoids data contamination by filtering out the video recordings that exist in benchmarks.
For each video recording, a program is first produced, and then our pipeline computes its reward with the same code that Real2SimLab uses for evaluation.
So far, it supports 47 coding agents and 5 non-agent methods on 6 benchmarks.
Both the platform and Awesome-Real2Sim, our research map of nearly 300 real-to-simulation papers, are open source, and we invite the Real2SimHub community to build them together.
introduction:
Real-to-simulation transfer has long been an active topic in both research and industry.
It takes real-world observations, such as images, videos, and 3D scans, to build simulations in which real objects, scenes, and events can be reproduced, analyzed, and reused.
This field spans computer vision, graphics, and robotics, and most of its methods are designed for one kind of input and one kind of output.
For example, some methods fit physical parameters, such as mass and friction, to videos of objects [35, 36, 15, 20, 16], some assign physical properties to reconstructed 3D scenes [37, 41], and others build sensor simulators from real scans [23] or simulated training environments for robots from real rooms [34, 10].
Each of these methods is a dedicated pipeline, which requires a new pipeline for a new kind of scene.

Recently, rapid progress in foundation models, such as Claude Fable 5.2 [2] and GPT-6 [25], has made coding agents capable of writing and debugging large programs in an evolving way.
This capability opens a new paradigm for real-to-simulation transfer (Figure 1, panel 1): instead of building a dedicated pipeline for each kind of scene, one can ask a coding agent to write a simulation program directly from a video recording [8, 7].
For example, given a video of a red drink being poured into a glass, an agent can write a program that sets up the glass and the liquid in a physics simulator and reproduces the pour.
While the video shows the event only once and from one viewpoint, the program can replay the event, render it from new viewpoints, and expose the state of every object at every moment.
The same agent can attempt many kinds of scenes, offering a promising step toward building simulations in an automatic way.
In this paper, we focus on such a setting, in which a method, such as a coding agent, receives a video recording and delivers a simulation program that can be run.

To measure the progress of the methods, several benchmarks have been proposed [24, 18, 32, 30, 33, 19].
They contribute valuable recordings, carefully designed tasks, and metrics.
However, each benchmark defines its own inputs, deliverables, and scoring pipeline.
For example, Physics-IQ [24] gives a method the first three seconds of a real video and scores the video frames that the method produces for the next five seconds, whereas Video2World [33] gives a whole robot manipulation video and asks for a simulation package that contains the reconstructed scene and the actions of the robot.
Other benchmarks ask for other types of deliverables: 4DCodeBench [32] asks for a script that builds a 4D world, that is, a 3D scene that changes over time, and PhysCodeGym [30] asks for a Blender scene that reproduces a reference video.
Each benchmark then scores its deliverable with its own code, in its own software environment.
As a result, a method built for one benchmark cannot be evaluated on another without a dedicated adapter, and evaluating NN methods on MM benchmarks requires N×MN\times M integrations (Figure 2a).
This cost discourages the evaluation of a method on more than a few benchmarks, and it is also hard to compare the results from different papers.

To this end, we present Real2SimLab, a unified platform for real-to-simulation transfer (Figure 1, panel 2).
It first runs the program that a method writes and scores the output simulation with the original scorer of a benchmark.
Since every method delivers a program and every benchmark scores what a program outputs, the program becomes a common interface between the two sides (Figure 2b).
On the method side, each method is connected once, through a method-wise adapter that passes a task to the method and collects its program.
On the benchmark side, each benchmark is connected once, through a benchmark-wise adapter that converts its data into tasks of one shared format and keeps the official scorer.
For example, on Physics-IQ, a method now delivers a program that writes the requested frames, and the official scorer evaluates these frames as the original benchmark.
Evaluating NN methods on MM benchmarks then requires only N+MN+M integrations instead of N×MN\times M.

Moreover, Real2SimLab provides a pipeline that creates training data with reward annotations for real-to-simulation methods.
These training data should be free of contamination. However, data contamination oftentimes happens in real-to-simulation transfer since one recording can appear in several datasets. For example, one benchmark could reuse the video clips from another benchmark.
The pipeline therefore compares the frames of every training recording with those of the evaluation tasks, and it filters out the recordings that appear in the evaluation tasks, including copies that are re-encoded, resized, or clipped.
For each remaining recording, a method first writes a program, and the pipeline then computes the reward of this program with the same code that Real2SimLab uses for evaluation.
Real2SimLab does not train models itself. Instead, the resulting programs and rewards can serve both offline fine-tuning and online reinforcement learning.

So far, Real2SimLab supports 47 coding agents and 5 non-agent methods, and it adapts 6 existing benchmarks.
All 47 agents, such as OpenHands and Aider, connect through a bridge to the Harbor framework [13], and 5 widely used ones, such as Codex, Claude Code, and Gemini CLI, can also run directly in the sandboxes of Real2SimLab.
The 6 benchmarks are Physics-IQ, Video2World, 4DCodeBench, PhysCodeGym, PhySimCode, and IRIS, to which we add a synthetic suite with exact ground truth, and we check each benchmark-wise adapter against the original release of its benchmark.
This paper focuses on the design of the platform, and we leave a systematic comparison of the connected methods to future work.

Last but not least, while positioning a new work, it is challenging to efficiently choose baseline methods and benchmarks. This is because the literature of real-to-simulation transfer scatters over multiple fields, including computer vision, graphics, and robotics.
These papers deliver the results in various ways and styles, from physical parameters and simulation-ready assets to scene-level simulations, simulation programs, and learned simulators.
We therefore also release Awesome-Real2Sim, a research map of nearly 300 real-to-simulation papers (Figure 1, panel 3).
It organizes the papers by motivations or deliverables, and we will keep it up to date as new work appears.

Both the platform and the research map are open source, and we hope that they will grow into a shared effort of Real2SimHub, an open community that we started around both projects, with a website linked under the paper title.
Researchers can connect their own methods, benchmarks, and datasets through the same adapters that we develop, and add their papers to the research map.

Our contributions are as follows:

A unified evaluation platform.
Real2SimLab considers the program that a method delivers as the common interface between methods and benchmarks. As a result, NN methods and MM benchmarks need only N+MN+M integrations.

A pipeline that can create training data and avoid contamination.
Real2SimLab creates training data by filtering the video recordings that appear in any evaluation task, and provides the reward scores for future fine-tuning.

An open-source ecosystem that is easy to use and extend.
So far, Real2SimLab supports 47 coding agents and 5 non-agent methods on 6 existing benchmarks.
Users can combine them in a short experiment file and add new methods or benchmarks as plugins.

An up-to-date research map.
Awesome-Real2Sim organizes nearly 300 real-to-simulation papers by motivation or deliverable, and we will keep extending it as new work appears.

title: Toward Agentic Robotics: A Large-Scale Study of Harness Design for Robot-Use Agents
authors: Yuxiang Lai,Jike Zhong,Yu-Jhe Li,Lan Wang,Chengzhi Liu,Youbao Tang,Ming Li,Xi Xiao,Xiaofeng Yang,Liang Zhao,Zheda Mai,Ruixi Fan
abstract: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can act as robot-use agents that understand diverse scenes and control robots through policy code and tools. However, they predict 3D gripper poses poorly even with extended reasoning, struggling with precise manipulation. Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action (WAM) models are the opposite: they execute fast, smooth control on trained tasks, yet fail under domain shifts or when tasks require long-horizon memory and reasoning. Agentic robots therefore combine VLM reasoning and perception with precise VLA/WAM control through a policy harness. Yet harness design spans thousands of configurations, shifting success by tens of points with the same models. Moreover, testing even one design takes thousands of rollouts at high API and GPU cost, so prior works often commit to a single design chosen from few alternatives. To guide harness design, we evaluate over 470,000 rollouts across eight simulation benchmarks, six VLMs, and 15 VLA/WAM checkpoints. Seven controlled studies show effective harnesses must adapt to both VLM and VLA/WAM capabilities. Our findings specify what structure the VLM’s policy code needs, where VLA manipulation needs help from tools and policy code, and when to involve the VLM at test time. The reference recipe X-Harness shows that these findings compose without weight updates, lifting base policies up to +42.8+42.8 points across memory, reasoning, and domain shifts.
introduction:
Recent vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as robot-use agents [16] that understand diverse scenes, recall past events, and—building on programmatic robot control [23, 14]—control robots through policy code and tools [11, 12]. However, they struggle with precise manipulation: they predict 3D gripper poses poorly even with extended reasoning and motion planners (§4.1), and calling them in the loop stalls the robot. Vision-language-action (VLA) [3, 2, 19] and world-action (WAM) [1] models are the opposite: they execute fast, smooth control on trained tasks, yet fail under domain shifts or when tasks require long-horizon memory and reasoning. For instance, π0.5\pi_{0.5} [2] exceeds 95%95\% on standard LIBERO [24] but drops to about a quarter once LIBERO-PRO [51] shifts object positions.

Agentic robots [32] therefore combine VLM reasoning and perception with precise VLA or WAM control, alongside motion primitives (functions that move the gripper). The interface that connects them is the policy harness (§3.1): it specifies what context the VLM receives, whether it acts in-loop or writes policy code (free-form Python or symbolic templates), and when it is called. Yet harness design spans thousands of configurations, shifting success by tens of points with the same VLM and action policy (§4–5). Moreover, testing even one design takes thousands of rollouts at high API and GPU cost, so prior works often commit to a single harness [23, 15, 12, 50] or restrict their ablations to a single regime and benchmark [42, 13]. As a result, how to build effective harnesses for agentic robots remains unclear.

To answer this question, we evaluate over 4,000 settings and 470,000 rollouts across eight simulation benchmarks (267 tasks), six VLMs, and 15 VLA/WAM checkpoints (Figure ). Controlled simulation enables one-factor-at-a-time ablations on matched seeds, complemented by supplementary physical validation on a bimanual robot (Appendix J). Starting from VLMs (§4), we study (1) action level: 3D poses versus VLA sub-goals, 2D visual prompts, and 3D target code; (2) context and perception: video history, task notes, pre-coding detections, and depth quality; (3) call timing: in-loop VLM calls versus closed-loop policy code; and (4) code structure: free-form Python versus symbolic templates. Starting from VLAs (§5), we study (5) where harnesses help across tasks and base policies; (6) pre-test evolution: revising policy code or a shared tool bank from training failures under regression checks; and (7) test-time VLM involvement: Offline does not call the VLM, Semi-online calls the VLM on failure signals, and Full-online calls the VLM per sub-goal.

Across these seven studies, we find that effective harnesses must adapt to both VLM coding strength and VLA/WAM capability rather than following one fixed design. To provide open baselines and practical guidelines for researchers stepping into agentic robotics, our contributions are:

Large-scale benchmark study and open baselines (§3), evaluating over 4,000 configurations across eight benchmarks under one protocol, releasing our evaluation suite, policy code, and 470,000+ rollout logs.

Seven empirical takeaways as a design guideline (§4–5; Table 1), specifying perception grounding, code structure, VLA-vs.-primitive routing, code evolution, and test-time VLM scheduling.

X-Harness, a reference recipe (§6) showing that these guidelines compose without weight updates to lift base policies under domain shifts, on memory tasks, and in precise manipulation.

1. Large-scale benchmark study and open baselines (§3), evaluating over 4,000 configurations across eight benchmarks under one protocol, releasing our evaluation suite, policy code, and 470,000+ rollout logs.

2. Seven empirical takeaways as a design guideline (§4–5; Table 1), specifying perception grounding, code structure, VLA-vs.-primitive routing, code evolution, and test-time VLM scheduling.

3. X-Harness, a reference recipe (§6) showing that these guidelines compose without weight updates to lift base policies under domain shifts, on memory tasks, and in precise manipulation.

title: Anytime-Valid Sequential Verification for Sensing-Efficient Robot Navigation under Perception Uncertainty
authors: Saad Korchi,Abderrahim Waga
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Route planning and move verification answer different questions. A planner can find a short route through cells that have barely been observed, while taking the same number of scans at each position can delay progress along a well-observed route. The following experiments ask how many scans a robot can save by verifying only the cells that its next move would newly occupy.

At each position, the robot updates evidence for visible cells, plans with a shared occupancy-dependent route cost, and tests the next swept footprint. If any newly entered cell lacks a certificate, it observes again or stops at a fixed scan limit. The policies share routing code and recovery logic, but their validation-selected routing weights differ. The comparison therefore includes matched-weight controls.

The evaluation compares this rule with four fixed scan counts, a posterior threshold, and routing controls on held-out MovingAI maps. A retrospective comparison at matched routing weights helps distinguish the effect of sequential sensing from the effect of route selection. A separate experiment on a different set of maps tests whether concentrating a fixed certification error budget near the initial start–goal rectangle reduces scan counts. The contribution lies in how the navigation policy uses established sequential tests and union bounds, and in the measured tradeoff between sensing and mission completion. Results are reported separately for the two test sets, which contain different mixes of map families.

The specific contributions are:

a move-level execution gate with an anytime-valid, cell-wise free-space certificate and an explicit conditional bound on episodic collision probability;

a paired benchmark comparing adaptive verification with fixed repeated sensing, including a retrospective matched-routing diagnostic to assess the role of routing weight;

a fixed spatial redistribution of the same certification budget, evaluated on previously unused maps with sensing, completion, and computation reported together; and

explicit stress tests and validation-set sensitivity analyses that identify where the model-based guarantee and practical completion diverge.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 places the method in the context of grid navigation, active sensing, and sequential inference. Section 3 describes the benchmark and observation model; Sections 4 and 5 specify the policies and their execution rule. Section 6 presents the benchmark, spatial-allocation, and robustness results. Section 7 examines parameter sensitivity, followed by discussion and limitations in Section 8 and reproducibility details in Section 9.

title: SOLVE: Sparse, Ordered Keyposes Make LLM Agents Versatile and Efficient Robot Manipulator
authors: Xiang Li,Hongyu Zhou,Ya-Li Li,Tao Li,Rui Zhang,Junjie Lai,Weihua Zhang,Shengjin Wang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
LLM agents have made remarkable progress in robot manipulation, yet they suffer from expensive inference, dense step-by-step control, and tool bottlenecks.
We introduce SOLVE, a training-free, versatile and efficient agent policy: a multimodal LLM agent writes a sparse, ordered sequence of 6-DoF end-effector keyposes per call, observes the result, and writes the next, while a motion planner interpolates between them. The agent decides the number and spacing of keyposes for both fast long-range motion and fine-grained manipulation.
This granularity matches the sparsity of teleoperated manipulation: most demonstrations in DROID can be compressed into a few keyposes instead of dense actions.
SOLVE grounds keyposes with sparse depth queries answered by noisy sources, such as multi-view triangulation, stereo, or monocular depth, and copes with that noise itself.
It also improves from execution feedback, reflecting on its own rollouts and distilling a few rules per task.
SOLVE reaches state-of-the-art performance of 74.5% on RoboDojo and 84.5% on RoboLab, with only $1.7 per episode on average, 12×\times less than previous dense-control agent policies.
On a real robot, the same agent achieves an 88% success rate (75 of 85 episodes) over 16 challenging zero-shot tasks.
Our project page is at https://serenos.github.io/solve-website.
introduction:
Robot manipulation policies have progressed from small task-specific networks trained with reinforcement or imitation learning [51, 26, 71, 14] to vision-language-action (VLA) models [3, 22, 35, 1] and world-action models (WAMs) [27, 7, 25], yet all remain data-hungry: they need large teleoperation corpora for each robot and benchmark, and transfer poorly beyond them.
Frontier multimodal LLMs offer a training-free alternative and can now control robots directly [64, 56, 69, 32], but current agents sit at one of two extremes.
Step-wise agents [69, 56, 64] issue one small step per model call, so every step costs seconds of latency and money, and errors compound.
Code-as-policy agents [40, 55, 19] instead generate programs over a primitive library, which becomes a bottleneck: uncovered tasks require new primitives, written by hand or searched offline [19, 39], and feedback arrives only when the program returns, too late to correct a failed step.

This raises a key question: what action granularity is appropriate for an agent policy?
We compress 57,534 successful DROID episodes [34] into end-effector keyposes joined by straight lines (Fig. 1b), and find that over 91% of the travel lies on segments longer than 5 cm, and that a grasp or release needs only 6 keyposes instead of 96 recorded actions.
We therefore hypothesize that, for an agent policy, a sequence of sparse end-effector keyposes suffices for manipulation, in place of a dense stream of actions.

We present SOLVE, a training-free framework in which a multimodal LLM agent writes sparse, ordered end-effector keyposes, and a motion planner [57] executes straight-line motions between them (Fig. 1c).
Each keypose is an absolute 6-DoF grasp-point pose with a gripper command; one call specifies up to five keyposes, roughly one primitive such as approach, grasp, and lift, and the gripper actuates only upon arrival.
The agent decides how many keyposes to use, how far apart, and how fast: a single keypose for a long free-space motion, and short, slow ones near contact.
After each sequence, the agent inspects the outcome before predicting the next one, so visual feedback enters its reasoning at every primitive rather than only at the checks a program anticipates.

Because each sparse keypose is an absolute commitment, it must be metrically accurate. SOLVE therefore grounds keyposes through sparse metric queries: the agent specifies the few pixels on which its next keypose depends, and a tool returns their 3D positions, each annotated with its measurement modality.
In RoboDojo and RoboLab simulation, which provide no stereo cameras, the tool triangulates each queried pixel across multiple views by epipolar matching, and falls back to monocular depth estimated by Depth Anything 3 [42], scaled by the known table height, when no multi-view match is found; on the real robot, it directly uses depth from FoundationStereo [58] on a stereo infrared camera.
Over multiple rounds of keypose reasoning, the agent adapts to the resulting depth noise by itself.
On difficult tasks, the agent further improves from its own execution feedback without training: it reflects on rollouts from layouts disjoint from evaluation, and consolidates the notes from several rounds into at most five bounded rules per task, which are provided to it at test time.

Since no component of SOLVE is trained, and keyposes live in end-effector space while the planner resolves embodiment-specific execution, the same agent deploys on different robots without modification.
SOLVE achieves 74.5% on the dual-arm RoboDojo under the leaderboard’s metric (Tab. 1) and 84.5% on the single-arm Franka RoboLab [63].
On a real UR12e, it completes 75 of 85 episodes across 16 challenging zero-shot tasks (Tab. 4), including table cleaning, peg-in-hole, sketch drawing, and playing Gomoku against a human.
It does so at $1.7 per episode on average, with one quarter of the model calls and 12×\times lower cost than a step-wise agent (Fig. 1d).

Our contributions are as follows:

We show that teleoperated demonstrations compress into a small number of keyposes and, building on this finding, propose SOLVE, a framework in which an LLM agent writes sparse, ordered keyposes for direct manipulation.

We propose sparse metric queries, combining cross-view epipolar matching with depth estimation to ground keyposes accurately and efficiently in 3D from RGB in simulation, and use stereo depth on the real robot.

We enable the agent to improve from rollouts, and show that SOLVE transfers without modification across robots and benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results on RoboDojo, RoboLab, and a real robot at 12×\times lower cost.

1. We show that teleoperated demonstrations compress into a small number of keyposes and, building on this finding, propose SOLVE, a framework in which an LLM agent writes sparse, ordered keyposes for direct manipulation.

2. We propose sparse metric queries, combining cross-view epipolar matching with depth estimation to ground keyposes accurately and efficiently in 3D from RGB in simulation, and use stereo depth on the real robot.

3. We enable the agent to improve from rollouts, and show that SOLVE transfers without modification across robots and benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results on RoboDojo, RoboLab, and a real robot at 12×\times lower cost.

title: How Well Do Vision-Language Scene Graphs Serve as Memory for Embodied Question Answering?
authors: Divyansh Pandey,Shubh Garg,Vedant Khandelwal,Niyati Rawal,Amit Sheth
comment: Accepted at the HOUR workshop, WACV 2027 (non-archival). (4-page main paper, references, supplementary material), 9 figures, 22 tables. Divyansh Pandey and Shubh Garg contributed equally
abstract: Embodied QA needs memory, but answer accuracy mixes retained evidence, reading errors and question priors. For a simulated multi-room scene-graph pipeline we define answerability: the fraction of questions a fixed rule-based reader answers correctly from the graph alone. The baseline recovers 24.1% of visible object types and its room labels flicker. Four targeted repairs double recall, raise answerability from 27.2% to 37.4%, and improve retrained QA from 71.4% to 75.9%, yet better object F1 can lower answerability. A question-type prior beats this reader on every predicted graph. In one real-video test, graph memory lowers accuracy. These exploratory findings favour scoring retained evidence alongside accuracy.
introduction:
An embodied assistant answering questions about a home must remember what it saw after leaving a room [10, 29, 48]. A common approach predicts each frame’s objects, relations and room as a scene graph, then lets a language model read the merged graph [39, 16, 44]. Final-answer accuracy mixes memory contents, the reader’s ability to use them, and question priors [42, 14]. A correct guess can conceal missing evidence; a reading error can conceal useful memory.

We audit a multi-room QA pipeline built on MomaGraph-R1 [21]. Its benchmark, baseline graphs, training recipe and no-memory/baseline QA runs are inherited (Supp. S1, S7, S11); our contribution is a diagnostic evaluation of memory evidence rather than a new memory method. We define answerability using a fixed rule-based reader, with abstentions counted as wrong. Four targeted repairs act as diagnostic interventions: higher object F1 can reduce question recovery, and better room continuity can hurt object–room queries (Figs. 1 and 2).

Related work. 
Across interactive/photorealistic QA [13, 45], long-horizon memory [55, 19, 3], egocentric video [15] and situated 3D QA [5, 27], answer accuracy evaluates end performance. Question-prior controls [1, 8] motivate separating that score from retained visual evidence. Saha et al. [38] likewise score evidence selection apart from final answers; we score evidence retention.

Scene graphs encode building hierarchies [4, 36, 20], reconstructed objects [43] and open-vocabulary semantics [22, 28] for planning [33], navigation [53] and QA [2, 39]. Image memories retain another form of evidence [51, 34]; we examine what graph evidence supports before a trained task reader.

Image scene-graph generation [47, 54, 40] and panoptic graphs [50] target object/relation recovery using annotations such as Visual Genome [24]. title: ELMO: Emergent Representations In Imitation Learning Via Dynamic Hierarchical Action Chunking
authors: Jasper Gerigk,Yang Xu,Nicholas Rhinehart,Igor Gilitschenski
abstract:
Robot trajectories naturally decompose into variable-length phases with distinct semantic intents, such as reaching, grasping, and lifting.
However, training policies to minimize MSE treats all actions as equal, obscuring their semantic structure.
While latent action models attempt to create a structured prediction target by compressing action chunks into latent representations, existing approaches rely on two-stage training and context-blind decoders.
Consequently, their representations are context-agnostic motion codes (e.g., “move down”) which fail to capture behavioural intent (e.g., “pick up the block”).
To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce the Emergent Latent-action MOdel (ELMO), an end-to-end framework that encodes robot trajectories as grounded semantic codes—representations that ground task-level behavioural intent in the current environment.
ELMO jointly trains a VLA planner and an observation-conditioned decoder over dynamically chunked trajectories, learning a semantically grounded action space without separate pretraining.
Across standard benchmarks, ELMO outperforms comparable prior methods by 9.6 percentage points on LIBERO-Plus and by +0.75 average task length on CALVIN.
Furthermore, on Blocks—our shortcut-free simulation and real-world generalization benchmark—ELMO reaches a 38.6% success rate while all baselines remain below 5%, demonstrating its ability to capture the semantic structure of demonstrations. Website: https://uoft-isl.github.io/elmo.github.io/
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies combine visual and language understanding with robot control by using pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) [17].
While the concept of using a VLM backbone is well established, it is unclear how to best parametrise the action prediction task on top of it.
Designs have tried predicting actions via discrete tokens [17, 31], diffusion [7, 41], or flow matching [4, 3, 39].
Further, it has been shown that making policies predict a chunk of actions rather than a single one improves performance [47], as these sequences capture the underlying non-Markovian behaviour and reduce compounding errors [18].
Going beyond the format of actions, training a VLM backbone to directly predict raw actions has been shown to hurt performance due to the large modality gap between language and raw actions [10].
Thus, research has explored alternative ways to represent actions [37, 34, 21].

At one extreme, hierarchical methods use language sub-tasks [1, 2, 35] as semantic codes to decompose instructions for a downstream controller.
However, language remains too coarse, leaving excessive execution uncertainty to the action policy that lacks the full context required to keep trajectories synchronised with the original intent.
At the other extreme, latent action models compress action chunks into continuous or discrete latents [19, 49, 31].
Yet, as we demonstrate in Section 4.2, these representations act merely as motion codes: context-agnostic encodings of kinematics without task-level intent.
Ideally, an intermediate representation should combine the best of both as grounded semantic codes—representations that capture exact behavioural intent and environmental context while allowing an action policy to reactively adapt execution to the live scene.

Why do existing latent action models collapse into motion codes rather than learning grounded semantic codes? We argue that they are held back by two architectural bottlenecks: context-blind decoding and two-stage training.
First, prior tokenizers and skill models (e.g., VQ-BeT, PRISE, and FAST [19, 49, 31]) reconstruct action sequences in isolation without an observation-conditioned decoder.
Because the decoder is blind to the visual scene, the latent code is forced to memorize exact kinematics rather than abstract behavioural intent.
Second, even when decoders utilize images [43], prior works adopt a hierarchical two-stage training paradigm: they first learn to compress actions into a fixed latent space in the first stage, and then train a planner to predict those frozen latents in the second step.
Decoupling action compression from latent prediction prevents the latent space from being shaped by task-level semantics and visual-language context, optimizing the representation for isolated reconstruction rather than grounded planning.

Overcoming these two bottlenecks requires unifying latent prediction and observation-conditioned decoding into a single end-to-end training stage.
To this end, we propose ELMO, an end-to-end hierarchical prediction framework that directly trains the VLA planner and the observation-conditioned decoder together, adapting the dynamic temporal chunking mechanism of H-Net [13] to continuous robot trajectories.
Instead of relying on fixed temporal windows, ELMO dynamically allocates latent representations across trajectory boundaries and jointly optimizes the entire hierarchy.
By training end-to-end in a single stage, the representation space is jointly shaped by vision-language planning and reactive visual control, allowing ELMO to learn a semantically grounded action space.
During deployment, the VLA planner predicts the resulting grounded semantic codes, which the observation-conditioned action policy maps to raw controls.
Grounded semantic codes serve as a compact, low-noise prediction target, improving VLM learning efficiency while preserving the reactivity and precision of receding-horizon control [47, 7].

Our contributions are threefold: (1) we introduce ELMO, an end-to-end hierarchical framework that unifies dynamic chunking with single-stage joint training of a VLA planner and an observation-conditioned decoder to learn grounded semantic codes; (2) we provide a comprehensive analysis of prior latent action methods, characterizing differences in their encoded information; and (3) we demonstrate strong performance on standard benchmarks (LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN) alongside superior generalization on Blocks, our specialized benchmark designed to eliminate evaluation shortcuts in existing suites.
