title: RoboEvo$^2$: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution
authors: Chenzhi Liu,Jiehong Lin,Wei Huang,Xuzhao Huang,Haoyuan Li,Yang Zhang,Junchao Huang,Chenyeyang Cai,Bo Wang,Kazuhiro Kosuge,Zhongrui Wang,Xiaojuan Qi
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice.
Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly.
Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo2, a framework for recursive harness–policy co-evolution.
In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory.
In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state.
The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop.
Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo2 improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D.
Our models and code will be publicly released.
introduction:
Robots should adapt rapidly to unfamiliar environments, acquire new skills through interaction, and execute those skills efficiently with practice. Human learning motivates this progression from deliberate problem solving to fluent execution, while retaining the flexibility to tackle new situations. Current robot systems offer complementary strengths toward this goal. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) [15, 3, 2, 45] and world action models (WAMs) [41, 11, 13] enable efficient visuomotor control, but remain vulnerable to task and scene shifts [46, 30]. Adapting them through imitation learning often requires collecting many additional human demonstrations, making continual skill acquisition costly. Foundation-model agents can draw on broad prior knowledge, reason about unfamiliar situations, and invoke robot-control APIs to discover and refine solutions [21, 10, 44, 43]. However, repeated reasoning, tool use, and repair introduce latency and API costs that limit reliance on agentic execution for routine behavior.

Realizing this progression requires a reciprocal learning loop between an agent’s harness—its executable skills, memory, and orchestration—and its low-level policy. Harness-centered recursive self-improvement methods refine programs and accumulate experience through feedback [9, 20, 32, 35], but keeping the motor policy fixed does not transfer newly acquired skills into the learned controller. Policy-centered methods use foundation models to guide autonomous data collection and improve learned controllers [12, 47, 23], but do not jointly adapt the harness to the controller’s changing abilities. Co-evolution must therefore connect learning efficient policy behaviors from harness discoveries with adapting the harness to the improving policy. This reciprocity is essential because policy improvement changes both the motor skills available to the agent and the failures that still require exploration and repair.

We introduce RoboEvo2, a framework for recursive harness–policy co-evolution that uses current-policy failures to drive both updates (). In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, a coding agent diagnoses failures, discovers verified corrections, and consolidates them into reusable skills, routing strategies, and persistent memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, successful trajectories and matched failure–correction pairs teach the policy to reproduce effective corrections and disfavor failed alternatives. The updated policy then supplies stronger motor skills for subsequent agentic search, while its remaining failures redirect harness refinement. Concurrent studies also investigate harness–policy coupling [7, 4, 36, 34]. RoboEvo2 connects failure-guided, multi-route solution discovery with explicit learning from matched failures and corrections, progressively reducing repeated agentic intervention as acquired skills are internalized into the policy.

First, to discover complementary capabilities, we develop a failure-conditioned, multi-route P2H repair engine. For each policy failure, it searches three solution routes in parallel: Code refines control programs, Code+ICL incorporates demonstration guidance, and Code+Policy composes programs with learned motor skills. Execution feedback drives iterative repair, and the successful candidate with the lowest normalized motion jerk is selected under matched conditions. This design combines complementary control capabilities to generate verified, smooth corrections targeted at current policy weaknesses.

Second, to internalize corrective capabilities, we introduce Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD). CPD pairs failed and corrected continuations from the same starting state and optimizes a margin between their action-prediction losses relative to a frozen reference policy. Asymmetric proximity penalties discourage degradation of corrective behaviors and excessive suppression of failed alternatives. Combined with supervised learning on verified trajectories, CPD teaches both which corrections to reproduce and which failed alternatives to disfavor. Failure-aware sampling and continual-learning regularization support targeted acquisition and capability retention.

Third, to sustain iterative capability reuse, we develop a harness update mechanism coupled with policy reuse across rounds. Compatible repairs update executable skills and routing logic, while persistent memory retains failure contexts, attempted solutions, and validated guidance. The updated policy then drives subsequent rollouts and participates in Code+Policy search, changing both the failures requiring exploration and the motor primitives available for repair. This closes the reciprocal loop: accumulated harness knowledge supports correction discovery, while internalized policy capabilities directly support subsequent search.

Experiments demonstrate recursive adaptation to distribution shifts without additional human demonstrations. Across eight rounds on LIBERO-PRO [46] and five rounds on RoboTwin C2R [5], standalone success improves from 11.0% to 84.1% and 46.0% to 77.5%, respectively, with hybrid success reaching 90.5% and 87.4% alongside reduced agentic API expenditure. On RoboTwin C2R, our method with 7.5K trajectories matches conventional training with 27.5K trajectories. Ablations validate reciprocal co-evolution, complementary solution routes in P2H, and counterfactual preference distillation in H2P. We further demonstrate autonomous task acquisition on MolmoSpaces [16] and cross-embodiment harness transfer. On the Unitree G1-D, a simulation-evolved harness enables the collection of 120 demonstrations, yielding 85.0% standalone success compared with 80.0% using 200 human demonstrations, while fixed-harness hybrid execution reaches 95.0%.

title: DemoFoundry: Toward Scalable Photorealistic Robot Data with Coding Agents and Generative Rendering
authors: Ruixiang Wang,Xinyue Yao,Xuanning Zhou,Yueci Deng,Yongyi Su,Kui Jia
abstract: Scaling robot learning requires demonstrations that combine realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision. Simulation-based synthesis faces a substantial visual gap relative to real environments, while video-only generation struggles to maintain physically consistent interactions and provide aligned action labels. We present DemoFoundry, an automated framework that couples coding agents with generative rendering to synthesize photorealistic and physically grounded robot demonstrations. Coding agents both construct aligned real–proxy video pairs from existing robot episodes to train a video renderer and write executable interaction programs to generate new demonstrations. Given a scene reference and task instruction, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and writes a control program without requiring target-task human demonstrations. Program execution in a physics simulator produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions. The video renderer translates these proxy videos into scene-consistent, photorealistic observations, reducing the need for detailed appearance modeling in each scene. Automated task-execution checks select successful trajectories for rendering and policy learning. Experiments show improved visual quality and action–video consistency. Policies trained on the generated demonstrations outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations.
introduction:
Generalizable robot policies require large-scale training data covering diverse interactions between robots and their environments. Such data should pair realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision across a broad range of objects, scenes, and tasks. Human teleoperation provides these demonstrations but requires sustained operator effort to execute tasks and reset the environment between trials. Expanding interaction coverage therefore calls for scalable alternatives to manual collection.

Simulation provides a scalable source of robot interactions [50, 53, 22, 7]. However, simulated observations still exhibit a substantial visual gap relative to real environments in object appearance, materials, lighting, and background detail. Domain randomization improves robustness to these differences [46, 7], although matching a particular deployment environment remains challenging. Generative video models can synthesize realistic observations across diverse scenes, but their outputs often exhibit inconsistent contact, object motion, and task execution [11]. Video-only generation also lacks an executable control trace that directly supplies robot actions. Recovering action supervision through inverse dynamics introduces an additional estimation problem [25].

These complementary strengths motivate separating interaction generation from appearance synthesis [9]. Executable programs provide a controllable source of behavior, and video rendering supplies scene appearance. Scaling this approach requires efficient construction of rendering supervision and task programs across scenes. Advances in program-based control and embodied reasoning [28, 42] make coding agents a practical means of coordinating the reconstruction, alignment, and control tools involved in this process.

We introduce DemoFoundry, an automated data engine combining coding agents and generative rendering, as illustrated in Fig. 1. First, a pair-construction agent reconstructs and aligns existing real robot episodes with proxy videos, forming a paired dataset for training a video renderer. The renderer learns to recover appearance from a scene reference while following robot and object motion. Second, for a novel scene, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and develops a program to execute the instructed task. Executing this program under different object layouts in simulation produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions. The renderer then converts these proxy videos into photorealistic observations using the corresponding scene references.

DemoFoundry enables zero-shot data generation for novel robot embodiments and scenes from reference images and robot/camera configurations, without target-scene demonstrations or human operator involvement during generation. We evaluate it on a real-world platform across three manipulation tasks using Diffusion Policy and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [10, 3]. Our renderers improve visual quality over baselines while maintaining strong action–video consistency. Policies trained on our generated data outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations. Policy performance improves with more synthetic training data, and estimated generation costs fall below human teleoperation at scale.

Table 1 places these components within existing robot data-generation pipelines. We make three contributions.

An automated data engine that couples coding-agent programs with appearance rendering to synthesize photorealistic, action-labeled robot demonstrations across diverse scenes and tasks without manual intervention during production.

An agent-constructed dataset of 1,884 aligned real–proxy video pairs from four public robot datasets, used to adapt two video-generation models for rendering newly programmed interactions. We plan to release the paired dataset upon publication.

Real-robot experiments demonstrating improved policy learning over raw simulation and performance comparable to real-demonstration training, complemented by visual-quality comparisons, paired-training ablation, and data-scaling experiments.

1. An automated data engine that couples coding-agent programs with appearance rendering to synthesize photorealistic, action-labeled robot demonstrations across diverse scenes and tasks without manual intervention during production.

2. An agent-constructed dataset of 1,884 aligned real–proxy video pairs from four public robot datasets, used to adapt two video-generation models for rendering newly programmed interactions. We plan to release the paired dataset upon publication.

3. Real-robot experiments demonstrating improved policy learning over raw simulation and performance comparable to real-demonstration training, complemented by visual-quality comparisons, paired-training ablation, and data-scaling experiments.

title: Autonomous Ergodic Robotic Palpation for Elastic Mapping of Curved Soft Tissues
authors: Luca Beber,Cem Bilaloglu,Edoardo Lamon,Matteo Saveriano,Daniele Fontanelli,Luigi Palopoli,Sylvain Calinon
abstract:
Autonomous robotic palpation offers repeatable, quantitative
estimates of tissue properties for stiff inclusion
localization. However, existing methods often rely on prior mesh
models or planar surface assumptions that do not generalize to
complex human anatomy. We propose an ergodic palpation framework that
operates directly on curved soft surfaces using point cloud
data. Central to our approach is the Laplace–Beltrami operator,
which grounds both online estimation and exploration in the surface
intrinsic geometry. We estimate local viscoelastic parameters using
an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) and fuse them into a surface-aware
Gaussian Process (GP). This probabilistic model drives a
diffusion-based ergodic motion planner, generating a continuous
exploration trajectory that feeds the new informative samples back
to the GP in a closed loop. Throughout this process, a hybrid
force-impedance controller regulates interaction forces to maintain
contact. We evaluate the approach against existing methods in
simulation and validate it in physical experiments on
tissue-mimicking silicone phantoms with varying geometries and
viscoelastic properties, demonstrating geometry-consistent mapping
and stiff inclusion localization under contact-rich conditions.
introduction:
Palpation is a clinical procedure in which physicians assess possible anomalies from the mechanical response of the patient’s tissues to touch. When performed manually, it is subjective and varies across practitioners, which limits diagnostic repeatability, particularly for small, deep-seated, or weakly contrasted lesions. Clinical workflows therefore complement palpation with imaging modalities such as mammography (Eisemann et al., 2025) and ultrasound (Dan et al., 2024), which are costly, require specialised staff and equipment, and can burden the patient (e.g., through ionising radiation).
Robotic palpation promises a more repeatable and objective interaction. Beyond revealing possible lesions, it can also quantify elasticity and viscosity (Palacio-Torralba et al., 2015), which are useful for instance to regulate robot–tissue interaction forces in robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery and ultrasound-guided procedures.

Approaches to tissue mechanical characterisation fall into imaging-based elastography and contact-based sensing. Ultrasound (Zhang et al., 2025) and magnetic resonance (Sack, 2023) elastography estimate spatial stiffness distributions, but integrating them into robot-mediated, contact-rich procedures requires dedicated hardware, accurate registration between imaging and robot frames, and workflow adaptations.
Contact-based approaches instead infer tissue properties from force and deformation at the tool-tissue interface, providing local mechanical feedback in real time. Force feedback during probing has been shown to reduce applied forces and procedure time (Trejos et al., 2009; Enayati et al., 2016), and force-based estimation can recover meaningful stiffness information without specialised tactile arrays (Haddadi and Hashtrudi-Zaad, 2012; Roveda et al., 2022). This motivates using a single wrist-mounted force-torque (F/T) sensor both to regulate the interaction and to estimate local viscoelastic properties.

Palpation sampling strategies have evolved from exhaustive grid probing (McKinley et al., 2016; Zevallos et al., 2018) to information-driven exploration based on Bayesian Optimization (BO) (Garg et al., 2016; Ayvali et al., 2017; Salman et al., 2018), which reduces the number of probing actions needed to localize abnormalities, and on ergodic exploration (Ayvali et al., 2017; Beber et al., 2026), which generates continuous, dynamically feasible trajectories whose spatial statistics match a target information distribution. However, these methods are typically formulated and validated on planar or locally flat surfaces (Garg et al., 2016) and assume rectangular exploration patches (Nichols and Okamura, 2015; Garg et al., 2016; Ayvali et al., 2017; Beber et al., 2026). This limits their applicability to curved anatomical surfaces and to irregular or non-convex admissible contact regions arising from safety constraints, anatomy, or kinematic limits.

We address these limitations with an autonomous palpation framework for elastic mapping on curved soft surfaces represented as point clouds, without requiring an anatomical mesh, a volumetric model, or a global surface parameterization. Figure 1 provides an overview of the framework. Local viscoelastic parameters are estimated online from force-displacement measurements using our previous force-based framework (Beber et al., 2025), in which a contact model based on the Dimensionality Reduction Method (DRM) (Popov and Heß, 2015) is embedded in a Kalman filter. These estimates are fused into a manifold-aware Gaussian Process (GP) (Borovitskiy et al., 2020)
defined directly over the point cloud, whose posterior drives an ergodic planner in the spirit of HEDAC (Bilaloglu et al., 2025). The ergodic planner, point cloud HEDAC (PC-HEDAC), is updated at a high rate and requires neither surface flattening nor discrete waypoint planning. Its Expected Information Density (EID) combines attraction towards regions of high estimated apparent stiffness with exploration of regions of high posterior uncertainty, progressively refining the map around mechanically informative areas, according to the prescribed ergodic metric.
The framework is evaluated through systematic simulation studies and repeated physical experiments.
The results demonstrated that the proposed method achieves lower reconstruction RMSE than all evaluated baselines under the same travel budget and requires approximately five times less travel than BO to reach the same RMSE. In addition, the proposed stopping criterion reduces exploration time by approximately 30%30\% compared with full exploration runs, with comparable reconstruction and localization performance.

A closed-loop robotic palpation framework coupling force-based
viscoelastic estimation, intrinsic probabilistic mapping, and
continuous exploration directly on non-planar point cloud surfaces.

title: FeaXDrive2: Body-Scene Spatial Grounding for Feasibility-Aware Generative Driving
authors: Bo Leng,Baoyun Wang,Wenxin Wen,Ming Liu,Weiqi Zhang,Ran Yu,Chongfeng Wei,Zhuoren Li,Lu Xiong
abstract: Generative driving planners may produce trajectories that appear feasible at their reference points but violate environmental constraints over the full vehicle body. We propose FeaXDrive2, an end-to-end generative planning framework that enhances vehicle-embodied spatial feasibility (VESF) through body–scene spatial grounding. The proposed method constructs spatial queries from actual vehicle-body corners and dynamically updates visual sampling locations using evolving trajectory estimates across Flow steps. Retrieved local visual features condition subsequent Action Flow-DiT velocity predictions, allowing trajectory generation to guide spatial information retrieval. Rollout-Consistent Safety Fine-Tuning (RC-F) combines high-risk trajectory supervision with reference behavior preservation, followed by planning-supervised VLM–Action Alignment. Vehicle-geometry counterfactual analysis reveals safety differences under identical trajectories but varying vehicle geometry. On NAVSIM, FeaXDrive2 reduces at-fault collisions by 36.5% relative to the base planner and improves PDMS from 87.0 to 88.8. Under NAVSIM v2 evaluation, EPDMS increases from 86.5 to 88.3. Ablation and body-clearance analyses further demonstrate the safety benefits of body–scene spatial grounding.
introduction:
The safety of end-to-end driving planning depends not only on the motion feasibility of planned trajectories but also on whether the full vehicle-body occupancy along these trajectories satisfies environmental constraints. Recent advances in generative models and vision-language-action (VLA) models have improved end-to-end driving planning. DriveVLM [1] and EMMA [2] incorporate vision-language modeling into driving through hierarchical planning and multimodal task modeling, respectively. DiffusionDrive [3] employs diffusion models to generate multimodal driving trajectories, while Alpamayo-R1 [4] connects driving reasoning with continuous action prediction. Nevertheless, even semantically reasonable and smooth trajectories may result in vehicle-body contact during narrow-road passing, close-range obstacle avoidance, or driving near road boundaries. We define vehicle-embodied spatial feasibility (VESF) as the extent to which the full vehicle-body occupancy induced by a planned trajectory satisfies environmental spatial constraints under given vehicle geometry and traffic conditions. VESF thus depends jointly on vehicle geometry, trajectory poses, and environmental constraints.

Vehicle-geometry counterfactual analysis further quantifies the influence of full-body occupancy on planning safety. On the NAVTEST scenarios of NAVSIM [5], we keep the rear-axle trajectories predicted by the base planner and the simulated motion states unchanged, varying only the vehicle geometry used for evaluation. The resulting geometric contact rates for Small, Pacifica, and Large vehicle configurations are 1.029%, 1.597%, and 2.972%, respectively, with Large exhibiting an 86.08% increase relative to Pacifica (Fig. 1(a)). These results demonstrate that vehicle geometry substantially affects geometric contact outcomes under identical scenes and trajectories. Further analysis reveals that changes in vehicle geometry can also lead to safety-metric failures without direct geometric contact, indicating that VESF involves not only geometric contact but also drivable-area constraints and potential collision risks.

A key challenge in VESF modeling is to establish dynamic spatial relationships between vehicle-body occupancy and the surrounding environment and incorporate them into trajectory generation. For a rigid vehicle with known geometry, its body occupancy can be determined from the trajectory reference pose and vehicle dimensions. However, identifying the environmental constraints relevant to this occupancy from visual observations remains challenging. Even within the same traffic scene, different candidate trajectories induce different body occupancies, changing which vehicle regions are subject to spatial constraints and which environmental information is relevant to planning. UniAD [6] and SparseDrive [7] connect perception, prediction, and planning through task queries and sparse scene representations, respectively, but these interactions do not explicitly establish correspondences between candidate-dependent vehicle-body occupancy and local image features. Therefore, visual information selection should account for both vehicle geometry and planned trajectories to identify local regions relevant to safe vehicle passage.

Prior studies have explored trajectory-guided visual retrieval and feasibility constraints in generative planning, but how these mechanisms can account for full vehicle-body occupancy remains underexplored. Think Twice [8] retrieves features around predicted future positions to refine driving decisions, while HiP-AD [9] employs trajectory-guided deformable attention to retrieve image features, demonstrating that candidate actions can guide environmental information selection. FeaXDrive [10] improves the kinematic and drivable-area feasibility of generated trajectories through adaptive curvature constraints and drivable-area guidance based on full vehicle-body occupancy. GuideFlow [11] incorporates constraint guidance and energy-based modeling into Flow Matching. Building on these studies, we investigate how vehicle geometry can define body-anchored spatial queries, while evolving trajectory estimates dynamically determine visual retrieval locations. The resulting body–scene spatial context can then condition subsequent trajectory generation to enhance VESF.

For Flow Matching-based driving planners, body–scene spatial grounding must also be translated into safe planning outcomes through the multi-step generation process. Flow Matching [12] learns a velocity field at sampled intermediate states, while the final trajectory is obtained through numerical integration. When intermediate trajectory estimates are used to update visual retrieval locations, evolving generation states also influence subsequent visual conditioning. Consequently, reducing local prediction errors does not necessarily ensure the safety of the final generated trajectory. DRaFT [13] investigated the direct optimization of differentiable rewards through diffusion sampling, motivating optimization strategies that account for generated outcomes. Meanwhile, R2SE [14] investigated targeted adaptation to challenging driving scenarios while preserving previously acquired driving capabilities. These considerations motivate safety optimization that accounts for actual generated trajectories while improving high-risk planning behaviors and preserving established safe behaviors.

To address these challenges, we propose FeaXDrive2, an end-to-end generative driving planning framework designed to enhance VESF (Fig. 1). The framework employs a pretrained vision-language model for multimodal scene conditioning and learns a base trajectory generator through Flow Matching with a DiT backbone [15]. Safety evaluation of the base planner identifies high-risk scenarios, while vehicle-geometry counterfactual analysis and body clearance measurements further identify challenging safe scenarios, yielding stratified training samples. FeaXDrive2 introduces body-anchored, trajectory-conditioned spatial visual retrieval to establish dynamic body–scene spatial grounding from actual vehicle geometry and evolving trajectory estimates. Rollout-Consistent Safety Fine-Tuning (RC-F) combines high-risk trajectory supervision with reference behavior preservation throughout the multi-step generation process to enhance planning safety. VLM–Action Alignment then jointly optimizes language-model LoRA parameters and selected Action Flow-DiT parameters through planning supervision, aligning multimodal representations with trajectory generation.

Extensive experiments on NAVSIM validate the planning performance and safety improvements of FeaXDrive2. On NAVSIM v1 NAVTEST, FeaXDrive2 reduces at-fault collision scenarios from 181 to 115, a 36.5% reduction, and improves PDMS from 87.0 to 88.8 under single-candidate inference. On the same scenarios evaluated using the NAVSIM v2 single-stage protocol [16], EPDMS increases from 86.5 to 88.3. Component ablations and vehicle-body clearance analysis further examine the contributions of spatial grounding and safety optimization.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We propose FeaXDrive2, an end-to-end generative driving planning framework for enhancing VESF. The framework uses vehicle-body occupancy to guide both environmental information acquisition during trajectory generation and the construction of safety supervision, integrating body–scene spatial grounding with safety-oriented learning of the generative planner.

We propose FeaXDrive2, an end-to-end generative driving planning framework for enhancing VESF. The framework uses vehicle-body occupancy to guide both environmental information acquisition during trajectory generation and the construction of safety supervision, integrating body–scene spatial grounding with safety-oriented learning of the generative planner.

We develop a body–scene spatial grounding mechanism and RC-F. Vehicle-body geometry defines query anchors, while evolving trajectory estimates update the corresponding visual retrieval locations to acquire body-relevant environmental information. RC-F further combines high-risk trajectory supervision with reference behavior preservation to improve planning safety and mitigate degradation of established safe behaviors.

We characterize and quantify VESF-related failures in end-to-end driving planning. Controlled vehicle-geometry counterfactual analysis quantifies geometric contacts and non-contact safety-metric failures under identical scenes and rear-axle trajectories. Planning evaluations, ablation studies, and vehicle-body clearance analysis further validate the effectiveness of FeaXDrive2.

title: Nav4Manip: From Navigation to Dexterous Mobile Manipulation through Co-Evolution
authors: Yusen Feng,Zixi Kang,Zhijun Yin,Changxiao Liu,Tianhong Gao,Jiazhao Zhang,Jiahang Liu,Libin Liu,Zhizheng Zhang,He Wang
abstract: Dexterous mobile manipulation is essential for robots to perform useful tasks in complex, unstructured environments. However, existing systems face two challenges. First, navigation remains too coarse for downstream manipulation, which often requires a precise base position and approach orientation rather than merely reaching a meter-scale goal region. Second, navigation and manipulation are commonly trained in isolation, lacking a feedback loop that enables the two capabilities to co-evolve. These limitations prevent current systems from reliably executing long-horizon dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks in real-world environments. To address them, we introduce Nav4Manip, a bidirectionally coupled co-evolution system for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation. It comprises two complementary architectures: Nav4Manip-N learns long-horizon navigation and refines its policy through manipulation feedback, while Nav4Manip-M trains a world-action model (WAM) for downstream dexterous manipulation. We train Nav4Manip-N in three stages: multi-task co-tuning learns navigation behavior and manipulation-aware affordance prediction; rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) rejects low-quality policy-generated paths and fine-tunes the model on retained trajectories; and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) uses counterfactual preferences to further improve navigation decisions. To support this framework, we establish the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs from benchmark rollouts, providing large-scale paired navigation–manipulation trajectories and affordance supervision. Extensive experiments on public vision-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, while real-world evaluations show that Nav4Manip completes diverse dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://nav4manip.github.io/.
introduction:
Dexterous mobile manipulation integrates navigation (Zhang et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2026a; Xue et al., 2026) and manipulation (Brohan et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2023; Team et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026). However, existing VLN methods are insufficient as upstream policies for downstream manipulation. First, VLN benchmarks typically consider navigation successful when the robot stops within 3 m of a reference goal (Anderson et al., 2018; Krantz et al., 2020). In contrast, manipulation success is highly sensitive to the robot’s terminal base pose, as workspace geometry, kinematic reachability, visibility, and collision constraints impose much stricter requirements on the final position and orientation. Consequently, an endpoint deemed successful by VLN metrics may still leave the target unreachable, occluded, or accessible only from an unsuitable approach direction. Second, existing mobile-manipulation systems typically adopt either a unified whole-body policy for room-scale tasks (Fu et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025) or separately trained navigation and manipulation modules (Yenamandra et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024). These approaches primarily focus on gripper-based manipulation rather than dexterous multi-finger interaction. Additionally, unified whole-body policies do not directly address long-horizon navigation, while modular pipelines lack a mechanism for manipulation outcomes to inform and refine the navigator. Moreover, independently fine-tuning navigation and manipulation policies provides no mechanism for the two capabilities to co-evolve toward a shared end-to-end objective.

We address these limitations by introducing Nav4Manip, a bidirectionally coupled co-evolution system with two complementary architectures: Nav4Manip-N learns long-horizon navigation and refines its policy through manipulation feedback, while Nav4Manip-M trains a WAM for downstream dexterous manipulation. As illustrated in Figure 1, navigation-only optimization yields limited joint capability, while alternating optimization repeatedly trains both modules. Our staged co-evolution strategy achieves a 17.83-point improvement in end-to-end task success (52.13% vs. 34.30%) over alternating optimization, while avoiding repeated manipulation policy training. Nav4Manip-N jointly predicts navigation actions and manipulation affordances. Multi-task co-tuning first establishes broad navigation competence and manipulation endpoint prediction. We then introduce verifier-guided RFT, which samples trajectories from Nav4Manip-N and uses downstream manipulation executions as a verifier to retain trajectories with feasible navigation endpoints and successful manipulation outcomes. Finally, RLAIF uses an execution agent to interpret navigation–manipulation outcomes and construct counterfactual preference pairs for further optimizing Nav4Manip-N. The resulting knowledge is distilled into the navigation model, enabling manipulation feedback to improve future navigation.

To support training and evaluation, we establish Nav-N-Manip, a benchmark that evaluates both long-horizon navigation and downstream manipulation. Rollouts on Nav-N-Manip yield Nav4Manip-Pairs, a 233-hour paired navigation–manipulation dataset. In summary, we make the following contributions:

We introduce Nav4Manip, a dexterous mobile-manipulation co-evolution system comprising three-stage Nav4Manip-N and WAM Nav4Manip-M.

We establish the Nav-N-Manip benchmark for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs, a 233-hour dataset of paired navigation–manipulation trajectories and affordance scores.

We conduct extensive experiments on established VLN tasks and Nav-N-Manip, together with real-robot evaluations, demonstrating strong navigation performance and reliable end-to-end dexterous mobile manipulation across diverse tasks.

1. We introduce Nav4Manip, a dexterous mobile-manipulation co-evolution system comprising three-stage Nav4Manip-N and WAM Nav4Manip-M.

2. We establish the Nav-N-Manip benchmark for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs, a 233-hour dataset of paired navigation–manipulation trajectories and affordance scores.

3. We conduct extensive experiments on established VLN tasks and Nav-N-Manip, together with real-robot evaluations, demonstrating strong navigation performance and reliable end-to-end dexterous mobile manipulation across diverse tasks.

title: $μ$MPC: Microsecond-Scale Nonlinear and World Model Control from Edge to GPU via Koopman-Linearized Precompilation
authors: Devesh Nath,Glen Chou
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
abstract: We present μ\muMPC, a fast model predictive control (MPC) framework that reduces online computation using learned Koopman-linearized dynamics. By precomputing finite-horizon control-to-output maps, μ\muMPC eliminates lifted-state trajectories, yielding an action-only Koopman-Compiled QP (KC-QP) with H​nuHn_{u} decision variables, independent of lifted dimension. A fixed, precomputed primal operator enables efficient primal-dual iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections, accommodating changing goals and constraints without refactorization. This efficiency also enables control-aware dynamics learning through differentiable KC-QPs in the training loop and batched DAgger-style data aggregation. μ\muMPC achieves solve times as low as 23​μ23\mus on a desktop CPU and 24 ms onboard a 168 MHz Crazyflie microcontroller. It scales to 4096D quadruped control in under 5 ms, visual planning with 2048D world models in 0.4 ms, and collision-aware planning for 200 quadrotors at over 30 Hz on the GPU. Across these benchmarks, μ\muMPC achieves up to 108×108\times faster constrained MPC and 1907×1907\times faster visuomotor planning than competing methods.
introduction:
Optimal control of complex robotic systems requires expressive dynamics models and real-time solvers for deployment, which is particularly difficult for resource-constrained and high-dimensional systems. Embedded aerial robots face strict compute, memory, and power budgets [1, 2]; whole-body legged control requires high-dimensional real-time optimization [3, 4]; visuomotor planning relies on learned world models with thousands of latent states [5, 6]; and multi-agent systems require many concurrent optimizations [7, 8]. Controllers must also plan over long horizons, react rapidly to observations, and satisfy complex constraints. Nonlinear model predictive control (MPC) addresses these requirements, but its computational cost grows with problem dimension, horizon length, and constraint complexity. Despite advances in sparsity exploitation, factorization caching, and GPU parallelism [4, 3], real-time deployment remains challenging.

This computational challenge is particularly pronounced for learned dynamics and world models. While these models can capture complex dynamics from high-dimensional observations, planning often requires repeated computationally-expensive evaluations of candidate action sequences through the learned dynamics [5, 9, 10]. One approach to reducing this cost is via Koopman linearization, which learns dynamics that are linear in a lifted space, yielding an affine dependence of finite-horizon predictions on the control sequence [11] that simplifies both prediction and trajectory optimization. However, nonlinear constraints can still require iterative linearization and expensive matrix refactorizations, limiting the computational benefits. This motivates an MPC framework that moves expensive computations offline while allowing goals and constraints to be updated efficiently online.

Another challenge is learning dynamics models that are suitable for control rather than prediction alone. Conventional Koopman dynamics learning emphasizes state-prediction accuracy [12], but low prediction error may not translate to high control performance. Moreover, training on fixed demonstrations neglects controller-induced distribution shifts, potentially degrading prediction accuracy at inference time. Differentiable MPC offers a way to address these limitations [13] by incorporating the learned Koopman dynamics into the MPC optimization during training, enabling direct supervision of control performance and generating training data arising from controller-induced state distributions. However, repeatedly solving and differentiating through MPC problems can be prohibitively expensive during training.

To address these challenges, we present μ\muMPC, an MPC framework for nonlinear systems that exploits learned Koopman-linearized dynamics to formulate Koopman-Compiled Quadratic Programs (KC-QPs) that can be solved in microseconds. We develop a tailored primal-dual solver that precomputes a fixed primal operator offline, reducing online constrained optimization to efficient matrix-vector products and projections. This operator can be reused across changing constraints, goals, and MPC steps, substantially reducing online computation. The efficiency of KC-QPs also enables scalable control-aware learning: we solve batches of KC-QPs in parallel, evaluate the resulting control performance under the original nonlinear dynamics, and differentiate through the optimization to train Koopman representations directly for control performance rather than prediction accuracy alone. Furthermore, fast batched KC-QP solves enable DAgger-style on-policy data aggregation, improving coverage of controller-induced state distributions and mitigating inference-time distribution shift. Together, this scalable learning of high-dimensional Koopman representations tailored to closed-loop control enables microsecond-scale online MPC.
Our contributions are:

μ\muMPC exploits the linear structure of learned Koopman dynamics to eliminate state variables and formulate MPC as an action-only QP (KC-QP). We precompute a fixed primal operator offline, enabling fast, “precompiled” primal-dual iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections, even as goals and constraints change, without requiring online matrix refactorization.

We exploit the compact, parallelizable structure of KC-QPs to train the Koopman dynamics to produce MPC control sequences that match expert demonstration data, by differentiating through the optimization. Batched KC-QP solves also enable fast DAgger-style data aggregation, reducing controller-induced distribution shift.

We demonstrate μ\muMPC across embedded, high-dimensional, multi-agent, and visual control. Our solver achieves MPC runtimes as low as 23 μ\mus on Dubins car and quadrotor systems, solves H=75H=75 MPC onboard a resource-limited Crazyflie microcontroller in 24 ms, and performs 4096-dimensional quadruped control in under 5 ms. We further demonstrate real-time collision-aware multi-agent planning for 200 quadrotors, with hardware validation on a system of seven differential-drive robots. For visual control, we train 2048D linear world models enabling sub-millisecond planning, outperforming evaluated baselines on navigation and bimanual rope manipulation, with hardware cube-manipulation validation.

1. μ\muMPC exploits the linear structure of learned Koopman dynamics to eliminate state variables and formulate MPC as an action-only QP (KC-QP). We precompute a fixed primal operator offline, enabling fast, “precompiled” primal-dual iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections, even as goals and constraints change, without requiring online matrix refactorization.

2. We exploit the compact, parallelizable structure of KC-QPs to train the Koopman dynamics to produce MPC control sequences that match expert demonstration data, by differentiating through the optimization. Batched KC-QP solves also enable fast DAgger-style data aggregation, reducing controller-induced distribution shift.

3. We demonstrate μ\muMPC across embedded, high-dimensional, multi-agent, and visual control. title: Geometric Acceleration Obstacles: Physical Boundary Structure and Affine Safety Certificates
authors: Xuheng Gao,Yuhan Pang,Bi-Ke Zhu,Ronghao Chen,Lingxiao Meng,Jiankun Wang,Max Q.-H. Meng
abstract:
Safe robot navigation in dynamic environments requires collision avoidance that respects motion constraints while remaining computationally efficient.
Conventional velocity-obstacle (VO) methods characterize collision-inducing motions in velocity space.
Although some formulations account for acceleration-limited velocity transitions, their collision constraints remain tied to specific velocity-tracking models.
Acceleration obstacles (AO) address this limitation by representing collision-inducing inputs directly in acceleration space.
However, existing AO methods either rely on conservative approximations or derive analytical structure expressions without verifying their geometric correspondence.
To address this gap, this paper presents Geometric Acceleration Obstacles (GAO), which provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first unified and physically validated characterization of AO geometry and its supporting structure.
Specifically, we derive configuration-dependent half-planes that globally support the collision set and establish their tightness, thereby separating certified collision-free acceleration inputs from collision-inducing parts.
These geometric results yield unified affine safety constraints.
Combined with actuator limits, these constraints define a quadratic program (QP) for real-time navigation.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that GAO achieves competitive success rates and the lowest control effort among the evaluated methods, with millisecond-level computational latency.
Further circle-interchange simulations demonstrate scalability to 1,000 agents.
Physical experiments validate the approach in pedestrian encounters, reciprocal multi-agent navigation, and high-speed maneuvering.
introduction:
Collision avoidance is a fundamental capability for autonomous robots operating in dynamic environments, enabling them to navigate safely among moving obstacles and other agents.
This problem arises in crowded indoor navigation [1, 2], warehouse logistics [3], and multi-robot systems [4].
In practice, a robot’s ability to maneuver away from collisions is constrained by its acceleration limits, which determine how rapidly it can change its speed and direction.
Biological studies of predator-prey interactions further highlight the role of acceleration and maneuverability in successful evasion [5, 6].
Consequently, safe avoidance requires not only selecting collision-free motions but also ensuring that the transitions toward them remain dynamically feasible under the robot’s acceleration limits [7].

Conventional geometric methods, including velocity obstacles (VO) [8] and collision cones (CC) [9], represent collision-inducing motions in velocity space.
Reciprocal VO (RVO) [10] and optimal reciprocal collision avoidance (ORCA) [11] extend this representation by distributing avoidance responsibility among interacting agents.
However, selecting a collision-free target velocity does not guarantee collision-free motion during the transition from the current velocity, particularly under bounded acceleration (Fig. 1(a)).
Dynamic window approach (DWA) [12] addresses this issue by restricting velocity selection to dynamically reachable commands and evaluating braking feasibility.
Other formulations incorporate control-induced motion into collision prediction:
generalized velocity obstacles (GVO) [13] consider trajectories generated by control inputs, continuous control obstacles [14] account for motion-continuity constraints,
acceleration-velocity obstacles (AVO) [15] characterize target velocities under proportional velocity tracking.
Although these methods account for motion constraints, their collision representations remain tied to specific control parameterizations or motion-generation mechanisms.
In contrast, acceleration obstacles (AO) [16] directly characterize collision-inducing acceleration inputs, without requiring a prescribed velocity-tracking mechanism.
However, characterizing the collision set in acceleration space does not by itself provide tractable safety constraints for real-time control.

To make AO suitable for real-time control, its geometric representation must be translated into tractable safety constraints.
Existing safety-control approaches derive tractable input constraints from predicted motion [17, 18, 19], collision-inevitability and reachability analyses [20, 21], or safe-set invariance [22, 23].
More directly, Wang et al. [24] derive affine acceleration constraints using braking-based safe sets and control barrier functions, while collision-cone CBFs [25] incorporate relative-velocity geometry into barrier-based control constraints.
These studies demonstrate the value of tractable input constraints for safety-critical control.
For AO, the challenge is to derive such constraints that exclude all collision-inducing inputs while retaining as many collision-free inputs as possible.

Existing AO studies have provided both collision-set characterization and analytical boundary construction, but important geometric questions remain.
Gonon et al. [16] represent the finite-horizon AO as a union of acceleration-space disks and derive conservative half-plane constraints for control.
However, their constructed local boundary curves can self-intersect, and the resulting constraints conservatively enclose the AO rather than exploit its exact boundary geometry.
Stern and Shiller [26] subsequently derive analytical grazing candidates for AO boundaries.
Yet, grazing conditions alone do not guarantee nonpenetration over the entire trajectory, so these candidates do not necessarily correspond to the physical AO boundary.
Moreover, the geometric structure of AO depends on the initial relative-motion configuration, requiring a unified analysis and corresponding geometric characterization.

To address these limitations, we present Geometric Acceleration Obstacles (GAO), which establishes a complete geometric characterization of AO and derives unified affine safety certificates from its validated structure.
The resulting contributions are:

Physical characterization of AO geometry.
A trajectory-wide nonpenetration criterion distinguishes physically valid grazing candidates from hidden penetrating candidates, establishing their correspondence with the actual AO boundary.

Configuration-dependent global support.
We characterize the AO geometry under approaching and bypassing configurations and derive tangent-based and spatially derived global supports, with proofs of translational and angular tightness (Fig. 1(b)).

Unified affine certificates and experiment validation.
We derive pairwise robot-input certificates and combine them with convex actuator limits to obtain a convex certified inner approximation of collision-free inputs for QP-based control. Large-scale simulations and physical robot experiments validate the proposed framework (Fig. 1(c)).

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section II reviews related work.
Section III formulates the relative-motion model and examines the global validity of grazing candidates.
Section IV establishes the geometric safety certificates.
Section V presents the control formulation.
Sections VI and VII report simulation and physical experiments, respectively.
Section VIII concludes this work.
Appendix A provides supplementary support and tightness proofs.

introduction:
Humanoid robots are expected to operate in unstructured environments, from disaster response and infrastructure inspection to household assistance. The ground in such settings is often far from an ideal rigid plane: rope bridges, protective nets, floating platforms, mattresses, and inflatable surfaces are compliant and deformable, yielding under load and rebounding when unloaded. Locomotion there means holding balance and tracking commands while the ground itself deforms and moves.

On an elastic terrain, loading changes surface shape and velocity, stores energy, excites motion that persists after unloading, and redistributes force from one foothold to the others. What the robot meets at its next contact therefore depends on the support’s evolving state and on its own preceding actions, so a training environment must expose the policy to these dynamics while resolving contact with the moving surface.

Reinforcement learning has enabled agile quadrupedal motion [1, 2], perceptive traversal [3], and humanoid locomotion from proprioceptive histories [4]. Terrain models and training curricula have also enabled locomotion on compliant and yielding surfaces [5, 6, 7], where the surface yields locally under the foot. Trampoline-like supports, whose entire surface deflects, stores energy, and keeps moving between footfalls, have only been traversed by a quadruped under model-based control [8]; learned humanoid control on such a support has not been demonstrated on hardware.

We present RIPPLE (

R

P

lastic terrain), a simulation-to-real learning framework for humanoid control on elastic terrains. Its principal model, ElasticMembrane, represents an elastic surface as a mass–spring mesh whose nodes are coupled by axial and diagonal springs. Robot contact excites the membrane, and its subsequent motion feeds back into the robot dynamics. We implement ElasticMembrane in MuJoCo [9] and integrate it into MJLab [10] for parallel reinforcement learning. Policies progress from rigid-ground skills to elastic-terrain balance and jumping through one shared proprioceptive interface, so deployment needs no cameras, foot pressure sensors, or other exteroceptive sensing.

A trampoline realizes local deformation, distributed motion, and rebound in one support. We demonstrate zero-shot deployment on a real MagicBot Z1 humanoid for balance, consecutive jumping, and entry from a rigid platform (Fig. ), against simpler baselines on the same trampoline and against three simpler terrain models — CompliantContact, IndependentSprings, and BouncyPlate — in simulation (Sec. IV).

We introduce humanoid locomotion and dynamic behaviors on large-deformation elastic terrains as a new and challenging setting. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study this task with reinforcement learning, and our learned policies generalize across terrain models and transfer zero-shot to a physical trampoline. Our contributions can be summarized in three points:

A simulation framework built on MuJoCo and MJLab that couples pretensioned ElasticMembrane dynamics with deformable robot–support contact for parallel humanoid policy learning.

A staged training and deployment pipeline that transfers rigid-ground skills to elastic-terrain balance and jumping through a shared proprioceptive interface, with real-trampoline demonstrations.

Generalization experiments that demonstrate policy transfer across multiple terrain models and seven additional simulated scenarios, and quantify performance under changes in stiffness, size, and external disturbances.

title: Compact Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environmentsvia On-Policy Training and Route-Bearing Output
authors: Reshad Ul Karim,Syeda Maliha Tabassum,Md. Khalilur Rhaman,Md Rashad Al Hasan Rony
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Instruction-following robots need navigation policies that reach high accuracy and remain inexpensive to train and to run on a single graphics processing unit (GPU).
The most accurate vision-language navigation policies for continuous environments rely on language models with 4 to 8 billion parameters, long observation histories, and large auxiliary corpora.
Two properties of the standard training setup limit smaller policies.
Imitation labels cover the states that an expert visits, whereas the running policy reaches states that its own errors produce.
In addition, an image-plane waypoint exists only while the route lies inside the camera view.
We present AlphaNav, a monocular red-green-blue (RGB) policy with 2 billion (2B) parameters that addresses both limitations.
AlphaNav adapts Qwen3-VL-2B with low-rank adapters and processes an eight-frame memory and the current view in one forward pass.
The policy predicts the route direction as a bearing in the body frame of the agent, which remains defined for every heading, and a deterministic controller converts this bearing into motion.
This design allows training to relabel the states that the policy itself visits.
On-policy correction improves success, while bearing decoding outperforms image-plane waypoint scanning across all evaluated start headings with identical weights.
On the Val-Unseen split, AlphaNav achieves 53.3% success on Room-to-Room in Continuous Environments (R2R-CE), averaged over three seeds, and 40.8% on its Room-Across-Room counterpart (RxR-CE).
Inference requires 65 ms and 4.3 GiB of memory, while training takes 30.6 GPU-hours on one 12 GB consumer GPU.
introduction:
Instruction-following navigation enables a robot to cross an unfamiliar building by following a route description.
Vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE) formulates this task with low-level actions, namely 0.25 m forward steps, 15∘15^{\circ} turns, and a stop action [15].
On the standard Room-to-Room in Continuous Environments (R2R-CE) benchmark, video-language models predict these actions from sequences of red-green-blue (RGB) observations.
NaVid [37] introduced this approach, Uni-NaVid [38] extended it to several navigation tasks, and NaVILA [8] and StreamVLN [34] scaled it further.
These systems are built on language models with 7B-8B parameters and long observation histories, and their training adds web video, question answering, or synthetic navigation episodes to the benchmark data.
StreamVLN and NaVILA report 270 and 595 ms per model call, respectively, on an RTX 4090 GPU, and training these 7B and 8B systems costs 544 to 2,816 data-center GPU-hours (details in Table 2).

In an instruction-following setup, a deployed robot must act several times per second on its own hardware, so the latency, memory footprint, and training cost of its policy determine where that policy can run and who can afford to train it. Fig. 1 demonstrates AlphaNav among published systems along two axes, language-model size and latency.
It is visible that a 2B-parameter policy is on par in success rate with the 7B StreamVLN and the 8B NaVILA and Aux-Think at the lowest reported latency, whereas the 2B MonoDream [29] requires 800 ms per call and the 2B Goal2Pixel [3] needs depth at test time.
We identify two limitations of the standard training setup that stand in the way of compact policies.
The first concerns the training data, since imitation covers only the states an expert visits, whereas a running policy drifts into new states after its own errors [25]. The second concerns the action representation, because an image-plane waypoint can express only routes inside the camera view, yet in 54.5% of the Val-Unseen episodes the first route step lies more than 90∘90^{\circ} from the start heading.

AlphaNav retains a standard vision-language backbone and instead changes the output representation and the training-state distribution (Fig. 2).
The instruction, eight memory frames, and the current frame form one sequence with 192 visual tokens for Qwen3-VL-2B [2], which we fine-tune with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [11].
A feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) layer [21] conditions the current-view tokens on known camera and body parameters.
Four heads then predict a waypoint heatmap, a visibility score, a stop probability, and a 24-bin route bearing, which encodes the direction of the route in the body frame and remains defined for every heading.
A deterministic controller converts these predictions into turns and at most four forward moves.
Training first imitates reference paths and then relabels the states of the policy’s own rollouts in rounds of on-policy correction (Secs. 3.5 and S11). The core contributions of AlphaNav are as follows:

We present AlphaNav, a compact monocular policy that adapts Qwen3-VL-2B with LoRA and processes eight memory frames and the current view in one forward pass.
Over three seeds, AlphaNav reaches 53.3 ±\pm 1.4% success rate (SR) and 49.3% success weighted by path length (SPL) on R2R-CE Val-Unseen.

We train the policy on the states that it visits, and this relabeling raises SR from 43.9% to 49.3%.
With oracle inputs the controller succeeds in 99.7% of the episodes, and an oracle stop raises the SR of one trained model from 53.6% to 72.5%.

We pair the image-plane waypoint with a 24-bin body-frame route-bearing head that remains defined for every heading, and we isolate its effect by decoding the same weights both ways.
The bearing raises SR from 39.7% to 53.6%, and on the baseline recipe the orient-then-go augmentation adds 4.6 points on starts that face away from the route.

AlphaNav has the lowest latency of the ten compared systems that report one and trains on one consumer GPU.
One decision requires 65 ms and 4.3 GiB of memory, and training requires 30.6 GPU-hours plus 11.2 GPU-hours of label rendering on one RTX 5070; training alone takes 18 to 92 times fewer GPU-hours than the 7B and 8B systems report.

title: M$^{2}$AdaptVLA: Multimodal Memory-Augmented Vision-Language-Action Model with Predictive Test-Time Adaptation
authors: Liufan Tan,Tong Wang,Yuehao Yin,Jian Chen,Yihang Yin,Ying Qu,Wenyu Li,Ruyi Gan,Hao Wang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Effective robotic manipulation calls for multimodal memory and rapid adaptation to shifts in contact dynamics.
However, many existing policies, which retain either visual or wrench history, may miss key cues from the other modality.
Moreover, even with wrench memory, fixed policies can struggle when contact conditions shift at deployment.
To this end, we introduce M2AdaptVLA, a vision-language-action model that integrates visual and wrench memories with predictive test-time adaptation.
For visual memory, the model uses test-time training (TTT) to encode observation history in fast weights.
Each entry in the bounded TTT bank combines the corresponding frame’s features with a readout from these weights, preserving cues that predate the oldest retained frame.
For wrench memory, a context gate controls how much the action expert draws on wrench history as it jointly denoises future actions and wrenches.
For predictive test-time adaptation, the auxiliary wrench prediction loss also provides online self-supervision.
Using measured wrenches as targets, we update low-rank policy adapters by backpropagating only through the final denoising step.
Real-world experiments show that the TTT bank outperforms visual memory baselines on progress tracking, scene recall, and demonstration following.
On contact-sensitive tasks, the context gate yields higher success rates than direct injection or gated cross-attention.
Predictive test-time adaptation improves robustness to shifts in contact dynamics.
On eight tasks requiring visual and wrench memory, M2AdaptVLA achieves a mean success rate of 82.71%, a 31.46% absolute gain over the strongest baseline.
The project page is available at https://tlf-tlf.github.io/M2AdaptVLAPage/.
introduction:
Recent work has incorporated memory into vision-language-action (VLA) models and demonstrated its effectiveness on robotic manipulation tasks in which the next action depends on sensory information gathered over time [26, 31, 18, 32, 36]. Many memory-augmented policies focus on a single sensory history, using either visual memory to retain earlier observations [46, 13, 23, 8] or wrench memory to retain the forces and torques measured during contact [17, 11, 19]. However, a policy that relies on a single memory modality may miss key cues from the other modality, making it difficult to perform tasks that require both.

Consider a robot entering a safe’s passcode (Fig. (a)). Visual memory helps the robot track which digits it has attempted and which key to press next. However, the gripper can look nearly identical as it approaches a key and as it lifts away after a press. Visual history alone may therefore leave the robot uncertain whether the key has gone down, causing it to move on before completing the press. Wrench memory supplies the missing cue: the rise and fall of contact force helps distinguish a completed press from an approach. This example motivates a multimodal memory-augmented VLA that integrates visual and wrench memory.

Recent multimodal VLAs such as DAM-VLA maintain fixed-size buffers for visual and force observations [33]. These buffers provide direct access to recent observations, but an earlier cue, such as which drawer was initially open (Fig. 4(a)), can be lost once its frame leaves the window. Test-time training (TTT) extends the memory horizon by summarizing earlier observations in recurrent fast weights [30, 14, 23, 34]. Compressing the entire visual history into these weights, however, can make details from a particular moment difficult to recover. For wrench memory, the task stage determines how much the policy should rely on contact feedback. Appending wrench tokens to the action expert leaves this weighting implicit [19]. DAM-VLA and DeCAL make the weighting explicit by gating cross-attention with pooled force features [33] and a global tactile token [7], respectively. Because these gates depend only on contact features, their weights cannot respond directly to changes in the instruction or visual cues to task progress. Moreover, even with wrench memory, a fixed policy can struggle when contact dynamics shift at deployment. For example, raising a whiteboard changes when the eraser meets the surface and how much force it exerts along the same stroke (Fig. (c)).

To this end, we introduce M2AdaptVLA, a VLA built on WALL-X [43] that combines multimodal memory with predictive test-time adaptation. For visual memory, we design a TTT bank to retain frame-specific detail while preserving cues beyond the explicit window. Each entry fuses the corresponding frame’s features with a readout from the fast weights at that time (Fig. (b)). For wrench memory, we introduce a context gate that uses the instruction, visual context, and wrench history to determine how strongly the action expert should draw on contact information at each task stage (Fig. (a)). For predictive test-time adaptation, we jointly denoise future actions and wrenches to obtain a wrench forecast for each action sequence. When measurements arrive, we backpropagate the forecast error only through the final denoising step to update low-rank adapters [12] (Fig. (c)).

To evaluate M2AdaptVLA, we design eight real-robot tasks with different demands on visual and wrench memory. Our model achieves a mean task score of 82.71%, an absolute gain of 31.46% over the strongest baseline (51.25%). Ablations show that the TTT bank outperforms the evaluated visual memory baselines on task progress tracking, initial-scene recall, and demonstration following. The context gate also achieves higher mean stage success than either direct wrench injection or the GCA approach. Across the two whiteboard contact shifts, predictive test-time adaptation raises mean wiping success from 85.0% to 97.5%, an absolute gain of 12.5% over the fixed policy. Each update takes 159.5 ms on average on an RTX 5090.

Our contributions are threefold.

We introduce M2AdaptVLA, a multimodal memory-augmented VLA that combines visual memory with context-gated wrench history to jointly predict future actions and wrenches. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness.

We introduce a visual memory bank that fuses each frame’s features with a readout from TTT fast weights, preserving cues from beyond the bank window.

We introduce a predictive test-time adaptation mechanism that updates policy adapters by backpropagating the wrench prediction loss through only the final step of joint action–wrench denoising.

1. We introduce M2AdaptVLA, a multimodal memory-augmented VLA that combines visual memory with context-gated wrench history to jointly predict future actions and wrenches. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness.

2. We introduce a visual memory bank that fuses each frame’s features with a readout from TTT fast weights, preserving cues from beyond the bank window.

3. We introduce a predictive test-time adaptation mechanism that updates policy adapters by backpropagating the wrench prediction loss through only the final step of joint action–wrench denoising.

title: Reference-Model-Guided Distributed MPC for UAV Swarm Formation Flying Under Switching Directed Graphs
authors: Yiming Wang,Yenan Wu,Junda Wu,Yanke Sun,Huizhe Li,Ke Yu,Youmin Gong,Guangfu Ma,Jie Mei
abstract: Distributed formation control of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms in complex environments faces several challenges, including switching inter-agent connectivity, limited communication, external disturbances, and collision avoidance. To address these challenges, we propose a reference-model-guided distributed model predictive control (MPC) framework for UAV swarm formation. Each UAV uses relative-position information from its neighbors as input to a local reference model, whose output serves as the formation guidance for the onboard MPC controller. Meanwhile, a Kalman filter is utilized to predict neighboring UAV motions, enabling the construction of inter-UAV collision-avoidance constraints solely from instantaneous relative-state information. By decoupling MPC optimization from distributed coordination, this control architecture preserves the look-ahead planning and constraint-handling capabilities of MPC while enhancing the swarm’s adaptability to switching directed graphs. Moreover, eliminating the exchange of neighbors’ predicted trajectories reduces communication bandwidth demands, offering strong scalability for large-scale UAV swarms. To improve robustness and safety, disturbance-observer-based feedforward compensation is employed, while the bounded residual disturbance is explicitly considered in the control barrier function (CBF)-based obstacle-avoidance constraints. Finally, the proposed framework is validated through both simulations and real-world flight experiments. Specifically, the flight verification is conducted on a fully distributed multi-UAV platform without external global localization.
introduction:
In recent years, with the rapid development of unmanned systems, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms have been increasingly employed in applications such as cooperative patrol [1, 2], target tracking [3, 4], and collaborative payload transport [5, 6]. Formation control plays a fundamental role in enabling multiple UAVs to perform complex tasks collaboratively and has therefore attracted extensive research attention [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13]. Compared with centralized architectures, distributed formation control relies primarily on information from neighboring UAVs, reducing dependence on a centralized controller and improving scalability for multi-UAV systems. However, practical deployment in complex environments remains challenging. Limited communication ranges, together with asymmetric or intermittent inter-UAV connectivity, can result in switching directed topologies, while external disturbances and collision-avoidance requirements must also be handled. This motivates the development of robust and scalable distributed formation-control methods for switching directed topologies.

For distributed UAV formation systems, the controller must achieve coordinated motion while satisfying safety and actuator constraints. Model predictive control (MPC) provides a natural framework for this purpose because it can explicitly incorporate system constraints and optimize predicted motion over a finite horizon.
Accordingly, distributed MPC (DMPC) has been extensively
investigated for multi-agent formation control over
graph-based communication topologies
[14, 15, 16].
For multi-UAV systems, recent studies have further explored
DMPC-based formation control under directed communication
structures [17, 18, 19].
However, many existing DMPC methods for cooperative multi-agent systems are formulated under predefined interaction structures [20, 21, 22] and rely on the exchange of predicted or assumed state trajectories among neighboring agents for distributed coordination, including collision avoidance [17, 23, 24]. Such horizon-wise information exchange inevitably increases the inter-UAV communication burden, since the transmitted data
volume grows with both the prediction horizon and the number of neighbors [25, 26], which is particularly undesirable in communication-limited networks with switching inter-UAV connectivity. These limitations motivate a distributed control architecture that can maintain formation coordination under switching directed topologies without requiring predicted-trajectory exchange.

In addition to communication and topology challenges, UAVs in practical flight inevitably encounter inter-UAV aerodynamic disturbances and external wind gusts. These disturbances degrade control accuracy and pose significant challenges to safe flight in dense-obstacle environments. To achieve disturbance rejection, existing studies have employed disturbance observers to estimate external disturbances and update the nominal model [27], while others have adopted disturbance-observer-based feedforward compensation to enable rapid adaptation with promising results [28]. However, such observers cannot comprehensively and accurately capture all disturbances, leaving non-negligible residual disturbances. Therefore, it remains challenging to guarantee safe flight in cluttered environments under residual disturbances.

To address these challenges, we propose a reference-model-guided distributed MPC framework for UAV swarm formation under switching directed topologies. For each UAV, a local reference model generates formation guidance using only instantaneous relative states. The onboard MPC controller then independently tracks this guidance while satisfying practical flight constraints. To avoid exchanging predicted trajectories for inter-UAV collision avoidance, each UAV locally predicts its neighbors’ future motions from these relative states. For robust and safe flight, disturbance-observer-based feedforward compensation is employed to attenuate external disturbances, while the bounded residual disturbance is explicitly accounted for in the control barrier function (CBF)-based obstacle-avoidance constraints. Finally, the proposed framework is deployed and validated on a fully distributed multi-UAV platform without external localization systems, as shown in Fig. 1.

The main contributions are summarized as follows:

Decoupling of Distributed Coordination and MPC Optimization: A local reference model is introduced as an intermediate coordination layer within the distributed MPC framework, generating formation guidance solely from instantaneous relative states. This architecture simplifies the onboard optimization formulation while adapting effectively to switching directed communication topologies. Meanwhile, it preserves the look-ahead planning and constraint-handling capabilities of MPC.

Instantaneous-State-Only Interaction without Trajectory Exchange: To preserve the trajectory-exchange-free property during inter-UAV avoidance, each UAV locally predicts its neighbors’ motions solely from instantaneous relative states. The predicted motions are then incorporated into the inter-UAV collision-avoidance constraints. This design reduces communication bandwidth overhead and facilitates scaling to large swarms.

Disturbance Compensation and Safe Obstacle Avoidance: Disturbance-observer-based feedforward compensation is integrated into the local controller to actively reject external disturbances. Meanwhile, the bounded residual disturbance is explicitly incorporated into the CBF-based obstacle-avoidance constraints. This formulation improves flight robustness and enhances safety against wind gusts in cluttered environments.

Fully Distributed Validation without External Localization: The proposed framework is implemented on a fully distributed multi-UAV platform without external localization systems (e.g., GPS or motion capture). Each UAV independently performs onboard state estimation, neighbor-state prediction, and local MPC optimization. Extensive simulations and real-world flight experiments validate the effectiveness and practicality of the overall system.

1. Decoupling of Distributed Coordination and MPC Optimization: A local reference model is introduced as an intermediate coordination layer within the distributed MPC framework, generating formation guidance solely from instantaneous relative states. This architecture simplifies the onboard optimization formulation while adapting effectively to switching directed communication topologies. Meanwhile, it preserves the look-ahead planning and constraint-handling capabilities of MPC.

The predicted motions are then incorporated into the inter-UAV collision-avoidance constraints. This design reduces communication bandwidth overhead and facilitates scaling to large swarms.
