title: Dynamic Task Update Benchmark (DTU-Bench): Evaluating Runtime Task Adaptation in Robotic Manipulation
authors: Yanran Jiang,Cécile Paris,Dana Kulić,Leimin Tian
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies perform well on fixed-instruction robotic manipulation benchmarks, but their ability to adapt to instruction changes during execution remains understudied. We introduce the Dynamic Task Update Benchmark (DTU-Bench), evaluating 40 task revisions across seven update types and three execution stages using LIBERO, a simulated robotic manipulation benchmark. We compare performance when a new instruction is given before execution starts versus during execution, and examine whether the new task instructions are followed. Across 13 representative VLA configurations, average task success is 95.8% on the original object-manipulation tasks, compared with only 1.6% when the instruction changes which object to manipulate during execution. Controlled diagnostics show that policies often complete the original task before the updated one, and that their responses depend on the robot’s physical state. We further test whether a simple scripted controller that releases the grasped object and moves the arm back helps robots respond to instruction changes. This improves success from 2% to 38% for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and from 8% to 48% for DM0.5, but can cause unwanted object motion. These findings reveal limitations that fixed-instruction benchmarks and task-success metrics alone can overlook in evaluating robotic manipulation. Project page: https://dtu-bench.github.io/.
introduction:
Robots operating alongside people may need respond to changes in instructions [24, 22]. A user may change where an object should be placed, request a different object, or withdraw part of an instruction after the robot has already begun acting. Unlike starting a new task, such updates arrive while the robot is executing and may have already made some progress on the initial task. When an instruction change arrives, some actions associated with the initial task may still be useful, while others may need to be abandoned or undone [15].

Recent advances in robot learning have greatly improved language-conditioned manipulation. Generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policies such as OpenVLA [14] and π0\pi_{0} [2] have demonstrated increasingly capable manipulation across tasks and environments. Benchmarks such as CALVIN [20] and LIBERO [19] have supported evaluation of VLA policies on long-horizon task execution, generalization, and knowledge transfer. However, success on tasks specified before execution does not necessarily mean a policy can adapt when the task changes during execution. A policy may successfully execute the original or the updated tasks independently, yet fail to transition between them once execution has begun.

Recent studies have addressed different challenges in dynamic robot execution. DynamicVLA [26] focuses on manipulating moving objects, while TIC-VLA [12] addresses reactive control. SwitchVLA [16] and ReSteer [6] develop training-based approaches to task switching. However, how existing VLA policies respond when different parts of a task are changed during execution remains insufficiently understood. Moreover, reaching the updated goal does not necessarily indicate that the robot has responded to the new instruction. This motivates a systematic evaluation of runtime task adaptation and post-update behavior.

We introduce Dynamic Task Update Benchmark (DTU-Bench) to systematically evaluate how robot policies respond to task instructions that change during execution. As illustrated in Fig. 1, DTU-Bench introduces new instructions while the robot is acting, without resetting its state. Built on LIBERO, the benchmark covers 40 task revisions across seven types of instruction changes and three execution stages. We evaluate each policy under three conditions: executing the original task, performing the revised task from the initial state of the original task, and switching to the revised task during execution. These comparisons allow us to assess whether policies can complete a revised task after making progress towards a different objective. Beyond task success, we examine whether robots maintain the requested outcome and how their behavior changes following an instruction update.

Our main contributions are:

We introduce DTU-Bench, a systematic, policy-agnostic framework for evaluating runtime task updates in robotic manipulation across seven task-revision categories and three execution stages. The benchmark and evaluation code will be released.

We evaluate 13 VLA configurations and identify limitations that fixed-instruction evaluation can overlook, including differences across update types, delayed satisfaction of updated goals, and substantial gaps between
temporary and final goal satisfaction.

We conduct controlled experiments to examine how the robot’s execution state affects responses to new instructions, including whether simple scripted interventions can help recover from failed task updates.

1. We introduce DTU-Bench, a systematic, policy-agnostic framework for evaluating runtime task updates in robotic manipulation across seven task-revision categories and three execution stages. The benchmark and evaluation code will be released.

2. We evaluate 13 VLA configurations and identify limitations that fixed-instruction evaluation can overlook, including differences across update types, delayed satisfaction of updated goals, and substantial gaps between
temporary and final goal satisfaction.

3. We conduct controlled experiments to examine how the robot’s execution state affects responses to new instructions, including whether simple scripted interventions can help recover from failed task updates.

title: AGLR: Attribute-Guided Latent Refinement for Fine-Grained Humanoid Motion Generation and Editing
authors: Shuai Yuan,Yuwei Gui,Mingshuang Luo,Zhuo Li,Siyuan Meng,Wenhao Cui,RuiBing Hou,Bingpeng Ma
abstract: Humanoid motion generation must accommodate evolving task requirements, where localized adjustments should satisfy new geometric constraints without disrupting desired motion details. However, language-based control lacks geometric precision, while joint-level constraints require explicit spatial targets. Local geometric constraints are also underdetermined, complicating target satisfaction and source preservation. We present AGLR (Attribute-Guided Latent Refinement), a unified framework for fine-grained humanoid motion generation and editing through source-anchored refinement. A compact geometric interface supports composable, time-varying control of limb extents, torso orientation, and root trajectories. Given a generated or encoded base latent, an Attribute Residual Adapter predicts a single-pass correction, with dual-level supervision enforcing target matching and selective preservation across attributes and motion coordinates. On HumanML3D-G1, AGLR achieves the highest controllable-generation and preservation-constrained editing success rates among evaluated methods. Editing take only 9.1 ms for a cached 500-frame motion, without additional sampling or test-time optimization. Zero-shot evaluation on BONES-SEED-G1 further demonstrates transfer without fine-tuning.
introduction:
Humanoid robots operating in dynamic environments must adapt their motions to changing task requirements. Recent methods generate diverse whole-body motions from natural language instructions [40, 47, 48, 19, 16, 6],
providing references for motion tracking policies. Many tasks, however, require only localized modifications to an existing reference.
For example, a humanoid may need to raise one arm while walking or adjust its torso orientation while maintaining its natural gait. Such tasks call for fine-grained motion editing that modifies selected geometric properties while preserving the rest of the reference motion.

The first challenge lies in specifying geometric edits with both precision and compositionality. While semantic control can describe high-level actions for individual body parts [53, 34], it offers limited direct control over the magnitude and timing of a geometric change, such as precisely how far an arm should extend forward at each phase of a step. Conversely, kinematic control specifies spatial targets through joint positions [49, 17, 35], full-body poses [41, 7], or task-space trajectories [24, 45, 38]. Depending on the edit, these inputs often demand burdensome kinematic details beyond what the task naturally specifies. This gap motivates a part-level geometric interface that supports numerical, time-varying targets and enables seamless composition of edits across different body parts.

The second challenge is to satisfy these targets efficiently while faithfully preserving the details of the source motion. Multiple whole-body trajectories can satisfy the same set of geometric targets; for instance, prescribing the forward extent of one arm during walking leaves the gait and the movement of the opposite arm underdetermined. Existing source-conditioned editors [1, 29, 11] leverage a reference trajectory to guide the transformation, where unselected attributes and motion coordinates are preserved.
However, diffusion-based editors [42, 1, 22] often require iterative sampling, whereas optimization-based methods [23, 30] rely on repeated gradient updates, significantly increasing inference latency. These limitations highlight the need for a framework that directly predicts motion corrections in a single forward pass, while providing robust supervision for both target satisfaction and source preservation.

In this work, we introduce Attribute-Guided Latent Refinement (AGLR), a framework for fine-grained
geometric adaptation of generated or existing humanoid robot reference motions.
AGLR specifies edits through the Whole-body Geometric Attribute Representation (WGAR), a 21-dimensional per-frame descriptor capturing directional limb extents, torso orientation, and root motion. A channel-wise mask dictates which attributes to edit, allowing time-varying targets to be combined across body parts. To preserve source motion details left underdetermined by the selected targets, AGLR refines the source trajectory within a robot-native latent space learned from dynamics-grounded motions.
An Attribute Residual Adapter (ARA) predicts an additive correction to the source latent in a single forward pass. The training objective encourages the edited motion to satisfy the selected targets while preserving unselected attributes and motion coordinates. Finally, a downstream motion tracking policy can use the refined trajectory as a reference to execute the motion on a physical humanoid robot.

We evaluate AGLR on HumanML3D-G1 for controllable generation and preservation-constrained editing. AGLR achieves state-of-the-art success rates among compared methods, reaching 80.34% for controllable generation and 76.81% and 77.28% for editing under attribute and joint preservation constraints, respectively. Furthermore, latent refinement and decoding take merely 9.1 ms for a 500-frame motion. Zero-shot evaluations on BONES-SEED-G1 demonstrate robust cross-dataset transfer without fine-tuning. Finally, real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid validate that AGLR can selectively and reliably modify whole-body motions during physical execution.

title: Long-Horizon Planning with Latent World Models via Graph Anchors
authors: Syed Nazmus Sakib,Abdul Monaf Chowdhury,Peizhen Li,Nafiul Haque,Chandak Chakma,Md Mehedi Hasan,Zehong Cao,Shifat E. Arman
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Project page:this https URL| Code:this https URL
abstract: Latent world models plan in a compact latent space by predicting the outcomes of actions. Their planners judge a plan by the latent distance between its predicted end state and the goal image. We show that this distance fails in two distinct ways. First, it loses directional signal a few steps from the goal, causing distant goals to fail. Second, it weighs the robot arm over the manipulated object, causing manipulation to fail at contact. We measure both failures directly on recorded data by asking whether a lower latent distance corresponds to true progress toward the goal. Across five environments, six visual representations (including raw pixels and V-JEPA 2), and nine Meta-World tasks, this ranking test cleanly separates the two failures, and the graph distance to a goal predicts where closed-loop planning breaks down. Both failures share a single remedy: replacing the distant goal with a nearby target that lies on a recorded trajectory. We realize this principle with Graph Anchors, a training-free planner for frozen latent world models. It builds a sparse graph once over the model’s own training frames and aims each planning step at a node a few moves ahead along the shortest path to the goal, keeping paths on recorded transitions wherever contact matters. On goals up to 400 steps away, Graph Anchors raise LeWM’s success from 13% to 85% on PointMaze-Medium, from 8% to 87% on PointMaze-Large, and from 5% to 71% on Push-T, where stronger search toward the goal fails and where prior training-free planners break down under missing step horizons, subsampling shortcuts, or fragmented contact.
introduction:
World models predict how actions change the world, allowing an agent to evaluate candidate plans in imagination before acting [14, 15, 16, 17]. Recent visual world models predict in the latent space of an image encoder [31, 38, 25] and plan by sampling action sequences, rolling out their predicted futures, and keeping the actions whose final latent state lies closest to a goal image [7, 35]. This approach works reliably for nearby goals. On PointMaze-Medium, LeWorldModel (LeWM) [25] solves 50% of goals 50 steps away, yet drops to just 13% at 200 steps, as illustrated in Figure 1. On Push-T it solves only 5% at 150 steps, often parking the pusher while leaving the T-block behind.

Why does a planner that easily solves short-range goals break down here? Rather than guessing, we test the latent goal cost directly. On recorded data, before running any planner, we measure how often a lower latent distance corresponds to a move that genuinely progresses toward the goal (Section 4.1). This simple test isolates two root failures. The first is range: latent distance ranks local moves accurately right next to the goal, but loses directional signal within a few graph hops across every navigation task and across six visual encoders, including raw pixels, DINOv2, CLIP, SigLIP, V-JEPA 2, and LeWM (Section A.1). The second is focus: whole-image distance weighs the robot arm far more heavily than the manipulated object, preferring an accurate arm pose over completing the task across all nine Meta-World [42] object tasks we measure (Section A.2).

Importantly, both failures have the exact same remedy. Whole-image distance works reliably whenever its target is nearby and lies along a route recorded in the data. On Meta-World, keeping the released cost untouched and simply aiming at a demonstration frame 20 steps ahead solves 65 of 72 object episodes that the final goal image never solves. We introduce Graph Anchors to provide such targets automatically without demonstrations or retraining. We construct a sparse graph once over the world model’s own training frames, compute a shortest path to the goal, and aim each planning step at an anchor node a few moves ahead on that path. Where object contact matters, penalizing cross-episode jumps keeps the route on continuous recorded transitions. With the released search and world model untouched, replacing only the distant goal with our nearby anchor lifts PointMaze-Medium at 200 steps from 12% to 85%, whereas stronger search aimed at the distant goal stalls at 9%. On Push-T, preserving recorded transitions raises d=150d{=}150 success from 30% to 71%.

Our main contributions are threefold:

A direct diagnosis of the latent goal cost. A local ranking test on recorded data separates two distinct failures, range and focus, across five environments, six image representations, and nine Meta-World tasks. Offline graph distance predicts where closed-loop planning fails, and a formal drift analysis (Section A.3) connects local ranking to linear versus quadratic reaching times.

Graph Anchors. A simple, training-free planner for frozen latent world models that cures both failures using nearby anchors on recorded routes, changing only the target and scoring rule of the planner while leaving the encoder, predictor, and CEM optimizer untouched.

Long-horizon evaluation and failure analysis of alternative planners. Across goals up to 400 steps away on navigation and manipulation, we benchmark against world-model planners, offline goal-conditioned policies, graph-guided policies (GAS [4], TTGS [30]), and training-free world-model planners (AP [23], NGC [41], Metro-WM [20]), showing how each missing diagnostic axis causes specific structural failures (Section 5.5, Appendix D).

Offline graph distance predicts where closed-loop planning fails, and a formal drift analysis (Section A.3) connects local ranking to linear versus quadratic reaching times.

2. Graph Anchors. A simple, training-free planner for frozen latent world models that cures both failures using nearby anchors on recorded routes, changing only the target and scoring rule of the planner while leaving the encoder, predictor, and CEM optimizer untouched.

Across goals up to 400 steps away on navigation and manipulation, we benchmark against world-model planners, offline goal-conditioned policies, graph-guided policies (GAS [4], TTGS [30]), and training-free world-model planners (AP [23], NGC [41], Metro-WM [20]), showing how each missing diagnostic axis causes specific structural failures (Section 5.5, Appendix D).

title: An Exact Branch-Price-and-Cut Algorithm for the Vehicle Routing Problem with Floating Targets
authors: Michał Paradowski,Anoop Bhat,Zhongqiang Ren,Howie Choset
abstract:
The Vehicle Routing Problem with Floating Targets (VRPFT) is a generalization
of the capacitated vehicle routing problem where targets may actively move to
locations “convenient” for the vehicles. In particular, each target may
leave its home location at a bounded speed. A solution to the VRPFT is a
sequence of targets for each vehicle to visit and a meeting point in
space-time for each target. In this paper, we solve the VRPFT exactly with a
branch-price-and-cut algorithm. Our key contribution is a dominance criterion
for the pricing labeling algorithm that utilizes closed-form lower and upper
bounds on a vehicle’s trajectory cost given a fixed sequence of targets. We prove that the criterion preserves
optimality, and the algorithm has smaller computation time than the exact dynamic program of prior work
on identical hardware. We also provide a relaxed criterion that prunes more
aggressively; the resulting heuristic is faster than our exact algorithm and matched every certified
optimum on the benchmark.
introduction:
The vehicle routing problem (VRP), introduced by Dantzig and Ramser [1], asks
for a set of minimum-cost vehicle paths that serve a set of static
targets subject to capacity constraints. It is among the most
studied problems in operations research, both for its practical importance in
transportation and logistics and for its computational difficulty [2]. A
defining assumption of the classical VRP and most of its variants is that each
target occupies a fixed, known location that a vehicle must visit.

This assumption does not hold in a growing class of applications in which the targets are themselves mobile and can cooperate with the fleet. In
ride-sharing and last-mile delivery, a passenger may walk a short distance to meet
a vehicle at a more convenient point than their home [3, 4, 5]; in aerial refueling, a target and an interceptor can jointly choose a rendezvous [6].

Motivated
by such settings, Gambella et al. [7] introduced the vehicle routing
problem with floating targets (VRPFT), a generalization of the VRP in which each
target may leave its home location and travel, up to a maximum speed, toward a selected meeting
point. Because a target can move in any direction, the set of locations at which it can be picked up by a given time is a disk
rather than a single point (Fig. 1).

Solving the VRPFT to optimality is challenging due to the coupling between the discrete routing decisions and continuous meeting-point decisions. In this paper, we solve the VRPFT exactly with a branch-price-and-cut algorithm. Central to the algorithm is a dominance criterion for the pricing labeling algorithm, built on closed-form lower and upper bounds on the minimum time required for a vehicle to meet a fixed sequence of targets. The criterion is provably optimality-preserving, and the resulting algorithm runs faster than the exact dynamic program of [5] on identical hardware. Relaxing the criterion yields a heuristic that prunes more aggressively and is faster than our exact algorithm by a factor ranging from 1.3 to 6.2 on the benchmark while matching every certified optimum.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews prior work and Section III states the VRPFT; the remaining
sections describe the branch-price-and-cut algorithm and report the
computational results.

title: SkySearcher: High-Altitude Onboard VLM Reasoning for Aerial Semantic Search
authors: Giacomo Vianello,David Morilla-Cabello,Juan Dendarieta Serrano,Ruggero Carli,Eduardo Montijano
abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have improved semantic and visual reasoning, enabling UAVs to search for open-vocabulary queries in unstructured environments at high altitude. However, existing systems mainly follow low-altitude strategies, focusing on close-range iterative exploration, requiring storage-intensive dense 3D metric-semantic reconstructions or relying on large cloud-serviced VLMs assuming constant internet access. We propose SkySearcher, an aerial semantic search navigation method designed for large outdoor scenes. SkySearcher integrates onboard VLM reasoning with a lightweight probabilistic representation that guides an information-driven exploration. The VLM extracts semantic information at high altitude about the target or cues informing about its location. This information is projected to the ground using the camera frustum instead of limited-depth sensors, actively exploiting the expansive field of view offered by elevated sensing. The information regarding the presence or absence of semantic cues is then integrated into a probabilistic map by modeling the spatial belief of the query, maintaining a task-driven memory for the mission and guiding the exploration towards semantically promising regions. Extensive simulations for Aerial Object Goal Navigation on public benchmarks demonstrate that SkySearcher significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in success rate, flight time, and navigation precision, while a deployment of SkySearcher running fully onboard a drone demonstrates the applicability of our approach.
introduction:
Aerial platforms operating at high altitude benefit from a wide effective field of view, which has proven valuable for tasks such as aerial surveillance [1], post-disaster search and rescue [2], and facility inspection [3]. Recent Vision–Language Models (VLMs) enable extracting rich semantic information and reasoning about the environment, which is promising for interpreting this broad spatial context and perform tasks autonomously.

The capabilities of VLMs have had a great impact in semantic tasks such as Aerial Object Goal Navigation (Aerial ObjectNav) [4]. In this setting, an autonomous aerial agent explores an unknown environment to identify an open-vocabulary target queried by the user while acquiring information from its sensors, as depicted in Fig. 1. However, existing solutions do not leverage the high-altitude flying capabilities of drones explicitly and usually adopt low-altitude search strategies. These strategies aim at exploration using range sensors and object detectors, and sometimes require dense reconstructions of the environment, such as semantic voxel maps [5, 6], and complex trajectory planning for efficient navigation[7, 8]. On the other hand, methods leveraging VLMs usually assume the availability of large cloud-served models to reason on images during the search mission [9, 10], restricting the applicability to settings with stable network connectivity and incurring on constant API usage costs. Furthermore, other methods give the VLM the full mission control by tasking it to directly analyze images, infer distances, and output movement commands [11, 12]. However, these models have not been trained for these tasks and can produce unpredictable behaviors.

In this work, we address the aforementioned limitations by introducing SkySearcher, a method that leverages the visual perception and semantic reasoning capabilities of a small VLM to enable fully onboard, open-vocabulary aerial ObjectNav at high altitude. Within the proposed system, the VLM processes camera observations to identify both the query and a set of semantically informative cues that may inform about its location. These observations are projected on a lightweight map representation integrating geometric information about already explored regions and semantic information expressing the spatial belief of the query. This representation supports the formulation of an information-theoretic optimization problem for selecting the next-best viewpoint for the high-altitude UAV exploration.

To validate our approach, we perform extensive Aerial ObjectNav experiments in a photorealistic simulator over a variety of objects and large environments. Results show that SkySearcher improves success rate by over 58% the strongest baseline while requiring no cloud connectivity or dense metric-semantic reconstructions. To further demonstrate the practical feasibility, we deploy SkySearcher running fully onboard a quadrotor in a real-world scenario.

To summarize, the contributions of SkySearcher are:

An aerial semantic search strategy from high altitude that relies on local VLM reasoning over images and frustum projection, exploiting the extensive visibility of high vantage viewpoints while running fully onboard.

A lightweight probabilistic representation that fuses metric and semantic information into a single map, encoding the spatial belief of the query from intermediate semantic cues without dense reconstructions.

An information-based next-best-viewpoint optimization for planning in open-vocabulary semantic search.

An open-source implementation of the full system in ROS2, deployable both in photorealistic simulation and on real hardware, supporting reproducibility and reuse by the community.

1. An aerial semantic search strategy from high altitude that relies on local VLM reasoning over images and frustum projection, exploiting the extensive visibility of high vantage viewpoints while running fully onboard.

2. A lightweight probabilistic representation that fuses metric and semantic information into a single map, encoding the spatial belief of the query from intermediate semantic cues without dense reconstructions.

3. An information-based next-best-viewpoint optimization for planning in open-vocabulary semantic search.

4. An open-source implementation of the full system in ROS2, deployable both in photorealistic simulation and on real hardware, supporting reproducibility and reuse by the community.

title: Least Restrictive Halfplane Control Barrier Functions for an Autonomous Hydrofoil Boat with Moving Obstacles
authors: Mattias Trende,Petter Ögren
abstract:
Finding valid Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) is difficult for non-linear systems subject to actuation constraints and moving in complex environments.
One way to enable analytically derived CBFs is to represent obstacles as supporting halfplanes, allowing the agent to move safely on one side.
In this paper, we propose such a CBF for an agent with Dubins car dynamics.
A potential drawback of halfplane CBFs is that they can be highly conservative, overestimating the obstacles and thereby restricting the agent’s motion.
To address this problem, we make the CBF halfplanes less restrictive as follows.
First, the orientation of the supporting halfplane for a single obstacle is optimised to find a safe control input as close as possible to the desired one.
Second, we use multiple halfplanes to better approximate complex geometries, and derive rules for handling halfplane intersections.
Comparative simulations show that our method reduces conservatism compared to existing CBF techniques, enabling tighter obstacle clearance and faster goal arrival, with delays reduced by more than 33%.
Finally, experiments on an autonomous hydrofoil boat demonstrate successful real-world implementation.
introduction:
Despite advances in maritime perception and situational awareness, including cameras, radars, and AIS transponders, serious accidents still occur [1].
This holds whether a human is in the loop, such as the captain of a small boat, or control is automated, such as an autopilot on a merchant ship.
The problem is not only the lack of information itself, but also acting on it to ensure safety.
In this paper, we design safe control for an autonomous hydrofoil boat, but much of the work will translate to other non-holonomic vehicles such as normal boats, cars, and fixed-wing aircraft.

A popular approach for safe control is based on Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) [2]. The main benefits of using CBFs are that they ensure provable safety while being computationally lightweight. However, CBFs also come with challenges, as it can be difficult to find a valid CBF for high-dimensional systems with actuation constraints [3]. A common solution is to use Higher Order CBFs (HO-CBFs) [4, 5], but purely distance-based designs require careful tuning to ensure both safety and actuation constraints [6].

Previous studies often construct CBFs using the signed distance function (SDF) for non-holonomic systems like Dubins cars, unicycles, and bicycles [7, 8, 5].
To handle the second-order dynamics, one can apply variants of Higher-Order CBFs (HO-CBFs) as in [7, 8, 5], or include a term containing the relative velocity between the agent and the obstacle [9, 10].

To investigate the relationship between SDF CBFs and a class of CBFs based on halfplanes,
we note that the distance from a vehicle to the closest point on an obstacle is the same as the distance to a supporting halfplane through that point, perpendicular to the line between the point and the vehicle.
Thus, the SDF CBFs are equivalent to
Minimum Distance Halfplane CBFs (MDH-CBFs), and to underline this connection, we adopt the MDH-CBF notation for the remainder of this paper.

Moving away from the MDH-CBFs, [11] adds a velocity component to the CBF that is derived from a velocity obstacle. None of the papers [7, 8, 5, 9, 10, 11] explicitly consider actuation constraints when designing the CBF function, instead compliance is achieved through parameter tuning. One that does include constraints is [12], which looks forward in time to determine the value of the CBF. This enables the CBF to handle actuation constraints at the price of higher computational costs.

In this paper, we will study CBFs for the Dubins car model [13]. This is a fairly accurate model for our
electric hydrofoil boat Evolo, see Figure 8, which has a limited turn radius and a narrow speed regime with high energy efficiency, motivating the fixed speed assumption. The Dubins car model ignores the tilting dynamics and the hydrofoil control surfaces, but describes the behaviour well at larger time scales.

Building upon Dubins car model, we propose an analytical CBF formulation similar in structure to the analytical solutions for the double integrator found in [14, 3]. Intuitively, we replace the braking distance derived for the double integrator with the turning behaviour of Dubins car, ensuring that it always has enough space to perform a turn without hitting the moving obstacle halfplane, up until the point when the closing distance to the moving halfplane is zero.

As noted above, halfplane obstacle approximations tend to be conservative. To reduce this effect,
building upon our previous work in [15], we optimise over the orientation of the supporting halfplane.
Ideally, we find an orientation that makes our desired control safe, and if that is not possible, we minimize the gap between the safe and the desired control. We call this the least restrictive halfplane CBF (LRH-CBF), as illustrated in Figure 1. For non-convex obstacle configurations, it can be beneficial to combine several halfplanes, as discussed in Section III-C.

The contribution of this paper consists of two main parts. First, the closed-form CBF for Dubins car and the handling of multiple moving obstacles and non-convex obstacle geometries. Second, the hardware experiment and the batch simulations show how the proposed approach leads to less conservative trajectories, making smaller detours that reach the target state in shorter time.

title: DynaRC: Dynamics-Robust 4-D Radar Relocalization with Rate-Adaptive Sequence Matching
authors: Chuan Cao,Xingyi Li,Tianchen Deng,Jingchuan Wang
abstract:
Four-dimensional millimeter-wave radar measures radial velocity within a
single scan and remains resilient under adverse weather and visibility.
Yet sparse directional returns, moving objects and occlusion make place
matching ambiguous. We propose DynaRC, a dynamics-robust framework encompassing
single-frame retrieval and sequence relocalization. Doppler evidence separates static returns and masks
motion-affected cells in a polar descriptor; median ring keys retrieve
candidates. Its sequence variant, Seq_DynaRC, couples endpoint-anchored rate alignment and candidate-index voting
with ordered verification to associate the latest scan under unequal
map/query advancement, without odometry or cloud accumulation.
Across four indoor and outdoor map–query pairs, Seq_DynaRC achieves
the highest conditional localization success within 2 m among tested methods.
On a campus-road revisit under changing traffic, success reaches 91.8%, exceeding
descriptor-matched SeqSLAM by 55.0 percentage points when each method retains
all its published outputs; output availability is reported separately.
Code and indoor/outdoor dynamic 4D radar data are available.
introduction:
Global relocalization recovers a robot’s pose in a known map without a
reliable initial estimate. It comprises place recognition, which
outputs candidate map locations, and pose recovery, which estimates
the robot’s six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) pose. Our contributions focus on
place recognition. Four-dimensional radar measures range, azimuth,
elevation and radial velocity, supporting localization under adverse
visibility [1, 2]. Sparse returns, dynamics, occlusion and repeated
structures nevertheless create false matches; a low descriptor distance
alone cannot establish a correct global pose.

Two challenges arise. Within a scan, limited field of view and occlusion
remove static structure, so empty descriptor cells need not represent
observed free space. Across a sequence, vehicle speed, keyframe density and
query sampling alter map/query index correspondence. Fixed one-to-one
progression can associate the latest scan with a map frame ahead of or
behind its location. Temporal matching must therefore preserve both
consistency and the identity of the observation being localized.

DynaRC denotes the overall framework, comprising single-frame retrieval and
its sequence extension, Seq_DynaRC. Their shared descriptor encodes a polar
height or intensity/RCS channel according to the environment and masks
cells with strong Doppler-derived dynamic evidence.
Median ring keys retrieve candidates for masked descriptor comparison.
Seq_DynaRC introduces endpoint-anchored rate alignment (ERA): each
hypothesis specifies the latest query’s map endpoint and the window’s index
advancement. Candidate-index voting selects supported hypotheses for aligned
multi-frame refinement. Iterative closest point (ICP) then registers the
current cloud to the chosen keyframe. Association requires neither odometry
nor inter-frame cloud accumulation.

The contributions are:

A training-free radar representation combining static polar features,
Doppler-based rejection of motion-affected cells, and median aggregation
to reduce extreme-cell influence during retrieval.

A candidate-supported sequence search coupling endpoint/rate proposals,
index-tolerant voting, and ordered verification to associate the current
scan under unequal map/query advancement.

title: HoloBrain-0.5 Technical Report
authors: Xuewu Lin,Jiahao Wang,Jiawei Li,Mengdi Li,Zhengmao Sun,Yiwei Jin,Hongyu Xie,Zhengyang Feng,Kun Wu,Zihao Chen,Lianzhou Zhang,Lichao Huang,Zhizhong Su
comment: Technical report. . Project page:this https URL
abstract:
We present HoloBrain-0.5, a family of vision-language-action (VLA) models for manipulation across heterogeneous embodiments.
Our goal is to plan motion in a shared action space across embodiments, using the robot state, kinematic structure, and calibrated camera observations as inputs.
Building on HoloBrain-0, we introduce three improvements.
First, we standardize joint axes, coordinate frames, and tool-center points in each robot description (URDF), then encode its kinematic graph in the policy.
Second, we release HoloBrain-0.5-Continuous, a diffusion policy, and HoloBrain-0.5-Discrete, which quantizes actions with residual finite scalar quantization (FSQ) and generates the resulting codes by delayed autoregression. Both use the same 3D embodiment representation, which accommodates arbitrary kinematic configurations.
Third, we scale pretraining to more than 10,000 hours of real-robot, simulation, and human-manipulation data spanning 15 embodiment categories, with calibrated camera geometry and canonicalized embodiment representations.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models ground visual observations and language instructions in executable robot actions, providing a scalable route toward general-purpose manipulation. Early large-scale systems established the value of vision-language pretraining and heterogeneous robot data Brohan et al. (2022); Brohan et al. (2023); Collaboration et al. (2023), while recent models have improved action generation, open-world generalization, and cross-embodiment learning Black et al. (2024); Intelligence et al. (2025); Intelligence et al. (2026); Robot and others (2026); Liu et al. (2026); Wu et al. (2026b).

A central challenge is that robot datasets differ not only in visual appearance and task distribution, but also in joint count, kinematic structure, camera configuration, and action conventions. Arbitrary coordinate choices in robot descriptions further obscure the relationship between an action value and its physical effect. HoloBrain-0 addressed part of this problem with a joint-centric architecture and explicit forward-kinematics features Lin et al. (2026). HoloBrain-0.5 extends this design with a canonical embodiment representation and two complementary action formulations. An overview is shown in Figure 1.

We introduce URDF standardization to remove embodiment-specific coordinate conventions before policy learning. Revolute joints are reparameterized about their local zz-axes, prismatic joints translate along the positive local zz-axis, and tool-center-point (TCP) frames point outward along zz.

HoloBrain-0.5 provides two model variants under a largely shared architecture. HoloBrain-0.5-Continuous models continuous action chunks with diffusion, whereas HoloBrain-0.5-Discrete applies finite scalar quantization (FSQ) Mentzer et al. (2023) in successive residual stages and multidimensional delayed autoregressive generation. The discrete formulation exposes an explicit token distribution and converges faster in our pretraining experiments. We pretrain both variants on more than 10,000 hours of data across 15 embodiment categories.

We track closed-loop performance at intermediate pretraining checkpoints using six simulation settings from three simulators, with a total of 21,430 evaluation episodes per model checkpoint across the six settings. We additionally evaluate out-of-the-box behavior, real-robot post-training, zero-shot task transfer between seen embodiments, and adaptation across substantially different robot morphologies. The first two real-robot benchmarks contain 18 tasks in total, while the additional morphology-adaptation suite spans 11 tasks across three further embodiments.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce a canonical 3D embodiment representation and a shared action space based on standardized URDFs. Both are defined on the kinematic graph rather than a fixed set of joints.

We release two policies built on this representation: the discrete policy converges faster during pretraining, while the continuous policy performs better after post-training.

In real-robot trials, HoloBrain-0.5 improves on HoloBrain-0 in closed-loop performance and performs complex dexterous tasks. It achieves 63.28% mean progress on tasks transferred zero-shot to a target robot and, with target-robot demonstrations, adapts to single-arm, humanoid, and mobile platforms.

2. We release two policies built on this representation: the discrete policy converges faster during pretraining, while the continuous policy performs better after post-training.

3. In real-robot trials, HoloBrain-0.5 improves on HoloBrain-0 in closed-loop performance and performs complex dexterous tasks. It achieves 63.28% mean progress on tasks transferred zero-shot to a target robot and, with target-robot demonstrations, adapts to single-arm, humanoid, and mobile platforms.

title: Calibration of Neuromusculoskeletal Models Using Differentiable Physics: Recommendations for Improving Model Accuracy
authors: Philip Sanderink,Yingfan Zhou,Shuzhen Luo,Cheng Fang
abstract: Differentiable physics has shown potential to usher in a new paradigm in human neuromusculoskeletal (NMS) model calibration. Early results from pioneering works have demonstrated that auto-differentiable NMS models can greatly reduce NMS model calibration time while achieving comparable accuracy compared to traditional calibration methods. The efficient gradient-based optimizers have enabled calibration of increasingly sophisticated human models with a large number of parameters, which seek to narrow the gap between simulation and reality. Several modules have been evaluated separately in different studies, but have never been directly compared within the same study. In this work, these modules are compared on the same differentiable upper limb model with a 3-DoF shoulder, a 2-DoF elbow, and 11 superficial and 5 deep muscles in the calibration to find an optimal pipeline for improving model accuracy. The considered modules include muscle synergy, learnable bone parameters, optimizable geometry of wrap objects, and constraint torque of the differentiable arm model. To evaluate the effect and interplay between the modules on calibration accuracy, one or more modules were used in each of 16 calibration configurations, which were compared in terms of the error between two joint torques calculated by the forward and inverse dynamics with the calibrated model on 9 distinctive testing movements across 4 subjects. Results showed that torque loss was reduced by 23.6% on average using muscle synergy extrapolation to estimate deep muscle activities, and by 10.9% on average through bone dynamic parameter optimization, which are both recommended to be incorporated in the calibration.
introduction:
Accurate neuromusculoskeletal (NMS) models are important for many applications within the science of sports and rehabilitation, exoskeleton and prosthesis development, and health monitoring [1, 2, 3]. NMS model calibration is the process of estimating the parameters of an NMS model for a subject, e.g., optimal muscle fiber length. Good calibration of an NMS model enables accurate estimation of unmeasurable biomechanical variables of subject-specific movement dynamics, e.g., muscle force and joint torque.

Typically, the model parameters are estimated or optimized by minimizing the error between the joint torque calculated by the inverse dynamics (ID) of the skeleton and that computed by the Forward Dynamics of the NMS model driven by muscle excitations which are measured by Electromyography (EMG). It is usually a highly nonlinear optimization problem, and
stochastic global optimization algorithms such as simulated annealing [4] or particle swarm [5] have been traditionally used to solve it [3], but they are extremely slow and take up to multiple hours to converge [6]. The issue worsens as the number of parameters increases, which prevents researchers from calibrating an NMS model with more parameters [7].

Recently, differentiable physics has emerged as a promising new paradigm to calibrate NMS models. A differentiable physics-based model enables the calculation of the gradients of the loss function with respect to a large number of model parameters with backpropagation through efficient automatic differentiation [8], which makes the calibration time more than 20 times shorter than the simulated annealing method with comparable model accuracy [7].
Thanks to the computational efficiency enabled by this new paradigm, the number of parameters to be calibrated can be increased significantly. Muscle synergies and the corresponding weights [7] and bone dynamic parameters [9] were separately incorporated into the differentiable NMS model calibration as learnable parameters in addition to Hill-type muscle model parameters, and early results showed that the accuracy of the calibrated model can be potentially improved with these additional modules. In this work, we explore which different modules/parameters can be added to the differentiable physics-based NMS model calibration, and evaluate how much adding these different parameters improves the calibration accuracy, which is defined by the joint torque loss on testing data. The main contributions of this work are three-fold:

We investigate how the inclusion of different modules in the NMS model calibration can impact model accuracy, including muscle synergy extrapolation to estimate deep muscle EMGs, bone dynamic parameter optimization, learnable geometric parameters of muscle wrap objects, and adding constraint torques in the loss calculation.

We conduct comprehensive experiments on nine testing movements different from the calibration movements with multiple subjects to evaluate the effects of the four modules and the generalization capability of the calibrated model.

Results show the torque estimation accuracy of the calibrated model can be improved by using muscle synergy and optimizing bone dynamic parameters together.

title: CHASE: Curiosity-Guided Skill Acquisition for Embodied Task Execution
authors: Zixuan Wang,Wei Zhang,Chenlei Zhu,Naiyu Chen,Xihua Wang,Jie Chen
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Humans are naturally curious. Faced with an unfamiliar situation, they formulate hypotheses, seek evidence, and learn new ways to act. This ability motivates a question for embodied intelligence: how can we endow robots with curiosity that supports task execution? A robot may know the desired outcome while lacking information about the environment or a skill needed to achieve it. We study the coupling between these information and capability gaps: useful interactions reveal what the robot needs to know, while acquiring a missing skill can make previously unavailable interactions possible.

A conventional execution pipeline restricted to current observations and a fixed skill library can stall when information or an operation is missing. Figure 1 illustrates this issue through a retrieval example. The robot on the left concludes, “I can’t see it. Task over.” The robot on the right asks, “Could it be in the drawer?” It seeks evidence, recognizes the missing opening skill, and acquires that skill before retrieval. This example illustrates a broader principle: task-directed curiosity connects task hypotheses, evidence-seeking interactions, and capability expansion, so that uncertainty and missing skills become explicit planning objectives.

Three research directions provide foundations. Semantic maps and scene graphs ground environmental reasoning [1, 2, 3], while interactive search reveals hidden targets [4, 5]. Generalist policies support adaptation [6, 7], and model-guided data generation supports skill learning [8, 9]. Agentic systems ground and compose operations with planning and feedback [10, 11, 12, 13]. CHASE connects these directions through an explicit loop: unresolved questions guide investigation and skill acquisition, while newly admitted skills enable further investigations. This coupling requires distinguishing a successful physical operation from an observation that actually answers the question.

We propose CHASE, a Curiosity-guided Harness for Acquiring Skills from Evidence, with four modules: dynamic scene understanding, hypothesis-driven curiosity planning, on-demand skill acquisition, and composition with verified execution. Scene memory grounds task hypotheses and retains observation support. A frozen high-level planner ranks investigations by information value, skill reuse, and total cost. Applicable skills execute directly; missing operations trigger bounded generalist exploration during acquisition. Verified segments support local-policy learning, and held-out validation determines skill admission. New skills expand the executable investigation set. Separate physical and evidence checks update the scene and hypotheses, while task-specific predicates verify completion. Held-out reuse evaluation freezes the registry.

The contributions are threefold: (1) a curiosity-driven task-execution framework that jointly ranks investigations by information value, capability-expansion value, and acquisition/execution cost, coupling task questions to skill acquisition and newly enabled investigations; (2) an on-demand skill-acquisition and verification mechanism that connects generalist exploration, feedback-guided refinement, verified-trajectory learning, and held-out admission to form reusable skills, with separate physical and information checks for composition; and (3) a simulation and real-robot experimental evaluation using interactive manipulation tasks to assess task execution, skill reuse, and the coupling between investigation and capability acquisition.

title: Embodied Lower-limb Exoskeleton Assistance: Survey, Challenges, and Perspectives
authors: Xiao-Yin Liu,Guotao Li,Robert Riener,Zeng-Guang Hou
abstract:
Over the past decade, artificial intelligence (AI) has enabled lower-limb exoskeletons to adapt to complex tasks and assist diverse users. Existing reviews, however, are organized around mechanical design, control strategies, or individual AI algorithms, and provide little systematic coverage of embodied lower-limb exoskeletons and their enabling technologies.
This review defines embodied lower-limb exoskeletons and organizes the literature around four dimensions: structural self-adaptation, task adaptation, user-specific adaptation, and control self-regulation. In each dimension, state-of-the-art and representative studies are classified and discussed in terms of the associated challenges, including lightweight and compliant design, data acquisition and fusion, optimization of complex policies, and robust, compliant control. The review then identifies the principal limitations of current research and outlines future directions along these dimensions.
From an embodied perspective, this review sets out the closed-loop relationship among mechanical structure, sensing, and control as a framework for analyzing lower-limb exoskeleton performance and for research on human–robot interaction. The directions it identifies point toward lightweight, comfortable, and practical physical assistance.
Project page: EmbExo.
introduction:
Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have improved the ability of lower-limb exoskeletons to adapt to unstructured and dynamic environments, offering new opportunities to enhance walking ability in older adults and reduce the risk of joint injury [1, 2]. However, exoskeletons operate within tightly coupled human–robot–environment systems, where assistance strategies must continually adapt to changes in the wearer’s movement, assistance needs, and environmental conditions [3, 4]. These interdependencies make reliable and effective adaptive assistance challenging. To address these challenges, a growing body of research over the past five years has incorporated AI into exoskeleton systems to improve autonomous perception and decision-making, with the aim of improving the effectiveness of assistance [5, 6].

An embodied exoskeleton is a human-centered wearable intelligent agent capable of perception, decision-making, and adaptation to its operating context. In contrast to adaptive assistance, which adjusts the assistance strategy to the wearer, the task, or the environment, embodied assistance for lower-limb exoskeletons starts from the coupling among the human, the exoskeleton, and the environment. Mechanical structure, sensing, and control are brought into a single closed loop and act jointly: the exoskeleton integrates information about human–exoskeleton states, environmental conditions, and task requirements, and optimizes assistance torque profiles. The objective is efficient, comfortable movement assistance in dynamic environments [7, 5, 8]. Because these elements share one loop, that objective requires mechanical structure, sensing, and control to be addressed jointly. These same three elements are the perspectives from which exoskeletons are studied and performance is analyzed.

Achieving the above assistance objective, however, presents four key challenges.
First, the mechanical structure must be lightweight, conform to human anatomy, and accommodate complex lower-limb joint kinematics to minimize additional interaction constraints and ensure wearing comfort [9, 10]. Second, diverse assistance tasks and changing environments require assistance strategies that adapt to task demands and operating conditions [1, 3]. Third, differences in body morphology, physical capabilities, and gait characteristics necessitate assistance tailored to individual users [11, 8]. Finally, the bidirectional coupling between human and exoskeleton motion creates interdependencies between state perception and assistance control, requiring continuous optimization of assistance torques to balance assistance effectiveness and interaction comfort [4, 12]. Accordingly, the core challenges for embodied lower-limb exoskeletons can be categorized into four areas: structural self-adaptation, task adaptation, user-specific adaptation, and control self-regulation.

To address these core challenges, existing research has pursued four complementary directions: joint self-alignment [10, 13] and compliant interaction [14, 9] to improve structural self-adaptation; multimodal information fusion [1, 5] and musculoskeletal-informed policy learning [3, 15] to support task adaptation; human-in-the-loop optimization [7, 11, 16] and cross-subject transfer learning [17, 8] to enable user-specific adaptation; and control compensation [18, 19] and human–exoskeleton control optimization [20, 4] to improve assistance control. From a system architecture perspective, structural self-adaptation primarily concerns the physical design of the exoskeleton, task adaptation and user-specific adaptation primarily concern the high-level controller, and control self-regulation primarily concerns the low-level controller. These components serve as the “body,” “brain,” and “cerebellum” of the embodied system, respectively [21]. Functionally, an embodied lower-limb exoskeleton forms a closed-loop system that integrates structural design, perception and representation, and control optimization. These interdependent elements work together to support efficient and comfortable movement assistance in complex, dynamic environments.

Existing reviews of lower-limb exoskeletons have established a systematic knowledge base covering mechanical design, perception and control, and the evaluation of assistive performance. For mechanical design, early reviews surveyed device evolution and key technologies, including actuation, sensing, power supply, and control [22, 23], and later reviews examined compliant mechanisms, attachment interfaces, bio-inspired structures, and human–robot interaction design [24, 25]. For perception and control, reviews of control and AI methods have addressed functional hierarchies, movement-intention recognition, user-specific parameter optimization, and reinforcement learning [26, 27, 28, 29], with increasing attention to gait planning that adapts to environmental conditions and to end-to-end, task-agnostic control [30, 2]. For evaluation, related reviews have broadened assistive outcomes to safety, embodiment, and physiological and clinical needs [31, 32, 33]. Together, these reviews provide a foundation for classifying technologies and understanding individual methods.

However, this foundation has three limitations. First, because the reviews are organized by device type, functional module, or algorithm category, they offer limited analysis of how mechanical structure, sensing, algorithms, and control jointly support assistance through closed-loop interactions among the human, the exoskeleton, and the environment [2]. Second, reviews that adopt an embodied perspective on perception, interaction, and cognition remain focused on the functions of individual technical modules, so perception, interaction, and cognition are not connected through that loop [34, 35]. Third, the integration of AI into the loop has yet to be treated systematically, leaving the mechanisms for wearer comfort, changing task demands, individual differences, and the coupling between perception and control unclear. This review examines those mechanisms as four interrelated dimensions: structural self-adaptation, task adaptation, user-specific adaptation, and control self-regulation, together with their interdependencies and key challenges. In doing so, it provides a system-level perspective on personalized and comfortable assistance in complex, dynamic environments.

This review adopts an embodied intelligence perspective to examine three interconnected levels: physical embodiment, high-level decision-making, and low-level control, which functionally correspond to the system’s “body,” “brain,” and “cerebellum,” respectively. The embodied perspective also provides an analytical framework for this review of lower-limb exoskeletons.
Specifically, Section II reviews the structural design of the physical embodiment. Sections III and IV examine task adaptation and user adaptation in high-level control, respectively, while Section V focuses on low-level control self-regulation. Building on these four parts, Section VI addresses practical system deployment, followed by an integrative discussion in Section VII.
Fig. 1 illustrates the functional roles and interconnections of these components. The physical embodiment provides the foundation for sensing and control. High-level controllers based on AI algorithms adapt assistance policies to task requirements and individual user characteristics, providing desired trajectories or reference torques to the low-level controller. The low-level controller further optimizes the generation and regulation of assistive torques. Together, these interconnected levels support efficient assistance in complex real-world scenarios.

Each technical section reviews the literature around key challenges, comparing the characteristics and applicability of different approaches.
Section II reviews human–exoskeleton kinematic compatibility [9], and lightweight design and compliant interaction [36], addressing two challenges: accommodating complex joint kinematics and interindividual differences for efficient assistance (Challenge 1.1), and reducing on-body mass and interaction impedance while preserving natural movement (Challenge 1.2).
Section III examines task adaptation through multimodal information fusion [5] and musculoskeletal policy learning [3]. The former addresses low-cost multimodal data acquisition when torque is difficult to measure directly (Challenge 2.1) and efficient fusion of high-dimensional multimodal features (Challenge 2.2), covering torque [1] and trajectory prediction [4]. The latter addresses training musculoskeletal policies in high-dimensional actuation spaces for complex terrain (Challenge 2.3), and designing learning objectives and training frameworks for exoskeleton assistance that account for human–exoskeleton coupling (Challenge 2.4), covering musculoskeletal locomotion [37] and exoskeleton assistance policies [38].

Section IV builds on these models and policies to examine user adaptation through human-in-the-loop optimization [7, 11] and cross-subject transfer [1, 17]. The former addresses efficient algorithms for rapid optimization with limited interaction trials (Challenge 3.1) and parameter optimization frameworks for complex network architectures that optimize policies on complex terrain (Challenge 3.2), covering optimization based on physiological signals [39] and preferences [40]. The latter addresses training objectives that improve the generalization of personalized motion-intention prediction models (Challenge 3.3), covering multi-subject data fusion [1] and domain adaptation [8].
Section V reviews control compensation [18] and control optimization that support efficient assistance [12]. It addresses accurate, real-time trajectory and torque tracking under uncertain human–exoskeleton systems (Challenge 4.1), and control optimization under task completion, safety, and users’ voluntary movement (Challenge 4.2).
These four aspects connect embodiment design, high-level adaptive decision-making, and low-level control self-regulation to support autonomous, adaptive assistance in complex, dynamic environments (Section VI). A comprehensive overview of the review framework is provided in Fig. 1.

Studies on embodied lower-limb exoskeleton assistance published through October 2026 were identified in two stages.
In the first stage, IEEE Xplore and Google Scholar were queried along the four dimensions of embodied exoskeleton assistance. Each query combined lower-limb exoskeleton or hip/knee/ankle exoskeleton with one keyword set: 1) Structural self-adaptation: kinematic/dynamic compatibility, lightweight design, compliant interaction; 2) Task adaptation: prediction, estimation, complex environment, musculoskeletal; 3) User-specific adaptation: human-in-the-loop optimization, preference, cross-subject; 4) Control self-regulation: compensation, tracking, optimization.

In the second stage, the retrieved literature was restricted to representative studies published in major robotics journals and conferences. Within each dimension, priority was given to work from the most recent five years. Where that interval contained few relevant studies, the search window was extended further back and representative studies were retained. The resulting corpus concerns exoskeleton assistance that augments lower-limb strength during walking in healthy adults. Rehabilitation methods were included when their design or control principles extended to such walking assistance. Relevant arXiv preprints were added when the reported methods or experiments had not yet appeared in a journal or conference; these preprints are identified as such and are distinguished from peer-reviewed evidence.

title: Beyond Natural-Language Instructions: Temporal Logic as a Task Language for VLA Models with Visual-Logical Fusion
authors: Zezhi Liu,Jingwen Sun,Hongjin Chen,Shaojie Ren,Peiyan Tu,Xin Jin,Zhibo Chen
abstract: Robotic tasks combine object relations, logical dependencies, and temporal requirements, which robot planning and industrial control commonly specify in temporal logic (TL). We introduce TL-VLA, a vision–language–action framework that replaces natural-language task instructions with temporal logic, making this spatiotemporal structure explicit. A typed graph encoder and visual–logical fusion condition continuous actions on the task specification and the current observations. To prepare a general vision–language backbone for this interface, we develop TL-aware robot pretraining with separate semantic and structural readouts: a frozen language teacher aligns task semantics, the structural readout encodes TL syntax to support complex, long-horizon tasks, and autoregressive action prediction connects the graph representation to robot behavior. Downstream policies inherit the pretrained backbone and TL encoder and learn new fusion and action modules. On CALVIN ABC→\rightarrowD, our TL-aware initializer reaches 3.800 average chain length and 62.3% five-task success, compared with 3.578 and 54.5% for a FAST initializer pretrained on the same data and 3.485 average chain length for a Qwen+NL baseline. On LIBERO-10, TL-aware initialization improves success from 91.2% to 95.8%. On LIBERO-Mem, our policy reaches 65.0% success without observation history, compared with 45.0% for a Qwen+NL reference. On held-out Panda planning specifications, it reaches 59.6% at Success@256 over three generation seeds, versus 48.4% for Qwen+TL and 37.0% for Qwen+NL. These results support explicit logical task conditioning and transferable TL-aware representations for robot action learning.
introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models connect broad visual and linguistic knowledge to robot control. RT-2, OpenVLA, and π0\pi_{0} show the value of this connection for learning diverse manipulation behaviors [1, 2, 3]. A central design choice is how a task enters the policy. Beyond naming an action, a task may specify which objects participate, how they relate, and which conditions must hold in a particular order. A short natural-language instruction often leaves some of this spatiotemporal structure implicit; we instead make it the explicit task input of the policy.

Consider placing an object in a drawer and then closing the drawer. Temporal logic (TL) represents semantic intent together with spatial relations, temporal dependencies, and compositional syntax. Predicate arguments bind participants; operators specify how requirements relate. This exposes richer, rule-governed structure than a short benchmark instruction, although natural language can express the same requirements. TL is less broadly used than natural language but is well established in robotics, control, and industrial systems. Its precise semantics provide a practical foundation for specifying task and system requirements and supporting systematic planning, control, and monitoring [4, 5, 6, 7]. This motivates bringing TL into VLA models: can an explicit logical task interface, supported by suitable pretraining, improve learned visuomotor behavior?

We introduce TL-VLA, which conditions actions on a TL graph, camera observations, and robot state. The graph represents task intent, and perception supplies the current scene. A typed graph encoder preserves operator structure and predicate arguments, and bidirectional visual–logical fusion connects them to visual features. The resulting continuous-action policy takes the graph, rather than an instruction, as its task input; training instructions only supply semantic supervision through a frozen teacher.

Because TL conveys both semantic intent and explicit spatiotemporal syntax, our pretraining splits graph representations into semantic and structural streams. The semantic stream aligns with task-matched training instructions, while the structural stream retains ordered graph information beyond that alignment target. Joint action-token prediction trains a Qwen3-VL backbone [8] to use these representations on a robot-data mixture. We then selectively transfer the Qwen backbone and the TL graph encoder, and learn the visual–logical fusion module and continuous-action head on downstream demonstrations.

We evaluate the capabilities this design targets: sustained execution of consecutive subtasks on CALVIN, long-horizon transfer on LIBERO-10, multi-stage manipulation without observation history on LIBERO-Mem, and logical satisfaction of held-out single-goal, multi-goal, sequential, and partial-order specifications on the Panda benchmark. Under a fixed task interface and downstream recipe, TL-aware initialization improves over original-Qwen and robot-pretrained initializers, and on Panda its gains concentrate on multi-goal, sequential, and partial-order specifications.

Our contributions are threefold:

Replacing natural language with temporal logic in VLA policies, with visual–logical fusion.
We adopt structured TL specifications as the policy’s sole task input and integrate them with visual observations through bidirectional fusion, conditioning continuous action generation on both task logic and scene information.

TL-aware pretraining for visual–logical policy learning.
We develop a multimodal pretraining framework that prepares TL-aware representations for visual–logical integration and transfers them to downstream policy learning.

Evaluation across diverse benchmarks.
Experiments across diverse robotic benchmarks demonstrate the benefits of our approach for downstream control, with gains on tasks involving complex structured specifications.

title: LUDIUS: A Benchmark for Embodied Social Intelligence in Everyday Human-Robot Interactions
authors: Chaewon Kim,Sangheon Lee,Seyeon Choi,Kangwook Lee,Yea Seul Kim
abstract:
Social intelligence in a robot requires interpreting a situation from the perspectives of the people involved and using that understanding to decide when and how to act. We introduce LUDIUS, a benchmark for evaluating how vision-language models exercise this judgment through a robot’s verbal responses and actions, organized around 15 social intelligence skills drawn from social psychology, sociology, and cognitive science. LUDIUS comprises six editions, each a collection of episodes spanning one simulated week. Three editions each cover all 15 skills in a different household. The other three focus on interactions involving multiple people, safety, and context-specific norms, respectively.
We evaluate frontier models and a smaller model finetuned on social-interaction data we generated, using a common evaluation harness.
The harness supplies each model with the robot’s camera views and residents’ reactions, retrieves relevant interaction history, and converts the model’s tool calls into robot verbal responses and actions. Models tend to perform worse when they must reason about what a resident saw or heard earlier, reconcile competing interests, or fulfill a request within safety constraints and household rules. Beyond the home setting, LUDIUS’s design pipeline offers a way to construct social intelligence benchmarks by translating social intelligence skills into context-specific judgments and observable robot behavior.
introduction:
A resident is tying their shoes by the door. “It’s raining,” they say. Should their household robot bring an umbrella? Suppose on previous rainy mornings, the resident said, “I cycle to work. When it rains, bring me my rain jacket.” The robot has reason to reach for the jacket instead of the umbrella. But if the resident had said, “I drive to work and don’t need rain gear,” there may be nothing to bring. The remark is the same, but the appropriate response depends on what the robot remembers from earlier interactions.

To design socially intelligent robots, we need to understand what makes an action appropriate for a particular person in a particular situation. In the opening example, both timing and context matter: the robot should help at the right moment even when the resident has not asked, and it should know how to help from what it learned on earlier mornings. Robots must put this judgment into practice as interactions unfold. This calls for a benchmark that evaluates how robots execute physical actions, respond to people’s reactions, and draw on accumulated context across interactions.

We introduce LUDIUS, a benchmark for Lifelong Understanding of Daily Interactions and Unspoken Signals, to evaluate whether vision-language models (VLMs) [3, 51, 53, 17] can choose socially appropriate actions for a household robot.
Each edition spans one simulated week of household life. Residents talk to the robot and react to its verbal responses and actions, and their remarks can guide its behavior days later. In Figure 1, Margaret mentions her drink preference on Tuesday, and the robot should recall it on Thursday.
Residents also convey their needs and states through social cues, such as gestures and posture, which the robot must interpret through observation and memory.
To design the benchmark, we first drew on research in social psychology, sociology, and cognitive science to identify 15 social intelligence skills relevant to everyday interactions (Table 1). We used these skills to design episodes and evaluation criteria, specifying the required social judgment and the robot’s verbal responses and actions that demonstrate it.

The benchmark comprises six editions, summarized in Table 2. To examine social intelligence across relationships and routines, three editions follow an older married couple (Margaret and Arthur), an engaged couple (Theo and Aria), and two roommates (Emily and Mina). The other three examine how the robot responds when a request affects several people (Multi-party management), when fulfilling it could harm someone (Safety), or when context-specific norms shape appropriate behavior (Context-specific norms).

We use LUDIUS to identify which social skills VLMs demonstrate reliably and when their verbal responses or actions fail. We evaluate several frontier VLMs [64, 65, 5, 4, 97] alongside a smaller model we trained, comparing their performance in each social intelligence skill and examining how their choices play out in individual episodes.
All the frontier models achieved their lowest success rates in the Multi-party management edition, especially when reconciling competing requests from multiple residents. Also, models generally performed well on Memory but struggled more with Theory of mind, suggesting that retrieving memories does not ensure the ability to reason with them about others’ beliefs. These skill-level observations surface gaps that can guide improvements to training data and memory systems for socially intelligent robots.

To summarize, our contributions are threefold:

We define 15 social intelligence skills by drawing on social psychology, sociology, and cognitive science around the judgments a robot faces in everyday interactions.

We define 15 social intelligence skills by drawing on social psychology, sociology, and cognitive science around the judgments a robot faces in everyday interactions.

We introduce LUDIUS, a benchmark of 750 scored episodes across six simulated household weeks, evaluating a VLM-controlled robot’s verbal responses and actions in ongoing interactions with residents.

We evaluate frontier and open VLMs on LUDIUS and analyze their failures. Fine-tuning an open-weight model on synthetic social-interaction scenarios, episodes from inZOI [43] (a life simulation game), and real-world trajectories
outperforms the base model on LUDIUS.

1. We define 15 social intelligence skills by drawing on social psychology, sociology, and cognitive science around the judgments a robot faces in everyday interactions.

2. We introduce LUDIUS, a benchmark of 750 scored episodes across six simulated household weeks, evaluating a VLM-controlled robot’s verbal responses and actions in ongoing interactions with residents.

3. We evaluate frontier and open VLMs on LUDIUS and analyze their failures. Fine-tuning an open-weight model on synthetic social-interaction scenarios, episodes from inZOI [43] (a life simulation game), and real-world trajectories
outperforms the base model on LUDIUS.
