title: Co-World Model for Human-Video-to-Robot Transfer via Co-Constructed Shared Latent Dynamics
authors: Xuetao Li,Xuan Jiang,Chen Liu,Zhongrui Rao,Yu Ling,Hui Wang,Sheng Liu,Miao Li
abstract: Human videos are abundant and cheap to obtain, whereas robot trajectories remain scarce and costly, making zero-shot skill transfer from a single human demonstration an appealing route to scalable robot learning. Existing methods, however, either retarget human-specific geometry or match only static visual goals, and thus stumble over the cross-embodiment dynamics mismatch and the ungrounded action execution. We present the Co-World Model (CoWM), a predictive framework jointly optimized from paired yet unsynchronized human and robot streams. To bridge the cross-embodiment dynamics gap, CoWM disentangles each observation into a shared object-relation state and embodiment-specific context. It aligns latent actions across embodiments using effect-swap and action-sensitivity objectives, such that actions are matched by their predicted effects on the manipulated objects rather than by embodiment-dependent kinematics. For grounded execution, a phase-aware receding-horizon controller estimates demonstration progress, projects the inferred human action prior onto the robot action-support density, and translates the resulting latent dynamics into executable robot commands. Extensive experiments in simulation and on two physical robot platforms demonstrate the effectiveness of CoWM, its cross-platform generalizability, and the contribution of each component. See the demo video in the supporting information for details.
introduction:
Robot manipulation learning has advanced markedly, from imitation policies and vision-language-action models [1, 2, 3] to generalist foundation policies that span tasks and platforms [4, 5, 6].
These advances, however, are fueled by robot trajectories that remain scarce and costly, as teleoperated collection demands per-platform hardware, expert operators, and hours of supervised recording [7, 8].
Egocentric human videos offer the opposite profile, capturing abundant and easily acquired observations of contact-rich manipulation [9, 10].
This asymmetry motivates human-video-to-robot zero-shot transfer, in which a robot acquires an executable skill from a single unseen human demonstration without any corresponding robot trajectory, as illustrated in Figure 1.
However, most existing transfer methods either retarget human motion while preserving human-specific geometry [11, 12, 13], or condition on visual goals or skill latents while discarding the intermediate interaction dynamics [14, 15, 16], and single-embodiment world models couple their predictive semantics to the one interface that generated the data [17, 18, 19, 20, 21].

Realizing such transfer presents two unique challenges.
First, cross-embodiment dynamics mismatch.
Humans and robots differ in morphology, sensing, and action interfaces, so different motions may produce the same object change while similar motions have state-dependent effects.
Latent proximity or marginal distribution matching cannot resolve this ambiguity, because a shared model may silently infer the embodiment, branch its transition rule, or ignore its action input.
Second, ungrounded action execution.
Human videos carry neither robot commands nor proprioception, and executions proceed at mismatched rates.
A plan induced from the video alone may therefore drift out of phase or request actions the robot has never been observed to perform, and direct kinematic mapping cannot certify feasibility. In light of these challenges, this work investigates two critical questions:
I) How can human observations and robot experience co-construct one predictive world model?
II) How can the latent plan induced by a single unseen human video be translated into feasible robot control at test time?

In response to question I), we propose the Co-World Model (CoWM), jointly optimized from paired but unsynchronized human and robot streams.
CoWM factorizes each observation into a shared object-relation state and an embodiment-private context, and encodes both human and robot motion into a common latent action space.
Rather than aligning raw kinematics, we bind action semantics through predicted object effects with two complementary constraints, where an effect-swap loss requires human and robot actions with matched effects to predict compatible object changes, and an action-sensitivity margin rejects nearby actions whose observed effects differ.
Together they prevent the shared dynamics from branching on embodiment or degenerating into action-agnostic prediction.

Leveraging the co-constructed latent space, we design a phase-aware grounded execution scheme for question II).
Online temporal matching tracks the demonstration phase against mismatched execution rates, a robot-state-conditioned residual corrects the human action prior, and an empirical action-support density confines proposals to actions supported by robot experience.
Receding-horizon planning under the shared dynamics then converts the demonstration-induced latent evolution into executable commands, replanning after each observation.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

Co-Constructed World Model. We formulate CoWM, in which human observations and robot experience jointly constrain a factorized predictive space over shared object relations and common latent actions, while embodiment-private variables retain the context tied to each embodiment’s own body and controller.

Effect-Grounded Action Semantics. We bind cross-embodiment latent actions through complementary effect-swap and action-sensitivity constraints, aligning actions by their predicted object effects rather than kinematics and rejecting action-agnostic shared dynamics.

Grounded Zero-Shot Execution. We translate CoWM predictions into robot control through phase tracking, residual proposals, an action-support prior, and receding-horizon planning. Extensive experiments in simulation and on two physical robots validate the framework and the contribution of each component.

1. Co-Constructed World Model. We formulate CoWM, in which human observations and robot experience jointly constrain a factorized predictive space over shared object relations and common latent actions, while embodiment-private variables retain the context tied to each embodiment’s own body and controller.

2. Effect-Grounded Action Semantics. We bind cross-embodiment latent actions through complementary effect-swap and action-sensitivity constraints, aligning actions by their predicted object effects rather than kinematics and rejecting action-agnostic shared dynamics.

3. Grounded Zero-Shot Execution. We translate CoWM predictions into robot control through phase tracking, residual proposals, an action-support prior, and receding-horizon planning. Extensive experiments in simulation and on two physical robots validate the framework and the contribution of each component.

title: BOT-Scale: A Traceable Evaluation Methodology for Robotic Manipulation
authors: Yunfei Xue,Kemi Chen,Weiling Chen,Wei Gao,Tiesong Zhao,Zheng-Jun Zha
abstract:
A successful manipulation rollout can still involve a mid-task object drop or a placement deviation. Existing evaluators reduce such deviations to a single score or attach explanations computed separately; the score itself explains neither its basis nor what to fix.
We show that a manipulation score becomes traceable when defined as the sum of outcome-conditioned penalties over retained behavioral-factor records. Explanation and score share the same computation, so each factor-level deduction names an inspectable deviation.
BOT-Scale applies this principle by adapting behavioral assessment scales from medicine. It organizes twelve candidate factors into four assessment layers; each factor is tied to observable evidence and an explicit decision criterion.
Reference calibration fixes a penalty per factor, and a closed-form rule aggregates the factor records into a score with per-factor contributions.
We developed BOTScorer, an automatic scoring system based on the seven factors retained by data-driven screening, to validate this methodology.
We provide BOT-Events, a dataset with eight-rater quality scores and factor-event annotations, alongside the traceable, interpretable score.
The code will be released publicly.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation is advancing rapidly with Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [12, 3, 2]. Sustaining this progress requires evaluation that attributes performance to behaviors a practitioner can fix. We show that a manipulation score becomes traceable when defined as the sum of outcome-conditioned penalties over retained behavioral-factor records: each score gap then decomposes into named, inspectable deviations that make its basis explicit.

Automated evaluation of robotic manipulation now extends beyond success rates: RoboJev [6] infers success probabilities from rollout video; PRM-as-a-Judge 1.5 (PRM-SQS) [16] derives fine-grained process metrics from dense progress curves; RoboMeter [13] learns rewards from comparisons of expert and suboptimal trajectories; and Eval-Actions/AutoEval [15] performs criteria-level expert grading with diagnostic explanations.

These evaluators share three limitations. First, a single score hides its behavioral basis because it does not specify which deviations occurred. It cannot distinguish a clean success from a rollout that succeeds despite a force-impedance control failure or a transient end-effector positioning failure, both of which directly affect stability, efficiency, and safety. Second, when explanations are available, they are computed separately from the score. That score cannot be recomputed from the supporting records. Third, no evaluator exposes per-factor contributions, leaving a score gap untraceable to named, fixable deviations. Comparing manipulation quality therefore requires both a score and process evidence explicitly linked to its computation.

BOT-Scale addresses these limitations (Fig. 1). Drawing on behavioral assessment scales in medicine, it records the behavioral basis of a score: each deviation becomes a behavioral factor, an assessment item with observable evidence and an explicit decision criterion. Twelve candidates, organized into four assessment layers (Table 1), are screened to seven. The score is then defined as the sum of outcome-conditioned penalties over the retained records (Eqs. 6–8). Explanation and score share the same computation, making every score recomputable. The closed-form rule yields per-factor contributions that decompose each score gap into named, fixable deviations.

BOTScorer is the automatic scoring system that implements this methodology; BOT-Events supplies the data for its calibration and validation. BOTScorer uses a discriminative detector to recognize deviation events of the seven retained factors in execution video. Reference calibration and a closed-form rule aggregate these records into a recomputable score with per-factor contributions. These scores agree more closely with human ratings than learned aggregators that use the same records and are trained on those ratings (Sec. 5.3). BOT-Events contains 800 rollouts with eight-rater quality scores and 2,394 factor-event annotations, used to validate BOT-Scale and to build BOTScorer.

Our main contributions are:

BOT-Scale. We define quality as the sum of outcome-conditioned penalties over retained behavioral-factor records. The explanation is the computation itself. Adapting the item-generation, evidence-and-criterion, domain-grouping, and item-analysis steps of clinical behavioral assessment scales, we specify twelve candidate factors in four assessment layers and retain seven through screening. Their pairwise correlations remain low, so the additive decomposition does not charge the same deviation twice.

BOTScorer. A discriminative detector recognizes factor events in execution video, reaching 90.38% event accuracy, 2.1 points below generative label decoding on the same backbone, at 1.94×1.94\times the speed. Among successful executions, scores computed from these records reach a mean per-task Spearman ρ\rho of 0.59, compared with at most 0.22 for three released evaluators; agreement with human quality judgments over all videos is 0.79. The same fixed penalties also distinguish two VLA checkpoints differing by only 0.2 points in Success Rate (SR).

BOT-Events. We provide 800 rollouts with 6,400 human quality ratings. The mean task-wise Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC), computed as ICC(2,8), is 0.951; eight-rater split-half reliability is 0.959. The dataset also includes 2,394 factor-event annotations and the calibrated penalties needed to recompute every reported score.

title: Rehearse in 3D, Render in 2D: Physically Consistent and Editable Robot World Models
authors: Guangyu Liu,Hanzhang Wang,Huijia Zhang,Hanbei Zhan,Linjie Hu,Bin Xiao,Xuan Zhou,Dong Zhang,Hanwei Liu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Embodied world models aim to predict future interactions that are both visually realistic and physically consistent. Yet explicit 3D motion prediction alone does not guarantee that object structure and contact relationships are preserved.
Beyond motion prediction, 3D representations provide an explicit state space for imposing structural and physical constraints.
Building on this insight, we introduce RehearsalWorld, an editable robot world model driven by 3D Interaction Rehearsal (3DIR).
Given an initial RGB-D observation and robot actions, Interaction-Consistent Rehearsal (ICR) uses a pretrained 3D point-flow model as a motion prior. It refines the predicted trajectories through response-aware object grouping, persistent grasp memory, and contact structure refiner, preserving scene stability, object structure, and grasp attachments. Rehearsal-Aligned Video Generation (RAVG) then uses geometric projections of the rehearsal as temporal conditioning. We fine-tune a video generator on projection–video pairs to synthesize realistic interaction videos.
Thanks to the decoupling of physical response from visual synthesis, RehearsalWorld also supports independent editing of material properties and camera viewpoints.
Compared with PointWorld on real DROID grasping sequences, RehearsalWorld reduces gripper-relative offset by approximately 79%–84% across deformable, articulated, and rigid objects and lowers reference motion error. For video prediction, it achieves a PSNR of 23.92 dB and an FVD of 149.
introduction:
Embodied video world models generate action-conditioned videos of future interactions to support planning, policy evaluation, and data generation [8, 11, 26, 27, 36].
Recent models produce visually realistic interaction videos with coherent motion.
Visual realism, however, does not guarantee physical consistency: generated interactions can still contain implausible object responses [1, 24].
In robotic manipulation, object motion must also be consistent with the given actions, contact relationships, and the objects’ physical properties.

Recent work has introduced explicit 3D representations to better ground interaction prediction in physics.
TesserAct [40], Aether [41], 4DNeX [4], and Kinema4D [35] jointly model RGB with depth or point maps to improve spatiotemporal consistency between appearance and geometry.
Yet joint training alone does not ensure RGB–geometry alignment, which depends on cross-modal fusion [4].
Even well-aligned predictions can violate structural or contact constraints.
Kinema4D, for example, notes that its generated environment responses can still exhibit penetration [35].

Other methods learn interaction dynamics directly in 3D, using particles or point clouds to predict action-induced displacement and deformation [9, 39, 20, 38].
For example, the 3D flow world model PointWorld [10] represents RGB-D observations and robot actions in a shared 3D point space and predicts future displacements of the initial scene points.
Its pointwise predictions can capture diverse interaction responses but do not explicitly enforce structural, material, or contact constraints.
On real DROID sequences, we observe background drift, excessive object stretching, and grasp slip in these predictions.
In addition, the predicted flow primarily describes the motion of observed surfaces. Generating complete videos requires additional appearance modeling [13].

Explicit 3D representations not only support geometric modeling and motion prediction but, more importantly, provide a state space for imposing physical constraints on object structure and interactions [12]. Prior work has explored video generation guided by physical simulation [3, 21, 6]. We focus instead on how to use motion priors learned from real interactions to construct more physically consistent 3D states under object-level constraints. Such states could ground both interaction prediction and visual synthesis.

To this end, we introduce RehearsalWorld, an editable robot world model that uses 3D interaction rehearsal to decouple physical response modeling from video generation.
During 3D Interaction Rehearsal (3DIR), a pretrained 3D point-flow model [10] predicts future interaction trajectories from the initial RGB-D observation and robot actions.
Interaction-Consistent Rehearsal (ICR) refines the predicted point displacements using response-aware object grouping, persistent grasp memory, and contact structure refiner. This reduces background drift, excessive object stretching, and grasp slip.
In Rehearsal-Aligned Video Generation (RAVG), we project the corrected 3D states into the target view to obtain temporal geometric conditions.
We fine-tune a video generator on paired dynamic projections and recordings to synthesize realistic videos that follow the rehearsed motion and scene layout.

This decoupling also enables independent editing of material properties and camera viewpoints.
Material edits resimulate the interaction with different material properties while keeping the robot action fixed. Viewpoint edits reproject the same 3D interaction.
Both reuse the video generator without retraining.
Compared with PointWorld [10] on real DROID [16] grasping sequences, RehearsalWorld reduces gripper-relative offset by about 79%–84% across deformable, articulated, and rigid objects and lowers reference motion error.
On DROID and BEHAVIOR-1K [18], RehearsalWorld improves video PSNR by 4.61 dB and reduces FVD by about 43% relative to Kinema4D [35].

Our contributions are:

We introduce RehearsalWorld, an editable robot world model that decouples 3D interaction rehearsal from video synthesis.

We propose ICR that refines 3D trajectories via persistent grasp memory and material-conditioned constraints, reducing slip and distortion.

We evaluate 3D rehearsal on DROID and BEHAVIOR-1K and test whether gains in grasp preservation, object structure, and motion accuracy carry over to generated videos.

1. We introduce RehearsalWorld, an editable robot world model that decouples 3D interaction rehearsal from video synthesis.

2. We propose ICR that refines 3D trajectories via persistent grasp memory and material-conditioned constraints, reducing slip and distortion.

3. We evaluate 3D rehearsal on DROID and BEHAVIOR-1K and test whether gains in grasp preservation, object structure, and motion accuracy carry over to generated videos.

title: DataForgeVLA: Fully Synthetic Manipulation Demonstrations for Vision-Language-Action Training
authors: Sergei Kurchev,Iaroslav Kolomiets,Filipp Maksimov,Elizaveta Semenyakina,Miguel Altamirano Cabrera,Artem Lykov,Dzmitry Tsetserukou
abstract: We present a dataset of 340 fully synthetic manipulation demonstrations generated from real seed data for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) training. The corpus contains 32,340 frames with synchronized RGB and actions across eight object categories, represented as LeRobot v2.1 episodes with H.264 video, per-frame robot states and pose-valued action labels, language task annotations, summary statistics and quality decisions. Each synthetic demonstration is produced without additional teleoperation: a LoRA-fine-tuned Cosmos-3 model generates a manipulation video, and RoboHaMeR recovers the corresponding robot trajectory from RGB. Quality screening accepted 300 of 340 episodes for policy fine-tuning. As preliminary evidence of feasibility, a pretrained GR00T N1.6 policy fine-tuned exclusively on the 300 accepted episodes reaches 16/20 (80%) real-world pick-and-place success on the Oreo-package task. A policy fine-tuned on 105 real teleoperated episodes achieved 18/20 (90%) under the same protocol. These results are based on one object and 20 trials per policy and are therefore reported as preliminary evidence rather than a general performance claim.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies for robot manipulation improve with the diversity of the demonstrations they are trained on – different objects, grasp poses, backgrounds, and task configurations. In practice, that diversity is bottlenecked by how the demonstrations
are collected: teleoperated data collection requires human operator time, and additional objects or scene configurations can require repeated
collection sessions.

A LoRA-fine-tuned Cosmos-3 video model (Hu et al., 2022) can generate robot manipulation clips from a starting frame, while RoboHaMeR can recover robot trajectories from RGB without proprioceptive logs. Together, they turn generated clips into labeled demonstrations.

DataForgeVLA controls the starting scene by removing the hands and object from a real seed frame, then inserting a MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012) robot overlay and reconstructed object at sampled poses. A transfer model converts this low-fidelity composite to a photorealistic first frame before video generation and action extraction (Section 3).

The primary artifact is a documented, machine-readable corpus of synthetic RGB demonstrations paired with pose-valued action labels, together with a description of its generation and processing procedure. By generating additional manipulation demonstrations from a limited set of human-teleoperated episodes, our approach may reduce the need for repeated teleoperation across different robot and object configurations. This capability is relevant to HRI settings in which collecting demonstrations requires substantial human involvement and may entail operator fatigue and cognitive load.
Our contributions are:

a LeRobot v2.1 dataset containing 340 episodes and 32,340 synchronized frames for eight object-conditioned pick tasks, including video, actions, language annotations, statistics, and per-sample quality decisions;

a description of a construction procedure combining controlled scene
recomposition, generative video, and RGB-to-action extraction, reusing
models trained on teleoperated demonstrations to create the
generated demonstrations without additional teleoperation;

preliminary evidence – a 16/20 (80%) real-world success rate
for a pretrained GR00T N1.6 policy fine-tuned exclusively on the
300 quality-screened episodes on one object – that the extracted
labels can support real-robot execution.

1. a LeRobot v2.1 dataset containing 340 episodes and 32,340 synchronized frames for eight object-conditioned pick tasks, including video, actions, language annotations, statistics, and per-sample quality decisions;

2. a description of a construction procedure combining controlled scene
recomposition, generative video, and RGB-to-action extraction, reusing
models trained on teleoperated demonstrations to create the
generated demonstrations without additional teleoperation;

3. preliminary evidence – a 16/20 (80%) real-world success rate
for a pretrained GR00T N1.6 policy fine-tuned exclusively on the
300 quality-screened episodes on one object – that the extracted
labels can support real-robot execution.

title: Escapingthe instruction blackhole of vision-language-action policies via optimal-transport wormholes
authors: Xuetao Li,Chen Liu,Jing Wu,Sheng Liu,Miao Li
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are trained to follow a fixed instruction, yet people change their minds while the robot acts. We identify the instruction black hole: once a VLA policy commits to a task, new instructions are absorbed and the robot completes the old task or freezes. We quantify it with a transmission ratio and an event horizon and prove it is a blind spot of static imitation, which cannot distinguish a policy that listens from a deaf one once the execution state reveals the task. We propose Wormhole, a training-free plug-in that relocates the robot instead of re-instructing it: optimal transport selects an approach-phase state of the new task, a rate-limited traversal carries the robot there, and the unmodified policy takes over. On LIBERO, Wormhole raises committed-switch success of π0\pi_{0} and π0.5\pi_{0.5} from at most 1.2% to 93.1%, matching or exceeding scripted retreat-and-restart with one fifth of its action discontinuity.

title: CamAct: Learning Robotic Manipulation from In-the-Wild Videos via Camera Motion
authors: Haoming Gu,Yunpeng Qing,Zhi Hou,Weinan Zhang
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models benefit from large, diverse datasets for robotic manipulation, yet collecting robot demonstrations remains costly. Recent work has explored egocentric videos as a source of supervision, primarily drawing on demonstrations of human–object interaction. We show that in-the-wild videos can improve robotic manipulation even when they contain no demonstrations of object manipulation. Specifically, camera motion recovered from these videos provides an additional source of motion supervision that complements robot demonstrations. Building on this finding, we introduce CamAct, which incorporates this camera-motion supervision into VLA policies alongside robot demonstrations, extending the use of human videos for manipulation learning beyond object interactions. Experiments show that incorporating this video supervision during fine-tuning improves success rates from 96.40% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 22.96% to 29.32% on RoboCasa 365. The resulting policy also demonstrates strong results in out-of-distribution generalization on LIBERO-Plus and real-world manipulation tasks.
introduction:
Developing manipulation policies that generalize across tasks and environments is a central goal in robotics. Vision-language-action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language understanding, and action generation within a single policy for robotic manipulation [23, 4]. These models benefit from diverse training data for generalization, including robot demonstrations collected in real-world environments, as well as egocentric human videos [3, 26]. Although recent efforts have built large-scale datasets from demonstrations collected across robot embodiments [37, 20], scaling robot demonstration data remains challenging due to the high cost of real-world collection and annotation, as well as embodiment-specific requirements. Egocentric human videos provide a lower-cost source of supervision for robot learning, yet existing approaches primarily focus on human–object interactions to complement robot demonstrations [19, 41]. In contrast, large language models benefit from diverse web-scale data [2, 36, 1], motivating us to explore whether robotic manipulation can benefit from broader video sources, including egocentric videos without explicit object manipulation demonstrations (Fig. 1).

Web-scale data have been widely used to train vision-language models (VLMs), with recent efforts further incorporating such data into VLA pretraining or adapting VLMs for downstream policy learning through vision-language tasks [17, 52, 12]. However, generalization in robotic manipulation requires understanding not only visual semantics but also the motion and dynamics of environments. This motivates us to explore whether the rich motion information in web videos can further benefit manipulation policy learning. CityWalker [34] demonstrates that camera trajectories recovered from in-the-wild videos can provide effective motion supervision for navigation policies. Moreover, recent unified frameworks show that jointly training on navigation and manipulation trajectories can benefit both domains [53, 48, 55]. Building on these insights, we investigate whether camera motion from in-the-wild walking videos can provide additional supervision for manipulation policies, even without explicit object interactions.

As humans walk through real-world environments, egocentric cameras capture rich spatial and motion information through changing viewpoints, as wrist-mounted cameras do during robotic manipulation. Although these videos contain no explicit object interactions, their camera motion provides a potential source of supervision for learning transferable spatial and motion representations. Building on this observation, we propose CamAct, a unified VLA framework that jointly learns from robot demonstrations and camera motion in in-the-wild videos. Specifically, we recover camera trajectories offline and convert them into pseudo-actions, allowing both robot actions and camera-derived pseudo-actions to be learned through a shared VLA backbone and action head. Through this joint training, CamAct aims to improve manipulation generalization by learning from diverse real-world camera motion.

We evaluate CamAct on LIBERO [32] and RoboCasa 365 [35] using StarVLA [11] as the base model. Joint training with camera motion improves success rates from 96.40% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 22.96% to 29.32% on RoboCasa 365. CamAct further demonstrates improved out-of-distribution generalization on LIBERO-Plus [14] and promising performance on real-world manipulation tasks. Extensive ablations and motion distribution analyses examine how video characteristics and training configurations influence downstream performance.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We explore the potential of in-the-wild videos for robotic manipulation beyond visual-semantic learning, showing that camera motion can provide useful supervision even without explicit object interactions.

We explore the potential of in-the-wild videos for robotic manipulation beyond visual-semantic learning, showing that camera motion can provide useful supervision even without explicit object interactions.

We propose CamAct, a unified VLA framework that jointly learns from robot demonstrations and camera-derived pseudo-actions, demonstrating consistent improvements in manipulation performance and out-of-distribution generalization.

We conduct extensive ablations and motion distribution analyses to investigate how video characteristics, data composition, and training design choices affect downstream manipulation performance.

1. We explore the potential of in-the-wild videos for robotic manipulation beyond visual-semantic learning, showing that camera motion can provide useful supervision even without explicit object interactions.

2. We propose CamAct, a unified VLA framework that jointly learns from robot demonstrations and camera-derived pseudo-actions, demonstrating consistent improvements in manipulation performance and out-of-distribution generalization.

3. We conduct extensive ablations and motion distribution analyses to investigate how video characteristics, data composition, and training design choices affect downstream manipulation performance.

title: Autonomous Vineyard Exploration using LiDAR Sensing: A Field Evaluation on Legged-Wheeled Quadruped Robot
authors: Spencer Sweeney,Hongbo Li,Michael Ziegltrum,Dimitra Koumoutsou,Andromachi Maria Delfaki,Taskin Padir,Dimitrios Kanoulas
abstract: Autonomous navigation in vineyards presents significant challenges due to uneven terrain, sparse vegetation, and the repetitive geometric nature of vineyard rows. This paper evaluates a LiDAR-based autonomous exploration system deployed on a Unitree Go2 Wheeled quadruped robot. Our approach utilizes an iterative RANSAC-based line detection pipeline to identify vineyard rows and a finite-state navigation strategy to govern row selection and traversal. Field evaluations conducted at Denbies Vineyard (UK) demonstrate the system’s ability to perform sustained autonomous row following, completing a 370​m370\,\mathrm{m} up-and-down traversal without intervention. We analyze the failure modes encountered, specifically focusing on line detection instability in sparse vegetation and the trade-offs of spatial filtering. The results suggest that, while RANSAC provides a robust geometric primitive, additional temporal filtering and adaptive perception are required for reliable lane-to-lane transitions in commercial vineyard environments. A video of the experimental results is available at: youtu.be/1om1HFGF4ps
introduction:
Autonomous navigation is a key enabling capability for agricultural robots tasked with monitoring, inspection, and field operations, but reliable autonomy remains difficult in unstructured outdoor environments due to terrain variability, sensing uncertainty, and seasonal change [bechar2016agrirobots, bac2014harvesting, sebastian2025stepp]. Vineyards present a particularly demanding setting: rows are narrow and repetitive, terrain is often sloped and muddy, and vegetation structure varies strongly across growth stages and management practices.

A range of sensing modalities have been explored for row-based agricultural navigation. GNSS/RTK solutions offer high accuracy but require costly infrastructure and prior surveying [lee2024compact]. Vision-based approaches exploit appearance cues from monocular or RGB-D cameras but remain sensitive to illumination, shadows, and seasonal canopy changes [mendez2023vision]. LiDAR, by contrast, provides direct geometric measurements that are largely invariant to lighting conditions, making it suitable for the high variability of the appearance of outdoor agricultural environments [shi2023row]. LiDAR-based perception has also been shown to support real-time mapping and terrain understanding at scale in unstructured outdoor environments [jiao2025metricsemantic], further motivating its use as the primary perception modality for field deployment.

Despite recent progress in LiDAR-based vineyard navigation, there remains limited reporting on deployment-time failure modes and perception–planning interactions during extended real-world operation, particularly under late-season conditions where row boundaries may only be intermittently observable.

In this work, we evaluate a LiDAR-based autonomous vineyard exploration system deployed on a Unitree Go2-W wheeled quadruped. Rather than proposing a new row-detection primitive, this paper contributes a deployment-driven evaluation: (i) we demonstrate sustained autonomous in-row navigation in a commercial vineyard, including a fully autonomous 370​m370\,\mathrm{m} up-and-down traversal; (ii) we analyze failure modes arising from intermittent observability under sparse vegetation; and (iii) we examine mitigation strategies and their trade-offs between in-row stability and lane-to-lane exploratory capability.

title: Ground Your Steps: Optimizing Sampling Schedules in Flow Matching Robot Policies
authors: Licheng Yang,Yonghao He,Lingfeng Qian,Xin Shi,Wei Sui,Hu Su
abstract:
Flow matching robot policies generate action chunks by integrating a
learned velocity field at inference.
However, under a fixed budget of neural function evaluations (NFEs),
the integration result depends on the sampling schedule.
This motivates optimizing the schedule to bring the generated action
distribution closer to the demonstrations and improve task success.
We propose Ground Your Steps (GYS), a training-free method that optimizes
the sampling schedule by matching the generated and demonstrated chunk
distributions at each observation.
GYS applies truncated fractional differencing along each arm
joint’s action sequence and compares two types of pairwise differences
between action chunks at each observation: differences of a generated
chunk against a demonstration, and differences of two independent
generated chunks against each other.
After fractional differencing, these two pairwise-difference distributions
coincide exactly when the
distributions of generated and demonstrated action chunks match.
GYS minimizes the energy distance between these distributions
to obtain an improved schedule for each task and NFE budget.
Compared with the uniform grid, GYS brings the
generated chunk distribution closer to
the demonstrated distribution and raises the
success rate through the sampling schedule alone.
On RoboTwin 2.0 benchmarks, GYS improves success rates at nearly every budget,
with gains of 2.82.8 percentage points for both π0.5\pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.7.
The gains also transfer to three real-world manipulation tasks,
reaching up to 3.33.3 percentage points.
Code is available at https://github.com/D-Robotics-AI-Lab/GroundYourSteps.
introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models translate visual observations and
language instructions into robot actions
(Ma et al., 2026b; Kawaharazuka et al., 2025).
Flow-based VLAs couple pretrained vision–language backbones with action
experts (Black et al., 2025b).
Recent models use flow matching
(Black et al., 2025a; NVIDIA et al., 2025) to generate these actions
in chunks (Zhao et al., 2023).
During training, the action expert predicts the velocities of straight
paths from Gaussian noise to demonstrated action chunks.
Under squared loss, the optimal prediction is the conditional average
of these velocities at a given state, flow time, and observation,
called the marginal velocity field
(Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023).
Exact integration of this field transports Gaussian noise to the
demonstrated action distribution (Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023).
In practice, however, the policy integrates a learned approximation to the
marginal field with finite neural function evaluations (NFEs), so the
generated action distribution can deviate from the demonstrated distribution.

Two mechanisms shape the generated action distribution under this finite-step
integration.
(i) Trajectory curvature—averaging differently directed path
velocities can produce curved marginal trajectories, which coarse
integration steps may fail to resolve
(Ma et al., 2026a; Kornilov et al., 2024).
(ii) Lipschitz window—near the action endpoint, the marginal
field can become highly sensitive to the action state, allowing small
deviations from the marginal flow to be amplified
(Gao et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026b) (Section A.3).
Since curvature and the amplification of small deviations vary along
flow time, evaluations at different times need not influence the
endpoint distribution equally.
Choosing these evaluation times, the sampling schedule, therefore
provides a way to change the generated distribution.
Our goal is to optimize the sampling schedule to bring the generated
distribution into agreement with the demonstrations and improve task
success for each fixed budget BB.

To see whether these distributional effects matter in closed loop, we vary
the NFE budget and sampling schedule for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.7 across
50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks (, panel (a)).
Under uniform sampling, success peaks at B=4B=4 for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and B=6B=6
for GR00T N1.7, then falls at larger budgets.
At fixed B=5B=5, a moderate bias toward the noise endpoint outperforms
the uniform grid, whereas concentrating nodes near either endpoint
lowers success.
The non-monotonic budget trend and fixed-budget schedule sensitivity are
consistent with the combined effects of trajectory curvature and
late-time amplification.
Taken with the mechanisms above, these observations identify the
sampling schedule as a lever on both the generated action distribution
and task success.
They motivate a demonstration-grounded criterion for selecting
evaluation times at each fixed budget.

We propose Ground Your Steps (GYS), a training-free method that
grounds the sampling schedule in the demonstrations, motivated by
Drifting (Deng et al., 2026), which trains a generator by
driving its generated distribution into agreement with the data
distribution.
GYS’s target is that the chunks the frozen policy generates be
distributed as the demonstrated ones at each observation.
GYS compares candidate sampling schedules using a
truncated fractional-difference operator: it applies finite
differences of a calibrated, possibly non-integer order along each arm
joint’s action sequence. This generalizes first-order differences
between consecutive actions and second-order differences between those
changes, using a fixed window of action steps.
One demonstrated chunk per observation still cannot estimate the
demonstrated distribution, so GYS instead compares two types of
pairwise differences: generated–demonstrated differences and
generated–generated differences, formed at the same observation using
independent noise draws. Both are transformed by the fractional-difference
operator. Under the stated identifiability assumptions, their distributions
coincide exactly when the transformed action distributions match,
so driving them into agreement realizes this target
(Section 4.2).
GYS optimizes the sampling schedule offline for each task by
minimizing an energy distance between the two transformed
pairwise-difference distributions
(, panel (c)), and the optimized schedule
replaces the uniform one.
At the same budget, GYS brings the generated distribution closer to
the demonstrated one and raises the task success rate.

We validate GYS on a simulation benchmark and on a real robot.
On 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks (Chen et al., 2026a) at 3 to 10 NFEs,
GYS raises the mean closed-loop success rate from 67.5% to
70.3% for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and from 49.2% to 52.0% for GR00T N1.7
(, panel (d)).
On three real-world manipulation tasks at 3 and 4 NFEs, it raises
the success rate from 67.7% to 69.5% for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and from 63.5%
to 66.5% for GR00T N1.7.
Across nearly every fixed budget, GYS raises the task success rate, and
the gain comes from the optimized sampling schedule alone, with the
weights and the inference cost untouched.

title: WorldPhy: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Physical Plausibility of World Models in Robotics
authors: Ziyuan Chu,Mingzhi Zheng,Kaiyue Zhang,Jinan Zhang,Linchao Zhu
abstract:
World models are increasingly used in robotics to improve the performance of embodied models. Compared with general-purpose video generation, robotics places more stringent requirements on world models. Generated videos must satisfy fine-grained physical constraints on robot motion and object interactions. However, existing world model benchmarks can overlook robotics specific physical details and struggle to assess them accurately. To address this problem, we introduce WorldPhy, a world model benchmark for accurate, fine-grained evaluation of physical plausibility in robotics. Our benchmark contains 300 tasks, each consisting of an initial-frame image and a task instruction, covering diverse robotics scenes, task categories, viewpoints, and robot configurations. We further collect over 12K high-quality human annotations, and use them to train WorldPhyReward to accurately provide scores and reasons across six fine-grained physical dimensions and an instruction-following dimension. Comparisons with general VLMs and existing reward models show that WorldPhyReward better aligns with human ratings. We systematically evaluate 13 frontier open and closed-source world models. The results reveal that current world models struggle to consistently maintain fine-grained physical plausibility across different robotics scenarios.
Our code is available at https://github.com/chuziyuan139/WorldPhy.
introduction:
World models predict future frames from observations, language instructions, or actions to support planning [1]. In robotics, they improve embodied models by generating training data and predicting future frames for policy selection [18, 35, 11].

Robotics differs from general-purpose video generation and places more stringent requirements on world models. To be useful in robotics, generated videos must satisfy a range of fine-grained physical criteria, such as robot joint rotation limits, the falling speeds of objects, and gripper opening ranges. As shown in Table 1, existing world model benchmarks can be grouped into two categories. One category targets general-purpose video generation, including VBench [16], WorldModelBench [19], VideoPhy-2 [4], and Physics-IQ [25]. These benchmarks offer broad evaluations of video quality, but may overlook robotics-specific physical details. The other category of benchmarks focuses on robotics, including RBench [8] and the benchmarks introduced in ReWorld [27], ABot-PhysWorld [6], and RoboGaze [26]. These works emphasize physical plausibility in robotic scenarios. However, their evaluation protocols use general vision-language models (VLMs) without task-specific fine-tuning. Evaluating robotic manipulation videos requires robotics specific knowledge such as joint connections, ranges of motion, end-effector contact, and object support. General VLMs may lack certain knowledge. Meanwhile, physical violations, such as interpenetration and contact failures, can usually occur briefly and within small image regions. General VLMs without targeted training may miss these details, limiting evaluation accuracy. These limitations motivate a robotics-specific benchmark with a reward model specifically trained to accurately assess fine-grained physical plausibility of robotic manipulation videos.

We introduce WorldPhy, a benchmark tailored to robotics with a specifically trained reward model that provides accurate and fine-grained evaluation. We collect a large number of real-world and simulated videos of robotics scenarios, extract the corresponding images and instructions, and select 300 image–instruction pairs covering diverse viewpoints and tasks to evaluate world models. We also generate a large collection of videos through multiple world models and develop a detailed pipeline to annotate scores and corresponding reasons along multiple evaluation dimensions. After filtering, we obtain over 12K high-quality human-annotated examples and use them to train a dedicated reward model WorldPhyReward. Given the task inputs and a video generated by a world model, WorldPhyReward produces fine-grained scores and reasons across six physical evaluation dimensions and an instruction-following dimension.

Using this trained reward model, we evaluate 13 world models. The evaluation results show that Kling-3.0, MiniMax-H3, and Seedance2 lead in overall scores, but all models receive their two lowest scores for contact and interaction causality and for support and motion dynamics. Instruction following is generally a relative strength, yet no model achieves a perfect score on this dimension, and stronger instruction following does not necessarily imply better overall performance. Furthermore, 12 of the 13 models score lower in gripper scenarios than in hand scenarios, and most models receive their lowest scores under the wrist view among the three evaluated viewpoints. These findings indicate that, although some existing world models have achieved strong overall performance, they still cannot consistently ensure fine-grained physical plausibility across different robotics scenarios. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We construct a world model benchmark for robotics scenarios that supports fine-grained evaluation of physical plausibility.

We construct a world model benchmark for robotics scenarios that supports fine-grained evaluation of physical plausibility.

We develop a detailed pipeline to collect over 12K high-quality human-annotated video-scoring examples with fine-grained labels and train WorldPhyReward using this data. This model provides scores and reasons for each evaluation dimension and outperforms general-purpose VLMs such as GPT-6 Astra and video reward models such as WorldModelBench on our test set.

We systematically evaluate 13 current open and closed-source world models. The results reveal shared weaknesses in contact causality and support dynamics, with additional limitations in gripper manipulation and wrist-view scenarios over these world models.

title: WAtcher: Watching Ahead for Safe Robotic Manipulation with Efficient World-Action Models
authors: Ziyu Shan,Xiao Ma,Kangrui Yu,Changjie Wang,Gaoyuan Wu,Zaijia Yang,Chuanrui Zhang,Qirui Li,Yanbo Zhang,Duomin Wang,Ziwei Wang
abstract: World-action models (WAMs) couple future imagination with action generation, but they execute every action chunk while ignoring the potential risk. To fill this gap, we present WAtcher, a safety-aware world-action framework in which the policy imagines the outcome of the candidate chunk before execution. For fast future preview, WAtcher builds on a compact WAM whose video expert imagines the visual outcome in only two denoising steps. In addition, we propose Safe-Guard, a lightweight module kept outside the WAM that scores each candidate chunk from its imagined outcome and triggers a bounded retreat when the risk is high. Safe-Guard is detachable and can be applied to other WAMs. To train Safe-Guard, we build an autonomous pipeline to collect hazard data from RoboTwin, LIBERO, and a real robot. Specifically, the pipeline perturbs expert demonstrations and labels each candidate chunk from the physical events recorded when it is executed, such as contacts and losses of support. Using the ∼{\sim}25,000 labeled windows from this pipeline, Safe-Guard reaches 92.1% balanced accuracy on a blind set, and cuts hazardous closed-loop trials on training tasks from 27.0% to 10.8% without lowering task success. On a held-out 300-question benchmark, it scores 94.2%, against 72.5% and 63.3% for zero-shot GPT-6-Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. WAtcher also reaches 90.4% and 82.4% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ManiSkill3, on par with or above leading WAMs, and 74.0% on five real-world tasks with Safe-Guard on, against 59.5% for π0.5\pi_{0.5}. Project page: https://zyshan0929.github.io/WAtcher.
introduction:
World-action models (WAMs) unify future forecasting and action generation in a shared generative model and have become a strong paradigm for robotic manipulation [59, 57, 41]. However, mainstream WAMs execute every action chunk they generate without a check. The training demonstrations also rarely contain hazardous outcomes such as collisions, slips, or dropped objects, and the training objectives never supervise risk. Whether a chunk is hazardous depends jointly on the scene, the robot state, and the commanded motion, so the same chunk can pass safely in one layout and collide in another. Detecting risk before execution requires anticipating the outcome of each candidate, at every decision step and within the latency budget of the policy.

Our key observation is that WAMs of a common design already contain the forward model that such a safety check needs. When the video and action experts share joint attention and are trained with decoupled noise levels and a video loss that reaches the action tokens [68, 28], the video expert can take a fixed candidate chunk as a clean condition and imagine a coarse outcome, as in the forward mode of Unified World Model (UWM) [68], so no additional world model has to be trained or used. To make this imagination fast enough for real-time use, WAtcher builds on an efficient architecture [28], a compact WAM trained in this way, whose video expert, distilled from a large video generator, imagines a candidate’s low-resolution outcome in only two denoising steps. This fast future preview provides a solid basis for a pre-execution risk check in practical deployment.

On top of this imagination, WAtcher places Safe-Guard, a lightweight risk head, between the policy and the robot (Fig. 1). Safe-Guard fuses the current views, the robot state, every command of the candidate, and its imagined outcome with a small Transformer, scores the action chunk, and executes low-risk chunks while replacing high-risk ones with a bounded retreat. Unlike monitors that read policy features [18] or train a separate world model [65, 52], Safe-Guard reuses the policy’s own video expert and learns from physical events recorded in executed hazards rather than from task failure [15, 13]. Because it is trained separately and leaves the policy weights unchanged, Safe-Guard can serve other WAMs. With Fast-WAM-Joint [60], the variant of Fast-WAM whose video and action tokens attend to each other, it also lowers hazardous executions compared with that WAM alone (Sec. 5.3).

To train Safe-Guard, we build an autonomous pipeline that perturbs expert trajectories in RoboTwin 2.0 [10], LIBERO [35], and on a real UR7e. The pipeline executes every candidate and labels it from recorded physical events, with an LLM agent reviewing ambiguous cases and a human verifying the real-robot labels. It constructs four hazard types: unintended contacts (e.g., collisions), losses of support (e.g., slips, failed hanging), generic motion errors, and semantic dangers (e.g., a knife moving toward a hand) that no contact threshold captures, yielding ∼{\sim}25,000 labeled windows. Trained on this dataset, Safe-Guard reaches 92.1% balanced accuracy on a blind set of 1,352 windows, ahead of a fine-tuned 8B vision-language model (VLM; 89.4%) and a ContactGuard-style monitor (87.9%). It also reduces hazardous closed-loop trials in new scenes of training tasks from 27.0% to 10.8%, against 15.3% for the ContactGuard-style monitor at the same rejection rate, without lowering task success rates.

For a fair comparison with zero-shot multimodal large language models (MLLMs), we also establish a held-out 300-question benchmark that covers every hazard type in RoboTwin and LIBERO. It also includes 101 same-state pairs that differ only in the candidate. On the 300-question benchmark, our lightweight Safe-Guard scores 94.2%, against 72.5% and 63.3% for zero-shot GPT-6-Astra and Claude Opus 5.5.
On simulation suites, our WAtcher reaches 90.4% and 82.4% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ManiSkill3, on par with or above leading WAMs such as Fast-WAM [60] and LingBot-VA [29].
On a UR7e robot platform, it reaches 74.0% on five real-world tasks with Safe-Guard on, against 59.5% for π0.5\pi_{0.5}. For safety on the real robot, Safe-Guard, adapted with 258 human-verified windows, reduces staged hazards from 43 to 6 out of 60.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose an autonomous pipeline that collects and labels hazardous executions in two simulators (i.e., RoboTwin and LIBERO) and on a real robot, with a comprehensive 300-question benchmark and a larger-size blind set for fair evaluation.

We propose Safe-Guard, a detachable risk head that scores each action candidate from the observations, commands, and the outcome imagined by the WAM’s own video expert in 32 ms. The head can also be applied to another WAM.

Based on the collected data and the Safe-Guard, we propose WAtcher, which runs a risk check before every chunk, retreats from risky ones, and reduces hazardous executions in simulation and on a UR7e robot while preserving original task success.

1. We propose an autonomous pipeline that collects and labels hazardous executions in two simulators (i.e., RoboTwin and LIBERO) and on a real robot, with a comprehensive 300-question benchmark and a larger-size blind set for fair evaluation.

2. We propose Safe-Guard, a detachable risk head that scores each action candidate from the observations, commands, and the outcome imagined by the WAM’s own video expert in 32 ms. The head can also be applied to another WAM.

3. Based on the collected data and the Safe-Guard, we propose WAtcher, which runs a risk check before every chunk, retreats from risky ones, and reduces hazardous executions in simulation and on a UR7e robot while preserving original task success.

title: CoTacWAM: Joint Modeling of Vision and Touch for Robotic Manipulation
authors: Lei Jin,Yiding Ma,Zhuohang Li,Jiachen Liu,Zibo Zhu,Kairui Liu,Chen Gao,Wei Wu,Yong Li
abstract:
We present CoTacWAM, a world-action model that learns shared contact semantics between wrist vision and touch, achieving the best observed performance in our nominal manipulation and missing-input evaluations.
The two modalities observe the same local interaction through different signals: wrist images reveal nearby geometry, while touch records physical contact.
Our approach connects their common contact meaning while preserving the evidence unique to each modality, giving the policy a joint description of interaction across available input combinations.
This representation supports predictive action learning alongside head-view scene context and conditions corrections after an independent detector confirms a failed attempt.
Experiments across four real-world tasks demonstrate improved manipulation performance over the evaluated baselines, robustness to missing local observations, and further gains from autonomous retries.
introduction:
Learning-based manipulation models increasingly translate visual observations and instructions into useful robot behavior [3, 41].
Generalist policies extend this capability through diverse robot demonstrations [9] and pretrained vision–language knowledge [17, 2, 27].
World-action models further connect action learning with prediction of future sensory changes [37].
For contact-rich manipulation, useful motion depends on understanding the physical interaction it produces.
Wrist vision and touch offer two observations of this interaction: an image shows the gripper closing around an object, while tactile measurements reveal the resulting contact.
Their signals differ, but both carry evidence about a common event.
Learning what these observations share could help a policy relate visible local changes to physical contact.

Recent policies integrate heterogeneous tactile sensors [36] and exploit visual–tactile relationships through cross-modal fusion and prediction [10, 38].
Visuotactile world-action models further connect future sensory prediction with control [31, 23].
However, making both streams useful to a policy does not by itself specify a common physical interpretation of their signals.
We therefore ask: how can wrist vision and touch express common contact meaning, and how can this shared understanding support control?
Wrist images contribute local geometry, while touch provides direct physical measurements.
A useful joint representation should therefore connect their common meaning while retaining the evidence unique to each modality.
With complete observations, both kinds of information can inform control; with an input missing, the remaining evidence should still support the contact concepts it can reveal.

We introduce CoTacWAM, which organizes wrist vision and touch around shared physical concepts: whether pad–object contact occurs and its coarse strength.
Alongside this common description, the representation preserves the sensory detail needed for manipulation.
By learning this description from paired observations and varying their availability, we form a joint representation that can be read through the same interface across input combinations.
Wrist vision enters through a lightweight trainable interface, while a separate head-view pathway supplies scene context.
We use the learned joint representation to describe current interaction and supervise its future evolution during predictive action learning.
When an attempt fails, an independent detector provides a failure event; the policy combines this context with updated joint observations to generate a correction and resume execution.

We evaluate this approach on four real-world tasks spanning insertion, surface interaction, liquid handling, and fragile-object manipulation.
CoTacWAM achieves 71.3% mean success without retries, compared with 35.0% for the strongest baseline.
Representation analyses show that contact semantics are readable from both modalities through a shared head, while the joint representation retains physical interaction detail.
Without wrist vision, the complete system retains 70% and 75% success on wiping and tofu grasping, where all three tactile baselines achieve 0%.
Autonomous retries further improve insertion and wiping success.

Our contributions are threefold:

A joint wrist–tactile representation that establishes shared contact semantics while retaining complementary sensory evidence under varying input availability.

Integration of this representation into predictive action learning and failure-conditioned correction, with head-view scene context supplied separately.

Four-task robot evaluations, representation analyses, and ablations connecting task performance with semantic accessibility, information retention, and temporal learning.

1. A joint wrist–tactile representation that establishes shared contact semantics while retaining complementary sensory evidence under varying input availability.

2. Integration of this representation into predictive action learning and failure-conditioned correction, with head-view scene context supplied separately.

3. Four-task robot evaluations, representation analyses, and ablations connecting task performance with semantic accessibility, information retention, and temporal learning.

title: xFORM: Accelerating Fixed-Lag LiDAR Odometry with Exact Factor Compression
authors: Ruogu Li,Easton R. Potokar,Michael Kaess
abstract:
A increasingly popular sensor, Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) have been successfully used for state estimation due to their precision, long range capabilities and high sensor rate.
Unfortunately, Light Detection and Ranging Odometry systems incur substantial computational cost when processing large point clouds, particularly those that jointly refine a window of scan poses.
While our prior Light Detection and Ranging Odometry work FORM is real-time, the costs of feature extraction, correspondence search, and the evaluation and linearization of residuals during pose optimization can introduce significant latency. This latency makes downstream tasks such as control and path planning difficult.
To overcome this, we present xFORM, which accelerates the three stages of FORM.
xFORM uses factor compression to reduce an optimization problem involving hundreds of thousands of feature matches to 34 scalar residuals per scan pair, while preserving the original objective and Gauss-Newton system in exact arithmetic.
We integrate this optimizer into two variants: xFORM-CPU, which additionally parallelizes feature extraction on the CPU, and xFORM-GPU, which accelerates feature processing, correspondence search, and factor compression on the GPU.
Across fifteen complete sequences from three datasets, xFORM-CPU and xFORM-GPU achieve overall speedups of 1.1–1.4×\times and 2.0–4.0×\times over FORM, respectively, with no numerically significant differences to the original implementation.
introduction:
Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) sensors have become the de facto sensor for many field robotic state estimation tasks due to their precision, reliability, and high speed scanning of environments. They have successfully been utilized in applications such as aerial vehicles, quadrapeds, and ground vehicles, with major improvements in accuracy and reliability over prior sensor modalities [1].

Most current state-of-the-art Light Detection and Ranging Odometry methods unfortunately have properties that often invalidate their usage as input to the underlying vehicle controller. To be able to properly used as a control input, state estimates must be high rate, accurate, and produce smooth trajectories. We note that our prior work, FORM [2], produces state-of-the-art accurate and smooth trajectories at real-time speeds, but often returns results at near 100 ms100\text{\,}\mathrm{ms} latency.

In feature-based LiDAR odometry, processing a scan involves three main stages: feature extraction, correspondence search, and pose optimization.
Feature extraction selects points that represent useful geometric structures and computes properties such as surface normals.
Correspondence search finds matching features in previous scans or a local map.
Pose optimization uses these matches to estimate the sensor poses by minimizing geometric alignment errors, called residuals.
Across our evaluated sequences, FORM extracts 5,000–18,800 feature points per scan on average, resulting in a final optimization containing 53,000–268,000 matches connecting 22–44 poses on average.
These numbers create substantial computational work in all three stages.

We present xFORM, which accelerates FORM through exact factor compression and optimized CPU and GPU implementation.
For each scan pair, xFORM compresses the fixed match data into small matrices called factor summaries.
Evaluating these summaries at the current poses produces 34 scalar residuals per scan pair, regardless of the number of matches, while preserving the original nonlinear least-squares objective in exact arithmetic.
This reduces the work required to evaluate and linearize the residuals during optimization.
Summaries remain valid as the poses change and need rebuilding only when their matches change.

Beyond pose optimization, xFORM accelerates feature extraction and correspondence search through CPU parallelism and GPU processing.
xFORM-CPU parallelizes planar-feature selection across scanlines and evaluates and linearizes factor summaries in parallel across scan pairs.
xFORM-GPU extends this implementation with GPU feature processing and correspondence search, constructing factor summaries directly within the GPU matching pipeline.

These changes give xFORM-CPU and xFORM-GPU end-to-end speedups of 1.1–1.4×\times and 2.0–4.0×\times, respectively, over FORM across the evaluated sequences.
For example, on Newer College Stairs, xFORM-CPU reduces mean processing time from 132.9 to 107.3 ms per scan, and xFORM-GPU reduces it from 132.9 to 32.9 ms while maintaining numerically identical results.

title: End-to-End Image-Goal Navigation for Agile Quadrotors via Recurrent State Distillation
authors: Simone Nascivera,Ismail Geles,Davide Scaramuzza
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Image-goal navigation asks a robot to reach the viewpoint of a target photograph without a map or goal pose.
In three dimensions, this requires not only recognizing the goal but also estimating 3D displacement and generating continuous control actions to approach and settle at the target view.
This is difficult because the same visual difference between current and goal image can require very different actions depending on the robot’s velocity, yet monocular images alone reveal neither metric scale nor body motion.
As a result, existing image-goal policies are limited to planar action spaces and rely on a state estimator for flight control.
Policies that map directly from images to low-level control commands have been demonstrated for agile flight, but not toward goal images in unseen environments.
We present the first image-goal navigation policy that directly commands thrust and angular rates for agile quadrotor flight in unseen 3D environments, without relying on state estimation (e.g., SLAM, VO, or SfM) or a separate velocity controller.
We train a recurrent vision-based policy through a four-stage pipeline that combines geometric and motion supervision with privileged-teacher distillation and end-to-end reinforcement learning fine-tuning.
On 1000 held-out flights in unseen environments, the policy achieves an 82.3% success rate with a mean terminal position error of 0.10 m across successful flights.
Deployed zero-shot on a real quadrotor, the policy reaches an 84% success rate over 25 trials in an unseen indoor environment.
introduction:
Human pilots navigate quadrotors through unfamiliar environments using only an onboard camera stream, without explicitly estimating the vehicle’s position, velocity, or attitude [10].
We investigate whether autonomous flight can similarly rely on visual feedback alone: given a goal photograph, a quadrotor must reach the viewpoint from which it was taken as quickly as possible (Fig. 1).
The photograph specifies a destination without requiring a map or a metric goal pose.
We study how to achieve this with a policy that maps visual observations and last applied actions directly to low-level control commands, without explicit state estimation such as Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), Visual Odometry (VO), or Structure from Motion (SfM) [2].

Extracting the information needed for flight control from onboard frames and policy’s past actions is challenging.
Reaching a goal viewpoint requires translating in three dimensions, aligning the camera, and braking to hover at the destination.
The appropriate control command depends not only on the displacement to the goal but also on the vehicle’s current motion.
However, velocity cannot be directly inferred from a single frame, and monocular observations leave metric scale ambiguous.

To address these limitations, we use a recurrent policy that integrates visual information over time, allowing it to implicitly infer the vehicle’s motion [32].
The previous control command provides additional information about the vehicle dynamics, helping reduce metric scale ambiguity [21].
Tilting the vehicle also changes its thrust direction and camera view together.
A visual policy must account for these coupled changes over time.

Recent work, such as SIGN [36], has explored aerial image-goal navigation.
While the authors demonstrate image-goal navigation on quadrotors, including real-world flight, the method outputs planar velocity commands, relying on a separate state-estimation-based controller for flight stabilization.
In parallel, vision-based policies have demonstrated agile flight by directly commanding low-level control inputs, without explicit state estimation [10, 11].
Combining image-goal navigation with such direct flight control remains an open challenge, particularly when requiring three-dimensional motion, precise settling at the goal, and generalization to unseen real-world environments.

We address this problem through a four-stage training pipeline (Fig. 2).
First, a state-based teacher learns to fly using privileged goal-relative pose and motion information.
We then train a visual representation from sequences of onboard images and a goal photograph, using geometric and motion supervision together with alignment to the teacher’s latent representation.
During the next stage, the student is trained through imitation learning using the teacher from the first stage.
Finally, reinforcement learning fine-tunes the student policy in closed loop.
At deployment, the policy receives only the current image, the goal photograph, and its previous command, with no access to position, velocity, attitude, or IMU measurements.

(1) To our knowledge, we present the first image-goal flight policy that directly commands low-level control inputs in unfamiliar environments without explicit state estimation.
(2) We introduce a four-stage training procedure that combines geometric and motion supervision, latent representation alignment, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning to learn a vision-based flight policy.
(3) We evaluate the policy on 1000 held-out flights in 100 unseen environments, achieving an 82.3% success rate with a mean terminal position error of 0.10 m\mathrm{m} across successful flights, and demonstrate zero-shot transfer to a real quadrotor with an 84% success rate over 25 trials in an unseen indoor environment.

title: WISER-RL: A Wake-Sleep Learning Mechanism for Robot Reinforcement Learning from One Demonstration
authors: Kwunhang Wong,Yang Bai,Qingyang Bao,Liudi Yang,Chenzhi Liu,Jiehong Lin,Wei Huang,Lin Li,Ziyuan Liu,Yujie Yang,Gitta Kutyniok,Zhongrui Wang,Xiaojuan Qi
abstract: A robot learning from one human demonstration may rarely succeed on its own, leaving reinforcement learning with little reward feedback. We introduce WISER-RL (Wake–sleep policy improvement loop, Imitation, and Selective Experience Replay), a composite reinforcement learning framework that turns assisted practice into autonomous control. During wake, GPTDAgger monitors disagreement among actions sampled by a diffusion policy. When disagreement crosses a threshold, a frozen GPT controller uses retrieved experience to continue the episode. During sleep, Conflict-Aware Experience Reweighting (CAER) compares visually matched successful trajectories and downweights conflicting action windows with more steps remaining to success. The policy imitates the reweighted successes and learns from both successes and failures through offline advantage-guided RL before collecting the next round. After final online PPO refinement, the autonomous policy succeeded in 100% evaluations on each of six LIBERO tasks and 100% trials on each of two real-robot tasks.
introduction:
A central goal of robotics is to acquire a new skill from one or a few human demonstrations and become proficient through practice [6]. A person can watch an example, reason about how it applies to a different scene, and gradually perform the skill with less deliberate effort. For robots, this motivates combining rapid adaptation from examples with lasting autonomous competence.

Reinforcement learning (RL) refines robotic policies through interaction [27, 16], but initially weak policies struggle to collect useful experience. With sparse success rewards, many attempts can fail before the robot discovers a useful behavior [3, 36, 22, 30, 11]. Recently, models such as GPT-6-Astra have demonstrated the ability to adapt from one or a few examples through in-context learning [4]. Drawing on strong reasoning and broad prior knowledge, these models can interpret a demonstration and apply it to a new scene. Yet this contextual ability does not automatically translate into a fast, efficient learned policy. The challenge is to turn adaptation from a few examples into an autonomous policy that improves through practice.

WISER-RL couples fast episodic adaptation with slow policy consolidation (Fig. 1). A frozen contextual controller bootstraps a demonstration immediately, while a diffusion policy learns from the interaction rollouts across rounds.

One human demonstration can bootstrap GPT rollouts to initialize diffusion policy, but very costly [5]. In wake phase, GPTDAgger acts decreasingly when small policy’s sampled actions acts improving. Retrieved experience and the executed prefix guide GPT intervention without training a task-specific teacher [38]. In sleep phase, the policy imitates selected successful actions and uses offline RL to finetune from both successes and failures. The updated policy collects the next round of experience. Final online refinement uses fresh autonomous interaction for 100% success.

A successful episode can contain a missed grasp and a recovery. When another episode reaches a visually similar state and grasps the object directly, both continuations receive the same terminal reward. Uniform imitation can therefore teach the retry alongside the direct grasp.

Inspired by adaptive forgetting, we propose Conflict-Aware Experience Reweighting (CAER) for reciprocal visual matches across successful episodes to modulate the sampling probability of action windows during behavioral cloning (BC). When matched action chunks conflict, CAER prunes imitating the window with more observed steps remaining to success. Offline RL can still learn from the outcomes of both trajectories. Our contributions are threefold:

Composite learning through WISER-RL. We introduce an offline recurring wake–sleep mechanism that connects contextual experience acquisition with imitation and outcome-guided policy improvement, followed by final online refinement. Each consolidated policy drives subsequent interaction, providing a route from limited human demonstrations to autonomous control.

Composite learning through WISER-RL. We introduce an offline recurring wake–sleep mechanism that connects contextual experience acquisition with imitation and outcome-guided policy improvement, followed by final online refinement. Each consolidated policy drives subsequent interaction, providing a route from limited human demonstrations to autonomous control.

Conflict-aware consolidation through CAER. We identify conflicting action replay memory across visually matched successful continuations and reweight imitation exposure according to observed efficiency, addressing direct imitate GPT policy unstable data source within the WISER-RL loop.

Simulation and real-robot evaluation. Starting from one human demonstration per task, we demonstrate reducing GPT token cost and increasing autonomous success across training stages. After online refinement, the policy succeeded in 50/50 evaluations across six LIBERO tasks and 20/20 across two real-robot tasks.
