title: Ask to Land: Learning a Mask-Conditioned Open-Vocabulary Landing Policy via Differentiable Physics
authors: Fangyu Sun,Guanyan Wu,Yang Deng,Jiahao Cui,Fanxing Li,Yuxiang Huang,Wenxian Yu,Danping Zou
abstract: Existing drone landing systems, whether model-based or learning-based, typically rely on predefined visual markers (e.g., ArUco tags) or are trained for specific platform categories, and often assume structured target motion. Recent open-vocabulary studies enable text-prompted target selection, but integrating this capability with learned closed-loop landing control remains underexplored. To this end, we present Ask to Land, a mask-conditioned framework that enables a quadrotor to land on various platforms described by a user in natural language, including randomly moving platforms. The core of our approach is the integration of a frozen state-of-the-art open-vocabulary perception frontend (YOLO-World with MobileSAM) and a control policy learned by differentiable physics. By providing real-time, task-agnostic semantic segmentation masks as policy inputs, our framework enables the drone to land on prompt-selected targets without target-specific fine-tuning while continuously tracking dynamic target motion during descent. The frozen frontend processes the prompt, while the policy receives the mask without text embeddings or category labels. To efficiently optimize the control policy, we leverage differentiable physics learning via Backpropagation-Through-Time (BPTT), and employ a carefully designed reward that enforces visual alignment with the landing target and altitude-adaptive descent speed, together with stable control. Real-world deployments validate that our approach achieves landings on diverse user-specified objects, including static and moving platforms.
introduction:
Imagine a rescue drone deployed in a disaster zone. Its mission is to land safely on a moving pickup truck or a distinctly colored supply box. The drone does not know the exact appearance of the target beforehand, and the target’s position changes unpredictably. Landing in such unstructured scenarios requires the drone to recognize user-specified targets on the fly and continuously adjust its descent speed to match unknown target motions.

Current autonomous landing systems struggle with these real-world conditions. Classical model-based methods often require predefined visual markers (like ArUco tags) or exact geometric priors of the landing pad [1, 2, 3, 4]. Learning-based methods typically train the drone for specific object categories [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. Recent open-vocabulary systems enable prompt-based landing-target selection, but do not learn a closed-loop policy that maps the selected target representation directly to low-level commands throughout the complete landing process [10, 11, 12, 13]. To address these challenges, we propose Ask to Land, a mask-conditioned framework designed to enable robust autonomous drone landing on diverse, user-specified platforms, including dynamic platforms that move along random trajectories. First, to overcome the limitations of predefined platform categories and achieve prompt-based target selection and controller transfer, we incorporate the semantic segmentation mask as the policy input. During real-world deployment, we leverage a frozen open-vocabulary detector, YOLO-World [14], in conjunction with a lightweight segmentation module, MobileSAM [15]. Guided by natural language prompts, this frontend generates real-time, task-agnostic semantic masks of the desired landing surface. By conditioning the control policy on these semantic representations rather than platform-specific labels or geometric priors, the learned policy can be applied to user-specified platforms of varying shapes, sizes, and categories, without requiring target-specific fine-tuning.

In addition, we employ domain randomization and curriculum learning during training. We randomize platform geometry and appearance, ground-plane motion with varying low speeds, as well as the initial positions of both the platform and the drone. The curriculum gradually increases task difficulty, starting from static platforms and progressing toward dynamic tasks with random trajectories and speeds. Finally, to improve training efficiency, we optimize the policy with Backpropagation-Through-Time (BPTT) through fully differentiable quadrotor dynamics, exploiting analytic gradients through the dynamics for faster convergence.

title: Hetero-Associative Visuomotor Memory: Soft Recall as a Base for Learned Residuals in Few-Demonstration Imitation
authors: Runcong Wang
abstract:
Retrieve-and-correct policies typically refine the nearest retrieved demonstration chunk, the readout that works best
when executed directly. We study what a demonstration memory should supply to the corrector instead and find that a
smooth, softmax-weighted recall over the whole memory is a much better base. On ALOHA cube transfer (40 human
demonstrations), soft recall is no better to execute alone than the nearest chunk; however, with keys, candidates, and
training fixed, correcting it raises success by 22.4 points on fresh resets with new encoders and by 7.4 against a
closed-loop-tuned top-1 corrector. On robomimic Square, it leads by 7.9 points with the two better operators and by 6.7
on a label-free draw of equal size. This gain holds on sparse, varied demonstrations under an action-aware key and
leave-one-demonstration-out training, and fades or slightly reverses on dense, scripted, or generated data. Building on
this finding, our hetero-associative visuomotor memory (HAVM, 14 M parameters) trains offline in about five minutes,
including a learned retrieval temperature β\beta, and runs in 1.1 ms. Across six fresh ALOHA encoders, it reaches
76.4 % within 24 s, comparable to a 264 M Diffusion Policy trained for 6.7 h (78.8 %) and ahead of ACT (71.7 %)
and fine-tuned VLAs (65.2–75.2 %), while leading every 40-demonstration baseline within the benchmark’s 8 s limit
(74.6 %; +6.5+6.5 over Diffusion Policy, +15.1+15.1 over ACT). On LIBERO, one 40-task memory reaches 92.2 % and loses far
less than SmolVLA to rewording; on a real SO-101 arm, it sustains 30 Hz control without stalling. Unlike pretrained
foundation policies aimed at zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks and workspaces, HAVM trades broad
out-of-distribution generalization for rapid adaptation to the available demonstrations.
introduction:
When learning a manipulation task, practitioners often have a few dozen teleoperated demonstrations, one GPU, and a
control loop that must re-plan in tens of milliseconds. Widely used policies, including action-chunking
transformers [2], diffusion policies [3], and vision-language-action
models (VLAs) [4, 5, 6, 7], use tens of millions to billions of
parameters and hours of training or fine-tuning. He et al. [8] found that
diffusion policies trained on small datasets largely reproduce training sequences and that an explicit action lookup
table (ALT) matches them far more cheaply, as our own Diffusion Policy experiments confirm (Appendix -D).

This motivates building the lookup table explicitly as an inspectable memory queried in milliseconds, a role suited to
associative memories. In our earlier work [1], a hetero-associative sequential memory recalled the next motor
pattern via the modern Hopfield update Z=softmax⁡(β​Q​K⊤)​VZ=\softmax(\beta QK^{\top})V [9], where
β\beta interpolates between one stored pattern and a prototype over several. Because lookup can only replay recorded
motions, a policy also needs to adapt when no demonstration matches the scene. Retrieve-and-correct
methods [10, 11, 12, 13, 14] add a learned network to
refine retrieved actions, usually passing it the nearest neighbors that retrieval alone would execute.

We study what readout a demonstration memory should supply to a learned corrector. A smooth recall over the whole memory
proves a better base when demonstrations are sparse and varied, given a future-action key and training on recall from
other demonstrations, even though alone it is no better to execute than the nearest chunk.

Our hetero-associative visuomotor memory, HAVM (Fig. 1), applies this finding. An action-aware ResNet
encoder maps frames with similar futures close together, and the memory stores one key and one future action chunk per
frame. Soft recall forms a draft chunk, and a 2.8 M-parameter attention head reads that draft, four retrieved chunks,
and the observation to predict an additive correction. Training uses leave-one-demonstration-out recall so the
head learns from recall errors on unseen demonstrations, needing only demonstrations without rollouts, rewards, simulator
labels, or robot pretraining. In summary:

We test what base a corrector should receive with all else fixed. On ALOHA Human, the soft base beats the nearest
chunk by 22.4 points on fresh resets across three encoder and three head seeds, holds against a closed-loop-tuned top-1
arm and under a second corrector, and acts mainly as the correction’s anchor. On robomimic Square, it leads by 7.9
points with the two better operators and by 6.7 on a label-free draw of equal size. Confirmed on additional data and a
controlled toy, the gain appears on sparse, varied demonstrations, fades on dense or scripted data, turns slightly
negative on generated data, and disappears with an appearance-only key.

We present HAVM, a 14 M-parameter policy trained offline in about five minutes (with a learned β\beta
validated on ALOHA) with a 1.1 ms call. Across six fresh encoders, it reaches 76.4 % at 24 s, comparable to a
264 M Diffusion Policy trained for 6.7 h and ahead of ACT and fine-tuned VLAs, and reaches 74.6 % within 8 s,
leading every 40-demonstration baseline (+6.5+6.5 over Diffusion Policy, +15.1+15.1 over ACT). On LIBERO, one memory reaches
92.2 % and loses far less to rewording than SmolVLA; on a real SO-101 arm, its 6 ms re-plan sustains 30 Hz control
without stalling.

We characterize where retrieval stops. Failures cluster at first contact where demonstrations are sparse, no
tested corrector extrapolates beyond the demonstrated workspace, and benchmark success can rank policies differently
from handover completion.

title: Aegis-VLA: Reliability-Gated Action Refinement via a Trajectory World Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
authors: Lennox Wei,Jiaqi Yao,Shixin Sun,Yuanzheng Zhang,Jianhua Han,Meng Tian,Shaohui Liu,Wangmeng Zuo
abstract: Dynamic object manipulation requires maintaining spatial and temporal alignment with targets that continue to move during inference and execution. Although future prediction can inform action correction, an accurate forecast does not establish whether modifying an existing action would be beneficial. We present Aegis-VLA, a world-model-guided vision-language-action (VLA) framework that generates predictive action corrections and separately determines whether and how strongly to apply them. A Trajectory World Model combines kinematic extrapolation with learned residual dynamics to predict object motion and estimate positional uncertainty. Discrepancy-Guided Action Refinement uses differences between history-only and base-action-conditioned end-effector forecasts to propose bounded arm corrections. A Reliability Gate learns when to admit corrections based on demonstration-relative improvements over base actions, and regulates their application during inference using predictive uncertainty and anticipated object–end-effector proximity. Rejected corrections preserve the corresponding base actions. Aegis-VLA introduces only approximately 2.45M trainable parameters. On the simulated Dynamic Object Manipulation (DOM) benchmark, Aegis-VLA achieves 56.72% success over 1,800 evaluation trials, exceeding our reproduced DynamicVLA baseline of 45.44% by 11.28 percentage points.
introduction:
Manipulating a moving object requires the robot and target to meet at the right place and time [1, 2, 3]. A grasp that is geometrically appropriate at planning time can become ineffective before contact if the object continues moving. The same observed position can demand different actions depending on whether the target is approaching, receding, or changing direction. Partial visibility obscures motion, while perception, inference, and physical execution introduce delays during which the scene evolves. Dynamic manipulation therefore requires maintaining spatial and temporal alignment between robot actions and target motion.

Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) and generalist robot policies provide increasingly capable foundations for language-conditioned manipulation [4, 5, 6]. Recent methods further incorporate motion history [7], improve inference efficiency [8], and coordinate action generation with execution [9, 10].
Temporal observations, continuous inference, and temporally aligned action streaming enable VLA policies to account for aspects of target motion and execution timing [3].
We therefore ask how predictive evidence can justify modifying a base action that may already be appropriate.

World models offer information about how a scene may evolve beyond the latest observation. Video and representation prediction can support policy learning and planning [11, 12, 13], while recent approaches explicitly incorporate target motion or predicted future observations into dynamic manipulation [14, 15, 16]. World-model-based approaches also evaluate or revise action proposals [17, 18]. However, predicting target motion alone does not establish whether applying a proposed correction would improve execution compared with leaving the base action unchanged.

As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), target motion can invalidate an anticipated contact during execution. A forward adjustment may improve alignment when the base action trails the target. If the base action already compensates for that motion, however, an additional adjustment may worsen alignment even with an accurate forecast. An apparently useful correction may also depend on an unreliable forecast. Useful refinement must therefore assess whether a proposed correction improves on the base action and whether the motion forecast is sufficiently reliable to justify the correction.

Residual learning provides a way to adapt an existing controller or policy [19, 20], including observation-conditioned per-step action correction [21] and uncertainty-guided corrective exploration [22]. However, freezing backbone weights does not by itself preserve task performance once residuals alter the executed actions. Aegis-VLA builds on this residual formulation by separating correction generation from admission through the three coordinated modules in Fig. 2.

Our contributions are summarized below:

Trajectory World Model. We combine kinematic extrapolation, learned residual dynamics, and positional uncertainty estimation to provide shared motion context for action refinement and predictive evidence for regulating corrections under uncertain target motion.

Discrepancy-Guided Action Refinement. We generate bounded arm corrections from position and orientation discrepancies between history-only and base-action-conditioned end-effector forecasts, linking each proposal to the base action it modifies.

Reliability Gate. We separate correction proposal from adoption by learning admission from demonstration-relative improvement of each candidate over its base action, while uncertainty and proximity regulate application at inference.

Aegis-VLA introduces only approximately 2.45M trainable parameters. On the simulated Dynamic Object Manipulation (DOM) benchmark [3], Aegis-VLA achieves 56.72% success over 1,800 evaluation trials, exceeding our reproduced DynamicVLA baseline of 45.44% by 11.28 percentage points. Ablations demonstrate that structured refinement already improves the backbone, while learned admission and reliability regulation further improve on an independently trained ungated alternative.

1. Trajectory World Model. We combine kinematic extrapolation, learned residual dynamics, and positional uncertainty estimation to provide shared motion context for action refinement and predictive evidence for regulating corrections under uncertain target motion.

2. Discrepancy-Guided Action Refinement. We generate bounded arm corrections from position and orientation discrepancies between history-only and base-action-conditioned end-effector forecasts, linking each proposal to the base action it modifies.

3. Reliability Gate. We separate correction proposal from adoption by learning admission from demonstration-relative improvement of each candidate over its base action, while uncertainty and proximity regulate application at inference.

title: QK-Bench: Benchmarking Quantitative Kinematic Understanding for Dynamic Spatial Intelligence
authors: Lennox Wei,Jiaqi Yao,Shixin Sun,Yuanzheng Zhang,Jianhua Han,Meng Tian,Shaohui Liu,Wangmeng Zuo
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Spatial intelligence concerns both scene structure and its temporal evolution. Yet a semantically correct description can conceal a quantitative error: recognizing that objects are approaching does not determine their closing speed or whether they will meet. Such errors are critical in collision avoidance, trajectory tracking, and reactive grasping, where actions depend on motion magnitude, timing, and relative geometry. We study quantitative kinematic understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs): resolving motion magnitude, rate, reference-frame dependence, and future spatial evolution from visual evidence. We introduce the Quantitative Kinematics Benchmark (QK-Bench), comprising 2,341 multiple-choice QA pairs from 379 videos and 17 tasks spanning Object-Centric Kinematics, Camera Ego-Motion Kinematics, and Multi-Object Kinematic Relations. Hidden geometric and temporal signals support trajectory construction and filtering, while fixed kinematic rules map physical quantities to verifiable answers, including categorical labels. Trajectory and question validation ensure target reliability and sufficient visual support in the sampled frames. All models receive a unified monocular RGB input. Evaluations of proprietary, open-source, and spatial MLLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest model achieves only 41.2% overall accuracy, and spatial MLLMs show no consistent advantage. These findings indicate that current advances in spatial intelligence do not reliably transfer to quantitative kinematic understanding.
introduction:
Spatial intelligence enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to perceive and reason about the geometric and relational structure of the physical world [1, 2, 3, 4]. In dynamic environments, object motion, camera ego-motion, and multi-object interactions continually change that structure. A system may describe motion correctly while using incorrect quantities to decide when or where to act. In autonomous driving, recognizing an approaching vehicle does not establish its closing speed; underestimating this speed can make the time available for avoidance appear longer than it is. Manipulator trajectory tracking requires estimating target motion relative to the robot, whereas reactive grasping depends on the target position at the intended contact time. Errors in these estimates can cause tracking deviations or failed grasps of moving object. For robotic and embodied systems, the quantities omitted by a qualitative description can therefore determine whether an action is timely and spatially appropriate. These applications motivate evaluating the motion information on which downstream prediction, planning, and control depend.

Recent benchmarks have extended spatial intelligence from static scenes to dynamic settings [5, 6, 7, 8] by assessing motion, viewpoint changes, and evolving spatial relations. This progress raises a further evaluation requirement: distinguishing motions that share a correct qualitative description but differ in quantitative properties and future outcomes. Two scenes may both show objects “approaching” yet differ in the time of closest approach; two trajectories may both be “turning” yet differ substantially in turning angle. A model can recognize either pattern correctly yet still misjudge these quantities. The distinction concerns the precision of spatial understanding, beyond the recognition of change alone.

We term this capability quantitative kinematic understanding. It extends spatial understanding from where entities are and how they change to how much and how fast they change, in which reference frame, and what spatial configuration follows from current motion. This spans individual object motion, camera ego-motion, camera–object relative dynamics, inter-object kinematic relations, and short-term prediction. Reliable evaluation requires constructing kinematic ground truth with consistent geometry and accurate timing. The resulting targets must distinguish motions that share a qualitative description but differ in magnitude, rate, or future outcome. Even categorical answers must be derived from measured quantities through fixed decision rules, so that selecting a plausible motion label alone is insufficient.

Figure 2 illustrates why reference frames matter for quantitative kinematic understanding. Similar leftward image changes arise from object motion in Clip A but primarily from camera ego-motion in Clip B. A model may correctly recognize this leftward change yet misjudge how far or how fast the object moves by attributing camera-induced changes to the object. Accurate quantitative judgments therefore require accounting for camera ego-motion and measuring change in the reference frame specified by the question.

We introduce the Quantitative Kinematics Benchmark (QK-Bench) to evaluate this capability. It comprises 2,341 question–answer pairs from 379 videos, organized into 17 tasks spanning Object-Centric Kinematics, Camera Ego-Motion Kinematics, and Multi-Object Kinematic Relations. The two-stage pipeline uses hidden geometric and temporal signals to construct trajectories, compute physical quantities, and derive answers through fixed task-specific rules. Each target can therefore be traced to its source evidence and derivation. Trajectory filtering and question validation ensure both label reliability and the visual evidence needed to answer each question.

QK-Bench uses monocular RGB video as a common evaluation interface, consistent with existing spatial-intelligence benchmarks and applicable to heterogeneous MLLMs. Models receive RGB observations, corresponding timestamps, and natural-language questions. Geometric signals remain hidden during evaluation, enabling verifiable target construction while testing what models can infer from a shared visual input. As shown in Fig. 1, evaluations of proprietary, open-source, and spatial MLLMs reveal substantial limitations. The strongest model achieves 41.2% overall accuracy, and the strongest open-source model achieves 39.1%. Spatial MLLMs do not exhibit a consistent advantage in quantitative motion, camera–object relative dynamics, or future relational reasoning.
These findings indicate that current advances in spatial intelligence do not yet translate reliably into quantitative kinematic understanding.

Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate quantitative kinematic understanding as an evaluation objective for dynamic spatial intelligence: resolving motion magnitude, rate, reference-frame dependence, and future outcomes that qualitative descriptions leave unspecified.

We introduce QK-Bench, with 17 tasks spanning object motion, camera ego-motion, and multi-object relations. Its two-stage construction pipeline connects hidden geometric and temporal evidence to quantitative targets through trajectory validation and fixed kinematic rules.

We evaluate proprietary, open-source, and spatial MLLMs, finding a best overall accuracy of 41.2% and no consistent advantage for spatial MLLMs. The results identify quantitative kinematic understanding as a remaining limitation of current spatial intelligence.

1. We formulate quantitative kinematic understanding as an evaluation objective for dynamic spatial intelligence: resolving motion magnitude, rate, reference-frame dependence, and future outcomes that qualitative descriptions leave unspecified.

2. We introduce QK-Bench, with 17 tasks spanning object motion, camera ego-motion, and multi-object relations. Its two-stage construction pipeline connects hidden geometric and temporal evidence to quantitative targets through trajectory validation and fixed kinematic rules.

3. We evaluate proprietary, open-source, and spatial MLLMs, finding a best overall accuracy of 41.2% and no consistent advantage for spatial MLLMs. The results identify quantitative kinematic understanding as a remaining limitation of current spatial intelligence.

title: Targeted Adaptation of World-Action Models via Interaction and Motion Heads
authors: Yuze Zhu,Jacky Li,Yusen Luo,Ken Jiankun Zheng,Chancharik Mitra,Trevor Darrell,Roei Herzig
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
World-Action Models (WAMs) are a promising new paradigm of robot manipulation policies that jointly generate future video and actions.
Successful manipulation requires both identifying where to interact and modeling how the robot and objects move.
Yet standard adaptation methods, such as full fine-tuning and LoRA, do not explicitly select parameters aligned with these manipulation-specific capabilities.
Motivated by this challenge, we discover two functionally specialized families of attention heads: Next-Interaction Heads, which localize upcoming grasp-and-release targets, and Motion Heads, which track movement across frames.
Furthermore, we introduce HeadLight, a parameter-efficient refinement method that jointly adapts Next-Interaction Heads and Motion Heads.
On RoboTwin tasks unseen during fine-tuning, HeadLight achieves 62.28% success, compared with 57.89% for full fine-tuning and 58.66% for LoRA, while updating only 1.1% of parameters.
Inference-time ablations further validate the functional importance of these heads: ablating Motion Heads reduces manipulation success from 57.89% to 0.94%, while ablating Next-Interaction Heads lowers it to 40.61%, both substantially more than ablating equally many random heads.
Finally, we show that our approach is effective across multiple WAM architectures and real-robot manipulation settings.
introduction:
Robot manipulation has been explored through various policy architectures [4, 39, 2], with World-Action Models (WAMs) emerging as a promising approach that generates both future video and actions [34, 36, 13]. Research in motor control and task-and-motion planning describes manipulation in terms of discrete contact events and continuous motion [6, 7]. These aspects translate into two complementary capabilities that WAMs need: anticipating where the next grasp or release should occur, and representing the continuous motion of the robot and manipulated objects across frames.

Current WAMs implicitly rely on large-scale video pretraining [27] to acquire these capabilities. Such pretraining allows them to generate visually plausible videos, yet visual plausibility alone does not ensure that the manipulation capabilities are actually learned [22, 26]. In practice, WAMs may fail to identify the correct interaction targets, and their generated actions may not accurately follow the motion in their predicted videos. These failures are especially pronounced when generalizing to unseen tasks. Although full fine-tuning and LoRA [11] can adapt WAMs, neither method explicitly selects parameters based on their roles in interaction targeting and motion. As a result, optimizing the prediction loss may encourage the model to fit visual details, such as appearance and texture, without necessarily improving interaction targeting and motion modeling. This raises two natural questions: Can we identify the model components associated with interaction targeting and motion? If so, can we selectively refine them to strengthen these capabilities rather than merely fitting visual details?

Previous work has shown that robot policies can be improved by adapting a small set of internal components, either through steering sparse features at inference [37] or by fine-tuning attention heads selected from demonstrations of a specific task [21]. In both cases, the identified components are selected separately for each task. We instead ask whether some heads support more fundamental capabilities shared across manipulation tasks, namely interaction targeting and motion. To answer this, we investigate attention heads in pretrained WAMs and identify two families associated with these capabilities: Next-Interaction Heads and Motion Heads. We identify the former by analyzing attention to upcoming interaction locations, and the latter by measuring the agreement between cross-frame attention and optical flow. Ablating Motion Heads reduces manipulation success from 57.89% to just 0.94%, while ablating Next-Interaction Heads reduces it to 40.61%, with both causing substantially larger declines than ablating equally many random heads. These experiments also reveal distinct failure modes: ablating Next-Interaction Heads often causes the robot to miss its intended targets, while ablating Motion Heads disrupts the motion in predicted videos. These results suggest that WAMs rely on a small number of specialized attention heads to localize interaction targets and to model motion.

Building on these findings, we introduce HeadLight, a parameter-efficient refinement method that uses these two head families to guide complementary adaptation pathways. We selectively fine-tune Next-Interaction Heads to improve target localization and use Motion Heads to guide the adaptation of action prediction, helping generated actions follow the predicted motion. By combining these two pathways, our method aims to improve both interaction targeting and motion execution without updating the entire model.

We evaluate HeadLight on RoboTwin [3] tasks unseen during fine-tuning. On Zero-WAM, our method achieves 62.3% success, compared to 57.9% for full fine-tuning and 58.7% for LoRA, while updating only 1.1% of parameters. Using either adaptation pathway alone does not achieve the same improvement, supporting the importance of their combination. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on LingBot-VA [15], which uses a different WAM architecture. Finally, we validate in real-robot manipulation using a Franka robot.

To summarize, our main contributions are threefold: (i) We identify Next-Interaction Heads and Motion Heads in pretrained WAMs and validate their distinct roles in interaction targeting and motion through attention analysis and controlled ablations. (ii) We introduce HeadLight, which combines two complementary adaptation pathways guided by these heads to improve interaction targeting and motion execution while updating only a small subset of model parameters. (iii) We demonstrate improvements over standard adaptation methods on unseen manipulation tasks, with effectiveness across WAM architectures and in real-robot manipulation. Together, these findings suggest that the functional structure of WAMs can guide which parameters to adapt, improving generalization to unseen tasks.

title: Beyond the Happy Path: Generalizing Robot World Models from Simulated Failures
authors: Zhiyue Zhao,Mingyu Liu,Bolin Zhang,Liyang Li,Guangyu Huang,Canyu Zhao,Jinchuan Shi,Haokai Zhang,Hao Chen,Chunhua Shen
abstract:
Robot world models are increasingly used to evaluate and plan policies, yet robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations. Off the happy path, when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed and the object is pushed, tilted, or slips, their predictions break down. Across five pretrained action-conditioned models, object-motion error is at most 10.4% lower than that of a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two models are worse than this baseline. We present WorldReforge, which teaches world models what happens when manipulation goes wrong. We construct the Reforge dataset of 62k simulated trajectories by perturbing reference grasps in position, orientation, and closure timing, recording each resulting push, slip, or failed pickup with ground-truth object pose, contact, and surface points. WorldReforge turns this ground truth into two training signals without additional inference cost. Interaction Alignment focuses reconstruction on the small object and contact regions that a global loss underweights, and Surface Correspondence trains backbone features to follow the same physical surface points across frames. On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on unseen objects, and it lowers the error in predicting how two actions’ outcomes diverge by 43.3%. Although trained only in simulation, it also improves reconstruction on DROID and on real failure videos. Controlled data studies show that failed contact and successful holding teach complementary physics: failed contact teaches how objects respond, and holding teaches how a grasped state persists.
Our code, data, and models are available at aim-uofa.github.io/WorldReforge/.
introduction:
Action-conditioned world models increasingly replace real-world rollouts for policy evaluation, data generation, and planning [43, 9, 56, 13]. Their value depends on predicting how different actions produce different outcomes. Manipulation is where this requirement is hardest to meet. A grasp shifted by a centimeter or closed too early does not simply fail. The object is pushed, tilted, or slips from the fingers. Yet their robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations [39, 27], so this branch of physics is rarely observed.

We find that this happy-path bias is severe. On our simulated evaluation, five pretrained models from three families [37, 13, 29] achieve object-motion error at most 10.4% lower than a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two are worse (Tab. 1). Their predictions keep objects near the initial pose even when the recorded object is pushed or rotated (). Such predictions risk overrating the policies being evaluated [51, 41].

Recent work fine-tunes on failures obtained by perturbing or executing actions [51, 47, 41, 28]. These methods keep the original generative objective [51], supervise outcomes through progress or reward signals [41, 47], or learn failure dynamics without ground-truth failure videos [47]. Two limitations remain. First, contact dynamics occupy a small fraction of each frame,
so a global reconstruction loss gives them little weight. Second, outcome-level signals indicate whether an interaction failed, not how the object moved. Simulation provides what real robot logs lack: failures can be produced at controlled offsets and timings, safely and at scale, each with exact object pose, contact, and surface geometry.

We present WorldReforge, a post-training framework that exploits this ground truth (Fig. 1). The Reforge dataset contains 62k simulated trajectories over 96 objects, generated by perturbing successful reference grasps in translation, rotation, and closure timing. Trajectories link execution variations to observed outcomes, including contact formation and loss, pushing, tilting, slipping, and whether a grasp is established and maintained. These labels support controlled training compositions. Reforge-Real provides 300 real failure trajectories for evaluation. WorldReforge adds two objectives to the generative loss. Interaction Alignment (IA) reconstructs object and contact regions with a dedicated, area-normalized signal. Surface Correspondence (SC) requires intermediate backbone features to locate the same physical surface points across frames, supervised by simulator-projected trajectories. Neither adds inference-time parameters.

Post-training on Reforge alone reduces object error by about a quarter for Cosmos3 Nano and LingBot-VA, and IA and SC further lower or match every motion error across all three model families. On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object ADE by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on objects unseen during post-training, and it predicts the divergence between two actions’ outcomes with 43.3% lower error. Trained only in simulation, it improves PSNR by 1.04 dB on DROID and 0.68 dB on real failure videos. Controlled data studies reveal a division of labor. Adding failures in which the gripper closes without securing the object reduces object error on such contacts by 18.0%, while successful holding remains the best teacher for keeping a grasped object stable.

Our contributions are:

A diagnosis that pretrained action-conditioned world models barely outperform a static predictor under failed contact, and the Reforge dataset, combining 62k simulated trajectories with dense physical ground truth, 300 real failure trajectories, and a paired-action protocol for measuring response differences.

WorldReforge, which converts simulator ground truth into interaction-region reconstruction and cross-frame surface correspondence objectives without inference-time cost.

Evidence that simulated failures improve object and gripper prediction across model families, transfer to unseen objects and real-world video, and play a role complementary to successful experience.

1. A diagnosis that pretrained action-conditioned world models barely outperform a static predictor under failed contact, and the Reforge dataset, combining 62k simulated trajectories with dense physical ground truth, 300 real failure trajectories, and a paired-action protocol for measuring response differences.

2. WorldReforge, which converts simulator ground truth into interaction-region reconstruction and cross-frame surface correspondence objectives without inference-time cost.

3. Evidence that simulated failures improve object and gripper prediction across model families, transfer to unseen objects and real-world video, and play a role complementary to successful experience.

title: iMFPO: Improving Mean Flow Policy Optimization with Drift-Aware Velocity Alignment for Embodied Control
authors: Lisiyu Pan,Ting Huang,Zeyu Zhang,Hao Tang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Flow-based generative policies offer expressive action modeling for embodied control, yet achieving efficient one-step generation under reward-driven policy optimization remains challenging.
In particular, evolving action distributions during online reinforcement learning may introduce inconsistencies between instantaneous-velocity learning and interval-averaged action generation.
To address this challenge, we propose iMFPO, a one-step generative policy optimization framework with decoupled velocity learning and drift-aware velocity alignment.
A shared interval-conditioned actor supports instantaneous-velocity supervision and interval-averaged action generation.
JVP-corrected velocity regression is jointly optimized with reward-driven policy objectives, with action-level guidance from a frozen PPO teacher during training.
At inference, iMFPO directly generates actions through interval-averaged velocity prediction, achieving one-step control without iterative flow integration.
Across Go2, G1, H1, and Spot, zero-latent evaluation yields mean returns of 35.6935.69, 34.4434.44, 416.23416.23, and 29.8629.86.
On Go2, action-generation latency drops from 15.5715.57 ms to 0.410.41 ms relative to 64-step RFPO.

introduction:
Recent advances in spatial understanding, video reasoning, and vision-language-action learning have expanded the capabilities of embodied intelligence [10, 11, 8].
However, reliable physical interaction requires expressive control policies with low inference latency.
Generative policies offer flexible modeling of complex action distributions.
Diffusion models generate actions through iterative denoising [7, 29] and have shown promising results in robotic manipulation and control [2, 31, 26].
Flow matching [18, 19] provides an alternative through continuous velocity fields.
Recent flow-based policy optimization methods, including FPO [21], FPO++ [32], and RFPO [9], further improve generative policies through reinforcement learning.
Nevertheless, iterative generation introduces substantial inference overhead, limiting its use in real-time robotic control.

One-step generative modeling offers a promising solution to this limitation.
MeanFlow [5] enables direct generation through interval-averaged velocity prediction, while Improved MeanFlow (iMF) [6] reformulates training as instantaneous-velocity regression.
Recent robotic methods extend these ideas through velocity constraints, directional alignment, and reinforcement learning [33, 4, 3, 37, 14].
However, integrating one-step velocity learning with online policy optimization remains challenging.
MeanFlow-based objectives involve model-dependent velocity predictions and Jacobian–vector products (JVPs).
Meanwhile, reward-driven policy updates continuously change the action distribution and its associated velocity targets.
This interaction can introduce inconsistencies between instantaneous-velocity supervision and interval-averaged action generation.
A key challenge is therefore to coordinate velocity learning with policy improvement under evolving rollout distributions.

To address this challenge, we propose iMFPO, a one-step generative policy optimization framework for embodied control (Fig. 1).
Our framework builds on a shared interval-conditioned actor that supports two complementary velocity representations.
At zero-length intervals, the actor estimates instantaneous velocities for training.
Over the full interval, it predicts the average velocity required for direct noise-to-action generation.
This design connects local velocity supervision with one-step action prediction without introducing separate networks.
It also allows both learning objectives to operate within a unified policy representation.

We further introduce drift-aware velocity alignment to keep instantaneous-velocity supervision, interval-averaged generation, and reward-driven updates consistent as the rollout distribution drifts.
Specifically, JVP-corrected velocity regression provides supervision for the shared velocity field, while a loss-induced policy surrogate aligns that field with reward feedback from online rollouts.
A frozen PPO teacher supplies additional action-level guidance during training.
These components jointly align the actor’s velocity predictions under evolving policy distributions.
At inference, the learned policy generates actions with a single network evaluation, without iterative flow integration or teacher guidance.
Experiments across four robotic embodiments demonstrate competitive control performance with substantially reduced inference latency.

The main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose iMFPO, a one-step MeanFlow policy optimization framework that decouples instantaneous-velocity learning from interval-averaged action generation through a shared interval-conditioned actor.

We introduce drift-aware velocity alignment, which couples JVP-corrected iMF regression with a velocity-based policy ratio so that reward updates reshape the same interval-conditioned field used for one-step generation under evolving rollouts.

We demonstrate competitive one-step control performance across four robotic embodiments, achieving mean returns of 35.6935.69, 34.4434.44, 416.23416.23, and 29.8629.86 on Go2, G1, H1, and Spot, respectively. On Go2, iMFPO reduces action-generation latency from 15.5715.57 ms to 0.410.41 ms compared with 64-step RFPO, with additional real-world locomotion demonstrations.

1. We propose iMFPO, a one-step MeanFlow policy optimization framework that decouples instantaneous-velocity learning from interval-averaged action generation through a shared interval-conditioned actor.

2. We introduce drift-aware velocity alignment, which couples JVP-corrected iMF regression with a velocity-based policy ratio so that reward updates reshape the same interval-conditioned field used for one-step generation under evolving rollouts.

title: SEEK: Self-Evolution through Execution Knowledge for Agentic Robot Manipulation
authors: Zeyang Guan,Qihao Zhao,Rui Gong,Zhang Haitian,Yalun Dai,Yangyu Huang,Lingao Xiao,Haozhe Du,Xuehui Yu,Ye Lu,Jianjun Gao,Ruoyu Wang,Haowen Bai,Hao Li,Scarlett Li,Kim-Hui Yap
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Recent advances in robot learning have been driven by scaling demonstration data and model capacity, producing policies with broader task coverage and stronger generalization [4, 28, 40, 10, 20, 27]. Yet these capabilities remain bounded by the distributions represented in the training data [4, 20, 13]. Extending these policies to new embodiments, tasks, or conditions beyond this coverage typically requires additional data collection, training, or fine-tuning [18, 10, 20, 9, 1]. As a result, capability growth remains closely coupled to pre-collected demonstrations and the imitation distribution they define [28, 13].

General-purpose multimodal models offer another route to robot adaptation through reasoning during deployment [17, 22, 14, 16]. By combining current visual observations with task instructions and execution feedback, these models can guide the robot’s actions and adjust its behavior as execution unfolds [15, 14, 24]. Through this interaction, the robot acquires execution knowledge: the effects its actions produce under given conditions and the procedures that prove effective. For example, it may find that a thin coin remains on the table when pinched at its center but lifts when pinched at its rim. However, the robot retains this knowledge only within the model’s working context. Once the task ends, the knowledge is lost. On its next attempt, the robot may again pinch the coin at its center before rediscovering the rim, taking just as long as before.

Avoiding this repetition requires retaining execution knowledge across attempts. Yet simply replaying past actions is insufficient. The same action can yield different effects under different conditions. The robot therefore needs reusable procedures that determine each action from the current scene. Existing and concurrent approaches have begun to retain such procedures as skills and programs [34, 33, 21, 23, 13]. However, retaining a procedure does not ensure that it will handle conditions beyond those encountered in earlier attempts. When a procedure encounters such conditions, measured action effects provide evidence for deciding how to revise it. This evidence should include actions from failed attempts. Procedures and measured action effects therefore need to be retained together, so that a procedure can act without the model where it applies and be revised from this evidence where it does not. Existing methods that keep action-level evidence still leave each action to the model or a learned policy [36, 35, 23], while programs that act without the model are frozen once developed [12].

To this end, we introduce SEEK, a framework for agentic robot manipulation that enables self-evolution through execution knowledge while keeping the underlying model fixed. SEEK retains this knowledge in two coupled forms. At the procedure level, a Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy (SEPP) encodes observation, action generation, verification, task progression, and recovery as executable procedures. During execution, these procedures use current observations to determine actions. At the action level, a Persistent Action-Effect Bank (PAEB) records the measured effect of each executed action with its execution context, including actions from failed attempts. Drawing on these records, the fixed model makes decisions or revises a procedure, and each revision retains references to its supporting evidence. Together, the two components form a continual self-improvement loop: execution supplies evidence for policy revision, and revised procedures carry the resulting capability into subsequent attempts. Once a retained procedure applies to the current scene, it can generate actions without another model request, so successive attempts reuse previously acquired behavior instead of repeating model deliberation.

We evaluate SEEK on RoboDojo [6], a simulation benchmark of 42 dual-arm manipulation tasks. To isolate the contribution of retained knowledge, we compare the same system with and without it on scenes unseen during self-evolution; both conditions allow adaptation within an attempt. Across the 42 tasks, knowledge retained over ten attempts more than doubles task performance. Compared with GPT-6.2 Astra acting directly on 34 of these tasks, SEEK with the same model raises the task score from 49.6 to 80.1 after five attempts and uses 77.6% fewer model requests. We further measure the fraction of executed steps generated by retained procedures, and ablate PAEB and SEPP to separate the contributions of action-level evidence reuse and procedure-level policy evolution. Finally, on a smaller set of tasks, we replace the underlying model and run SEEK on a real robot; in both settings, SEEK again improves task performance.

4. 是否属于 Humanoid Loco-manipulation：是。理由：SEEK在RoboDojo上评估，涉及双臂操控任务，虽然没有明确提到使用humanoid机器人，但其任务性质涉及到协调多个动作，符合humanoid的操控和运动控制的联合任务。

5. 最终标签总结：
该论文属于World Model和Humanoid Loco-manipulation。

6. 如果有歧义，请说明最容易混淆的点：
可能的混淆点在于SEEK是否直接依赖于视觉和语言输入来生成动作，这可能让人联想到VLA。然而，SEEK的重点在于通过执行知识的自我演化来改进动作，而不是通过视觉和语言的结合来生成动作。

title: X-World: Transferring Video Priors to Cross-Embodiment Robot Control
authors: Chun Gu,Xiaofei Wei,Yiming Chen,Juntong Zhang,Li Zhang
abstract:
Language-instructed manipulation requires robust closed-loop policies, yet action-labeled robot trajectories are costly and limited in coverage.
Human and robot videos provide complementary spatiotemporal priors for cross-embodiment control.
We propose X-World, which adapts pretrained video diffusion to variable views. A Q-Former compresses hidden states into tokens for a shared flow-matching expert that predicts action chunks.
Dataset-specific projections map native states and actions.
We adapt the backbone on large-scale robot and human videos, freeze it for action-only pretraining of the Q-Former and action expert, then post-train on the target platform.
At inference, X-World responds at 20 Hz and overlaps updates with execution via asynchronous real-time chunking.
X-World performs strongly on LIBERO and under zero-shot shifts on LIBERO-Plus. On hardware, it averages 81.7% success across six bimanual tasks on the side-mounted dual-arm UR5e, one of three real-robot configurations presented.
introduction:
Language-instructed robotic manipulation [8, 7] requires policies that translate high-level instructions into robust low-level actions under diverse contacts, partial observability, and long horizons.
Recent vision-language-action (VLA) policies [8, 7, 30, 37, 3, 4, 42] rely on large collections of action-labeled trajectories that are costly to obtain and often limited in task, embodiment, and viewpoint coverage.
Internet-scale videos of humans and robots capture spatiotemporal patterns such as motion and contact.
How can video world priors improve closed-loop manipulation across embodiments with limited action supervision?

Prior work [52, 18, 23] suggests that pretrained video diffusion models can aid action generation. Many methods assume a single view or a fixed camera layout, making them harder to deploy on robots with different numbers of cameras.
Multi-view adaptations [33] can shift the backbone away from its pretrained behavior and weaken transfer.
Across robot embodiments, datasets [38, 9, 49, 27, 48] define states and actions in different coordinate frames, units, and control conventions.
Directly pooling these action targets in one space can produce incompatible supervision and destabilize learning.
Iterative sampling and large backbones can hinder real-time control by increasing latency.

To address these limitations, we propose X-World, which (i) adapts a pretrained video diffusion backbone (LTX-Video [22]) to variable-view robot observations via view embeddings and a zero-initialized cross-view attention module, (ii) distills diffusion hidden states into a compact token sequence via a Q-Former as a world-prior interface for action generation, (iii) trains a shared action expert across embodiments and, following X-VLA [56], uses dataset-specific projections to encode states and actions and decode predictions into native actions, and (iv) supports continuous control via asynchronous real-time chunking that decouples inference updates from action execution to avoid waiting latency.
We train X-World in three steps to separate learning a transferable video world prior from learning control. First, we adapt the pretrained video diffusion backbone on large-scale robot [38, 9, 49, 27, 48] and human videos [21, 54] to acquire a strong spatiotemporal prior. Then, we freeze the video diffusion backbone and optimize the Q-Former and action expert with the action-only objective ℒa​c​t\mathcal{L}_{act} for knowledge isolation, so action gradients do not perturb the learned prior. Finally, we post-train on target-platform data to adapt the policy for benchmark or real-world deployment.

We evaluate X-World on LIBERO [34] and test the same checkpoint under zero-shot distribution shifts on LIBERO-Plus [19].
The policy performs well on both benchmarks, with its largest gains over OpenVLA-OFT [28] on LIBERO-Plus occurring under robot, language, and layout perturbations.
On real hardware, we evaluate X-World on six bimanual tasks on the side-mounted dual-arm UR5e.
Figure  shows task examples from all three configurations, including textile handling on the shared-frame dual-arm UR5e and interaction with a household appliance on the Unitree G1.

Our contributions are threefold.
(i) We upgrade a pretrained video diffusion backbone to variable-view robot videos via view embeddings and a zero-initialized cross-view attention module.
(ii) We distill diffusion hidden states into a token sequence via a Q-Former and train a shared flow-matching action expert across embodiments, with dataset-specific projections for native state and action spaces.
(iii) We train in three stages by adapting the video diffusion backbone on large-scale videos and learning action generation with the backbone kept frozen for knowledge isolation, and deploy with asynchronous real-time chunking for low-latency control.

title: CoTAMP: Cooperative Task and Motion Planning for Quadruped Robots with Large Language Models
authors: Woojin Kim,Jemin Hwangbo
abstract: Some environments cannot be traversed by a single quadruped robot, for example a ledge that one robot can climb only from its partner’s back or a gap that must be bridged with boxes. Solving them requires cooperative task and motion planning (TAMP). Previous works are limited to the motions of a single robot or only select actions from a predefined set of skills. We propose a framework with two parts: task planning that invents motions not defined in advance, and motion generation that realizes the invented motions. Both parts consist of large language model (LLM)-based modules and code-based modules. Task planning divides the trajectory of the whole task into steps and fixes the robot poses at the step boundaries. Motion generation produces keyframes that describe the motion of each step and turns them into a continuous trajectory through kinematic synthesis. The code-based modules check every plan and motion and return failures to the LLM-based modules for correction. The whole trajectory is then refined by trajectory optimization to satisfy the dynamics. On three simulated courses with two RAIBO2 robot models, our framework produced kinematically valid references in all 30 trials, all of which converged in trajectory optimization. Compared with several baselines, our framework showed advantages in success rate, dynamic feasibility, execution time, and generation time and cost.
introduction:
Task and motion planning (TAMP) has enabled legged robots to complete long-horizon tasks in cluttered environments, combining decisions about what to do with motions that respect contacts and geometry [1]. Many environments, however, cannot be traversed by a single robot: a ledge higher than its legs can reach, a gap between two platforms, or a path blocked by boxes that must first be pushed into place. Two robots can overcome such obstacles if one serves as a step (Fig. 1) or a bridge for the other, or if they rearrange objects together. Planning such behavior requires a cooperative TAMP that decides who supports whom and in which order, and at the same time where each foot lands on the partner’s back.

Existing approaches to TAMP fix the set of available actions in advance. Classical TAMP requires hand-designed action schemas with preconditions and effects, and computes the motion of each action with a motion planner [2, 3]. Large language models (LLMs) have made it possible to plan cooperation directly from a description of the scene; Delfaki et al. [4], for example, use an LLM to decompose a task so that one quadruped helps another over a high obstacle. Like most LLM-based planners [5, 6, 7], however, their method composes the plan from a predefined or pretrained set of skills, in its case GoTo, Sit, and Stand commands. In both cases a task that requires a motion outside the given set cannot be solved, which limits how far such planners generalize to new obstacles.

We therefore let the task planner invent the motions it needs instead of selecting them. The task planner decomposes the task into steps according to the kind of motion required and fixes the robot poses at the step boundaries, while the motion within each step is described freely: either a solo motion of one robot or a coupled motion of both robots in physical contact. Because solo steps of different robots are independent, they can be executed in parallel, which shortens the execution.

Turning such freely invented motions into trajectories is itself difficult. Learning-based controllers need training for every new skill, and trajectory optimization (TO) needs a contact sequence and a good initial guess [8, 9]. LLMs can write the reward or cost of such controllers [10, 11], but these methods target a single robot. Motions in which two robots touch each other, such as stepping onto a partner whose back moves under the load, are particularly hard because the contacts of both robots are coupled.

Recent work shows that LLMs can also generate motions directly, by writing trajectories or programs that produce them [12, 13]. These methods, however, generate the motion of a single robot and do not produce motions in which two robots physically support each other. Our motion generator produces such coupled motions of both robots. To keep generation fast and inexpensive, the LLM specifies only the landed contact states (keyframes), and code-based modules fill in the motion between them with interpolation and a local kinematic optimization, instead of the LLM writing every sample of a long trajectory. The resulting kinematic reference is finally refined by a TO so that it satisfies the dynamics of both robots.

The contributions of this letter are:

An LLM planner that invents solo and coupled motions without a predefined skill set and executes independent motions in parallel.

A motion generator that produces coupled motions of two robots in physical contact, in which the LLM outputs only keyframes and code-based modules fill in the motion with kinematic optimization, which takes less time and fewer tokens than generating dense trajectories directly.

An evaluation on three cooperative courses showing that the framework successfully performs cooperative TAMP and has advantages over baselines in success rate, dynamic feasibility, execution time, and generation time and cost.

title: Integration of Vision-Language-Action Control for Autonomous Forklift Unloading with Limited Real-World Data
authors: Koshi Oishi,Seigo Ito
abstract:
Forklifts play a critical role in warehousing and distribution, but existing automation systems remain limited in handling complex tasks that require sequential decision-making.
Recently, vision–language–action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach for multi-step decision-making by directly generating control actions from visual observations and language prompts.
Although VLA-based control has been extensively researched for manipulators, to the best of our knowledge, its application to forklifts remains unexplored.
Therefore, this study demonstrates the integration of VLA control for an autonomous forklift unloading task with limited real-world data.
Moreover, training VLA models typically requires large-scale datasets.
As there is currently no public dataset for forklift operations, we use a VLA model pretrained primarily on robotic manipulator data and construct a training dataset via simulation, which can be scaled up at low cost.
We then adapt the pretrained VLA model to forklift control using 9.38 h of simulation data and 0.8 h of real-world demonstrations, with the latter accounting for approximately 8% of the collected forklift data by duration.
The integrated system was validated through 72 real-world trials across four model variants.
The results show that the proposed system can accomplish an unloading task even with limited real-world data.
introduction:
Forklifts are among the most widely used industrial vehicles in warehousing and distribution.
In the context of rapidly expanding global logistics, forklifts are indispensable material-handling equipment, and their automation has become increasingly important.
Forklift automation has already been implemented in restricted environments, using system designs broadly similar to those reported by Walter et al. [1] and Teller et al. [2].
However, these approaches rely heavily on accurate state estimation using multiple sensors and hard-coded logic tailored to constrained spaces  [3].
In real-world deployments, where forklifts operate under diverse and changing conditions, hard-coding decisions for all possible situations is prohibitively costly to engineer and maintain.
This motivates the need for an alternative approach to conventional systems that depend heavily on human-engineered design.

Recently, with the rapid progress of vision–language models (VLMs), there is a growing interest in vision–language–action (VLA) models that extend VLMs to directly output actions [4, 5, 6, 7].
VLA models address decision-making scenarios that are challenging for conventional approaches, enabling automation in long-horizon and complex tasks [8, 9, 10, 11]. This capability can reduce reliance on hard-coded logic, which is inflexible and costly to maintain as operating conditions vary.
Applying VLA models can potentially automate decision-making in complex forklift operations.
However, most VLA research has focused on manipulators, and forklift-specific studies remain limited.

In this study, we integrate a VLA model into a forklift unloading system and automate the unloading sequence by directly generating actions from language and visual observations (Fig. 1).
Our integrated system can handle task goals in natural language and generate action sequences while jointly predicting the current task phase, eliminating the need to manually enter numeric targets or implementing extensive hard-coded logic.
Moreover, training VLA models requires large-scale datasets.
However, to the best of our knowledge, no public dataset currently exists for forklift operations.
Therefore, we employed a VLA model pretrained primarily on robotic manipulator data and constructed a simulation dataset so that the embodiment gap between manipulators and forklifts could be bridged without large-scale real-world forklift data.
We performed real-world evaluation of our approach on a 1/14-scale forklift platform by conducting 72 trials, including baseline comparisons.
Although full-scale forklifts are the intended target, the 1/14-scale platform enables safer, real-world iterations during early-stage learning-based development.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first real-world integration study of VLA-based end-to-end action generation for a forklift unloading task.
The main contributions are as follows:

We integrate a VLA model into a forklift unloading system, enabling phase inference and action generation from onboard sensor observations while supporting low-latency execution.

We integrate a VLA model into a forklift unloading system, enabling phase inference and action generation from onboard sensor observations while supporting low-latency execution.

We present a cross-embodiment adaptation recipe that combines simulation-based mid-training with post-training on 0.8 h of real-world forklift demonstrations.

We evaluate the proposed integrated system through 72 real-world trials across four model variants and demonstrate that it can accomplish the unloading task even with limited real-world data.

Section II reviews related work, Sections III–V describe the integrated system, Section VI reports real-world experiments, and Sections VII and VIII discuss limitations and conclusions.

1. We integrate a VLA model into a forklift unloading system, enabling phase inference and action generation from onboard sensor observations while supporting low-latency execution.

2. We present a cross-embodiment adaptation recipe that combines simulation-based mid-training with post-training on 0.8 h of real-world forklift demonstrations.

3. We evaluate the proposed integrated system through 72 real-world trials across four model variants and demonstrate that it can accomplish the unloading task even with limited real-world data.

title: Measuring the Value of One Shared Image at Robot Handoffs in Vision-and-Language Navigation
authors: Yuze Lu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: When the lead robot cannot continue, what should it send the teammate that must finish the route? We replay a frozen receiver at each contact under alternative messages. Across 3,920 autonomous departures in 106 environments, adding the view before the lead’s last action block to its executed actions raised success by 7.51 percentage points (pp) per RxR handoff and 8.54 pp per SAGE handoff. Per departure the gains were 2.23 and 1.44 pp, respectively. The lead continuing in simulation defines the empirical full-history ceiling (Solo). At contact, the lead had accumulated a median of 41 frames. Sending one frame when available recovered 24% of the full-history advantage over actions alone in SAGE and 30% in RxR. Over an estimated progress cue in SAGE, the image rescued 100 routes and reversed 54 successes. Near-goal receivers finished outside less often (63.1% to 51.7%, post hoc). In secondary comparisons the earlier view outperformed the contact view by 6–7 pp per handoff. Exact-route specificity and image gains at controlled starts with mostly unknown progress or outside the goal region remained unresolved. Gains were detectable from about 7 kB per handoff. Random transmission matched within size bins nearly equaled the learned sender’s team success. At a required handoff, a view of the approach to the last maneuver helps the receiver finish.
introduction:
A delivery can pass from a truck to a drone or between robots assigned to different legs [1, 2]. We study the case in which the lead cannot finish a navigation instruction. Its battery may be depleted, the next segment may require another platform’s capabilities, or the team may have assigned that segment to a partner. At contact the receiver must take over. The communication decision is what to send it from the stretch of route it has never seen.

Consider a lead robot that turns left and meets its teammate in a corridor. The receiver can see the corridor ahead and can receive the exact turn sequence in a few bytes. A photograph from just before the turn shows the approach, but costs thousands of times more to transmit. Does that view change which routes the team completes?

Navigation policies already use their own visual history [3], and cooperating navigators can share peer observations [4]. We isolate the value of a message by running the lead once and replaying a frozen receiver under each candidate packet at the same physical contact (Fig. 1). All packet branches share the receiver’s view, residual budget and instruction. For an empirical full-history ceiling (Solo), we allow the original lead to finish in simulation with its own history. In the deployment task, only the receiver can finish the route.

The lead had accumulated a median of 41 camera frames by first contact. The median was 40 in SAGE (interquartile range [IQR], 23–57) and 43 in RxR (26–62). Sending one pre-block frame when available recovered 24–30% of the full-history advantage over actions alone at those same contacts. The image raised success by 7.5–8.5 percentage points (pp) per handoff, translating to 1.4–2.2 pp per team departure because a packet can help only when the lead reaches the receiver (17.6% of SAGE departures). Most additional successes in designed interiors came from receivers that started near the goal, whereas on human-instructed RxR routes most required travel into the goal region.

Our contributions are

A paired handoff protocol that restores the same contact state for every packet, counts missed contacts in team success, and reproduced the archived outcomes on all 6,330 same-batch baseline reruns.

An empirical full-history ceiling, Solo, that quantifies how much of the actions-only receiver’s success deficit one earlier image recovers at a required handoff. Paired outcomes also identify the routes an image rescues or loses over an instruction-progress cue.

Evidence on which frame to send. In both cohorts the view before the lead’s last action block outperformed the contact frame. In designed interiors an image mainly helped receivers retain a position near the goal. On human-instructed routes most additional successes required travel into the goal region.

A byte-priced evaluation of seven encodings with measured delivery costs. Comparing a learned sender with random senders at matched spending shows how a preference for inexpensive images can resemble a preference for informative handoffs.

title: Learning a Whole-Body Pivot-Walking Gait for Heavy-Box Transport with a Humanoid
authors: Rikuto Hidaka,Tsung-Yuan Chen,Kento Kawaharazuka
comment: Accepted to IEEE-RAS Humanoids 2026. . Project page:this https URLVideo:this https URL
abstract:
Through pivot walking, humans can transport objects that are too
heavy to lift.
Previous humanoid studies have relied on planned sequences
in which object manipulation and stepping are executed separately and the
object is brought to rest between successive rotations. However,
few studies have developed a single learned controller for humanoid pivot walking.
In this paper, we propose a single reinforcement-learning policy that jointly
coordinates stepping, balance control, and object manipulation. The policy is
trained using rewards that promote alternating pivot motions and a phase
reference that progresses according to the displacement of the object.
In simulation, we confirmed that the humanoid
can pivot a box. For deployment, we fine-tuned the policy into an
object-blind version that follows a periodic clock instead of the
progress reference. On the real robot, the deployed policy transported
the box forward by more than 1 m1\text{\,}\mathrm{m} in all five trials; each
trial ended at a base-tilt safety stop.
These results demonstrate that coordinated humanoid pivot walking can be
learned with reinforcement learning and transferred to a physical
humanoid robot without direct object-state sensing.
introduction:
Humanoid robots are becoming increasingly capable of dynamic locomotion,
yet many useful tasks require moving objects that are too large or heavy
to lift. Direct lifting may exceed the robot’s arm capacity, while pushing
or dragging can require large sustained forces and substantial sliding at
the floor. Humans can instead exploit ground support through pivot
walking: the object is rocked between its bottom corners and rotated
forward while most of its weight remains supported by the ground. Pivot
walking may therefore provide humanoids with a useful transport mode for
heavy objects (Fig. 1).

Pivoting has been studied extensively as a nonprehensile manipulation primitive,
including for humanoid transport (Section II). Existing
humanoid systems, however, rely on explicit contact models and planned
quasi-static sequences. Object rotation and robot stepping are scheduled as
separate phases, and the object is nearly stationary between rotations.
These methods demonstrate reliable task-level planning, yet they do not
realize pivot walking as a continuously executed learned gait in which
stepping, balance, and object rocking are generated jointly.

In this work, we propose such a whole-body pivot-walking gait with
reinforcement learning. In the six separately trained routes we
tested, a basic transport objective produces tilted dragging or unstable
pushing rather than repeated pivoting. We introduce box-level rewards that encourage
alternating rocking and a spatial reference indexed by realized box
progress. This reference remains synchronized with the object when
motion slows or stalls. We then transfer the learned gait to a
proprioceptive policy by removing box-state observations and continuing
reinforcement learning with clock conditioning
(Section IV-E). Progress pacing is thus used
during training, while the deployed policy follows an internal clock.

In simulation, πpath\pi_{\mathrm{path}}
transports a 14.9 kg14.9\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{g} box 4.12 m4.12\text{\,}\mathrm{m} in 20 s20\text{\,}\mathrm{s} with
zero observed terminations across 128 initial box orientations
(Section V). In real robot experiments, the object-blind policy reproduces repeated lean and yaw
reversals and achieves more than 1 m1\text{\,}\mathrm{m} of forward transport in all
five trials. All trials terminate at the robot’s base-tilt safety
trigger, so the present result demonstrates repeatable short-horizon
gait transfer rather than sustained autonomous delivery
(Section V-G).

Our contributions are:

A whole-body humanoid policy that walks, balances, and pivots
a free-standing box with both hands in a single gait, learned
without an explicit object-contact model or a planned settling
phase.

Box-level pivoting rewards and a progress-paced
reference with which the alternating gait is learned; in our
tests, a transport reward alone led to dragging or unstable
pushing.

Repeatable short-horizon transfer to the physical G1 without
box-state sensing, achieving repeated lean and yaw reversals
and transporting the box forward by more than 1 m1\text{\,}\mathrm{m} in
all five trials.
