title: $\widetilde{\varepsilon}$: Does Initial Noise Induce Directional Bias in Vision-Language-Action Models?
authors: Junmyeong Lee,Dongmin Shin,Wooseok Jeon,JunGyu Lee,Seunghyun Shin,Hae-Gon Jeon
abstract:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have widely adopted diffusion-based action generation for continuous robot motions, enabling fine-grained control across diverse tasks.
However, recent studies have shown that their performance is highly sensitive to initial noise, with resulting action errors that make recovery difficult during execution.
Existing approaches search for favorable noise initializations to improve performance, yet the action expert itself remains sensitive to noise.
In this work, we reveal that initial noise induces a consistent directional bias in action space that closely aligns with the noise’s temporal mean.
We thus introduce a simple yet effective framework that improves robustness to initial noise through interventions during both training and inference.
During training, we enforce consistent action predictions from antithetic noise pairs (ϵ,−ϵ)(\epsilon,-\epsilon) and, at inference, remove the noise’s temporal mean.
Our method substantially reduces action deviation and improves task performance across simulation benchmarks.
In real-robot experiments, our method increases the average task success rate of π0.5\pi_{0.5} from 40% to 68%, with more stable and consistent execution.
introduction:
Recent advances in diffusion models [12, 40, 35, 24] have enabled vision-language-action models (VLAs) to generate continuous action sequences for smooth robot control [7, 3, 2, 1].
As a result, VLAs can perform an increasingly broad range of tasks, from simple pick-and-place operations to long-horizon manipulation [20, 19, 6, 5, 52, 36, 46, 42].
However, recent studies identify initial noise as a key factor contributing to inconsistent task performance [34, 49].
Since a single inaccurate motion can significantly alter the next observation and trigger cascading failures, robustness to initial noise is crucial for consistent manipulation. Also, recovery can be particularly difficult when such errors change the physical state of objects, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (a), where a cube falls during stacking. Therefore, improving robustness to initial noise is essential for reliable real-world deployment of VLAs.

Prior works have explored two main approaches to address initial noise sensitivity in diffusion-based policies.
One research direction is to improve manipulation performance by searching for favorable initial noise or evaluating multiple generated action candidates [34, 43, 21, 49].
Another line of work learns the noise distribution or modifies the noise-to-action mapping during training [8, 53, 27].
However, both approaches often require additional computation during inference or training for task-specific adaptation.
Furthermore, they do not fully explain the systematic changes that initial noise induces in action space, and the resulting policies remain sensitive to noise initialization.

To address this limitation, we analyze how initial noise affects action generation.
We find that it inherently induces directional deviations in generated actions, which we refer to as directional bias.
We empirically reveal that the same noise sample produces similarly directed deviations despite different observations and language instructions, while antithetic noise pairs tend to induce biases in opposite directions.
These observations suggest that the initial noise is a primary driver of directional bias.
Further analysis reveals that this direction closely aligns with the temporal mean of the initial noise.
By assuming the action distribution as Gaussian, we theoretically show that the directional bias remains aligned with the initial noise’s temporal mean.
These findings motivate a method that reduces directional bias for more stable action generation across noise initializations.

Guided by these insights, we propose intuitive solutions that address directional bias at both training and inference time.
Specifically, during training, we enforce consistency between action predictions obtained from antithetic noise pairs to reduce the effect of initial noise.
This encourages the action expert to generate more consistent actions across different noise initializations.
At inference, we directly subtract the temporal mean from each sample and use it to initialize the action generation (see Fig. 1 (b)).

Through comprehensive evaluations, we confirm that reductions in noise sensitivity are generally accompanied by improved task performance, supporting the importance of addressing the directional bias.
These gains are achieved through simple corrections that can be readily applied to a variety of VLA models.
The improvements also extend to real-robot execution, where our method increases the average task success rate of π0.5\pi_{0.5} from 40% to 68%, while improving motion stability.

title: LSRP*-LA: Scalable and Anytime Multi-Agent Path Finding for Large Agents with Asynchronous Actions
authors: Dachuan Liu,Shizhe Zhao,Zhongqiang Ren
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
abstract:
Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) seeks collision-free paths for multiple agents from their start locations to their goal locations while minimizing path costs. Most MAPF algorithms assume that each agent occupies a single vertex
and that the actions of all agents are synchronized. These assumptions may limit the use of MAPF planners in practice. Existing planners that get rid of both assumptions either handle only a few agents or cannot improve their solutions. Recently, a planner called LSRP* was proposed, which is scalable and anytime with asynchronous actions, but still limited by that each agent occupies a single vertex. This paper develops a new planner called LSRP*-LA for MAPF for large agents with asynchronous actions (LA-MAPF-AA), where an agent can occupy several cells. LSRP*-LA is scalable
and complete, and it keeps improving solution quality after the initial solution is obtained until the runtime budget depletes. We analyze the properties of LSRP*-LA and test it against several baselines with up to 800 agents on various maps. LSRP*-LA can handle twice as many agents as baseline methods and its solution cost is about half that of recent synchronous planners for large agents.
introduction:
Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) seeks collision-free paths for multiple agents from their start locations to their goal locations while minimizing the path costs. It arises in applications such as logistics and automated warehouses. MAPF is NP-hard to solve to optimality [yu2013structure],
and existing planners trade solution quality for scalability: optimal planners such as conflict-based search (CBS) [sharon2015cbs], rule-based planners such as PIBT [okumura2022pibt], which handle thousands of agents, and anytime planners, which keep improving a first solution while time
remains [li2021lns, okumura2023lacamstar].

Most of these MAPF planners rely on two assumptions: (i) the point-agent assumption, where every agent occupies a single vertex of the graph, and (ii) the synchronous-action assumption, where every action of the agents, either wait or move, takes one time step, and all agents start and end their actions at the same integer time steps.
In practice, robot fleets may satisfy neither of the two assumptions. In the car plant of Fig. 1(a),
automated tugger trains and Smart Transport Robots (STRs) share one hall. A tugger train is several times longer
than an STR, so it occupies several cells and can block several STRs at the same time (Fig. 1(b)).
Tugger trains and STRs also move at different speeds, so they do not start and finish their moves at the same time.

Some existing work drops one of the two assumptions but keeps the other. In MAPF with asynchronous actions (MAPF-AA), every agent has its own action durations. Optimal planners for MAPF-AA solve instances with tens of agents [ren2021lss, wu2026cbsaa]. The rule-based planner LSRP [zhou2025lsrp] scales to hundreds of agents, and its extension LSRP* [liu2026lsrpstar] is in addition complete and anytime. In MAPF for large agents
(LA-MAPF) [li2019lamapf], an agent occupies several cells, and even finding a feasible solution is
NP-hard [agafonov2025intractable]. Several variants of MAPF have been developed to address this problem, such as generalizing CBS [atzmon2020gmapf], Multi-Dependency PIBT (MD-PIBT) [jiang2026mdpibt], and
Layered LA-MAPF [yao2024layeredlamapf]. These planners assume synchronous actions.

Only a few planners drop both assumptions. CCBS [andreychuk2022ccbs] plans in continuous time for agents with a
geometric body that traverse edges of different lengths, and AOC-CBS [combrink2026aoccbs] handles
heterogeneous fleets and keeps improving its solution while time remains. These planners build on CBS and aim at
optimal solutions. Their runtime grows quickly with the number of conflicts, and large agents cause far more conflicts, leading to poor scalability. Prioritized planning with safe-interval path planning (PP-SIPP) handles robots of different sizes and speeds and scales to hundreds of robots [yakovlev2019diffdrive], but it is incomplete and cannot improve its solution.

Different from these planners, this paper develops LSRP*-LA, a planner that drops both assumptions while being able to scale to a large number of agents with anytime solution refinement.
LSRP*-LA builds upon LSRP* [liu2026lsrpstar], which does not consider large agents but can handle many point agents by employing a rule-based procedure to complete joint actions quickly, and a search over joint actions in the style of LaCAM [okumura2023lacam] to make the planner complete and anytime.
However, extending LSRP* to large agents is challenging. First, a large agent may be blocked by several agents at once, and each of them may need several actions to get out of its way. Planning one action of a large agent thus couples many agents over several actions, and these
agents have to be planned together in their joint space, whose size grows exponentially with agents number. Second, due to asynchronous actions, the later actions of a push start at different times, and other agents are planned in between. Such an agent sees only the current footprints of the agents in the push, so it may move into the cells that one of their later actions will occupy. Synchronous planners for large agents (such as [jiang2026mdpibt]) bypass this challenge by deciding the actions of all agents together at each time step.

To address these challenges, LSRP*-LA builds upon the search process of LSRP*, and checks collisions between the footprints of the agents.
First, a pusher agent pushes all agents that block the pusher within an action, as in MD-PIBT [jiang2026mdpibt], and each pushed agent plans a short sequence of actions, called an evacuation, to leave the pusher’s way. Second, a pre-execution check tests each planned action for collisions right before it starts.
With these techniques, we show that LSRP*-LA is complete and guaranteed to eventually find an optimal solution given sufficient runtime.

In our tests, we compare LSRP*-LA against several baselines, including LSRP [zhou2025lsrp], CBS-AA [wu2026cbsaa] extended to large agents, PP-SIPP [yakovlev2019diffdrive], and the synchronous planners MD-PIBT [jiang2026mdpibt] and Layered LA-MAPF [yao2024layeredlamapf], using various maps from a popular MAPF benchmark [stern2019mapf]. The results show that LSRP*-LA can handle up to 40 times as many agents as the baselines. Specifically, on den312d, our LSRP*-LA can solve instances with up to 800 agents, twice as many as LSRP alone, whereas CBS-AA and PP-SIPP solve no instance with more than 20 and 200 agents. The anytime search in our LSRP*-LA refines the cost of the initial solution by up to about 34% within the runtime budget. LSRP*-LA often finds nearly optimal solutions, as its solution costs are at most 2% higher than that of CBS-AA-LA, an optimal planner, on small scale problems. Planning with asynchronous actions is also important, as the solution costs of LSRP*-LA are about half of that of the synchronous planners (MD-PIBT [jiang2026mdpibt], Layered LA-MAPF [yao2024layeredlamapf]) which ignores asynchronous actions.

title: Triage Before Fine-Tuning: Feasibility-Gated Selection and Monitored Adaptation of Embodied Foundation Models for a Fixed Physical Platform
authors: Zilin Huang,Zhengyang Wan,Zihao Sheng,Boyue Wang,Ruolin Yang,Yuhao Luo,Sikai Chen
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Embodied foundation models are increasingly deployed by selection: a practitioner picks a public checkpoint by benchmark rank and fine-tunes it on local data. The platform is fixed before the model is chosen: its sensors, onboard compute and operating site are set by the task, and at the start there is little or no local data. We ask what such a checkpoint loses on a fixed physical platform and which part of the loss local data can buy back. Our answer is to split the gap by what can repair it. A sensing gap, information the sensors do not capture, cannot be closed with their data; a latency gap, output arriving after the control loop needs it, belongs to the loop, not the weights; only a distribution gap is fine-tuning’s to repair. We turn this into Triage, a procedure for feasibility-gated selection and monitored adaptation in five stages: gates on the sensor contract and on end-to-end latency that no score can override, probes on ten minutes of local logs, a ranking by target-relevant score among the candidates that pass, and fine-tuning that is monitored and checked in closed loop before release. On driving benchmarks, a deadline below a leading closed-loop model’s latency makes it collide on 80 to 90% of routes, and losing field of view moves plans 2.2 to 5.7 times more than losing resolution at equal pixels (1.6 to 2.4 in manipulation) and costs more driving score in closed loop. Local frames close 75% of a stability gap but raise perturbation sensitivity at small budgets, fine-tuning removes more of a moderate crop’s cost than of a strong crop’s, and picking by score violates a gate in two of four deployment profiles. On a full-scale vehicle, the factory camera failed the sensing gate and an added camera repaired it. The latency gate, applied to the end-to-end latency measured on board, removed the two highest-scoring candidates, neither of which completed a closed-loop trip. The selected model passed closed-loop acceptance in 4 of 5 trips, and the closed-loop check withheld a fine-tuned model that had improved offline. Triage lets organizations that cannot train foundation models from scratch find out, before buying data or hardware, whether a public checkpoint can run on the robot or vehicle they own, and what to fix if not.
introduction:
Public checkpoints of embodied foundation models, released by research
groups and industry teams, now span end-to-end driving systems
(Chitta et al., 2023; Liao et al., 2025), vision-language-action
policies (Renz et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b; Kim et al., 2024),
video world models (Liu et al., 2026) and generalist robot policies
(Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024; Octo Model Team et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024), and public benchmarks built on
recorded datasets (Caesar et al., 2021; Dauner et al., 2024; Walke et al., 2023)
and simulated environments
(Dosovitskiy et al., 2017; Jia et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025) evaluate and
compare them. It is increasingly practical to begin a new deployment with an existing model: select a pretrained checkpoint and adapt it.

A benchmark evaluates candidates under its own observation, environment,
and execution conditions, whereas a deployed policy acts through a
particular platform’s sensors, onboard compute, and controller, and its
actions change the state from which its next observations come. The
order of these decisions matters. A deployer, such as a campus shuttle
operator, a mining or construction fleet, or a hospital delivery robot,
chooses the platform for the task: payload, ruggedness, cost, and sensing
are fixed long before any model is considered and are not changed merely
to suit a checkpoint. Such a deployer does not train a foundation model
from scratch and starts with little or no local data, since collecting it
on the target platform is the expensive step the model is meant to make
worthwhile. Benchmark scores are thus evidence of capability, not of
compatibility with the platform. In our experiments a leading closed-loop model of a standard driving benchmark (SimLingo; Renz et al., 2025) consumes a single
110∘110^{\circ} camera that neither the 64∘64^{\circ} front camera of a
nuPlan-style monocular camera setup nor its surround ring reproduces as
one view, and under an inference deadline shorter than its own latency it collides on 80 to 90% of routes; the
failure belongs to the deployment loop, not to the model. Rank alone is
therefore not a sufficient criterion; the question is which model is a
viable starting point for the platform and what must change to make it
work: the model, the sensing hardware, the execution architecture, or the
training data.

Fine-tuning is the natural response to such differences, but the
first question is not how to fine-tune; it is which part of the gap
between a public checkpoint and the platform fine-tuning can reach at
all: more data cannot recover
information the observations do not preserve, and lower open-loop
error does not resolve delayed execution. Our insight is
that deployment gaps should therefore be diagnosed by
repairability, by whether their dominant cause is missing
information, late outputs, or distribution shift, since these call for
interventions that are not interchangeable (Figure 1a–c). A sensing gap arises when task-relevant distinctions cannot
be recovered from the deployed observations (Proposition 1, Section B.2);
the repair is a different sensing configuration or a model whose
requirements match the platform. A latency gap arises when model
outputs arrive too late for the control loop; its consequences depend
on whether the controller replays stale commands or tracks a delayed
plan with fresh state
(Katsikopoulos & Engelbrecht, 2003; Ramstedt & Pal, 2019), and the repair
is faster computation or a different output-consumption architecture,
not more data. A distribution gap arises from differences in
appearance, scene structure, or behavior, the mechanism target-domain
adaptation is designed to address (Ben-David et al., 2010).

Building on this diagnosis, we introduce Triage
(Figure 1d), a staged diagnostic framework for the
feasibility-gated selection and monitored adaptation of embodied
foundation models. It checks each candidate’s sensing requirements
against the platform and measures its end-to-end latency, from camera
frame to plan, on the deployment hardware against the deadline of the
intended control interface. Candidates
that violate either requirement are excluded, and a higher score cannot
bring them back: that takes a change to sensing, compute, model
implementation, or the execution interface. Among the remaining
candidates the target-relevant benchmark score selects, while passive
probes on short local logs confirm each candidate’s tier and check that
it responds to its images as it should; adaptation is evaluated on tracking
performance, perturbation sensitivity (Kumar et al., 2022), and
reliance on the image. When no candidate satisfies the
requirements, Triage reports the limiting constraints rather
than forcing a choice. Beyond a benchmark ranking, Triage
contributes three things: gates with operational definitions, and
evidence that selecting by score or by closed-loop rank violates them; a split of the gap by
what repairs it; and monitoring of adaptation for the robustness it can
cost. Within the feasible set it ranks as the benchmark does, since no
cheaper evidence we tested ranked better. Its purpose is to determine when benchmark
evidence applies to a deployment and where effort should go, not to
produce another universal ranking.

Contributions.
(i) We formulate the deployment of pretrained embodied foundation models
on a fixed platform as a problem of repairability rather than
benchmark ranking, distinguishing sensing, latency, and distribution gaps
by their causes and interventions, and turn it into Triage, a
staged framework that returns either a viable starting point or the
constraint preventing deployment.
(ii) We evaluate Triage on 1,085 closed-loop runs in
CARLA/Bench2Drive, thirteen driving configurations on four-city nuPlan
logs (eleven scored under the official NAVSIM evaluator), and six
open-weight manipulation models on Bridge V2. Restricting field of view
costs 2.22.2–5.7×5.7\times more than reducing resolution at a matched pixel
budget in driving and 1.61.6–2.4×2.4\times in manipulation, and whether
fine-tuning compensates a sensory restriction depends on the model, on whether its vision encoder adapts and on how much is cropped.
(iii) We run all five stages of Triage on a full-scale vehicle
(Sections 5 and A): its factory camera fails the sensing gate; the latency gate, applied to the end-to-end latency measured on board, removes the two highest-scoring candidates, neither of which completed a closed-loop trip; Stage 4 returns a model that passes closed-loop acceptance; and the closed-loop check withholds a locally fine-tuned model that had improved offline (Table 3).

title: FailPoint-X: A Policy-Matched, Failure-Anchored Benchmark for Offline VLA Post-Training from Human Takeovers
authors: Zirui Li,Yujie Yan,Jingxuan Qian,Yangang Ren,Haizhou Yin,Haoran Xu,Chen Lv
comment: (8-page main paper, references, and 24-page supplementary material), 9 figures, 20 tables. Zirui Li and Yujie Yan contributed equally. Project page:this https URL; Code:this https URL
abstract: Human takeovers offer corrective supervision for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, but their contribution to offline post-training must be separated from that of continued optimization. We introduce FailPoint-X, a benchmark for offline VLA post-training with human takeovers. To represent uncertainty in failure onset, an annotator marks an interval for each failure, and training takeovers start at seeded frames sampled within it. From one fixed π0.5\pi_{0.5} checkpoint, which also initializes post-training, we assemble 629 natural failures across 10 LIBERO-X task families at up to five difficulty levels. All 2,823 takeover attempts are logged; 2,400 are accepted recoveries, of which 2,320 are used for post-training. Evaluation restarts every method from the fixed midpoints of 384 held-out failure intervals. Under matched actor-update counts, we compare behavior cloning of recoveries, value-based offline learning on recoveries and failed rollouts, and continued training on existing demonstrations. Within 1,200 steps on the 240 L1–L3 held-out failures, cloning improves recovery by 29.4 percentage points (pp) over the demonstration-only control; the value-based learner does not establish a further gain (1.5 pp). In exploratory evaluation from L1–L5 nominal starts at the same horizon, cloning loses 30.0 pp of success relative to the base policy; mixing in demonstrations reduces the loss to 16.5 pp, a reduction that shrinks under a stricter, pre-specified horizon. Restorable failure states and a shared evaluator let all methods be compared from identical starts.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies map visual observations and language instructions to robot control actions. Embodied agents more broadly must decide and act reliably under partial observation, from judging whether a target is present to searching unseen environments for it [15, 11, 3]. Reliable manipulation, however, requires handling states induced by the robot’s own errors, including missed grasps, misplaced objects, and interrupted task progress. At such states, a human takeover can supply corrective actions that restore progress toward the original goal. Offline post-training seeks to make such recovery autonomous, learning from human corrections or from the robot’s own mixed-quality deployment experience [26]; we study it on human recoveries recorded at a fixed policy’s own failures. Training uses failed policy executions and human takeovers from their intermediate states; the resulting policy must autonomously complete the original task from held-out failure states of the same task configurations.

The contribution of takeover data is difficult to isolate from overall task success alone. From a nominal start, a higher success rate may reflect either avoiding an error or recovering from one. Moreover, post-training adds optimization steps, so comparing a post-trained policy directly with the base policy conflates the effect of new data with that of continued optimization. LIBERO-RECOVER [18] reports recovery gains from fine-tuning on recoveries mixed with demonstrations, without a demonstration-only control matched in training recipe and optimizer steps. RePO-VLA [19] includes a matched-budget ablation of value conditioning on the real-robot Fold Towel task and evaluates recovery under injected perturbations, and SimPT [30] compares post-training methods at matched policy-update counts on held-out environment seeds; neither reports recovery from the base policy’s own held-out failures against a matched demonstration-only control. We therefore ask two questions about using recovery data for offline post-training. Q1: At matched actor updates, does training on human recoveries improve failure recovery more than continued training on existing demonstrations? Beyond the successful corrections, the preceding failed executions provide an additional negative training signal. Q2: Does value-based post-training on both recoveries and failed rollouts improve upon behavior cloning of recoveries alone?

Collecting recovery data also requires deciding when to intervene. Selecting a single frame, whether by a model or a human, commits data collection to a single temporal judgment, yet perceived event boundaries depend on physical changes, interpreted goals, and temporal granularity [14]. We therefore let an annotator bracket the failure onset with an interval [a,b][a,b] and start training takeovers from seeded frames sampled within it.

We introduce FailPoint-X, a policy-matched benchmark for offline VLA post-training with human takeovers: one checkpoint both generates the failures and initializes post-training (Fig. 1, Table 1). Because simulation can restore exactly the same recorded physical state across policies, the benchmark’s failure-anchored protocol (Sec. 4) restarts every evaluated policy (arm) from the interval midpoints of the same 384 held-out failures and, separately, from nominal starts to measure retained task performance. The unchanged base policy (Base-restart) provides a reference. Demo-continue continues training on existing demonstrations for as many actor updates as the takeover-trained arms: Takeover-BC clones accepted recoveries, IQL-R2 adds failed training rollouts and a learned critic, and Mix-BC mixes recoveries with demonstrations. Q1 and Q2, paired over task families, are confirmatory on the 240 held-out L1–L3 failures of all 10 families; Mix-BC, the 144 L4–L5 failures, and nominal starts are exploratory.

Our collection pipeline (Sec. 3, Fig. 2) supplies recovery supervision from restorable failure states and logs its human cost. From rollouts of a fixed π0.5\pi_{0.5} [10] checkpoint, we assemble 629 natural failures across 10 LIBERO-X [31] task families at up to five difficulty levels, split by seed into training and held-out sets. Takeovers are protocol-timed: the protocol, not the operator, draws 10 seeded start frames per training failure, and unsuccessful attempts are retried at the same frame. We retain all 2,823 attempts, including 2,400 accepted recoveries, of which 2,320 are used for post-training.

Within a 1,200-step horizon on L1–L3, Takeover-BC improves recovery by 29.4 percentage points (pp) over Demo-continue, whereas IQL-R2 does not establish a further gain over Takeover-BC (1.5 pp; Fig. 3a). In exploratory evaluations from L1–L5 nominal starts at the same horizon, Takeover-BC loses 30.0 pp of nominal success relative to the base policy; mixing in demonstrations reduces this loss to 16.5 pp but lowers recovery (Fig. 3b). This smaller loss depends on the evaluation horizon: under the stricter, pre-specified 1.1​T1.1T horizon (TT: mean demonstration length), Takeover-BC and Mix-BC change nominal success by similar amounts (−-33.2 and −-30.9 pp; Sec. 5). Thus, takeover data improve recovery in this study, while nominal-task evaluation reveals an accompanying retention loss.

Our contributions are:

FailPoint-X, a policy-matched benchmark for offline VLA post-training with human takeovers, combining restorable failure states from one base checkpoint (reusable across policies, policy-matched when initialized from it), fixed splits, matched actor updates, and joint recovery and nominal-task evaluation (Secs. 3 and 4).

FailPoint-X, a policy-matched benchmark for offline VLA post-training with human takeovers, combining restorable failure states from one base checkpoint (reusable across policies, policy-matched when initialized from it), fixed splits, matched actor updates, and joint recovery and nominal-task evaluation (Secs. 3 and 4).

Interval-based takeover collection and a failure-and-recovery dataset with human-annotated failure intervals, seeded takeover starts within each training interval, and complete attempt logs of human collection cost (Sec. 3).

A controlled empirical study of recovery benefit and nominal-task loss for a fixed checkpoint, with pre-specified L1–L3 comparisons of behavior cloning against continued demonstration training (Q1) and value-based learning (Q2), and exploratory analyses of Mix-BC, L4–L5, nominal starts, task families, and additional training and inference variants (Sec. 5).

title: RegHarness: Regulating What Code-as-Policy Agents Keep from Steps to Skills
authors: Shengming Liu,Yunyi Gao,Xinyi Wang,Jianyong Sun,Shuai Wang,Yi Deng,Li Chenye,Mingcai Zhou,Sim Kuan Goh
abstract:
Code-as-Policy agents generate, execute, and revise robot programs, but often lack explicit mechanisms to govern what persists across executions: which actions are retained within a trial and which code modifications carry over to subsequent runs. This leaves two critical aspects of agent behavior insufficiently controlled: step-level execution and cross-run adaptation.
We present RegHarness, a two-level harness that governs both forms of persistence for the RATs agent team, without relying on a vision-language-action (VLA) policy or demonstrations. Within each trial, run-time governance evaluates each proposed step from a reset scene, replaying the committed steps, while a fixed-rule controller commits the step only when both RATs’ verifier and a task-long LLM auditor approve it. Between runs, a coding agent uses logged failures to develop and test revisions to skills, primitives, and rules, which remain disabled by default until explicitly enabled by the authors.
Using a single low-cost model across all run-time roles, RegHarness achieves an 87.8% success rate (158/180) on paired LIBERO-PRO trials, compared with 39.4% for RATs, and a 72.0% success rate on MolmoSpaces trials. A 2×\times2 ablation study of RegHarness’s two levels shows that its skill refinement alone increases RATs’ successful trials from 71 to 135, whereas run-time governance alone achieves 105 and RATs’ native stepwise reset-and-replay mode achieves only 46.
These findings suggest that, for Code-as-Policy agents operating with low-cost models, task success depends not only on how generated programs are executed, but also on the quality of the reusable skills they invoke and how those skills evolve across runs.
introduction:
Consider the task in : pick the black bowl on top of a cabinet and place it on a plate.
RATs [26], a Code-as-Policy [15] agent team that we run with a low-cost language model, makes six attempts at this LIBERO-PRO [32] task, each a program for the whole plan.
Its static checker rejects one program before it runs, and none of the five that run lifts the bowl: the first leaves it on the cabinet, the last two knock it onto the table.

Over the 180 paired LIBERO-PRO trials, RATs solves 39.4% (71/180) within six attempts but only 13 on the first.
In its published loop, RATs judges each step only after the whole program has run; a retry, though prompted to keep what worked, is a complete program run again from the reset scene, so a passed step can change and must pass again.
All 692 retries are complete programs, and 86% (493/574) of those that follow a diagnosed failure change code outside the failed step (criteria in the supplementary material).
Nor does a clean verdict mean the work is done: in 117 of the 670 failed executions, the verifier flags no failed step.

What these agents lack is a rule for what to keep: which executed steps stay committed within a trial, and which code changes carry over to the next run.
Testing one step at a time does not supply it by itself: the released RATs code already contains a stepwise mode, off by default and not described in its paper, that resets the scene and replays the passed steps before every try, but it commits a step on the verifier’s pass alone and, once a step’s tries run out, commits the step unverified so that the plan can go on.
A reset protects a retried step from what the failed test left behind, but it also erases what that test revealed; a trial therefore needs a memory that outlives the reset, and a commit rule that never keeps an unverified step instead of letting the coder’s next program decide which code survives.
Between runs, the code itself must change: even after we add such a commit rule to RATs (+ Harness, Sec. 4.3), 75 of the 180 trials still fail, 30 of them at a grasp that never lifts a non-flat object (19) or at a placement off target (11).

RegHarness regulates what persists at these two time scales (Fig. 2).
Within a trial, it wraps RATs’ planner, coder and verifier and reuses the executor of the stepwise mode, so every step test resets the scene and replays the committed steps (reset-and-replay); one LLM auditor per trial audits plans, code, step tests and finished plans that fail the benchmark’s task check, and a controller of six fixed rules turns its proposal and the remaining budget into commit, retry, replan or abort, never committing a step that the verifier has not passed.
Between runs, a coding agent (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code) reads full trial logs and frames and turns each fix to skills, primitives or rules into a default-off switch that must pass tests, and a byte-for-byte equivalence check when off, before the authors can enable it.
Reset-and-replay, which needs a scene that software can reset, is confined to simulation.

Coding agents and optimizers already revise robot harnesses and skills between runs [6, 18, 25, 4, 29, 5], most of them behind an automatic acceptance test that our author-gated loop lacks, and the concurrent RegenHarness separates a model’s proposal from a deterministic commit gate on a quadruped [23].
RegHarness is a new harness framework that improves RATs in two ways, without a VLA policy or demonstrations: within a trial it replaces RATs’ loop with a commit rule over steps tested from a reset scene, and between runs it refines the skill library that RATs shares across tasks.

With one low-cost model in every role, RegHarness solves 158 of the 180 LIBERO-PRO trials on initial states 0–2 (87.8%), where RATs solves 71 (39.4%), and 260 of 300 (86.7%) over five initial states; on MolmoSpaces it solves 72.0% (144/200).
The 2×\times2 splits this gain unevenly between RegHarness’s two levels: its refined skills add 64 trials under RATs’ loop and 53 under run-time governance, whereas replacing RATs’ loop with run-time governance adds 34 trials with the released skills and 23 with the refined ones (exact McNemar p=1.2×10−4p=1.2\times 10^{-4} and 2.9×10−42.9\times 10^{-4}).
RATs’ own stepwise mode solves 46, fewer than RATs itself, so the reset alone does not explain the margin of run-time governance.
A RegHarness trial costs an estimated CNY 2.16 (about US$0.32 at CNY 6.67 per US$) in model calls, against 1.51 (US$0.23) for RATs (Sec. 4.5).
Both levels were debugged on initial state 0 only and tested directly on states 1–4 (Sec. 4.1).

Our contributions are:

Rule-decided commits over steps tested from a reset scene, paired with author-gated refinement of a shared skill library, around an existing Code-as-Policy agent and without a VLA policy or demonstrations (Sec. 3).

A 2×\times2 over the control loop and the skill library on the same 180 paired LIBERO-PRO trials, with RATs’ own stepwise mode as a control (Secs. 4.2 and 4.3).

An account of what happens inside trials, what still fails and what it costs, failures caused by run-time governance included (Secs. 4.4, 4.5 and 4.6).

1. Rule-decided commits over steps tested from a reset scene, paired with author-gated refinement of a shared skill library, around an existing Code-as-Policy agent and without a VLA policy or demonstrations (Sec. 3).

2. A 2×\times2 over the control loop and the skill library on the same 180 paired LIBERO-PRO trials, with RATs’ own stepwise mode as a control (Secs. 4.2 and 4.3).

3. An account of what happens inside trials, what still fails and what it costs, failures caused by run-time governance included (Secs. 4.4, 4.5 and 4.6).

title: PROVE: Predict-to-Specify and Observe-to-Verify for Human-Aligned Evaluation of Mobile Manipulation
authors: Bowen Lyu,Yunan Liu,Liaoyuan Fan,Qinchuan Cheng,Jiafei Duan,Cheston Tan,Shijie Li
abstract:
Judging open-world robot manipulation is hard because layouts, articulated fixtures, and valid goal configurations vary widely.
On RoboCasa365, simulator predicates agree with human judgments on only 69.09% of rollouts, and a frontier VLM judge on 86.12%.
We present PROVE (Predict-to-Specify, Observe-to-Verify), which first specifies what success should look like and then checks the outcome.
PROVE refines success conditions from the instruction,
the initial scene, a target-object reference image,
and a generated goal image.
The goal image only sharpens the conditions and never serves as evidence.
On 6,500 human-annotated rollouts over 65 atomic actions, PROVE reaches 96.83% agreement.
Applied to open-source policies, it reports far lower success than native checks and changes their ranking.
To reduce evaluation overhead in policy learning, we distill PROVE into PROVE-Lite, a 4B evaluator that needs no reference images.
In one forward pass, PROVE-Lite predicts the outcome and the terminal state of each task condition.
It reaches 91.20% agreement while running about 38×\times faster than PROVE.
Mapped to a severity-aware reward, its diagnoses improve PPO post-training over both simulator and binary rewards.
Project page: https://sj-li.com/projects/prove/.
introduction:
Mobile manipulation benchmarks decompose household tasks into atomic actions such as grasping, placing, closing doors, and turning knobs.
Judging these actions reliably matters for benchmark credibility [30, 31, 52] and for policy improvement [48].
In open-world scenes, this is harder than it looks.
Layouts and articulated fixtures vary across kitchens, and one instruction often admits several valid goal configurations.
An evaluator should tell whether the robot succeeded and which physical conditions remain unmet.
Ideally, this diagnosis should also help improve the policy.

Existing evaluators fall short.
Simulation benchmarks check fixed predicates over privileged object states.
These states are unavailable on physical robots, and the predicates cannot anticipate every valid outcome.
On RoboCasa365 [31], they agree with human judgments on only 69.09% of rollouts.
They err in both directions, accepting failures and rejecting successes, and never explain why (1).
VLM judges [11, 43] avoid privileged state, but instruction-and-terminal-only judging omits the initial scene context.
Prompted with the instruction alone, they turn plausible yet irrelevant expectations into requirements.
For example, they may demand closing a cabinet door that was already open.
Such a judge reaches 82.52% agreement with our 8B backbone and 86.12% with a frontier model, GPT-6.1 Sol [36].

Human judges do better because they separate two questions.
What should success look like in this scene, and did it actually happen?
They first set the standard from the task, the scene, and the expected outcome, and only then consult the evidence.
VLMs understand instructions, objects, and spatial relations [3].
Image-editing models can predict the intended post-action configuration [8, 7].
Generated images, however, contain artifacts and implausible contact.
They tell us about the goal but are unreliable as a reference for matching.
We therefore let predictions specify and observations verify.
The goal image only sharpens the success conditions.
The terminal observations alone decide whether those conditions hold, so the outcome never shapes its own standard.

Following this principle, we build PROVE, an evaluation harness that mirrors the human process (2).
One frozen MLLM refines success conditions in three stages.
It starts from the instruction alone (M1) and adds the initial scene and target object (M2).
The last stage adds a generated goal image (M3).
On 6,500 human-annotated rollouts over 65 atomic actions, this progressive grounding raises agreement to 96.83%.
Ablations confirm that the goal image helps only as specification, and that the gain transfers across backbones.
Applied to four open-source policies, PROVE reports far lower success than native checks and reorders them.
When the two disagree, blind human review sides with PROVE in 95.42% of cases.

PROVE suits offline evaluation, where each rollout is judged once.
Policy training is different: thousands of rollouts must be judged on the fly.
There, PROVE’s multi-stage inference and reference assets become too costly.
We therefore distill [14] it into PROVE-Lite, an evaluator that needs no reference images (3).
In a single forward pass, PROVE-Lite predicts the outcome and the terminal state of each task condition.
Trained only on PROVE’s pseudo-labels, it reaches 91.20% agreement while running about 38×\times faster.

We validate PROVE-Lite where it is meant to be used: as the reward in policy post-training.
Its diagnoses describe how far each condition is from its target.
They can therefore grade failures instead of treating them alike.
A narrow door gap, for instance, is penalized less than a wide-open door.
We map each diagnosed state to a fixed severity.
The resulting terminal reward gives failed rollouts bounded partial credit while keeping binary success dominant.
In controlled PPO [42] post-training, it beats simulator rewards by 4.58 points and binary PROVE-Lite rewards by 2.00 points.

Our contributions are three-fold:

Predict-to-Specify, Observe-to-Verify evaluation. PROVE grounds success conditions in the task, the scene, and a generated goal image. It verifies them against real observations only.

Reference-free evaluation for policy learning. PROVE-Lite is distilled from PROVE without manual labels. Beyond the outcome, it diagnoses the terminal state of each task condition in one forward pass.

Diagnosis-guided terminal reward. The reward grades failed rollouts by the physical severity of their unmet conditions. It outperforms simulator and binary rewards in PPO post-training.

1. Predict-to-Specify, Observe-to-Verify evaluation. PROVE grounds success conditions in the task, the scene, and a generated goal image. It verifies them against real observations only.

2. Reference-free evaluation for policy learning. PROVE-Lite is distilled from PROVE without manual labels. Beyond the outcome, it diagnoses the terminal state of each task condition in one forward pass.

3. Diagnosis-guided terminal reward. The reward grades failed rollouts by the physical severity of their unmet conditions. It outperforms simulator and binary rewards in PPO post-training.

title: RoboJackVR: Turning Robot Tasks into VR Games for Scalable Demonstration Collection
authors: Ben Ma,Jixuan Cai
abstract:
Scaling robot demonstration datasets requires collection systems that
accommodate more participants and diverse tasks, yet teleoperation barriers
and task-adaptation effort limit this expansion. We present RoboJackVR, a
standalone virtual reality (VR) game in which players manipulate simulated
robots to execute combat skills and contribute demonstrations. MuJoCo
simulation and demonstration recording run locally on the headset, removing
the need for an external PC or simulation server during collection. Tutorials, skill
selection, combat consequences, and character progression organize repeated
task attempts within a continuing game. Task contracts declare assets,
controls, resets, success criteria, and recording semantics; separate game
configurations specify guidance, attempt groups, skill effects, and course
placement. Shared bindings connect these declarations to task execution,
outcome handling, and recording, allowing tasks to reuse the game flow while
retaining their control and success semantics. Batch tools package supported
resources and generate configurations, with manual adaptation and review for
new interfaces and unsupported predicates. We instantiate the approach with
SO101-Nexus-derived and LIBERO tasks. On the 66 LIBERO-90 tasks covered by the collected data, ACT policies
trained solely on VR demonstrations retain approximately 91% of the
full-standard simulation-demonstration baseline’s success rate on held-out
initial states, averaged over four training seeds. These results support the
utility of play-collected VR demonstrations for policy learning in this setting.
introduction:
Scaling robot demonstration collection requires broader participation and
more task coverage, but teleoperation barriers and the effort of adapting
new tasks limit both [1, 2]. DROID illustrates the
value of diverse demonstrations alongside the hardware, labor, and
coordination needed to obtain them [3]. Extended reality (XR) interfaces to
simulation may still depend on an external simulation host [2];
running task execution on the headset removes this additional computing
requirement from the participant’s collection setup. Accessible interfaces
and reusable task infrastructure address parts of this challenge; games
provide a way to organize repeated contributions within an activity that
players can understand and choose to continue.

We ask: How can existing robot task collections become VR game content
through a reusable gameplay and collection workflow, and can demonstrations
collected during play support robot learning? Our central idea gives each
task two connected roles: an operation challenge that players choose and
master, and a demonstration unit with explicit controls, success criteria,
and recording semantics. The design must connect task execution to game
consequences while preserving the information needed to interpret the data.

We present RoboJackVR, a VR adventure game built around robot manipulation.
Players select skills according to the battle state, operate simulated robots,
and progress through subsequent challenges. Opening a drawer, for example,
executes an attack skill: the task outcome changes the battle state and
produces a demonstration record. Task contracts declare execution and
recording interfaces; separate game configurations specify guidance, attempt
groups, skill effects, and course placement. Shared bindings connect them to
instruction, control, feedback, progression, and recording
(Figure 1). New tasks can extend the same game while
retaining their task-specific control and success semantics.

The paper focuses on expanding playable task coverage, instantiated with
SO101-Nexus-derived [4] and LIBERO tasks [5]. Concrete bindings
identify reusable components and the configuration or implementation that
remains task-specific. A policy-learning study on LIBERO-90 using Action
Chunking with Transformers (ACT) [6] compares full and reduced
standard-data budgets, VR-only training, and joint training on VR and reduced
standard data. Standard demonstrations here are LIBERO’s public
simulation data, not physical-robot recordings. The study connects
on-headset demonstration collection, trajectory conversion, and downstream
policy training within a common experimental pipeline.

Our contributions are:

A reusable task-to-game interface that preserves declared task controls
and success conditions while connecting robot-task execution to shared
guidance, combat feedback, progression, and demonstration recording.

A standalone VR game that runs MuJoCo simulation and demonstration
recording on consumer Quest headsets, with default combat configurations
for 130 LIBERO and four SO101 tasks.

A pipeline that converts VR records into the standard LIBERO
demonstration format, and a LIBERO-90 ACT study comparing
standard-data budgets, VR-only training, and joint VR and standard-data
training.

1. A reusable task-to-game interface that preserves declared task controls
and success conditions while connecting robot-task execution to shared
guidance, combat feedback, progression, and demonstration recording.

2. A standalone VR game that runs MuJoCo simulation and demonstration
recording on consumer Quest headsets, with default combat configurations
for 130 LIBERO and four SO101 tasks.

3. A pipeline that converts VR records into the standard LIBERO
demonstration format, and a LIBERO-90 ACT study comparing
standard-data budgets, VR-only training, and joint VR and standard-data
training.

title: Practice Makes Fluent: Learning to Use Earlier Predictions in Looped Models
authors: Minseok seo,Hee-Seon Kim,Changick Kim
abstract:
People become faster at a task through practice, but models that improve with experience do not necessarily learn to use less computation.
We train looped models, whose intermediate predictions allow earlier exits, to perform tasks with fewer iterations through practice.
This is difficult because shared-weight updates can degrade the final-loop prediction while improving early ones, and the exit gate must track early predictions as their quality changes.
We propose FLUENT, which requires no additional task labels or rewards: it distills the initial model’s final-loop prediction into early predictions, anchors the current final-loop prediction to the same frozen teacher, and trains the exit gate to balance disagreement with the current final-loop prediction against computation cost.
FLUENT improves performance at shallower depth in new Crafter worlds, raises LIBERO success with fewer action-head iterations, and maintains language-model accuracy at lower selected depth.
On a real robot, success rises from 62.3% to 74.6% while mean time over successful episodes falls from 69 s to 31 s. The project page is available at https://msseok96-cpu.github.io/FLUENT/.
introduction:
A person who repeats a task gets faster at it. Execution time often falls
steeply over the first attempts and more gradually thereafter [31, 29]
(Fig. 1, left).
Robots and agents also perform similar tasks repeatedly, from
visual manipulation [4, 21, 3, 42]
to language-guided interaction [39, 43].
Yet better task performance through experience does not necessarily
mean less computation at inference.

Early exit and adaptive-depth methods allocate computation according
to the current input [37, 47, 28, 55, 50, 42].
Our question is complementary: can experience make a previously
difficult task require less computation?
Methods that reuse reasoning traces [33, 39, 6],
skills [43, 32], or cached
computation [13, 49, 7]
exploit previous experience through external records.
These records must be stored, retrieved, and matched to the current task.
We instead store experience in the model’s weights: the model
learns through self-distillation from the task inputs it encounters,
without additional labels or rewards. We call this process practice,
and aim to improve task performance while reducing the computation needed
to perform the task.

We study this question in looped models [55, 19, 42].
In the architectures we consider, a shared block repeatedly updates
a latent state, and a shared output head can read a prediction
after each loop.
This makes earlier predictions available, but availability alone
does not make them useful.
Practice must both improve these predictions and enable the policy
to act on them.
A natural starting point is to use the frozen initial model as a
teacher, distilling its deep predictions into shallow loops.

However, this addresses only part of this problem.
It directly supervises agreement between the first loop and the
teacher, not the task performance of every subsequent loop.
Because the weights are shared, later predictions also change,
but they need not improve together.
Moreover, even an improved first-loop prediction saves computation
only when the exit gate selects it.
Improving early predictions and learning to use them are
distinct aspects of practice.

We present FLUENT, a self-distillation procedure that addresses
these two parts together.
Translate trains early predictions to match the final-loop output
of the frozen initial model.
Because these updates also affect later loops,
Anchor keeps the current final-loop prediction close to the
same frozen teacher.
This anchored prediction provides the reference for training the gate.
Gate adapts the exit policy to the updated predictions, balancing
agreement with the current final loop against the cost of further
computation.
Practice uses no additional task labels or rewards, and inference
requires no external experience store.

We evaluate FLUENT in four settings, examining both prediction
depth and task performance.
In Crafter [14], FLUENT improves performance
in new worlds while selecting shallower predictions.
On LIBERO [26], FLUENT executes 36.7% fewer
action-head iterations than RD-VLA [42],
while improving success.
On a real robot, relative to the SFT policy, FLUENT increases
success from 62.3% to 74.6% and reduces mean completion time
over successful episodes from 69 s to 31 s.
In language-model distillation, compared with the vanilla model
using its original gate, FLUENT maintains mean accuracy
while reducing mean selected depth by 18.7%.

title: A general-purpose safe manipulator planning framework for diverse environments without retraining
authors: Mingkang Long,Rong Su,Luhang Hong,Qingqing Wang,Ruochen Tai
abstract: Nowadays, robots need to be retrained whenever their operating environment changes, and this prohibitive training cost keeps them far from daily use. The community is calling for innovations that bestow on a robot the ability to safely grasp different objects under different conditions without excessive training data and computing power. In response to this call, we present a general-purpose manipulator mission-planning framework, allowing a robot to safely perform manipulation tasks, such as grasping objects that fit in its gripper, across different operating environments without retraining its controllers. The framework rests on two innovations: a finite-state abstracted model, bisimilar to the original system dynamics, that describes accessibility of the space in front of the robot under its given arm and gripper, and a block-conservative specification generation method that turns each manipulation task under any specific operational environment into specifications about state accessibility of the abstracted model. A task proven feasible and safe on the abstracted model is guaranteed to be safe and achievable by the robot. Real-world case studies conducted on a Unitree G1 U1 humanoid show that manipulation tasks commonly encountered in daily life, such as grasping an object, pressing an elevator button or picking up a berry, can be handled within this framework, where an abstracted model of the G1 U1 robot is built only once to avoid costly model reconstructions, and different tasks are simply captured by specific block-conservative specifications, achievable by a generic mission planner with vision-based feedback control.

title: $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM: Efficient Hierarchical Memory Across Modalities and Timescales for World-Action Models
authors: Xiaopeng Zhang,Weiqi Yuan,Xin Zhu,Jiaxi Huang,Yueqi Hu,Yin Zhang,Jian Yao,Yanjie Li
abstract:
Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires historical context, yet retaining extensive visual histories incurs growing storage and retrieval costs, while aggressive compression risks losing fine-grained information needed for subsequent decisions.
Moreover, executed action histories capture intermediate behaviors that sparse visual observations may miss.
Preserving this complementary context efficiently calls for modality-specific memory mechanisms that balance recent detail with long-term retention.
To this end, we introduce M2-WAM, a world-action model equipped with hierarchical visual and interaction memories.
M2-WAM preserves recent visual observations in dense short-term memory while consolidating entries evicted from this window into fixed-size associative long-term memory through gated delta updates.
Within the same short- and long-term hierarchy, interaction memory encodes executed action prefixes into compact temporal representations, complementing visual observations with behavioral context.
These complementary memories are integrated into world-action modeling through layer-wise retrieval, enabling memory-augmented action generation with a bounded online memory footprint independent of episode length.
On the memory-dependent simulation benchmarks MIKASA-Robo and RMBench, M2-WAM achieves +53.2% and +61.2% absolute improvements in average success rates over Fast-WAM, respectively.
These gains extend to real-world manipulation, where M2-WAM achieves a +29.3% absolute improvement over LingBot-VA in average success across three tasks.
These results suggest that M2-WAM offers a promising approach to efficient memory-augmented world-action modeling.
introduction:
Long-horizon robotic manipulation often requires reasoning beyond the current observation [52, 38, 22]. For example, in a shell game task, a robot must track a target object as it is occluded and moved beneath visually identical cups, relying on historical observations to identify its location [10, 13]. Such tasks are inherently non-Markovian with respect to instantaneous observations, requiring policies to reason over past observations and interactions [17]. Recent world-action models (WAMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities by jointly modeling visual dynamics and robot actions [42, 19, 44]. However, many WAMs still rely on current observations or limited contexts, making it difficult to exploit information from earlier stages of execution.

Historical context must support ongoing decisions while preserving
information from earlier task stages. Recent observations provide
spatial detail, whereas earlier observations may
contain cues that remain relevant after they leave view.
As shown in Figure (a,b), a memoryless WAM lacks
access to earlier observations, whereas retaining full visual history
incurs storage and retrieval costs that grow with episode length.
A sliding window preserves recent detail but discards older observations
[37, 39].
Alternatively, compact or recurrent memories reduce storage costs,
but compression can limit access to fine-grained historical information
[40, 49].
We argue for allocating memory capacity across timescales:
retaining recent observations explicitly and consolidating older
entries into a compact, persistent state. This design preserves
recent detail without compressing all observations and
extends historical coverage beyond a fixed window, drawing inspiration
from short- and long-term memory [1] and
complementary learning systems [26].

However, retaining history across timescales is only part of the
challenge: memory must also capture complementary information
from observations and executed actions. Visual observations
describe scene configurations and changes, but may omit behavior
between sampled frames.
Denser sampling increases visual encoding and storage costs
for the same duration.
Executed action prefixes complement these observations by
recording the intervening actions, providing compact, temporally
denser behavioral context
[53, 50, 27].
This motivates modality-aware memory that preserves
both scene observations and executed actions.
We therefore adopt visual and interaction memories that preserve
spatial details and temporal action patterns, respectively,
within a common short- and long-term hierarchy.

Building on these considerations, we propose M2-WAM, which augments a mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architecture with complementary visual and interaction memories across timescales, as illustrated in Figure (c). The visual memory preserves an initial observation anchor and recent observations as dense spatial key-value (KV) representations, while consolidating older information into fixed-size, layer-wise associative states through gated delta updates [41, 14]. To accommodate robot image sequences, we apply temporal decay once per observation according to elapsed time, rather than repeatedly across its spatial tokens. We further replace channel-wise erasure with a scalar erase gate per token and head to improve numerical stability. In parallel, the interaction memory encodes executed action prefixes into compact temporal representations and maintains a shared associative state. These memories are integrated into world-action modeling through layer-wise, query-conditioned retrieval. By combining bounded short-term memories with fixed-size associative states, M2-WAM enables persistent history conditioning with online memory storage and retrieval costs independent of episode length.

Our main contributions are as follows:
1) We propose M2-WAM, a world-action model equipped with modality-specialized hierarchical memory that jointly preserves visual observations and executed interactions across short and long timescales.
2) We develop modality-specific memory representations and associative consolidation mechanisms, together with complementary retrieval pathways that incorporate historical information into world-action computation with bounded online memory and retrieval costs.
3) We conduct extensive experiments on MIKASA-Robo
[10], RMBench [9],
RoboTwin 2.0 [8], and three real-world tasks,
complemented by ablation studies and qualitative and quantitative
analyses. Results demonstrate improved performance on memory-dependent
tasks with bounded online memory and retrieval costs,
supporting the effectiveness and efficiency of our method.

title: Lab2Sim: Agentic Generation of Interactive Laboratory Equipment from Operation Videos
authors: Yuxin Lin,Pei Ren,Yirong Yang,Xuxin Lv,Xingchuang Liao,Diyuan Hou,Jiale He,Zhengping Che,Yongfei Zhang,Wenjun Wu,Zhaoxin Fan
abstract: Generating laboratory assets that faithfully reproduce the appearance, structure, and joint motions of real equipment remains challenging. Existing asset generation methods struggle to directly generate simulation assets for all equipment observed in operation videos and to faithfully reproduce the appearance, joint motions, and internal cavities of the real equipment. To address the challenge, we present Lab2Sim, an agentic framework that generates editable, simulation-ready laboratory equipment assets from egocentric or multi-view operation videos. Lab2Sim comprises four specialized agents. The Evidence Agent combines video observations with laboratory knowledge to specify equipment parts, materials, and functional requirements, which guide the Asset Agent in constructing editable Blender assets. The independent Verifier checks the generated geometry and appearance against the evidence and requirements, providing targeted feedback for revision. The Simulation Integration Agent converts verified Blender assets into simulation instances with physical properties and articulated mechanisms, using execution feedback to refine their behavior. Experiments on human and robot laboratory scenes show that Lab2Sim achieves higher visual fidelity and stronger interaction capability than coding-agent and real-to-sim baselines, including a Codex baseline using the same underlying model. We further demonstrate valve-controlled drainage and use the generated asset library to reproduce laboratory scenes and operations in RoboTwin, supporting reusable simulation environments for robotic laboratory tasks.
introduction:
Robotic automation is increasingly enabling scientific experimentation [4, 37, 8]. Simulation provides an important environment for developing and evaluating these robotic systems, supporting policy training, demonstration generation, and task development before deployment in real laboratories [28, 6]. These applications rely on simulation assets that faithfully represent laboratory equipment in appearance, structure, physical properties, and mechanical interactions. The need for such assets is particularly acute in scientific laboratories [4, 8, 21], where real-world experiments consume reagents, may expose operators to hazardous substances, and require repeated setup and resetting. Simulation can reduce these costs and risks, but its effectiveness depends on interactive assets that faithfully represent laboratory equipment.

Existing approaches to generating such assets can be broadly grouped into three categories. Laboratory simulators [21, 22, 18] typically rely on manually modeled or curated equipment libraries, with assets prepared for specific environments and benchmarks. Articulated reconstruction recovers object geometry and joints from observed states or part motions [15, 23, 24, 17, 29]. Real-to-sim pipelines convert images, videos, or demonstrations into interactive assets and environments [5, 26, 19, 40, 7, 33]. However, these approaches face distinct limitations when applied to laboratory operation videos. Specifically, although existing methods have achieved promising results on everyday objects, we observe substantial shortcomings in the laboratory equipment assets they generate. These include inaccurate material appearance, incomplete internal structures, and inoperable articulated components such as stopcocks and screw caps.

The limitations arise from two aspects. First, video-based methods often rely on object-centric videos that provide clear and sufficiently complete observations of the target object’s motion. This reliance limits their applicability to laboratory operation videos, which capture multi-object experimental workflows rather than systematically demonstrate each apparatus and its mechanisms. Second, modeling pipelines that prioritize external shape often lack targeted inspection of local material and structural details, as well as explicit construction of the cavities and connected internal passages required for laboratory operations. For example, reproducing a separatory funnel’s exterior and assigning a rotational joint to its stopcock does not establish the internal channel through which the valve controls drainage. Addressing these bottlenecks requires extracting equipment-specific evidence from multi-object operation videos and translating functional requirements into construction constraints on materials, internal geometry, and mechanical relationships.

To address the challenge, we propose Lab2Sim, an agentic framework that generates editable laboratory equipment assets and their simulation instances from operation videos, as illustrated in Fig. Lab2Sim: Agentic Generation of Interactive Laboratory Equipment from Operation Videos. The framework comprises four specialized agents. The Evidence Agent combines video observations with laboratory domain knowledge to establish the structure, materials, and functional requirements of each apparatus, which guide the Asset Agent in constructing editable Blender assets and exporting their meshes. An independent Verifier checks the generated assets against the evidence and requirements and guides revisions, while Simulation Integration converts verified assets into interactive simulation instances with physical properties and articulated mechanisms. A Coordinator orchestrates the workflow and routes tasks and feedback among these modules.

We evaluate Lab2Sim on a human-performed chemistry workflow and a multi-camera robot scene, testing required part motions and valve-controlled drainage in simulation. title: FreshVLA: Frequency-Regularized Time Scale Hierarchical Latent Actions for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Jiaming Liang,Yifeng Zhan,Rongyi He,Mu Li,Jiaqi Fan,Zhiyuan Zhang,Qiwei Liang,Zhengjie Zhang,Boyang Cai,Ningyuan Zhang,Xingjian Jing,Qiang Nie
abstract: Learning reusable latent actions from action-free videos offers an effective route to improving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies. However, reconstruction-oriented latent actions do not necessarily benefit policy learning: as they may encode task-irrelevant static appearance with scene identity, or entangle slowly varying task progress with fine-grained execution dynamics in limited discrete code. We propose FreshVLA, a VLA framework built on a frequency-guided, dynamics-sensitive learning paradigm for acquiring temporally hierarchical continuous latent actions. FreshVLA uses a high-pass prior to guide visual transition encoding toward dynamical regions, thereby reducing reliance on static appearance cues. It further organizes latent actions into coarse-grained task progress and fine-grained execution dynamics through cross-timescale sampling and frequency-domain regularization, enhancing their capacity to represent long-horizon behaviors. During policy training, we freeze the pretrained latent action encoder and transfer its representations to robot control through joint flow-matching of latent and robot actions. FreshVLA achieves 98.2% average success on LIBERO and 98.0% on LIBERO-Long, exceeding GR00T-N1.6 on the latter by 3.6%. It also reaches an average sequence length of 4.52 on CALVIN and strong overall success rate of 80.4% in the zero-shot LIBERO-PLUS evaluation. Furthermore, FreshVLA exhibits greater robustness to visual perturbations and a more distinct division of roles between two branches in modeling low- and high-frequency motion, respectively. In 35-step action regression, it achieves a 51.3-percentage-point higher relative error reduction than its hierarchical discrete counterpart. Real-world experiments demonstrate that FreshVLA improves the average success rate over π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 7.5%. The FreshVLA project page is available at https://freshvla.github.io/.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models aim to translate language-conditioned visual understanding into executable robot behavior. Recent systems have advanced this paradigm through larger multimodal backbones, broader robot datasets, and more expressive action decoders [1, 2, 3, 4]. Nevertheless, a fundamental interface challenge remains: policies must transform visual intent into temporally coherent control behavior. This requires representing the visual transitions that should occur in a scene, including which object should move, how contact relationships evolve, and how local execution supports longer-horizon task progress.

Latent Action Models (LAMs) provide a natural means of learning such representations. By predicting or reconstructing observation transitions, LAMs infer latent actions from adjacent frames or observation sequences [5, 6, 7]. These variables can provide supervision for policy pretraining while reducing the need to directly align raw action spaces across embodiments. However, reconstruction objectives do not guarantee that latent actions capture controllable and task-relevant changes. They may instead encode background layouts, static appearance, or other cues that help predict future observations but are only weakly related to control [8, 9, 10]. Furthermore, manipulation trajectories contain both slowly evolving task progress, such as approaching and transporting an object, and local execution dynamics, such as grasp adjustments and release timing. Many prior LAMs represent fixed-interval visual transitions with vector-quantized codes [11, 5, 7], or continuous formulations with a single latent transition scale [6, 12], which may obscure this multi-timescale structure and hinder downstream policies from modeling the temporal dependencies of long-horizon manipulation.

To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose FreshVLA to construct dynamics-sensitive hierarchical latent actions from visual transitions, as is described in Figure 1. In the visual feature space, temporal high-pass responses provide localized cues of change and guide the patch-level attention module toward regions exhibiting task-relevant visual dynamics. In the latent action space, temporal downsampling and upsampling, together with temporal-frequency regularization, encourage the substage-scale transition to model persistent long-horizon dependencies, while the execution-scale representation captures immediate dynamic residuals. Both representations are further used in bidirectional future prediction to explain changes in visual observations. During VLA learning, the pretrained latent action model is kept frozen to preserve the transition space learned from action-free videos. Conditioned on visual-language context, a latent-action flow-matching mechanism jointly models latent actions and robot actions [13, 14].

With 2B parameters, FreshVLA achieves an average success rate of 98.2% on LIBERO, reaches 98.0% on LIBERO-Long, and attains an average sequence length of 4.52 on CALVIN. These results exceed those of GR00T-N1.6 [15] by 1.2 and 3.6 percentage points on the two LIBERO metrics, respectively, and by 0.28 subtasks on CALVIN, highlighting its strength in long-horizon manipulation. In zero-shot LIBERO-PLUS evaluation, it achieves 80.4% macro-average success and outperforms OpenVLA-OFT [16] across all seven perturbation categories, reaching 88.9%, 97.0%, and 97.1% under language, lighting, and background shifts, respectively. Representation analyses further show that FreshVLA’s latent actions are more robust to visual perturbations and exhibit complementary frequency preferences across temporal scales. On the 35-step action-regression probe, FreshVLA achieves a relative error reduction 51.3-percentage-points higher than that of its hierarchical discrete counterpart. Across four real-world tasks, FreshVLA improves mean success by 7.5 percentage points over π0.5\pi_{0.5}, suggesting more reliable object interaction and long-horizon execution.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce a temporally hierarchical continuous latent action representation that organizes visual transitions into substage-scale components capturing long-horizon task progress and execution-scale residuals preserving local dynamics.

We propose FreshVLA, which learns this representation using a temporal high-pass visual prior and frequency-domain regularization. A frozen latent action encoder then provides targets for VLA policy training through joint flow matching over latent and robot actions.

FreshVLA achieves strong results on LIBERO and CALVIN and generalizes well to perturbations in zero-shot LIBERO-PLUS evaluations. Additional experiments and real-world deployments further demonstrate its effectiveness on long-horizon manipulation tasks.

1. We introduce a temporally hierarchical continuous latent action representation that organizes visual transitions into substage-scale components capturing long-horizon task progress and execution-scale residuals preserving local dynamics.

2. We propose FreshVLA, which learns this representation using a temporal high-pass visual prior and frequency-domain regularization. A frozen latent action encoder then provides targets for VLA policy training through joint flow matching over latent and robot actions.

3. FreshVLA achieves strong results on LIBERO and CALVIN and generalizes well to perturbations in zero-shot LIBERO-PLUS evaluations. Additional experiments and real-world deployments further demonstrate its effectiveness on long-horizon manipulation tasks.
