title: Greedy Decoding Hides Good Plans: Sample-and-Verify Planning for Vision-Language Driving Models
authors: Zhipeng Bao,Wenjie Zhao,Yiping Li,Haohua Que,Qianwen Li
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly adopted for end-to-end driving planning, yet their performance is typically evaluated based on a single greedily decoded trajectory. However, greedy decoding may overlook better trajectories within the model’s output distribution. Experiments on WOD-E2E and NAVSIM reveal a consistent performance gap between greedily decoded trajectories and the best sampled candidates, showing that planning errors can arise from trajectory selection, rather than trajectory generation alone. On WOD-E2E, when the ego vehicle should start moving, the model often assigns probability to different possible start times, causing greedy decoding to repeatedly favor waiting and produce a stationary plan even though moving trajectories are available. Motivated by these findings, we propose Sample-and-Verify (SaV), which keeps the VLM planner frozen and samples multiple candidate trajectories. A lightweight verifier is trained from ground-truth futures to estimate the relative quality of these candidates. It uses trajectory kinematics, candidate-set agreement and likelihood, and ego-motion features to select the final trajectory. On WOD-E2E, SaV reduces ADE and FDE by approximately 15% across three VLM planners on the validation set. Changes in RFS are smaller: two planners show slight decreases on val-456, while Alpamayo-1.5 improves from 7.74 to 7.81 RFS on the official test set as ADE@5s decreases by 11%. On NAVSIM, SaV reduces ADE@4s by 10–24% across three VLM planners, while PDMS changes are less consistent. These results show that trajectory selection can substantially improve displacement accuracy without additional planner training. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/hzxbzp/sample-and-verify.
introduction:
Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as end-to-end driving planners, mapping visual observations and ego states to future trajectories, often together with intermediate reasoning [14, 33, 27, 38]. In several recent approaches, trajectory planning is formulated autoregressively by representing future motion as sequences of textual coordinates or discrete action tokens [14, 27, 38]. Research has largely focused on improving what these models learn through stronger visual reasoning and grounding, better action representations, additional driving supervision, or reinforcement-learning post-training [29, 2, 37, 27, 38].

How these planners are decoded at inference time, however, has received less attention. An autoregressive planner learns a distribution over possible future trajectories, but inference requires decoding a single trajectory from that distribution. Greedy decoding makes this selection locally, choosing the most likely token at each generation step. Choosing the most likely token at each step does not necessarily produce the best trajectory overall, especially when the model assigns probability to several plausible behaviors or different timings of the same behavior. Consequently, the quality of a greedily decoded trajectory may not faithfully reflect the planning capability represented by the model distribution.

This distinction raises a fundamental question:
When a VLM produces a poor plan, does the model fail to contain an appropriate trajectory, or does its decoding procedure fail to recover one that is already represented in its output distribution? These two failure modes call for fundamentally different solutions. The former motivates additional data, supervision, or model training. The latter is an inference-time search and selection problem. Existing evaluations, which typically judge only the final decoded trajectory, do not distinguish between them.

We study this question on the Waymo Open Dataset for End-to-End Driving (WOD-E2E) [35] and NAVSIM [8]. Across both benchmarks, we find a gap between the trajectories selected by greedy decoding and the better alternatives available in the same model distribution. A prominent example occurs when the ego vehicle is stationary and should proceed: greedy trajectories from three backbones frequently remain stopped, while alternative moving trajectories remain present in the model distribution. We trace this failure to uncertainty in start time, which causes greedy decoding to repeatedly favor waiting. More broadly, the results on both benchmarks show that greedy decoding can fail to recover better trajectories already generated by the same planner.

Motivated by this observation, we introduce Sample-and-Verify (SaV), a test-time planning framework that separates trajectory generation from trajectory selection. The frozen planner first generates its greedy trajectory together with KK sampled candidates. A lightweight verifier then scores each candidate using its kinematics, agreement with the candidate set, model likelihood, and the ego-motion history, and selects the highest-quality plan. Experiments show that SaV consistently improves trajectory accuracy. On WOD-E2E, SaV reduces 5-s average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) by approximately 15–16% across three VLM planners, reduces failed starts, and transfers across VLMs without retraining. On the official WOD-E2E leaderboard, it improves Alpamayo-1.5’s RFS from 7.74 to 7.81 while reducing ADE@5s by 11%. On NAVSIM, SaV reduces ADE@4s by 9–25% across three publicly released planners. Together, these results suggest that decoding can affect the planning performance of autoregressive VLM-based driving models.

Our contributions are:

We identify trajectory selection as a distinct failure source in autoregressive VLM driving planners, showing that greedy decoding can miss better trajectories already present in the model distribution. This distinction separates decoding failures from trajectory-generation failures and motivates evaluating them independently.

We introduce SaV, a test-time framework that samples candidate trajectories from a frozen VLM planner and ranks them with a lightweight supervised verifier. The planner requires no additional training; only the verifier is trained from logged ground-truth futures.

title: DFLAT: Model-based Diffusion on Differentially Flat Spaces for Long-Horizon Trajectory Optimization
authors: Ege Yuceel,Taekyung Kim,Keyvan Majd,Hideki Okamoto,Bardh Hoxha,Sayan Mitra,Georgios Fainekos
abstract:
Long-horizon diffusion-based planning for kinodynamically constrained systems requires both scalability and feasibility, yet existing diffusion planners typically sacrifice one for the other. We present DFLAT, a diffusion-based planning algorithm that operates directly on a differentially flat trajectory representation. Instead of diffusing over time-discretized controls, DFLAT denoises a compact set of Hermite curve parameters in the flat-output space, consisting of intermediate waypoints together with the endpoint tangents of each segment. Every denoised sample maps to a dynamically consistent trajectory, so feasibility holds by construction rather than being restored afterward. Experiments on challenging tractor–trailer planning benchmarks show that DFLAT matches or exceeds the success rates of existing baselines at consistently
lower planning times, particularly on long-horizon problems requiring multiple forward–reverse maneuvers. In cases where kinodynamic RRT requires over 100 seconds, DFLAT plans in subsecond time, enabling practical deployment. [Project Page]11

introduction:
Planning motions that are both collision-free and dynamically feasible is a long-standing challenge in robotics, particularly for nonholonomic systems operating over long horizons [1]. Recent advances in generative modeling, including diffusion models and flow matching, have introduced powerful new approaches to robot policy learning and motion planning [2]. Diffusion-based planners, in particular, have demonstrated strong performance across a broad range of robotic planning tasks [3, 4].

These results are harder to sustain once the dynamics are constrained and the horizon is long. Every candidate trajectory must remain
dynamically consistent, yet the sample budget must not grow with the
horizon, and existing representations trade one against the other. One
route to feasibility is to diffuse over the control sequence rather than
the state trajectory: samples are drawn from a distribution favoring
low-cost controls and rolled forward through the known dynamics, so the
resulting trajectories are dynamically feasible by
construction [5, 6]. This representation
scales poorly with the horizon: low-cost controls occupy a shrinking
fraction of the sample space, so the sample budget must grow
accordingly. An alternative is to diffuse over the
trajectory directly [7, 4, 8], which avoids this conditioning problem, as obstacle and
goal constraints act on the sampled variables themselves rather than
through a long composition of dynamics steps. The resulting trajectory is
no longer the rollout of any admissible control and is therefore not
necessarily dynamically feasible, requiring projection or post-hoc
refinement to recover a trackable solution [9, 10, 11, 12]. To the best of our knowledge, no existing diffusion-based planner is both feasible by construction and efficient as the horizon grows for such systems.

We resolve this tension through the choice of trajectory representation.
A particular class of systems, called differentially flat, admits a set
of outputs from which the states and inputs can be
recovered [13]. In the flat-output space, a
sufficiently smooth curve is therefore already a valid state and input
trajectory, so feasibility follows from the representation rather than
being restored after the fact. Our method diffuses over a compact
parametrization of such a curve: a sequence of waypoints together with
the in-segment parameters that join them into a smooth path. Because
these parameters describe segments rather than time steps, the design
space scales with the number of segments and the structure of the
maneuver, not with the resolution of the discretization, and stays small
as the horizon grows. Our method thus retains the dynamic consistency of control-sequence diffusion without the large sample budget it requires.

Model-based diffusion (MBD) uses the dynamics model to compute a training-free score function for trajectory optimization [5],
and Safe Model Predictive Diffusion (Safe MPD) combines this with shielded rollouts to guarantee safety
throughout sampling process [14]. Barrier-rate guided MPPI
embeds barrier constraints into the sampling distribution for tractor–trailer
maneuvers in narrow spaces [15]. These methods achieve kinodynamic
feasibility by construction, but they operate on representations whose
dimension grows with the planning horizon, causing sample efficiency to
degrade on long-horizon problems. Recent work has also explored more
compact parameterizations for diffusion planning. Guided Polynomial Diffusion (GPD) performs diffusion directly over Bernstein
polynomial trajectory coefficients [8], and sparse control
points with spline interpolation have been used to obtain smooth control
trajectories from few samples in MPPI [16]. Hierarchical
diffusion methods instead plan over temporally abstracted
sub-goals [7, 4], and coupled hierarchical
diffusion tightens the interaction between the two levels for long-horizon
tasks [17]. Although these approaches
improve horizon scalability, the sampled coefficients and sub-goals need
not correspond to admissible motions. Feasibility is instead recovered afterward, for instance by filtering out
samples that violate the constraints [18], or by projecting the
sampled variables onto the constraint
set [9, 11].
A representative instance related to our work diffuses over control points
rather than over the trajectory itself, and recovers dynamic feasibility with a
quadratic program [12], which is convex only when the relevant
bounds are affine in the sampled variables and does not extend to nonholonomic
models.

A different way to obtain feasibility is through the choice of coordinates. Differential flatness provides a change of variables under which
trajectories in the flat-output space map back to recoverable state-input
trajectories [13]. Beyond recoverability, flatness
provides a compact trajectory representation that has been widely
exploited for motion planning and trajectory
generation [19]. Existing
planners operating directly in the flat-output space are largely
sampling-based. Flat-RRT* [20] precomputes motion
primitives to expand the search tree in the flat-output space, but
planning performance depends strongly on the primitive library, with finer
discretizations increasing both memory requirements and computation time. The
same dependence appears in DE-AGT [21], which pairs a
precomputed primitive library with a learned cost-to-go heuristic for
tractor–trailer parking. More recently, [22] connects sampled states with
closed-form segments, at the cost of restricting the objective to costs
quadratic in the control.
All of these operate by search. We instead pose planning in the flat-output space as diffusion based trajectory optimization, which places no restriction on the cost and
requires no primitive library.

In this paper, we propose DFLAT, a diffusion-based trajectory
optimization algorithm for long-horizon kinodynamic planning. The main
contributions of this work are:

We formulate model-based diffusion directly in the differentially flat
output space, shifting the optimization problem from time-discretized control
sequences to a low-dimensional trajectory parameterization.

We introduce a segmented Hermite representation that guarantees every
denoised sample corresponds to a dynamically consistent trajectory.

We validate DFLAT on long-horizon tractor–trailer planning, where it
solves every benchmark instance orders of magnitude faster than
baselines, reaching subsecond latency on short parking scenarios.

We release a benchmark library of long-horizon tractor–trailer planning

title: DexEngine: Scaling Human Demonstrations into Physically Executable Whole-Robot Data
authors: Wongyun Yu,Honggeun Kim,Donguk Lee,Minchan Kim,Kyoung Whan Choe,Minsu Cho
comment: Project page:this https URLCode:this https URLData:this https URL
abstract:
A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of human hand–object demonstrations to robotic hands. To train whole-robot policies, however, the retargeted motions must be kinematically feasible and physically executable, and be produced efficiently at scale.
We present DexEngine, a simulation pipeline that turns human manipulation data into train-ready, physically executable arm–hand trajectories. DexEngine first places each clip’s hand–object motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human hand–object datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10×\times faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after a floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. Mid-training on our data further improves them at equal fine-tuning budget, in simulation and on a real robot.
introduction:
Dexterous robot policies learn from demonstrations, which are slow and costly to collect by teleoperation [29, 17, 53].
Human hand–object interaction, in contrast, is easier to capture [1, 52, 24, 42, 12, 19, 46, 48] and covers more diverse tasks than teleoperation [16, 55].
Many recent methods therefore convert human data into robot data [53, 16, 25, 21, 28, 34, 56, 20, 40, 15].
Kinematic methods map human hand keypoints to robot joint angles by optimization or inverse kinematics (IK) [47, 53]. Physics-based methods search for a robot motion that reproduces the object motion in simulation, using sampling-based optimization [34] or reinforcement learning (RL) [21, 28, 56].
Several of these methods build robot datasets this way [53, 16, 34, 21], and UniDex [53] and HuRo [16] pretrain policies on them.

Yet these data fall short as training data for whole-robot policies in three ways.
First, kinematic methods [53, 16] ignore dynamics: without contact and force, the robot may fail to move the object, and HuRo [16] uses its trajectories as pretraining supervision only.
Second, most physics-based methods [21, 28, 56, 34, 23, 20] ignore the arm: they drive floating hands and leave the arm’s joint limits, reach, and collisions unchecked, even though a policy must control both arm and hand joints.
Third, physics-based methods do not scale: the few that include the arm [40, 15, 14] cover fewer than a thousand human demonstrations, and most are either slow or inaccurate on many clips.

We present DexEngine, a scalable pipeline that turns human capture data into physically executable, train-ready simulation data for bimanual robots with dexterous hands.
It rests on two key ideas.
First, it solves the arms before physics: it searches each clip’s scene placements for one that the arms can follow, and keeps nearly every clip that has such a placement.
By contrast, attaching the arms after a floating-hand correction keeps 26% fewer clips, even at our placements (Sec. 4.1).
Second, it reuses this arm IK solution in residual RL, whose policy acts on the wrist pose in task space and never observes the arm joints.
Since IK has multiple solutions for a wrist pose, each random start [36] resets the arm to this solution instead of re-solving IK, which would switch branches and lower accuracy (Tab. 3).
With this recipe, even with the arms attached, DexEngine corrects up to 64 clips with one policy, more accurately than existing floating-hand methods, and is the fastest training-based method, at 3.9 GPU-minutes per clip (Tab. 2).

Our contributions are fourfold:

DexEngine, a scalable pipeline that turns human demonstrations into simulation data for a whole bimanual robot by solving the arm motion before physics (Sec. 3).

DexEngine, a scalable pipeline that turns human demonstrations into simulation data for a whole bimanual robot by solving the arm motion before physics (Sec. 3).

An arm attachment for residual RL, acting in wrist space [15] with the arm reset to the kinematic reference at random starts, that keeps the policy accurate and lets it run on a rigidly transformed scene without retraining (Tabs. 3 and 3.5).

Experiments showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction and mid-training on our data helps at equal fine-tuning budget, also on a real robot (Sec. 4).

A train-ready, physically executable dataset of 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) with contact forces and depth for a bimanual robot with each of four dexterous hands, released (Tab. 1).

title: Skeptic: Grounding Failure Diagnosis for Robot Skill Discovery
authors: Wenfang Sun,Jianghao Deng,Wenzhe Yin,Yingjun Du,Cees G. M. Snoek
abstract:
Robot agents discover reusable skills by revising programs from execution feedback and retaining experience for later tasks.
This process can fail when an agent treats an unsuccessful program as evidence that the task is physically impossible, ending exploration with revision budget remaining.
We study this failure in Qwen3.8-27B and examine two decisions that shape skill discovery: I) how execution failures are diagnosed, and II) which lessons enter the shared skill library.
Failure diagnosis requires the agent to reconstruct physical action effects from multimodal traces, while independent reproduction of a proposed repair does not require adequate task performance from its source program.
We introduce Skeptic, a training-free protocol that uses measured action outcomes to guide repair and measured task success to govern skill admission.
A grounded event log reports action effects and object end states from depth images and proprioception, separating sensor observations from inferred diagnoses.
Verified promotion adds a development-success requirement on the source program to the existing independent reproduction check.
Across 60 audited tasks, the mean number of tasks with false impossibility judgments decreases from 19.5 to 8.5 per campaign.
On 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks and seven Robosuite tasks, Skeptic improves held-out success by 14.9 and 11.7 percentage points, with frozen model weights and the same program-revision budget.
introduction:
Agentic skill discovery enables robots to improve control programs and accumulate reusable skills through interaction [16, 34, 12, 20].
Its progress depends on how unsuccessful executions guide subsequent exploration.
An incorrect failure diagnosis can rule out a viable strategy and cause the agent to abandon a solvable task.
We use a frozen Qwen3.8-27B [32], a 27B open-weight model, to study this problem in a robot-programming loop with persistent skill memory.
We focus on how evidence about an unsuccessful program becomes an unsupported judgment of physical impossibility, and how changing the evidence used for diagnosis and skill admission affects discovery.

Physical feedback makes failure diagnosis difficult because completing an API call does not establish that the intended interaction occurred.
Coding agents receive images, primitive outputs, and execution traces [43, 20], from which they must reconstruct the physical effects of their programs before choosing a repair.
In Fig. 1, the gripper closes without reaching the drawer handle, but the agent attributes the unsuccessful pull to a mechanical stop.
The coordinator then uses this explanation to close another task involving the same drawer.
The agent has generalized evidence about one unsuccessful interaction into a statement about task feasibility.
Such a conclusion can terminate exploration with revision budget remaining and constrain subsequent attempts.

We examine the distinction between using a strategy and discovering one on seven Goal tasks where Qwen3.8-27B initially fails every held-out episode.
Providing strategies and code sketches curated by Claude Opus 5.5 on these same tasks yields 342 successful episodes out of 350 (Tab. 4 in the supplement).
The model still adapts these recipes into task programs.
Rewriting or removing claims of impossibility from its own library and requiring three distinct strategies, however, yields only 9 successes out of 350.
The workers continue to explore local variations of their original approach while retaining the same explanation of failure.
On these tasks, the model can adapt an effective strategy but struggles to discover one through its own interaction.
Further attempts provide little progress when they are guided by the same mistaken explanation.

We introduce Skeptic, a training-free protocol that uses measured action effects to guide program repair and measured task success to govern skill admission.
A grounded event log organizes depth and proprioceptive measurements into action outcomes and object end states, distinguishing sensor observations from inferred diagnoses.
The worker can compare this record with its explanation of failure and the task instruction, locate an unfinished step, and preserve earlier actions supported by the execution record.
For skill accumulation, verified promotion retains the existing independent reproduction check and adds a requirement on the source program of each proposed skill.
Reproducing a repair does not establish adequate task performance from the program that produced it; Skeptic therefore requires the program to meet a measured development-success threshold before its proposal can enter the shared library.
An admission service computes success from execution records and checks the verifier’s result before updating the library.

On all 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks [47], Skeptic raises the held-out success of Qwen3.8-27B from 63.4% to 78.3%, a gain of 14.9 percentage points, with the same model, starting library, and program-revision budget.
Applied unchanged to seven Robosuite tasks [48], it increases mean success from 35.3% to 47.0%, a gain of 11.7 points.
Across the 60 audited Object, Goal, and Spatial tasks, the mean number of tasks with false impossibility judgments decreases from 19.5 to 8.5 per campaign.
Model weights remain frozen throughout skill discovery.

title: Model Predictive Control of a Multirotor UAV with a Cable-Suspended Payload: A Comparison of Shifted and Transformer-Based Warm Starts
authors: Athanasios Zeris
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: Multirotor drones carrying cable-suspended payloads require coordinated regulation of vehicle motion and suspended-load oscillations while respecting rotor constraints and cable dynamics. In this study, the drone is modeled as a multirotor unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). This study develops a physics-based model predictive control (MPC) framework for a multirotor with an elastic cable and a reduced double-pendulum representation of its suspended load, and compares two approaches to initializing its sequential convex programming (SCP) optimizer: conventional receding-horizon shifting and Transformer-based sequence prediction. The controller combines numerical propagation of a coupled mechanical model with move-blocked control decisions, finite-difference sensitivities, constrained quadratic subproblems, and feasibility projection of the initial control sequence. Expert SCP solutions are used to train the Transformer, and the learned and shifted initializations are evaluated using the same prediction model, constraints, and solver settings. Mechanical consistency checks, data-generation and feasibility studies, tests of independently solved MPC problems, and sequential closed-loop experiments establish a common basis for the comparison. Although Transformer initialization improves computational performance relative to zero initialization in the tests of independently solved MPC problems, the shifted solution is more efficient in the sequential closed-loop benchmark and achieves comparable tracking behavior. The results show that learned sequence accuracy and downstream optimizer efficiency are distinct properties, and that previous-solution shifting is an essential baseline when assessing learning-assisted MPC. The measured optimization times remain above the nominal control sampling period, so the study does not demonstrate real-time deployment.
introduction:
Multirotor unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) carrying suspended loads are coupled mechanical systems: changes in rotor thrust and vehicle attitude affect the payload trajectory, while cable deflection, extension, and payload swing feed back into the forces acting on the vehicle. A controller intended for constrained tracking must therefore represent the relevant coupled dynamics without making repeated online prediction prohibitively expensive. This balance between mechanical fidelity and computational effort motivates the present comparison of model predictive control (MPC) initialization strategies.

The suspended-load literature offers different levels of mechanical detail. Goodarzi, Lee, and Lee [1] derive a coordinate-free quadrotor–payload formulation with a flexible cable represented by serially connected links and develop a geometric stabilization controller with stability analysis. Tolba and Shirinzadeh [2] instead consider a fifteen-degree-of-freedom multirotor and rigid-body payload model that includes elastic cable behavior, slackening and tightening, shifted centers of gravity, arbitrary attachment locations, and double-pendulum motion; they investigate an output-weighted linear-quadratic regulator. These studies establish the importance of cable and payload dynamics, but neither is an evaluation of Transformer initialization for a common predictive optimizer. Our control-oriented model has eleven generalized coordinates, including vehicle translation and attitude, an extensible suspension segment, and two swing-direction pairs. It does not reproduce all the effects represented in the more detailed models, and the reported results must be interpreted within that modeling scope.

Predictive control provides a framework for handling tracking objectives and explicit constraints [6, 7, 8]. For quadrotors, Ru and Subbarao [3] formulate constrained trajectory-tracking MPC using a state-dependent-coefficient representation and sequential quadratic programming. Rohr et al. [4] develop and flight-test predictive velocity control for a tiltwing UAV using an identified aerodynamic model; their use of preceding solutions as optimization references should be distinguished from using a shifted solution as the initial iterate. These works illustrate the importance of selecting a control-oriented prediction model and a practical numerical optimization procedure, but do not directly establish the performance of the coupled suspended-payload controller considered here.

Computational cost remains a central issue in receding-horizon control. Wang and Boyd [9] demonstrate that exploiting quadratic-program structure can substantially accelerate online MPC. Move blocking reduces the number of independent control decisions, but Cagienard et al. [10] also show why blocking choices cannot be assumed to preserve stability and constraint-satisfaction guarantees. Diehl, Bock, and Schlöder [14] develop a real-time iteration scheme for approximate online optimization, providing a complementary example of trading iterative solution accuracy against the time available between control updates. In the present sequential convex programming (SCP) implementation, the numerical workload also includes repeated integration of the coupled mechanical model to construct finite-difference sensitivities and evaluate trial steps. Faster quadratic-program solutions alone therefore need not imply faster control updates.

Learning-based models address different parts of this computational problem. Gu, Primatesta, and Rizzo [5] investigate physics-informed neural modeling of quadrotor dynamics, highlighting model accuracy and physical consistency; their network serves a different purpose from the initialization predictor studied here. Davoudi et al. [12] likewise illustrate the influence of aerodynamic and wind-model fidelity on quadrotor flight simulation. Our Transformer does not replace the mechanical prediction model or estimate the wind field. It predicts an initial control-decision sequence for subsequent physics-based SCP optimization.

Transformer-assisted trajectory optimization provides the immediate methodological motivation. Celestini et al. [11] use sequence modeling to generate initial guesses or target plans for constrained trajectory optimization and report improvements in convergence and runtime in their evaluated settings. Such benefits cannot be presumed for a different plant, solver, and prediction horizon. In particular, a shifted previous solution is an inexpensive and informative baseline in receding-horizon control, and learned inference and feasibility projection add their own computational costs.

We therefore compare three initializations of the same move-blocked SCP controller: zero deviations from hover, a shifted and reblocked previous solution, and a Transformer-generated candidate. The shifted and Transformer-generated initial control sequences are adjusted, when necessary, to satisfy the imposed input constraints before optimization. Zero initialization already satisfies these constraints. The reported experiments assess both isolated optimization behavior and matched closed-loop episodes, including measured initialization-and-optimization time, solver iterations, and physical tracking outcomes. The principal contribution is a controlled numerical comparison of zero, shifted, and Transformer-based initialization strategies within a common SCP-MPC framework for a coupled UAV–cable–payload system. The study evaluates their effects on computational effort, optimization iterations, and closed-loop response under identical modeling and control constraints. The results establish the relative performance of these initialization strategies for the investigated numerical scenarios, without implying formal closed-loop stability or real-time flight readiness.

title: OnCue: Generating Safety-Critical Driving Scenarios under Occlusion with Temporal Control
authors: Kailang Ma,Li Song,Weining Ren,Zirui Li,Xianjie Dai,Jingguang Li,Zuyi Guo,Benwang Chen,Heye Huang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Occluded hazards challenge autonomous driving because visibility timing determines available avoidance actions. Existing scenario generators control hazard motion without jointly specifying exposure and reference-contact times. We propose OnCue, a framework that generates safety-critical encounters in real driving logs with these temporal conditions. Scene geometry provides hidden starts and timed waypoints for pedestrian, cyclist, and vehicle trajectory generation. An offline response oracle labels encounters as Reactive (avoidable after exposure) or Anticipatory (avoidable only with earlier visibility) and stores safe maneuvers as training demonstrations. On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, 90.1–96.6% of valid trajectories meet both requested times within ±0.2\pm 0.2 s. OnCue matches the requested reaction window between them in 92.8% of shared vehicle requests versus at most 42.1% for adapted adversarial generators. Across matched cyclist encounters, longer windows lower PDM-Closed collision from 59.1% to 5.5%, while the learned planner LatentDriver shows the opposite trend. OnCue demonstrations reduce LatentDriver target collision by 54.8 points on held-out Reactive tests, but reduce overall no-target progress by 12.7 m. These results highlight the value of temporal control for evaluating and improving planners under occlusion.
introduction:
Safe autonomous driving requires timely responses to hazards hidden behind surrounding traffic. A pedestrian emerging from behind a parked vehicle or a cyclist crossing through a queue can leave little time to react. In such encounters, the interval between first visibility and potential conflict determines which avoidance actions remain feasible. These encounters thus test both reaction to visible hazards and anticipation of hidden ones [18]. Evaluating planners under occlusion therefore requires controlling when a hidden hazard first becomes visible while keeping the conflict location and time fixed.

Scenario generation makes such rare encounters available for controlled evaluation [16, 17, 51]. Driving logs such as the Waymo Open Motion Dataset (WOMD) [14] provide realistic traffic context, but replay fixes when road users become visible, so each encounter can only be tested with its recorded timing. Existing generators manipulate target motion to create safety-critical interactions [55, 43, 33], while controllable motion models guide trajectories with rules or costs [57, 26]. Occlusion-focused methods further construct hidden encounters and evaluate ego responses [13, 45, 27, 25]. However, these approaches mainly control how a hazard moves and generally lack joint control over when it becomes visible and when it reaches the ego. This makes it difficult to test the same conflict under earlier or later exposure. Moreover, collision outcomes alone cannot reveal whether safe avoidance remained possible after exposure or required earlier information.

This raises a key question: can we specify both event times while preserving the surrounding traffic? The challenge is that target placement, motion, and visibility are coupled. Changing target speed can shift exposure, while moving the hidden start can alter arrival at the conflict. Matching the reaction window alone is also insufficient, as equal errors in both event times can shift the entire encounter within recorded traffic. Temporal control therefore requires jointly constraining exposure and reference-contact times.

To address this challenge, we propose OnCue, a framework for generating safety-critical driving scenarios with joint temporal control. The key idea is to make exposure and reference contact explicit conditions of target motion. A fixed reference ego defines the conflict independently of the tested planner. The target’s first confirmed visibility defines its exposure time [40], while first contact with the reference ego defines its reference-contact time [32]. Their interval specifies the reaction window WW (Figure 1). OnCue converts these temporal conditions into geometry-derived hidden starts and timed waypoints to guide learned trajectory generation within recorded traffic. An offline, planner-independent response oracle then searches for safe maneuvers, providing response labels and executable demonstrations.

As a general framework, OnCue turns hazard timing from a fixed property of replayed logs into a controllable test variable. By varying exposure while fixing the reference contact, it reveals how planners respond to different reaction windows. Its response oracle distinguishes encounters with available post-exposure maneuvers (Reactive) from those where safe actions are found only under earlier visibility (Anticipatory), within the evaluated action library. Moreover, the resulting safe maneuvers serve as training demonstrations, connecting failure diagnosis with planner adaptation.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We propose OnCue, a framework for generating safety-critical driving scenarios under occlusion with temporal control. It enables systematic evaluation of planner responses as hidden hazards become visible earlier or later.

We develop geometry-guided conditional trajectory generation, combining constructed hidden starts and timed waypoints with learned motion generation. A planner-independent response oracle labels available avoidance and stores executable demonstrations.

We demonstrate how temporally controlled hazards support planner evaluation and adaptation. Closed-loop experiments across target classes and planners reveal how available reaction time affects driving behavior, and training with oracle demonstrations improves target avoidance.

1. We propose OnCue, a framework for generating safety-critical driving scenarios under occlusion with temporal control. It enables systematic evaluation of planner responses as hidden hazards become visible earlier or later.

2. We develop geometry-guided conditional trajectory generation, combining constructed hidden starts and timed waypoints with learned motion generation. A planner-independent response oracle labels available avoidance and stores executable demonstrations.

3. We demonstrate how temporally controlled hazards support planner evaluation and adaptation. Closed-loop experiments across target classes and planners reveal how available reaction time affects driving behavior, and training with oracle demonstrations improves target avoidance.

title: An Adversarial Multi-Agent Pursuit Game for Locomotor Agility Pretraining
authors: Nathan A.C. Hogg,Matt Hyatt,Neil Klingensmith,George K. Thiruvathukal
abstract:
Agile humanoid locomotion requires controllers that can adapt to rapidly changing motion demands while remaining stable and robust.
Recent locomotion controllers are typically designed with either a dense reward that is carefully shaped to encourage steps and penalize falling, or by using a reference tracking reward which teaches the controller to follow predetermined motions.
Once a behavior that maximizes the reward is discovered, the controller ceases to learn. While generally stable, reference-tracking methods focus on motor control separately from motion generation.
Self-play has been proven as an effective technique for superhuman performance on several multiagent games like Go, Starcraft, hide-and-seek, and capture-the-flag. We train neural networks to play the game of multiagent tag in a physics simulator to study
if new motion generation and control strategies can emerge through sparse feedback and competitive self-play.
introduction:
Agile robotic locomotion is essential for robots to be widely useful in real-world problems such as delivery, exploration, search and rescue, and healthcare.
Current approaches often rely on supervised imitation of reference trajectories and reinforcement learning (RL) for high frequency control.
While imitation learning provides stable training from prior demonstrations [8] , it depends on high-quality motion data. Such data is limited in scale, and it is highly dependent on the capture environment [16]. Often, motion capture must be post-processed to become physically plausible. A generative locomotion controller is limited to move only in ways that fall inside the training distribution.

In contrast, RL allows agents to learn from experience but often stagnates once a reward is maximized. Standard curriculum learning is frequently used to make the environment more difficult but the curriculum is seldom aware of the capabilities of the policy leading to impossible or trivial tasks [5]. This eventually dilutes the quality of training data. Advanced environment tuning results in a difficult high-dimensional optimization problem [15].

We hypothesize that the shortcomings of locomotor RL and motion generation are not due to any poor quality of locomotor skills but rather due to the eventual plateau of behavior when maximizing the reward function under the training environment. Additionally, the manual effort required to tune both the environment difficulty and reward shape are undesirable traits of RL.

Neither supervised learning nor dense RL offer a simple recipe for policy improvement that is resistant to plateau. This differs from RL on Atari-style games or manipulation tasks, where the reward being maximized is itself the desired behavior [6]. Conversely, terrain traversal is open-ended and any dense reward imposes a bias that is not guaranteed to be aligned with locomotion.

In competitive games, self-play is often used to enforce an adaptive curriculum.
A weak model can begin to learn by dominating a weak opponent, and successive training rounds will prepare the policy to learn counter-strategies in order to receive a scalar reward [14, 10, 1, 7]. In this case, even though the earned reward is unchanged, the model still adapts since a skilled opponent will force the player into undesirable state-space which it will need to overcome.

Recently, self-play was used as a strategy in drone pursuit [12], demonstrating impressive low-level flight control at high frequency.
Previously, tag has been used in quadrupedal motion [13] although their method has some notable differences to ours, with the primary difference being that their evader is a 2D dot coordinate rather than another identical robot entity.
This makes their training protocol more similar to goal following than self-play.
Moreover, they report that their model cannot learn from RL and they opt for evolutionary algorithms. Han et al. also train quadrupeds using a game of tag [3], but they freeze the locomotion controller and train a goal-proposal policy. This means that the game does not teach locomotor strategy. Instead, it teaches the high-level selection of planar coordinate goals. Similar to us, Han et al. are inspired by the parkour game World Chase Tag.
Finally, Prioritized Fictitious Self-Play (PFSP) [14] has been used in the learning of character controllers [18] for boxing matches.

To address limitations in environment difficulty and reward modeling, we propose competitive tag as a surrogate objective that is well aligned with terrain-traversal. We hypothesize that the policy should continue to improve even on simple terrains since PFSP enforces adaptive difficulty.

Our contributions include (1) the development of a multiagent competitive league environment for humanoids,
(2) a data sampling strategy to balance role-difficulty imbalances, and (3) a comparative analysis of state exploration under self-play and dense reward shaping.
We demonstrate that competitive league-based play with sparse feedback can train a locomotion controller to develop strategic skills like lunging, tackling and ducking.

title: Best-of-$N$ Test-Time Steering Can Lead to Reward Hacking in Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Vanshaj Khattar,Jing Liu,Toshiaki Koike-Akino,Ming Jin,Ye Wang
comment: to be presented at 1st Workshop on Physical World AI at NeurIPS 2026
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but adapting to changing environmental conditions still remains challenging.
Recent test-time steering methods have shown promise in enabling adaptive VLA policies by utilizing additional computation during deployment. In this paper, we consider best-of-NN test-time steering for VLA models, where multiple action candidates are sampled from a fixed policy and a verifier is used to select the best one during deployment.
We show that increasing NN does not always improve performance when the verifier is inaccurate, and can favor candidates whose scores exploit prediction errors, a form of reward hacking.
We study this effect on 60 LIBERO-Safety task-level cases using a π0.5\pi_{0.5} policy, with ten repetitions per case.
We introduce controlled errors in a MuJoCo trajectory verifier and show that as NN increases, selected candidate rewards diverge from the accurate verifier rewards, leading to reward hacking.
We also show that verifier calibration and softmax-based candidate selection can mitigate reward hacking in some settings.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions and have shown broad manipulation capabilities (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025).
However, their performance can deteriorate when deployment conditions differ from those seen during training (Fei et al., 2025).
There are two ways to improve the generalization capabilities of VLAs.
The first is to collect additional demonstrations and retrain or fine-tune the policy; however, this can be computationally expensive (Lu et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025).
Another widely used and less computationally expensive approach is test-time steering, where additional computation during execution is used to steer the VLA actions (Nakamoto et al., 2024; Dai et al., 2025) or select the best one from a few sampled candidates (Kwok et al., 2025; Zhang and Shah, 2026).

Recent test-time steering methods such as RoboMonkey and VERITAS have shown promising results with best-of-NN (BoN) test-time steering, which samples multiple action candidates and uses a verifier to select the best one for execution (Kwok et al., 2025; Zhang and Shah, 2026).
However, its benefit depends on the verifier’s ability to rank those candidates.
In practice, perception errors, inaccurate predictions of physical motion, or an imperfect scoring rule can cause a poor action to receive a high score.

This problem has been identified in large language models (LLMs), where a reward model or verifier is used to pick the best of several sampled responses.
Gao et al. (2023) showed that when best-of-NN selection uses an imperfect reward model, the true quality of the selected response first improves and then drops as NN grows.
Similar effects have been shown when selecting solutions to math problems with a learned verifier Cobbe et al. (2021) and when selecting code with unit tests Stroebl et al. (2026), where wrong answers that pass the check limit the benefit of more samples.
Recent work explains this pattern in theory and shows that it is expected for best-of-NN selection when NN is large Huang et al. (2025); Khalaf et al. (2025), and terms it inference-time reward hacking.
These works also suggest ways to mitigate this effect, such as down-weighting candidates with uncertain scores Huang et al. (2025) or using softmax-based selection instead of always taking the top-scoring candidate (Khalaf et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026).

Similar effects have recently been reported in robotics literature.
Luo et al. (2026) showed that optimizing robot policies against a learned visual critic can increase failures in which the robot acts on the wrong object, because the critic scores some of these failures above real successes.
Bakshi and Bose (2026) showed that sampling-based planning with rewards learned from human preferences can reduce the true task return by up to 76%, and that best-of-NN selection with such a reward can perform worse than taking a single action.
A recent survey of verifiers for robot policies notes that how far a policy can be optimized against a verifier before its score stops tracking the task is still largely unexplored (Wan et al., 2026).
These studies use learned scores and focus on task success. In contrast, we use a MuJoCo simulator whose errors we control, and a proxy reward function. We measure both safety violations and task completion.

This raises the central question of our study: when the verifier is imperfect, does additional search still improve robot behavior, or can it reduce task performance and safety?
We study this question on the LIBERO-Safety benchmark Cui et al. (2026), which requires robots to complete manipulation tasks while following constraints on how objects are grasped and avoiding contact with nearby obstacles and simulated human hands.
In these tasks, task progress and safety can conflict: an action can move an object toward its goal while violating a safety constraint.
We keep the VLA policy and the execution environment fixed, and add controlled errors only inside the verifier, either by adding noise to the predicted object positions or by changing the simulated dynamics.
For each selected action, we compare the proxy score from the perturbed verifier with its clean score from the unperturbed simulator.
We find that best-of-NN steering of VLA policies is prone to inference-time reward hacking: as NN increases, the gap between predicted and clean reward grows, and for some tasks the gains in safe completion seen at small NN are lost while violations increase.

title: RoboARC: Physical Puzzles for Robotic Manipulation under Spatial Constraints
authors: Qineng Wang,Jianwen Lyu,Pingyue Zhang,Reuben Tan,Xiaoyu Huang,Tonghe Zhang,Kangrui Wang,Yelong Shen,Jianfeng Gao,Guanya Shi,Ruohan Zhang,Manling Li
abstract:
Many hard manipulation tasks come down to a spatial constraint that only a few motions satisfy, such as passing a part
through a gap barely wider than itself or separating two interlocked parts. These motions depend on the exact geometry of
each scene, so demonstrations and skills recorded elsewhere rarely transfer. We
therefore ask: when manipulation hinges on spatial constraints, can robots reason out the right motions? We introduce RoboARC, a benchmark of 9090 tasks in six constraint types over rigid and soft materials, on three robots in MuJoCo. Every task is a frozen scene with a physics-based grader and a verified reference solution that replays
bit-identically. Each task comes in a Privileged regime, with the full simulator state and resets, and a
Standard regime with real-sensor inputs (camera images and proprioception) and a single attempt without resets.
We evaluate seven coding agents and four VLA
policies, none trained on these tasks. The strongest agent, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, solves 86%86\,\% of the tasks in the Privileged regime and 43%43\,\% in the Standard regime,
and the four VLA policies, run zero-shot, solve none of their 1818 one-arm puzzles. On 1515 puzzles that GPT-6 Astra solved in the Privileged regime and failed in the Standard regime, object poses add 44 points and part geometry 1313, but both together add 3636, from 24%24\,\% to 60%60\,\%. Only 7%7\,\% of the coding agents’ failed runs pass more than half of a task, and 53%53\,\% of the failed runs in the Standard regime are stuck on a single step. Frontier coding agents already reason out
the right motions for many of these tasks once they know where the parts are and what shape they have. From their own sensors,
in a single attempt, the strongest solves fewer than half of the tasks.
introduction:
In some manipulation tasks only a few motions succeed. Untangling a cable, threading a rope through a fixture or sliding
a board into a frame [30, 78, 49] succeeds only along the few
motions that a spatial constraint leaves open: a gap barely wider than the part, two parts that interlock, or a
rope that must not pass through itself. Which motions remain is set by the exact geometry of the scene and changes from
scene to scene. Policies learned from demonstrations, as in vision-language-action (VLA)
models [114, 45, 8], and programs composed from known
skills [53, 36] succeed when the right motion resembles one seen before, such as
a grasp, a push or a placement. Coding agents built on models that reason well in symbolic domains, from abstract
puzzles [17] to computer use [98, 64], already control robots through
code [22] and could work out a motion for the scene at hand. This raises the question:

Existing benchmarks do not address this question. Manipulation benchmarks draw their difficulty from the number of
steps and the variety of objects [40, 62, 56, 70, 50, 86],
rarely from the geometry a motion must clear (Table 1). Reasoning benchmarks pose puzzles in text, images or
abstract environments [17, 26, 96], where no motion has to satisfy a contact. Motion
planning has long used physical puzzles such as the alpha puzzle as tests for planners that are given the exact geometry [3, 107].
RoboARC poses them to complete systems and grades the motion the robot executes.

To answer this question, we introduce RoboARC, a benchmark of physical puzzles under spatial constraints
(Figure 1), built on three principles.

First, difficulty comes from spatial constraints. Like ARC [17], each task is easy to
state, but its solution is specific to its geometry, and the agent is given no demonstration of it. Unlike
ARC, the answer is a motion. RoboARC has 9090 tasks, 7878 from 1919 puzzle families and 1212 IKEA scenes, in six constraint types: interlocking, narrow passage, assembly,
untangling, threading and shape control (Figures 2 and 4). They span
rigid and soft materials and three robots in MuJoCo [90].

Second, each task comes in two regimes. A policy can fail because it cannot see the constraint, because it cannot reason through it, or because it cannot carry out the motion. Each task therefore comes in two regimes that share the scene, the physics and the grader
(Figure 2). The Privileged regime gives the simulator itself, with its full state and resets. The Standard regime gives real-sensor inputs, calibrated cameras and
proprioception, and one live episode. The gap between the regimes measures what access to the simulator is worth, and Section 5.1 gives it back to GPT-6 Astra one kind at a time.

Third, the tasks are open to any policy. Coding agents reach
the tasks through Harbor [32], and general policies through a Gymnasium
environment [91] that VLA policies join as openpi policy servers [8]. Policies range from VLAs that map images to actions to coding agents that write planners. All are
judged by the same physics-based grader on the motion they execute.

We evaluate seven coding agents, each a complete system of harness, model and reasoning effort, and four VLA
policies, none trained on these tasks (Section 4). To find which information an agent lacks in the Standard regime, we give it back to
GPT-6 Astra at high effort, one kind at a time (Section 5.1). We then replay the runs of all seven agents and read their transcripts to find where the failed runs stop, what form the failed attempts take and whether the agents plan before they act
(Section 5.3). Our main findings are as follows.

the task object but solve none.

title: FOCI: Trajectory Optimization on Gaussian Splats for Gaussian Robots
authors: Mario Gomez Andreu,Carlos Martinez Cuenca,Maximum Wilder-Smith,Victor Klemm,Vaishakh Patil,Marco Hutter,Jesus Tordesillas
abstract:
3D Gaussian Splatting has recently gained popularity as a faster alternative to Neural Radiance Fields in 3D reconstruction and view synthesis methods.
Leveraging the spatial information encoded in 3D Gaussian Splatting,
this work proposes FOCI (Field Overlap Collision Integral), an algorithm that is able to optimize trajectories directly on the Gaussians themselves. FOCI leverages a novel and interpretable collision formulation for 3D Gaussian Splatting using the notion of the overlap integral between Gaussians.
The formulation presented applies to different robot morphologies (e.g., fixed and mobile base manipulators, legged robots, UAVs) and handles both static and dynamic Gaussian-Splat environments.
Contrary to other approaches, which represent the robot with conservative bounding boxes that underestimate the traversability of the environment, we propose to represent the environment and the robot as Gaussian Splats. This not only has desirable computational properties, but also allows for orientation-aware planning, allowing the robot to pass through very tight and narrow spaces.
We extensively test our algorithm in both synthetic and real Gaussian Splats, showcasing that collision-free trajectories for legged, aerial and manipulator robots can be computed in seconds, even with hundreds of thousands of Gaussians making up the environment.
introduction:
Trajectory planning is integral to autonomous mobile robotics to ensure guided and safe operation.
However, in order to make an informed decision, these planning algorithms heavily depend on the underlying environment representations.
Popular representations include occupancy grids, signed distance fields, 3D Meshes, and point clouds.

Recently, Neural Radiance Fields [27] have been proposed as a novel neural representation of the environment. However, they suffer from having slow inference speeds because new views have to be created using a computationally expensive ray-casting procedure. More recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting [22] has been proposed as a promising alternative to Neural Radiance Fields. Instead of using a neural network to represent the radiance field, it is defined explicitly by a set of 3D Gaussian ellipsoids. Because of this, new views can be efficiently generated by projecting these ellipsoids into the view plane.

Given the advantages that 3D Gaussian Splatting offers when compared with Neural Radiance Fields, the natural question is how a robot can leverage this Gaussian representation for navigation. In this paper, we propose an algorithm that enables a robot to perform trajectory optimization directly on the 3D Gaussians. Furthermore, the proposed formulation is robot-agnostic and makes no assumption of a static environment, enabling trajectory optimization across a wide range of robotic platforms and in dynamic scenarios (see Figs. 1 and 2). Although some steps have been taken in this direction [6, 23, 14, 25], the huge number of Gaussians a scene can have, together with the specific formulation of an explicit collision measure, makes this problem especially hard.

To overcome these challenges, we propose FOCI, a trajectory optimization algorithm that leverages the overlap integral – the spatial integral over the multiplication of two functions – as a proxy measure for the collision between two Gaussians. By representing both the robot and the environment with 3D Gaussians, evaluating the full-body collision between them reduces to a sum of normal distribution evaluations. Furthermore, the resulting expression is fully differentiable, yielding expressive gradients in the optimization step.

This work extends our conference paper [3], and its contributions are summarized as follows:

A novel collision measure between Gaussian Splats based on the overlap integral between Gaussians.

A robot-agnostic, fully differentiable trajectory optimization pipeline compatible with arbitrary robot morphologies and dynamic environments.

A GPU implementation of the trajectory optimization.

An evaluation of the proposed algorithm on the ANYmal legged robot in simulation and the real world, and on manipulator and aerial robots in simulation.

Formulation: extension to arbitrary robot morphologies (fixed and mobile-base manipulators, legged robots, and UAVs) by optimizing the robot joint trajectories, and to dynamic environments through time-varying environment Gaussians.

Experiments: new experiments with a manipulator and UAVs, including a UAV navigating among moving obstacles.

Comparisons: benchmarks against the trajectory optimizers CHOMP [34] and STOMP [20].

1. A novel collision measure between Gaussian Splats based on the overlap integral between Gaussians.

2. A robot-agnostic, fully differentiable trajectory optimization pipeline compatible with arbitrary robot morphologies and dynamic environments.

3. A GPU implementation of the trajectory optimization.

4. An evaluation of the proposed algorithm on the ANYmal legged robot in simulation and the real world, and on manipulator and aerial robots in simulation.

title: Why Does Sensor Depth Fail Learned Manipulation Policies? Finding the Failure Mode with ACT
authors: Inayat Rasool,Chulwoo Pack,Shabbir Ahmed
abstract: Learned manipulation policies, from task-specific imitation policies to vision-language-action (VLA) models, rely primarily on RGB images. While some studies report gains from sensor depth, others avoid depth cameras because of measurement noise. Depth cameras introduce both noise and missing depth values (holes), whose relative effects remain unclear. In this study, we calibrate a sensor model using a real wrist-mounted stereo camera and separately evaluate noise and holes on RGB-D imitation policies with three visual encoders in simulation. We found that complete depth improves success by approximately ten percentage points, and most of this gain persists even at twenty times the camera’s noise level. In contrast, holes covering about one-sixth of the wrist image eliminate the detectable benefit of depth. The validity mask strongly influences depth reliance: marking a small fraction of pixels as invalid reduces reliance, while filling holes and marking them valid restores most of the benefit. Policies trained on clean depth also lose performance when holes appear only at deployment, sometimes falling below RGB-only performance. These findings suggest that depth cameras for learned policies should therefore be judged by depth coverage more than measurement precision.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a prominent approach
to robot manipulation and are pretrained on large-scale images and texts datasets, which gives them a strong sense of what objects are and what an instruction asks for [1, 2, 3]. However, robotic manipulation is also a geometric problem, and a robot must know about the position of an object relative to its gripper to grasp or place it precisely. While an RGB image provides indirect cues about the pose and relative distance of a three-dimensional geometry, a depth sensor can directly measure distances in metric units. As a result, VLA models and task-specific manipulation policies are increasingly incorporating depth maps or point clouds as additional inputs.

However, existing studies differ on whether depth information should be acquired directly from sensors or inferred through learning-based policies. Studies such as 3D Diffusion Policy [4], RISE [5], iDP3 [6], FP3 [7], 3D Diffuser Actor [8], Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) and Vision Language Action (VLA) policies [9, 10] etc. incorporates depth maps or point clouds through direct sensor measurements and report improved performance. In contrast, several other studies seek to eliminate the need for depth sensors during deployment by estimating or predicting depth from images, thereby distilling geometric information into the policy, or add 3D supervision during training for inferring depth [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. A common motivation for these approaches is the susceptibility of depth sensors to measurement noise and missing depth information [18, 19, 12, 13, 17].

One possible explanation for these differing findings is that “sensor quality” encompasses two distinct limitations: measurement noise and missing depth values (holes). Measurement noise affects the accuracy of valid depth measurements, whereas holes occur when the sensor fails to return a depth value. A camera or sensor can be very precise where it provides a measured value, and at the same time, may leave a large part of the image without any depth information (holes). Consequently, a sensor may provide accurate measurements while exhibiting substantial missing data. Previous studies have extensively characterized measurement accuracy of depth and associated noise [20, 21, 22],however, the impact of missing depth or holes on robotic manipulation remains less understood.

We therefore ask three questions: (1) Does complete depth information improve manipulation performance? (2) How do measurement noise and missing depth values (holes) independently affect this benefit? (3) What causes the performance degradation, and how can it be mitigated? To address these questions, we characterize the distance-dependent noise and missing-depth rate of a real wrist-mounted stereo camera on a teleoperated robot. Using noise-free depth rendered in simulation, we independently introduce measurement noise and missing values at the measured levels and under scaled perturbations. We evaluate Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policies [23] using three visual encoders: ResNet-18 trained from scratch, DINOv2 [24] with 2D pretraining, and MoGe-2 [25] with geometric pretraining. We quantify the contribution of depth using two metrics: benefit, defined as the improvement in task success relative to an RGB-only policy with the same encoder, and reliance, defined as the reduction in success when depth input is removed at deployment. All policy evaluations are conducted in simulation using ACT, without training VLA models.

Fig. 1 summarizes the key findings. Complete depth information improves manipulation performance, and most of this benefit persists even when measurement noise increases to 20 times the measured level. In contrast, depth holes eliminate the benefit by causing policies to disregard depth information. This behavior is driven by the validity mask, which distinguishes missing depth from measured depth values. By filling the holes and marking them as valid restores most of the benefit. Moreover, policies trained on complete depth can perform worse than RGB-only policies when depth holes are introduced at deployment. These trends are consistent across all three visual encoders.

This paper makes four contributions: (1) a controlled evaluation of depth noise and holes, with a sensor model fitted to a real wrist camera; (2) provide evidence that the holes, not noise, remove the benefit of sensor depth for the studied policies; (3) provide evidence that validity masks cause policies to disregard incomplete depth information; and (4) provide practical guidance for depth sensor selection and preprocessing, along with a metric (reliance) to quantify whether a trained policy uses depth information.

title: Effect-Driven Skill Abstractions for Offline Reinforcement Learning
authors: Burcu Kilic,David Drexel,Emre Ugur,Justus Piater
comment: The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, NeurIPS 2026
abstract: We seek to learn discrete skill abstractions to facilitate long-horizon, goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning (RL) tasks. Recent approaches have shown success by quantizing actions via clustering or reconstruction. However, these objectives lead to skills that are not directly related to what the current state affords or what the goal requires. Instead, we argue that goal-directed skills should be driven by how they affect the state of the agent. To realize this, we introduce a novel quantization method for action chunks that optimizes next-state predictions conditioned on the current state and action. This objective encourages skills to be distinguished by the future states they lead to, resulting in a vocabulary that spans diverse outcomes reachable from a given state. Our framework can easily be paired with common offline RL methods by replacing their continuous actor head with a discrete one that selects among the learned skills. We can execute these skills in the environment by converting them back to continuous actions using a trained low-level controller. Experiments on benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks largely show substantial and consistent improvements over both the continuous-actor baselines and reconstruction-based discretizations. Our project page can be found at: https://burcukilic.github.io/projects/effect-driven-skill-abstractions/
introduction:
Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) aims to learn decision-making policies from collected interaction data to eliminate the safety and sample-efficiency issues of online exploration Levine et al. (2020). This paradigm is especially useful in goal-conditioned settings Kaelbling (1993); Park et al. (2025); Schaul et al. (2015) where a single policy must reach various targets in the environment, making online exploration unsafe and expensive. However, training stable goal-conditioned policies remains challenging for long-horizon tasks in sparse-reward settings, especially in high-dimensional continuous action spaces, where the policy may output actions outside the training dataset’s support, leading to unstable training and unreliable value estimates.

One way to mitigate this is to convert the continuous problem into a discrete one. It is generally more straightforward to optimize a policy over a finite set of actions than over an uncountable set Dadashi et al. (2022). The simplest approach to discretizing a continuous action space is to uniformly partition each dimension into discrete bins. However, such a partition would suffer from the curse of dimensionality in high-dimensional spaces. A better alternative is to learn the discretizations from data. AQuaDem Dadashi et al. (2022) and SAQ Luo et al. (2023) learn state-conditioned action discretizations, improving both training stability and task performance over continuous baselines. These methods discretize actions at the level of a single timestep. However, for long-horizon tasks, behavior should be temporally extended as a prerequisite for tractable learning and reasoning Sutton et al. (1999); Konidaris (2019). Recent studies quantize action chunks rather than single-step actions to produce discrete skills Shafiullah et al. (2022); Lee et al. (2024); Zheng et al. (2024); Mete et al. (2024). These methods perform quantization by reconstructing or clustering actions, which is a sensible objective to capture the multimodality of the demonstrator’s behavior.

We argue that for goal-conditioned tasks, what makes a learned skill useful is the effect it has on the state, not the particular sequence of low-level control commands that produces it. In this respect, in the unsupervised skill discovery literature, DIAYN  Eysenbach et al. (2019) learns diverse skills by making the states they visit distinguishable, and DADS Sharma et al. (2020) trains skills whose next state, given the current state, is predictable. However, neither approach performs explicit discretization; they observe diverse behavioral patterns in the data but do not represent them as separate entities or leverage them as reusable primitives. Inspired by this consequence-driven perspective, we quantize action chunks based on next-state predictions, grounding each discrete skill in its effect on the state rather than in its low-level execution. Conditioning this effect prediction mechanism on the current state further ensures that each discrete skill corresponds to an outcome that the state already offers in the dataset.
In this sense, the resulting skill codes behave as state-dependent affordances Gibson (1977); Khetarpal et al. (2020), which are skill possibilities available to the agent in the current state provided by the environment. Through this quantization framework, we aim to discover a discrete vocabulary of skills that yield meaningful outcomes, i.e., outcomes that allow the system to effectively sequence these skills to achieve given goals.

In summary, we introduce a novel action chunk quantization method that discovers goal-driven discrete skills by predicting the outcomes they generate. Our system also learns a separate low-level controller network to translate the discrete skills back to continuous actions. Both the skill vocabulary and the controller are policy-independent, meaning that they can be paired with various offline RL methods. To demonstrate policy independence, we derive discrete variants of four standard offline RL methods, which are trained as high-level policies that output discrete skills instead of continuous actions. We evaluate our method across state- and pixel-based navigation and manipulation domains, including Maze, Puzzle, and visual tasks from the Offline Goal-Conditioned RL Benchmark (OGBench) Park et al. (2025), Push-T dataset Chi et al. (2023), and D4RL Kitchen Fu et al. (2021) against both continuous baseline policies and reconstruction-based or single-step action quantization alternatives, demonstrating that our method consistently outperforms all baselines.

title: BOP-Refer: Benchmark for Monocular 3D and 2D Object Grounding
authors: Tomas Hodan,Vineet Bhat,Martin Sundermeyer,Jonathan Tremblay,Yash Patel,Médéric Fourmy,Stephen Tyree,Junwen Huang,Varun Burde,Martin Cífka,Eric Brachmann,Vincent Lepetit,Stan Birchfield,Jiri Matas,Carsten Rother
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
We introduce BOP-Refer, the first benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of everyday and industrial objects sourced from 9 diverse BOP datasets.
We pair images from these datasets with VLM-generated and human-verified referring expressions, and derive accurate ground-truth 3D and 2D bounding boxes of the referred objects from their 3D models and 6DoF pose annotations.
Our systematic evaluation of 17 frontier VLMs across the major proprietary and open-weight families (Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, Gemma)
shows that the best model, Gemini 4 Carbon, reaches 72.6% APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}} in 2D but only 12.4% APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} in 3D,
despite the more lenient IoU thresholds in 3D.
The predicted 3D boxes are usually centered on the target objects in the image but often off in depth by more than the object’s size, suggesting that metric scale estimation, which needs reliable object size priors, is currently by far the main source of error.
introduction:
3D object grounding, which is the task of 3D localization of objects referred to by a natural-language expression from visual or 3D input,
is important for systems that act in the physical world [16, 1].
Robots need 3D information for grasping, AR systems for augmenting objects with virtual content, and navigation systems for reaching named targets.
We focus on the monocular variant [99], predicting 3D bounding boxes from a single image with known intrinsics rather than from the reconstructed point cloud assumed by most 3D grounding methods. This variant needs only a calibrated camera, as found on phones, robots, and AR/VR headsets.

While 2D grounding has been studied extensively, with task-specific detectors [58, 68]
and more recently general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) [80, 6, 36],
the 3D counterpart remains underexplored. Three factors make it harder: (1) the expected output is an oriented 3D box rather than an axis-aligned rectangle, (2) ground truth is hard to obtain at scale, and (3) a single monocular view leaves object scale and distance jointly underdetermined.
Existing 3D grounding benchmarks focus on room-scale indoor or traffic scenes [16, 1, 99, 48], open-vocabulary 3D detectors are evaluated with category-level queries rather than free-form referring expressions [93, 56, 71], and few evaluate 2D and 3D grounding together [23, 27], leaving it unclear whether errors arise in localizing the referred objects in the image or in estimating their 3D position, size, or orientation.

To address these limitations, we introduce BOP-Refer, a benchmark for 3D and 2D object grounding built on top of BOP (Benchmark Object Pose) [52, 75], an established benchmark suite for 6DoF object pose estimation that includes a wide range of datasets with accurate 3D object models and pose annotations. Our key contributions are:

First benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of diverse objects from referring expressions.
BOP-Refer covers 225 diverse everyday and industrial objects from 9 BOP datasets, with 1,400 validation and 1,400 test image-query pairs.
We provide VLM-generated, human-verified referring expressions (Fig. BOP-Refer: Benchmark for Monocular 3D and 2D Object Grounding) with high-quality ground-truth 3D and 2D boxes, for direct comparison of 3D and 2D grounding on the same data.

First benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of diverse objects from referring expressions.
BOP-Refer covers 225 diverse everyday and industrial objects from 9 BOP datasets, with 1,400 validation and 1,400 test image-query pairs.
We provide VLM-generated, human-verified referring expressions (Fig. BOP-Refer: Benchmark for Monocular 3D and 2D Object Grounding) with high-quality ground-truth 3D and 2D boxes, for direct comparison of 3D and 2D grounding on the same data.

Comprehensive evaluation of frontier VLMs. We evaluate 12 proprietary and 5 open-weight VLMs from the Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, and Gemma families, revealing that monocular 3D grounding remains far from solved, whereas the strongest models already localize most referred objects well in 2D. Our analysis points to metric scale estimation (the distance and size of the objects) as the main source of error in 3D grounding.

Symmetry-aware 3D evaluation. We introduce two symmetry-aware 3D box comparison functions that treat symmetry-related 3D boxes as equivalent: a variant of the popular IoU3D, and NCD (Normalized Corner Distance), which can distinguish near and far misses.

Online evaluation system. We developed an online evaluation system that scores submissions on the test split with private ground-truth annotations and provides a public leaderboard of submitted methods. The validation split has public ground truth for development.
