title: HOG-WAM: Improving Visual Robustness through Future Gradient Prediction
authors: Boxuan Dong,Yupeng Qian,Ying Wu,Heshuai Li,Junhao Tan,Zhenxiong Tan,Weijia Wu,Weihao Yu
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies.
We introduce HOG-WAM, which adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision derived directly from demonstration images.
An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) module reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, allowing its objective to shape the visual representation used for control.
The module is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving FastWAM’s RGB-to-action architecture.
We evaluate four controlled observation corruptions through a visual-corruption extension of RoboTwin, termed RoboTwin-Plus; HOG-WAM achieves the highest success among the compared policies under all four.
Mixed-noise success increases from 78.86% to 82.86% relative to FastWAM, with comparable performance on clean scenes.
On LIBERO Plus, overall success increases from 74.49% to 75.26%, with the largest gain under sensor noise, from 74.14% to 78.89%.
Across four Franka tasks, average success increases from 40% to 59% under clean observations and from 17% to 24% under noisy observations.
A representation ablation favors combining RGB observations with auxiliary HOG prediction over replacing RGB with HOG.
These findings support future-gradient prediction as complementary supervision for visually robust control, with larger absolute gains on physical tasks than in simulation.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation requires recognizing task-relevant objects and anticipating how their spatial relations change during interaction.
Vision-language-action policies use pretrained visual and language representations to map observations to actions [40, 17, 5].
World-action models (WAMs) additionally learn to predict future observations, making demonstrated scene evolution a source of policy supervision [35, 18, 3].
Fast-WAM [38], denoted FastWAM here, preserves this predictive objective during training while generating actions from the current observation at inference.
The prediction target therefore determines which visual information this training objective emphasizes.

RGB prediction supervises object structure together with color, texture, and illumination.
These appearance cues help identify objects, but they also vary with lighting and sensor conditions while the manipulation goal remains unchanged.
An RGB objective alone thus ties the learned features to appearance factors that can change at deployment.
For placement, stacking, and insertion, local boundaries describe the image-space arrangement of objects and their surroundings.
Requiring a visual representation to predict these boundaries provides an explicit structural learning signal alongside RGB reconstruction.
The question is how to introduce this signal while retaining the appearance information needed for language-conditioned control.

Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) [10] summarize local edge orientations through spatial pooling and contrast normalization.
MaskFeat [30] demonstrates that predicting HOG features in masked image and video regions can learn useful visual representations, identifying local contrast normalization as an important component.
This motivates a different prediction problem for manipulation: learning the gradient structure of future demonstration frames alongside actions.
The target emphasizes where local intensity transitions occur and how they are oriented, making spatial organization explicit without object annotations or a learned target generator.

A descriptor useful for supervising a representation need not replace its sensory input.
Our HOG raster compresses orientation statistics and removes chromatic information; RGB retains cues for object identity and instruction grounding.
WAM4D [19] offers a related architectural principle: future-depth supervision shapes the visual features used for control through a removable readout.
We apply this principle to deterministic gradient targets, which require no additional sensor or pretrained estimator.
In HOG-WAM, an auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, and its loss updates the RGB backbone.
Action prediction remains independent of HOG tokens, allowing the auxiliary module to be removed at inference while retaining its effect on the learned RGB representation.

We evaluate visual robustness on RoboTwin 2.0 [7], LIBERO Plus [13], and four Franka tasks.
RoboTwin-Plus denotes our visual-corruption extension of the existing RoboTwin evaluation, with fixed tasks and controlled changes to image inputs.
On LIBERO Plus, gains concentrate under sensor noise.
A LIBERO Plus ablation compares HOG as auxiliary supervision with HOG as a replacement for RGB.
The physical experiments show larger absolute gains over FastWAM than the simulation averages, extending the evidence to manipulation with real camera observations.
Our contributions are:

A deterministic future-gradient target that makes local structure an explicit supervision signal for world-action learning.

An asymmetric coupling of RGB, HOG, and action DiT modules that transfers this supervision to the visual backbone while preserving RGB-based inference.

Evidence from controlled visual-corruption tests and physical manipulation, together with a representation ablation that supports complementary HOG supervision over RGB replacement.

1. A deterministic future-gradient target that makes local structure an explicit supervision signal for world-action learning.

2. An asymmetric coupling of RGB, HOG, and action DiT modules that transfers this supervision to the visual backbone while preserving RGB-based inference.

3. Evidence from controlled visual-corruption tests and physical manipulation, together with a representation ablation that supports complementary HOG supervision over RGB replacement.

title: Was the Model Given the Right Action? Auditing and Repairing Action Interfaces in Navigation World Models
authors: Ajmain Istiak Apon,Md Mehedi Hasan,Sejuti Rahman
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
World models are evaluated through rollouts: starting from real camera frames of a recorded robot run, or trajectory, the model receives the run’s actions and predicts the frames that follow, each prediction feeding the next. Evaluations use segments of trajectories, called clips. We study Navigation World Models (NWM) [5], a model that predicts future camera frames from past frames and navigation actions; later work reuses its rollout code, so one error can affect several evaluations. Preprocessing maps poses to action inputs, choosing a reference frame, a normalization offset, an angle convention and a rule for aggregating raw-step displacements. This action encoder has no learned weights: it is neither NWM’s image encoder nor its learned action embedding. A difference between the encodings used in training and in evaluation is a mismatch; the error it causes is charged to the model.

Existing benchmarks ask whether a model follows the action it is given [42, 8, 9]; we ask whether the model received the action it learned to interpret. Our main result is an audit of NWM’s action interface: its released rollout code prepares actions differently from its training code, through three interacting mismatches that change one frozen checkpoint’s predictions (Figure 1). We call the action inputs built by the released rollout code released actions, and those built from the same poses by the training code repaired actions; replacing one with the other, with the checkpoint unchanged, is repair. A chunk spans one prediction call, which predicts one future state a fixed time shift ahead. The two encodings agree only on the first chunk, so a one-chunk check passes.

Detecting that two action encoders differ is differential testing; knowing what to fix is harder, because mismatches interact: fixing only NWM’s offset increases error. The encoding also spans the rollout loop, dataset code and normalization, so reading one function can miss what the model receives. We therefore query action encoders, with a tool we call ActRosetta. Our NWM repair itself used NWM’s own training code; ActRosetta lets others run the same check on their own encoders. Our contributions are:

An action-interface mismatch that changes model evaluation. NWM’s rollout code differs from training in reference frame, normalization offset and yaw wrapping. Repair, without retraining, reduces mean DreamSim error on RECON from 0.240 to 0.139 (42%) and removes or shrinks two alternative models’ leads (Sec. 3).

A repeatable audit with witnessed attribution. ActRosetta queries paired training and evaluation encoders on controlled paths, names a differing field only when a test path witnesses it, and repairs only when the whole contract, an encoder’s full set of encoding choices, is determined. Unlike ActionABI [2], which shares its principles but recovers contracts from logs, it diagnoses paired code, identifying the interacting choices a patch must address (Secs. 4–5).

Evidence separating detection, attribution and repair. ActionFaultBench, our benchmark of action-encoder pairs whose differences are known in advance, tests whether a checker can find differences, explain them and recover the training encoder’s inputs, on four sealed test sets written by separate automated agents after our code was frozen; an audit of 40 public repositories complements it. On the final 240-pair test, ActRosetta detects all 91 differing pairs, recovers their differences exactly in 73 cases, and repairs all 38 differing pairs supported by output conversion (Secs. 6–7).

title: Motion Beyond Pixels: Learning Future Visual Representations for Object-Centric Dynamics
authors: Chengzhi Zhao,Juelin Li,Zhennan Wang,Sheng Wang,Zhuoman Liu,Yuhao Lu,Jiongxu Chen,Haitang Feng,Yanjie Li,Lin Shao
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Many embodied world models predict future states in latent spaces optimized for RGB reconstruction, which do not explicitly prioritize object-level semantics and geometry relevant to motion generation.
We present MotionRep, a visual representation world model that jointly generates future DINO representations and 3D object flow, coupling semantic and geometric information with object-centric dynamics.
To make high-dimensional DINO features amenable to generative modeling, we introduce DINO-VAE, which combines temporal and channel compression with latent regularization to produce compact latents while preserving semantic and geometric information.
Conditioned on an initial observation, object query points, and a language instruction, a unified diffusion transformer predicts future visual representations and 3D object flow through joint attention.
MotionRep employs asymmetric modality-specific noise schedules to keep the visual stream ahead of 3D object flow during joint denoising, allowing progressively refined future visual representations to guide flow generation.
Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that MotionRep outperforms pixel-based baselines in 3D object flow accuracy and generalization to unseen scenes, while requiring only three denoising steps for inference.
These results support predictive visual representations as an effective future-state space for object-centric dynamics modeling.
introduction:
Effective robotic manipulation requires reasoning beyond the current observation to anticipate future object dynamics.
3D object flow explicitly represents the trajectories of object points in 3D space, providing a natural description of future physical dynamics (Yuan et al., 2024).
Recent 3D object flow world models incorporate future visual state modeling to support motion generation, making the choice of visual representation a critical design decision (Li et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026b).

Existing 3D object flow world models commonly predict future states in pixel-reconstruction-oriented latent spaces (Li et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026b), which preserve substantial low-level texture and appearance details but do not explicitly prioritize object semantics and spatial geometry relevant to motion prediction (Yu et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025). Modeling such complex appearance details can increase inference cost and limit generalization to unseen scenes.
In contrast, visual representation world models predict future states rich in semantic and geometric information (Zhou et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026).
However, these approaches primarily focus on visual representation prediction, while jointly modeling visual representations and 3D object flow remains underexplored.

To address this challenge, we introduce MotionRep, a visual representation world model for object-centric dynamics that jointly generates future DINO representations and 3D object flow, modeling future visual states in the DINO representation space rather than pixel-reconstruction-oriented latent spaces (Fig. 1).
Although DINO representations capture rich semantic and geometric information (Siméoni et al., 2025), their high dimensionality and unregularized feature distributions limit direct diffusion modeling (Zheng et al., 2026; Bi et al., 2026).
We therefore introduce DINO-VAE, which combines temporal and channel compression with latent regularization to produce compact generative latents while preserving informative feature structure.
Building on this representation, MotionRep generates future visual representations and 3D object flow using a diffusion transformer, enabling direct interaction between visual states and object dynamics through joint attention.
Furthermore, we introduce decoupled timestep sampling and modality-specific noise schedules, allowing future visual representations to be progressively denoised ahead of 3D object flow and continuously guide motion generation in a latent-forcing manner.

Experiments on simulated and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that MotionRep achieves state-of-the-art 3D object flow prediction performance, generalizes to unseen scenes, and enables efficient generation with only three sampling steps.
Representation analyses show that DINO-VAE preserves semantic and geometric information in compressed latents.
Ablation studies further validate the contributions of DINO-VAE, future DINO generation, modality-specific noise scheduling, and representation world model pretraining to 3D object flow generation.
Conditional inference experiments demonstrate that MotionRep supports both visual-conditioned inverse dynamics and flow-conditioned forward dynamics within the same model, revealing bidirectional dependencies between future visual representations and 3D object motion.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We demonstrate the value of explicitly predicting future visual representations for 3D object flow generation, and introduce MotionRep to jointly model future DINO representations and object motion.

We introduce DINO-VAE, which makes dense DINO features amenable to generative modeling through temporal and channel compression and latent regularization, while preserving semantic and geometric information.

We develop an asymmetric denoising strategy with decoupled timesteps and modality-specific noise schedules, enabling representation-guided flow generation and bidirectional conditional dynamics modeling.

1. We demonstrate the value of explicitly predicting future visual representations for 3D object flow generation, and introduce MotionRep to jointly model future DINO representations and object motion.

2. We introduce DINO-VAE, which makes dense DINO features amenable to generative modeling through temporal and channel compression and latent regularization, while preserving semantic and geometric information.

3. We develop an asymmetric denoising strategy with decoupled timesteps and modality-specific noise schedules, enabling representation-guided flow generation and bidirectional conditional dynamics modeling.

title: Who Is Ego? Scaling Cross-View Camera Wearer Identification and Segmentation beyond Humans
authors: Yifan Jin,Zheng Zhang,Tianwen Qian,Dong Wang,Bo Zhao,Yanwei Fu,Yuqian Fu
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
A first-person (ego) image reveals what a camera sees, but not who or what carries it. Given a synchronized third-person (exo) image, camera wearer identification asks who is ego: which candidate carries the ego camera? We extend this task beyond humans to robots, vehicles, animals, and drones, and broaden its spatial scope (where is ego) from selecting a provided candidate mask to wearer segmentation with absence prediction and mutual camera localization across ego–exo views. We introduce FindEgo-1M, comprising 1.16M real and simulated ego–exo pairs across 12 wearer types, 17 domains, and 111 test settings. Our approach exploits a geometric relation: the ego camera’s projection into the exo image, i.e., the epipole, lies on or near its wearer. We introduce EgoRay-ZS, the first method to turn a frozen feed-forward 3D reconstruction model, VGGT-Ω\Omega, into a training-free solution for wearer identification and segmentation. Its geometric readout ranks candidate masks or segmentation proposals by angular offset and distance to the ego camera, while the relative pose provides mutual camera directions. We then develop the full EgoRay model through pose-supervised training on FindEgo-1M and label-free test-time adaptation constrained by candidate masks.
Without task-specific training, EgoRay-ZS achieves 78.0% identification accuracy on TF2023’s original labels [121], versus 52.9% reported for the dataset-trained PEN [121].
On FindEgo-1M, EgoRay achieves state-of-the-art chance-corrected accuracy of 87.1 and 77.7 on seen and unseen settings. On matched queries, EgoRay also outperforms GPT-6 Astra by 31.6 and 21.3 points on seen and unseen settings, respectively, while running 18×\times faster.
Data, code, and models will be released.
introduction:
Given synchronized first-person (ego) and third-person (exo) images, camera wearer identification asks who is ego: which person in the exo view carries the ego camera [24, 121]? This task connects a person’s first-person footage to their presence in an external view, supporting applications such as body-camera analysis in broadcast or surveillance footage. When identifiers, GPS, and camera calibration are unavailable, this association must be inferred visually.

Benchmarks such as TF2023 and TF2025 [121, 122] have supported progress on this task. However, existing research remains limited in three respects.
(1) Narrow wearer scope: studies focus on humans, overlooking the need to associate onboard and external observations in other settings.
(2) Limited data scale and diversity: existing datasets constrain both training and systematic evaluation of generalization to new environments and wearer types.
(3) Limited task scope: existing evaluations mostly identify the wearer among provided candidates or select a detected mask for segmentation [121], leaving segmentation without given candidates, absence prediction, and mutual camera localization underexplored.

We therefore ask whether who is ego can scale beyond human-centric identification, and address this question along three dimensions.
First, we broaden the wearer scope to robots, vehicles, animals, and drones, recognizing cross-view camera wearer identification as a shared problem across camera-bearing agents. These settings introduce distinct challenges: robots of the same model can look nearly identical, while birds and drones may occupy only a few pixels in the exo view.
Second, we scale training and evaluation through FindEgo-1M, combining public recordings, such as TF2023 [121] and Ego-Exo4D [36], with new simulations to provide 1.16M ego–exo pairs across 12 wearer types, 17 domains, and 111 test settings. Real recordings capture real-world variability, while simulation broadens coverage and supplies exact geometry.
Evaluation spans four levels of generalization relative to training: new recordings at seen locations (L0), new locations within seen domains (L1), unseen data sources or scene types with seen wearer types (L2), and unseen wearer types (L3). The top of Fig. 1 illustrates FindEgo-1M.
Finally, we move beyond candidate-mask selection to wearer segmentation without given candidates, requiring methods to delineate the wearer or report its absence. We further study mutual camera localization, estimating each camera’s direction from the other.

Existing methods associate ego and exo views through appearance or motion matching [24, 1, 121, 122]. Appearance is ambiguous among similar-looking candidates, while motion requires video and distinct trajectories. We instead exploit a geometric relation: the wearer is where the camera is. The ego camera’s projection into the exo image, i.e., the epipole, lies on or near its wearer [11, 12]. The bottom of Fig. 1 illustrates how relative camera geometry reveals wearer identity. We are the first to use a feed-forward 3D reconstruction model, VGGT-Ω\Omega [103], for this task. Our EgoRay-ZS combines the angular offset to each candidate mask with camera distance to distinguish candidates along similar rays. The same readout ranks SAM 3 proposals [9] for segmentation and predicts absence through angular offset, while relative pose provides mutual camera directions.
The full EgoRay model improves pose generalization through pose-supervised training on FindEgo-1M and test-time adaptation, which constrains the projected ego camera to lie on or near a candidate mask, providing a geometric learning signal without wearer labels.

Without task-specific training, EgoRay-ZS identifies 78.0% of wearers on TF2023’s original labels [121], compared with 52.9% reported for the dataset-trained PEN [121] (Sec. 5.2). On FindEgo-1M, EgoRay achieves state-of-the-art identification accuracy at all four generalization levels. For the most challenging unseen wearer types (L3), it reaches 71.1 chance-corrected accuracy, versus 42.1 for the strongest competing 3D model. It further outperforms strong multimodal LLMs, including Claude Opus and GPT-6 Astra, by 16.5 and 21.3 percentage points, respectively, on matched unseen identification queries (Tab. 4).

Our contributions are fourfold.
(1) Task: we extend wearer identification beyond humans and to segmentation without given candidates, absence prediction, and mutual camera localization.
(2) Data: we introduce FindEgo-1M, with 1.16M real and simulated ego–exo pairs for large-scale training and systematic generalization evaluation.
(3) Method: we explore a geometric perspective on camera wearer understanding and present two models: zero-shot EgoRay-ZS and trained EgoRay.
(4) Results: we achieve state-of-the-art results on FindEgo-1M and TF2023, outperforming prior wearer identification methods, competing 3D models, and strong multimodal LLMs.

title: ProManO: Beyond Sim(3) for Metric Upgrade of Feed-Forward Geometry with Visual-Inertial Anchors
authors: Lingxiang Hu,Zhenjun Zhao,Qi Shao,Naima Ait Oufroukh,Fabien Bonardi,Raymond Ghandour,Shenghai Yuan,Javier Civera,Baoru Huang
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Upgrading feed-forward geometry to metric scale with visual-inertial odometry (VIO) raises the question of which correction should align dense feed-forward prediction with sparse metric VIO anchors.
Existing methods use either a similarity transformation, which cannot represent depth-dependent distortion, or a projective transformation, which alters pre-calibrated intrinsics.
We prove that the transformations compatible with pre-calibrated intrinsics form a ten-dimensional manifold.
Beyond Sim(3), this manifold contains three degrees of freedom (DoF) that locate the plane at infinity and leave residuals growing quadratically with depth range after any similarity alignment.
These DoF are invisible in the image and can be resolved only by metric depth along viewing rays or by multi-view constraints.
To estimate them, we propose ProManO, a probabilistic manifold optimization framework in which every anchor is weighted by its along-ray uncertainty and inlier probability within a single expectation-maximization (EM) procedure.
ProManO certifies the similarity synchronization and refines the plane at infinity only where it is observable, which guarantees an objective value no worse than that of the optimal similarity alignment.
Experiments on EuRoC, CID-SIMS, Oxford Spires, and KITTI-360 demonstrate that ProManO achieves the highest mean F1F_{1} and outperforms Sim(3) alignment on all four datasets.
The project page is available at https://h0xg.github.io/ProManO/.
introduction:
Dense metric reconstruction underpins robot navigation, simulation, and digital twins.
Recent 3D foundation models [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] can predict dense, multi-view consistent geometry in a single forward pass, but do not provide reliable metric scale.
In contrast, visual-inertial odometry (VIO) provides metric camera motion and 3D structure, but only sparsely [6, 7, 8].
Combining the two offers a natural path to dense metric maps.
However, the key challenge lies in the metric upgrade itself: feed-forward geometry exhibits depth-dependent distortions that cannot be captured by a global similarity transformation.
Specifically, distant structure is unevenly compressed across the image, causing residual errors to increase with depth after similarity alignment to the VIO anchors (), eventually leading to the rejection of distant anchors as outliers.

Existing approaches upgrade feed-forward geometry using correction models chosen by design rather than derived from geometric constraints.
Monocular depth pipelines estimate per-image scale and shift parameters [9, 10, 11].
Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) systems built on feed-forward models align each submap using either a similarity transformation [12, 13, 14], which cannot capture depth-dependent distortions, or a projective transformation in SL(4) [15, 16], whose additional degrees of freedom (DoF) may change pre-calibrated camera intrinsics.
Visual-inertial systems that fuse feed-forward geometry [17, 18, 19, 20] use metric measurements as alignment targets but retain these same correction
models.
However, none of these approaches derive the correction model from an analysis of the residual geometric ambiguity after camera calibration, nor do they explicitly account for the reliability of the available metric evidence.

We model the residual error of feed-forward geometry as a transformation of the scene and prove that, with calibrated cameras, the intrinsics-consistent transformations form exactly a ten-dimensional manifold (Theorem 1), namely a similarity and three modes that locate the plane at infinity.
These modes add the inverse-depth map of a plane to the prediction, are invisible in the image, bias any similarity alignment quadratically in depth (Proposition 2), and are resolved by metric depth along rays (Fig. 2).
This evidence is weakest where it is needed: a triangulated anchor is least precise along its viewing ray, wrong anchors cannot be exposed by the image, and constraints shared between submaps fix only their relative correction.
Building on this analysis, we present ProManO (Probabilistic Manifold Optimization), which weights every anchor, overlap, and loop constraint by its along-ray uncertainty and inlier probability in one expectation-maximization (EM), certifies the similarity synchronization, and upgrades a submap from Sim(3) to the full correction only where an observability test shows that the data determine it.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

We prove the intrinsics-consistent transformations are exactly Sim(3) and the position of the plane at infinity, derive its invisibility, depth-dependent bias, and degeneracies, and unify scale-shift, Sim(3), and SL(4) models.

We propose ProManO, a probabilistic manifold optimization framework with along-ray anchor uncertainty, a single EM with monotone block updates across all stages, certified similarity synchronization, and an observability-gated refinement.

On four indoor and outdoor benchmarks, ProManO achieves the highest mean F1F_{1} and improves F1F_{1} over a certified similarity with the same anchors on every outdoor sequence, by 9.8 points on average on Oxford Spires.

1. We prove the intrinsics-consistent transformations are exactly Sim(3) and the position of the plane at infinity, derive its invisibility, depth-dependent bias, and degeneracies, and unify scale-shift, Sim(3), and SL(4) models.

2. We propose ProManO, a probabilistic manifold optimization framework with along-ray anchor uncertainty, a single EM with monotone block updates across all stages, certified similarity synchronization, and an observability-gated refinement.

3. On four indoor and outdoor benchmarks, ProManO achieves the highest mean F1F_{1} and improves F1F_{1} over a certified similarity with the same anchors on every outdoor sequence, by 9.8 points on average on Oxford Spires.

title: Can Visual World Models See Force?
authors: Felix Tristram,Benjamin D. Killeen,Nassir Navab
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: World models and vision-language-action policy models are increasingly proposed as foundations for robot manipulation. They predict how scenes evolve and which actions to take, yet successful manipulation depends not solely on following observable trajectories but also on the hidden variable of interaction force. Neurophysiology has shown that humans possess a visual prior for this hidden variable, motivating us to ask the question: Do the representations of visual foundation models also capture the forces involved in an interaction? We define force awareness as the ability of representations to (1) indicate when contact force is applied, (2) track how it changes during an interaction, and (3) reflect how large it is. We probe frozen image, video, world- and policy model representations with a lightweight readout trained on synchronized video and force measurements from two manipulation datasets. Our experiments show that most models capture when contact occurs but not how much force is being applied. Surprisingly, robot post-training does not improve this either, highlighting an important gap in current models capabilities.
introduction:
World-action models may enable generalist robot manipulation by learning to predict how the world changes together with the actions a robot takes. DreamZero, for example, jointly predicts future video and actions, building on large-scale video pretraining [40]. Related approaches use predictive video representations for planning or train vision-language-action models across diverse robot demonstrations [2, 21, 5, 4]. These efforts raise the prospect that physical understanding can emerge from more video, larger models, and more robot data. Yet inaccurate force application has been identified as a failure mode of robot foundation models [31, 42], which commonly predict motion targets while leaving force control to low-level controllers [2, 21, 5, 4, 1]. These failures raise the question of whether the models’ representations capture the forces involved in manipulation, beyond the motion they predict.

An example of similar motion trajectories but different force application can be seen in everyday activities such as opening a fridge vs. a cabinet door. The doors can follow similar trajectories but require different forces because of friction or resistance that is difficult to see. Vision can provide useful cues here: humans use visual appearance to anticipate an object’s weight and scale their initial lifting forces [7], while visual feedback during lifting helps correct expectation-driven force errors [6]. These findings motivate us to investigate whether visual world models also acquire representations that implicitly encode interaction force.

Prior evaluations of visual foundation models reveal difficulties with hidden mechanical properties and broader physical understanding [35, 8]. At the same time, probing studies find geometric information, physical plausibility signals, and motion variables in pretrained representations [10, 18, 12]. Readouts of elasticity, viscosity, and friction provide further evidence of accessible physical information, although accurate value prediction in real-world videos remains challenging [41].
Together, these studies establish the systematic evaluation of physical and geometric information in pretrained representations as a research contribution in its own right. We extend this line of inquiry to interaction force by asking: how much force can be decoded from models trained for general visual, generative, and action objectives?

We probe 13 different models spanning image and geometry encoders, self-supervised video encoders, generative world models, and vision-language and policy models, on synchronized video and force measurements from the Hoi! dataset [11], and the larger robotic RH20T [14] dataset. The model set contains matched comparisons: base checkpoints and their robot-trained counterparts, different sizes within the Wan and Cosmos3 families, and two camera views of the same interactions. We separate three capabilities that are often conflated: detecting when contact force is applied, tracking how it changes within an interaction, and recovering how much force is applied. Our main findings are:

Detecting contact is easy, recovering magnitude is not. Most representations detect when force is applied, including single-image encoders, but not how much. Nearly all compress the measured force range, and on Hoi! most are less accurate than predicting the mean contact force.

Detecting contact is easy, recovering magnitude is not. Most representations detect when force is applied, including single-image encoders, but not how much. Nearly all compress the measured force range, and on Hoi! most are less accurate than predicting the mean contact force.

V-JEPA is the exception. In the Hoi! gripper view and on RH20T, it tracks force best and explains the most variance in contact force, although at most 17%17\%. Neither video input nor model size accounts for this: VideoMAEv2 observes the same clips, and world models of up to 14B parameters remain below the 1B-parameter V-JEPA encoder.

Robot training does not reliably improve force awareness. Of four robot-trained world and VLA models, only DreamZero tracks force better than the model it builds on, and only on Hoi!. On RH20T it does not, although its predictions cover more of the measured force range.

Together, these results suggest that force awareness does not come for free with video generation or robot training. It can be learned though, through direct force supervision: fine-tuning V-JEPA on RH20T force labels improves force tracking there and transfers to Hoi! without retraining. This makes force supervision a promising direction, and force a quantity worth evaluating alongside geometry, video quality and task success.

title: FoundSurface: Feedforward Ray-Based 3D Scene Surface Reconstruction from Unposed Images
authors: Shenxing Wei,Jinxi Li,Zihui Zhang,Ajay Kumar,Wei Wang,Bo Yang
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computational Geometry (cs.CG); Graphics (cs.GR); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation. Code and data are available at: https://vlar-group.github.io/FoundSurface.html
introduction:
Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from multiple images plays a key role in emerging applications such as embodied AI and augmented reality. In recent years, significant progress has been made in the field of 3D reconstruction through the development of various 3D representation techniques [82]. These include coordinate-based methods such as radiance fields (NeRF) [56], and point-based methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [43], and their variants [29, 12]. While these approaches achieve impressive results in novel view synthesis, they usually rely on highly accurate camera poses, which are often unavailable in practice, and typically struggle to recover precise 3D surfaces. Furthermore, they generally require time-consuming per-scene optimization rather than functioning as generalizable, feed-forward models [99].

Recently, the pioneering feedforward method DUSt3R [81] has enabled precise 3D geometry reconstruction by directly predicting pixel-aligned pointmaps from unposed image pairs. Subsequent methods [101] have extended this pointmap representation to handle multiple views [78, 92], to improve computational efficiency [65, 52], etc.. Leveraging powerful Transformer architectures and large-scale training datasets, these approaches achieve excellent accuracy in recovering surface points from image collections. However, the reconstructed pointmaps are inherently discrete and sparse, lacking the continuous and fine-grained geometric details required for many downstream applications, such as robot manipulation and scene editing.

Another recent line of work focuses on ray-based representations such as RayDF [53] and RayletDF [84]. Their key innovation is learning a ray-surface distance field for any query light ray conditioned on visual inputs, thus enabling the recovery of continuous and high-fidelity surfaces. However, they still rely on accurate camera poses or sparse point clouds as inputs to reconstruct detailed surfaces.

In this paper, we present a generalizable, feed-forward 3D surface reconstruction pipeline that takes only a set of unposed images as input and directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces. We achieve this by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. In particular, as illustrated in Figure 2, our pipeline comprises four key components: 1) a pre-trained pointmap-based model such as VGGT [78], which extracts visual tokens and generates pixel-aligned pointmaps along with estimated camera poses; 2) a query-view-centric selection module designed to identify geometrically relevant reference views; 3) a coarse ray-surface distance regressor utilizing cross-attention layers; and 4) a raylet-based surface module for refining surface details and normals.

Among the four modules of our pipeline, the core is the second and third modules, which seamlessly integrate pointmap- and ray-based representations, effectively estimating continuous surfaces for any query views conditioned on the recovered pointmaps from unposed input images. In contrast, directly applying RayletDF to VGGT pointmaps can lead to inaccurate raylet initialization, resulting in multi-surface artifacts and missing regions.

Our pipeline is based on large Transformer and standard neural layers with sufficient capacity, without relying on domain specific assumptions. Therefore, it is rather suitable to consume various indoor and outdoor datasets. We train a single foundation 3D surface model on a mixture of 9 public datasets with depth annotations, including BlendMVS [94], WildRGB [86], ScanNet [21], HyperSim [63], MVS-Synth [37], ARKitScenes [4], S3DIS [1], SceneNN [33], and GTASfM [79]. Our model is termed FoundSurface and Figure 1 shows qualitative results. Our contributions are:

We introduce a large feed-forward model to recover continuous 3D scene surfaces from an arbitrary number of images without needing poses.

We introduce a large feed-forward model to recover continuous 3D scene surfaces from an arbitrary number of images without needing poses.

We design a query-view-centric selection module together with a cross attention based fusion module to seamlessly integrate pointmap- and ray-based 3D representations.

We train a single foundation model and demonstrate superior 3D surface reconstruction accuracy across multiple datasets, clearly surpassing existing baselines.

1. We introduce a large feed-forward model to recover continuous 3D scene surfaces from an arbitrary number of images without needing poses.

2. We design a query-view-centric selection module together with a cross attention based fusion module to seamlessly integrate pointmap- and ray-based 3D representations.

3. We train a single foundation model and demonstrate superior 3D surface reconstruction accuracy across multiple datasets, clearly surpassing existing baselines.

title: A Simple Yet Effective Agent for Open-World Aerial Object Search
authors: Jitai Hao,Liangxing Yang,Zhenyang Li,Fan Liu,Qiang Huang,Jun Yu
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Open-world aerial object search methods often rely on persistent spatial maps, learned world models, or task-specific policy training.
To examine how far a minimal, training-free design can go, we introduce SimpleUAV, an agent built around a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM).
SimpleUAV separates current-view target assessment from history-conditioned action selection, combining fresh candidate evidence with lightweight search context.
Local geometry converts visual selections into bounded straight-line movements, depth-based checks halt blocked segments, and measured execution feedback guides subsequent decisions.
This closed loop sustains search without persistent spatial maps or task-specific training.
SimpleUAV achieves 41.61% Success Rate (SR) on UAV-ON and 11.98% on AerialDojo-200K, compared with 23.80% and 3.20% for the strongest prior baselines, respectively.
With limited benchmark-specific adaptation, the same core agent transfers to aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) on TravelUAV, improving Full SR by at least 19.66% across all three splits under L1 assistance.
These results establish a strong baseline for evaluating when additional architectural complexity benefits aerial search.
introduction:
Aerial object-goal navigation requires an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to locate and approach a target described in natural language in an unfamiliar outdoor environment [47, 19, 10].
This capability supports applications such as search and rescue [45] and infrastructure inspection [40].
Given neither the target location nor detailed route instructions [59], the UAV must decide where to search, which observations warrant further inspection, and when the available evidence supports stopping [18].

These decisions are tightly coupled in large, partially observed outdoor environments.
The target may remain outside the UAV’s field of view for much of an episode, requiring contextual cues to guide exploration [23, 46].
Even if a candidate appears, distance, occlusion, and visually similar distractors can make its identity uncertain [50].
Moving closer or changing altitude may reveal discriminative attributes, but also changes the visible scene and exposes the UAV to new obstacles [8].
Thus, effective search requires semantic judgments, search context, and three-dimensional motion to remain coordinated as observations evolve.

Recent aerial search systems address these challenges with specialized spatial representations and predictive models.
Three representative directions are shown in Figure 1:

Semantic Maps and Beliefs.
Task-oriented semantic, attraction, uncertainty, or value maps turn local observations into sustained search guidance  [19, 51, 8].
AeroBelief further separates contextual cues from target-specific evidence through dual-layer semantic-spatial belief maps [46].

Explicit Spatial Memory.
Semantic voxel-ray memory [23], sliding local maps with sparse global history [15], and adaptive octree memory with instruction-guided queries [59] organize fragmented observations across changing viewpoints.

Learned World Models.
SearchWorld combines explicit spatial memory with learned dynamics to reason about action consequences and improve its exploration policy through imagined rollouts [18].

These approaches introduce persistent representations, dedicated memory-processing modules, or task-specific model and policy training.
At the same time, pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) offer broad semantic knowledge and open-vocabulary visual understanding [2, 36].
These capabilities provide a basis for interpreting target descriptions, identifying promising search regions, and assessing visible candidates without navigation-specific fine-tuning.
They motivate a systematic evaluation of how effectively a frozen VLM can support aerial search when paired with lightweight search context and local geometric execution.
This leads us to ask:

How far can a minimal, training-free VLM-based agent go in open-world aerial search?

We investigate this question with SimpleUAV, a closed-loop agent built around a frozen, off-the-shelf VLM.
The VLM first assesses candidate targets from current multi-view observations alone, then selects actions using localized candidates, recent interactions, and a bounded text summary.
This separates current visual assessment from the context needed to maintain search continuity.
Local geometry converts visual selections into bounded straight-line movements, while depth-based obstacle checks halt blocked segments.
Measured execution outcomes inform the next observation and decision cycle, connecting semantic reasoning to actual motion without persistent spatial maps or task-specific policy training.

Without task-specific fine-tuning, SimpleUAV improves success rate (SR) over the strongest compared baselines by 17.81% on UAV-ON [47] and 8.78% on AerialDojo-200K [10].
On the aerial VLN benchmark TravelUAV [44], it improves Full SR by at least 19.66% across all three evaluation splits under L1 assistance.
Even with a compact 4B VLM, SimpleUAV exceeds the strongest prior UAV-ON baseline by 14.13% in SR.

Our main contributions are summarized below.

We show that a minimal, training-free agent built around a frozen VLM can substantially outperform specialized systems in open-world aerial search without persistent spatial maps or task-specific policy training.

We propose SimpleUAV, separating current-view target assessment from history-conditioned action selection and closing the loop through local geometric execution feedback to sustain search, while requiring fresh visual and geometric evidence for approach and stopping.

We demonstrate generalization across environments and navigation tasks, transferring SimpleUAV from UAV-ON to AerialDojo-200K and TravelUAV with limited benchmark-specific adaptation and no additional training, achieving the highest SR among compared methods.

1. Semantic Maps and Beliefs.
Task-oriented semantic, attraction, uncertainty, or value maps turn local observations into sustained search guidance  [19, 51, 8].
AeroBelief further separates contextual cues from target-specific evidence through dual-layer semantic-spatial belief maps [46].

2. Explicit Spatial Memory.
Semantic voxel-ray memory [23], sliding local maps with sparse global history [15], and adaptive octree memory with instruction-guided queries [59] organize fragmented observations across changing viewpoints.

3. Learned World Models.
SearchWorld combines explicit spatial memory with learned dynamics to reason about action consequences and improve its exploration policy through imagined rollouts [18].

1. We show that a minimal, training-free agent built around a frozen VLM can substantially outperform specialized systems in open-world aerial search without persistent spatial maps or task-specific policy training.

2. We propose SimpleUAV, separating current-view target assessment from history-conditioned action selection and closing the loop through local geometric execution feedback to sustain search, while requiring fresh visual and geometric evidence for approach and stopping.

3. We demonstrate generalization across environments and navigation tasks, transferring SimpleUAV from UAV-ON to AerialDojo-200K and TravelUAV with limited benchmark-specific adaptation and no additional training, achieving the highest SR among compared methods.

title: CARE-WM: Same-Horizon Self-Conditioning with Constraint-Adaptive Regularization for Latent World Models
authors: Yuchen Lin,Kai Zhao
abstract:
Planning with latent world models requires both accurate multi-step predictions
and latent distances that reflect physical proximity to the goal.
However, models are typically trained on ground-truth observations but must rely
on their own imaginations during planning, while closer latent distances do not
necessarily correspond to better task outcomes.
Existing methods resort to auxiliary training objectives or additional
task-cost readouts, which respectively incur extra training overhead or leave
the latent geometry itself misaligned with task cost.
We introduce CARE-WM, a drop-in training method that meets both requirements without
additional supervision, a separate cost model, or any change to LeWM’s architecture
and Euclidean-cost planner.
CARE-WM trains the predictor on its own predictions and adaptively calibrates
the strength of latent regularization.
With a single hyperparameter configuration, CARE-WM improves mean planning
success over LeWM across all evaluated continuous-control tasks and matches
or exceeds the best results of other LeWM-family methods on most tasks.
Further analyses show lower open-loop latent prediction error and
closer agreement between latent-cost rankings and physical task costs.
The code is available at
https://github.com/KaidRommel/CARE-WM.
introduction:
World models support planning by predicting the consequences of candidate
actions [2, 10, 12].
LeWorldModel (LeWM) [19] jointly learns visual
representations and action-conditioned latent dynamics from pixels,
without reconstructing them [15].
At planning time, the predictor recursively rolls out future latents, and
the cross-entropy method
(CEM) [23, 32] ranks candidate action
sequences by the Euclidean distance between their predicted terminal
latents and the encoding of a goal image. The model must both predict where
an action sequence will lead and judge how close that outcome comes to the
goal.

Planning can fail in two distinct ways as illustrated in Fig. 1.
First, a predictor that is accurate on observed histories may become unreliable
when it repeatedly uses its own predictions as inputs [6, 28]. During training,
teacher forcing provides encoded observations, whereas planning feeds
predictions back into the model. Errors can propagate and alter candidate rankings.
We refer to accurate multi-step prediction under such model-generated inputs
as rollout accuracy.

Second, even a correctly predicted endpoint can receive a misleading planning cost.
The Euclidean distance between its latent representation and the goal may not
reflect the actual task outcome [16, 29].
For example, in a two-room environment, an endpoint separated from the goal by
a wall may appear closer than one along a feasible route. We refer to the agreement
between latent distances at executed endpoints and
their physical task costs as planning-cost alignment.

Existing methods address rollout error by supervising latent predictions
at multiple depths of recursive rollouts [11, 13, 16].
Other approaches replace recursive rollout with direct prediction
of future states conditioned on the initial observation and action
sequence [9, 17].
On the cost side, reachability and decision-related objectives give the
representation information about which futures are attainable or
preferable [16, 29, 18, 30].
These objectives can use the original trajectories while adding
supervision beyond next-latent prediction.
This motivates our central question.
Can we improve both aspects of planning reliability through
training alone, without additional task supervision or changes to the
prediction and planning interfaces?

We introduce CARE-WM, a training method with two components for improving
rollout accuracy and planning-cost alignment.
We hypothesize that exposure bias from the mismatch between observed
training and generated rollout contexts [6, 22]
is a key source of recursive error.
The first component, Same-Horizon Self-Conditioning (SHSC), therefore trains
the predictor on its own outputs as inputs and backpropagates through them
within the original supervision window.
To improve planning-cost alignment without task-specific objectives, we
seek to relax unnecessary regularization constraints [26].
LeWM uses Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization
(SIGReg) [3] to prevent collapse, yet we find that
finite-sample bias sustains its regularization pressure even at the
Gaussian target.
Manually tuning the regularization weight to temper this pressure
requires additional hyperparameter search.
CARE-WM’s second component, Constraint-Adaptive SIGReg (CA-SIGReg),
therefore adjusts this weight automatically using a finite-sample-calibrated
discrepancy from the Gaussian target.

CARE-WM improves mean planning success over LeWM across all evaluated
continuous-control tasks and matches or exceeds the best results of other
LeWM-family methods on most tasks.
It achieves lower open-loop latent MSE at every
evaluated horizon on all four tasks in the rollout evaluation.
Its predicted costs better
preserve realized latent-cost rankings, and realized costs rank candidates
more consistently with physical task costs.

The strict simplicial complexity SCstrict​(K)\mathrm{SC}_{\mathrm{strict}}(K), González’s simplicial
complexity at subdivision level zero, is one less than the least number of contiguity domains covering the
ordered product K×KK\times K. We bound it from both sides. For upper
bounds, every product of two vertex stars is a domain, which gives
SCstrict​(K)≤ρ⁡(K)−1\mathrm{SC}_{\mathrm{strict}}(K)\leq\rho(K)-1 for an exactly computable set-cover number
ρ⁡(K)\rho(K); the bound is sharp on every even-dimensional simplex boundary. A
GPU annealer that evolves whole systems of contiguity chains finds
three-domain covers of ∂Δ3,…,∂Δ7\partial\Delta^{3},\dots,\partial\Delta^{7} and of the
cube boundary. Seeded by star covers, it descends from 2424 to 55 domains
on the icosahedron boundary, and an exact SAT completion of its stalled
state gives SCstrict≤3\mathrm{SC}_{\mathrm{strict}}\leq 3 there. For lower bounds, a subcomplex of K×KK\times K
is rigid if its two projections are joined by no contiguity chain of any
length; kk domains can cover K×KK\times K only if kk classes of facets
avoid every rigid subcomplex, a finite SAT problem. Rigid subcomplexes
arise from hollow triangles over essential empty triangles and, on
complexes without dominated vertices, from the graph of every
order-preserving simplicial self-map other than the identity. The
resulting chain-length-free bounds give

almost every uncovered facet closes a rigid subcomplex in every domain,

Farber’s topological complexity TC⁡(X)\mathrm{TC}(X) [6] is the least number of
continuous motion-planning rules on a space XX, minus one (we use the
reduced convention throughout, one less than in [6, 8], so a
cover by kk domains certifies TC≤k−1\mathrm{TC}\leq k-1). González’s simplicial complexity [9] discretises
it. On the ordered product K×KK\times K of a triangulation KK of XX,
continuity is replaced by contiguity of simplicial maps
(Section 2), and a motion planner on a subcomplex becomes a
chain of contiguous simplicial maps joining the two projections. The strict
invariant SCstrict​(K)\mathrm{SC}_{\mathrm{strict}}(K), which is González’s SC0\mathrm{SC}^{0} [9] in the
notation of [11], counts such planners on K×KK\times K itself,
without subdividing. It is finite and checkable and satisfies
SCstrict​(K)≥TC⁡(‖K‖)\mathrm{SC}_{\mathrm{strict}}(K)\geq\mathrm{TC}(\|K\|); the analogous count on iterated barycentric
subdivisions of K×KK\times K becomes equal to TC\mathrm{TC} [9]. At subdivision level 00 it is an
invariant of the triangulation, and it is the quantity bounded by the covers
that the randomized greedy algorithm of Ortiz, Lara, González and Borat
[11] constructs; values were known for the circle and the wedge of
two circles [11].

We compute or bracket SCstrict\mathrm{SC}_{\mathrm{strict}} at level 00 for the

Section 3 gives the star cover, which needs no search; on
